When a child adds blocks on a desk: 1. They place two blue blocks on the table. 2. They place three red blocks on the table. 3. They push them together into a group of five.

They do not write an equation, wrap it in parentheses, and push an invisible "equals" button. They choose their quantities first, and then execute the operation.

StackCalc formalizes this through Jerome Bruner's Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) framework:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       THE CRA PROGRESSION IN ACTION                     |
|                                                                         |
|   1. CONCRETE                2. REPRESENTATIONAL      3. ABSTRACT       |
|   Desk Workbench Lids        Digital Twin             Bare-Metal RP2350 |
|   (19mm Miniblocks)          (Apple Watch/iPad)       (SC-32 Hardware)  |
|                                                                         |
|   [ 2 Blocks ]               [ Y: 2.0000 ]            [ 2 ] [ENTER]     |
|   [ 3 Blocks ]   ===>        [ X: 3.0000 ]    ===>    [ 3 ]             |
|   [ Pushed Together ]        [ X: 5.0000 ]            [ + ]             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Every physical kit in the StackCalc Learning Lab maps \(1:1\) to a calculator function: * Ten-Frames & Carry Cube \(\leftrightarrow\) Base-10 regrouping and the [▦] stack key. * Fraction Studio Proportional Towers \(\leftrightarrow\) Height-parity equivalence and the [FDISP] key. * Classroom Planetary Clock \(\leftrightarrow\) 12:1 internal gear kinematics and the [CLK] time key. * Algebra Boxes & Factoring Tiles \(\leftrightarrow\) Archimedean area multiplication and the [EQN] polynomial solver.

docs.title: 4. Open Hardware & Material Honesty
docs.text:
We believe educational instruments must belong to the communities that use them. StackCalc rejects proprietary planned obsolescence:

  1. Perpetual Reproduction License: Buy a kit once, and print unlimited classroom lab worksheets forever. We never charge monthly seat fees or software subscriptions.
  2. "No Lost Piece Left Behind": Classrooms lose parts. When a block goes missing, teachers shouldn't have to replace an entire kit. We ship individual replacement parts for a flat $4, or teachers can download our 100% free open-source .3MF files and print replacement parts in their school's maker lab for pennies.
  3. Apollo-Era Instrumental Brutalism: We engineer in durable technical thermoplastics (Midnight Navy PLA 2.0+, Space Gray, Black PETG), and 400g metal snap-dome switches built for hundreds of thousands of actuation cycles.

The era of in-fix parentheses fatigue is over. Welcome to tactile Postfix computing.

Explore the Master Catalog or download free open-source project files in the Download Center. For department quotes and tax-exempt school purchasing, contact quotes@stackcalc.io.

docs.title: Notes from the PCBWay Assembly Floor: Header Pins, JST Footprints, and Switch Jumper Routing
docs.text:
Passing local Design Rule Checks (DRC) in KiCad is a satisfying milestone, but it is not the same thing as passing physical assembly on the factory floor.

Shortly after we submitted our initial 4-layer calculator mainboard (calculator.kicad_pcb), BOM (bom.csv), and pick-and-place centroid files to PCBWay for turnkey SMT and through-hole assembly, their engineering team paused the line and sent back a set of real bench inspection photos. Those photos caught four physical integration bugs that a software DRC never flags: through-hole MCU header pins colliding with a front-side tactile switch, a through-hole JST battery header paired with undrilled surface-mount pads, mirrored silkscreen layers, and implicit jumper connections across the 4-pad tactile switches.

Here is what the PCBWay team found on the bench and how we fixed the board layout and jumper routing with Python scripts in KiCad's pcbnew API.

docs.title: 1. The Red Box: Rear MCU1 Header Pins vs. Front Tactile Switch SOFT6
docs.text:
In our prototype architecture, the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (MCU1) mounts horizontally on the back of the mainboard (B.Cu), while the 43 tactile switches (B1–B37 and SOFT1–SOFT6) mount on the front (F.Cu).

In our initial BOM, we accidentally specified part number SC1632 (the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 with pre-soldered through-hole header pins) alongside a plated through-hole (PTH) footprint in KiCad. When PCBWay's technicians dry-fitted the module from the rear, the header pins poked straight through the \(1.6\text{ mm}\) FR-4 substrate and emerged on the front face—right inside the courtyard of softkey SOFT6:

Figure 1: PCBWay bench inspection photo (headers.png). The red box highlights the rear MCU1 through-hole header pins poking through the front of the board directly between the four SMD pads of tactile switch SOFT6.

Even if those protruding pins were clipped flush after soldering, the exposed solder fillets and pin tips sat directly beneath the metal snap-dome body of SOFT6, preventing the switch from seating flat on its F.Cu pads and risking a dead short against the switch housing.

docs.title: The Fix: Castellated SMD Mounting (SC1631) & fix_mcu_pads.py
docs.text: Because the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 features castellated edge pads along all 40 pins, through-hole headers are completely unnecessary when mounting the module flush against the rear copper layer. We: 1. Updated MCU1 in bom.csv from SC1632 (pre-headered) to SC1631 (bare castellated Pico 2). 2. Wrote a pcbnew script (Hardware/fix_mcu_pads.py) to convert all 40 MCU1 pads from PAD_ATTRIB_PTH to pure bottom-side PAD_ATTRIB_SMD (B.Cu, B.Paste, B.Mask) with zero drill holes, leaving the front switch surface unbroken.

docs.title: 2. The JST1 Footprint Mismatch & Stranded Front Silkscreen
docs.text:
The second photo from PCBWay flagged JST1, our 2-pin right-angle battery connector at the top-right corner of the board:

Figure 2: PCBWay bench photo (jst.png) showing the through-hole S2B-PH-K-S header next to the surface-mount JST1 pads.

Two things had gone wrong simultaneously: 1. Through-Hole Part vs. SMD Pads: Our BOM listed S2B-PH-K-S(LF)(SN)—a through-hole right-angle JST PH header with bent metal pins—while the footprint on the board used undrilled surface-mount pads. We updated bom.csv to specify the surface-mount S2B-PH-SM4-TB right-angle connector (and coordinated the jumper/lead seating for the initial boards with the PCBWay assembly team). 2. Mirrored Silkscreen on the Wrong Layer: Notice how the text JST (ON BACK) in Figure 2 and the MCU1 outline in Figure 3 below were printed in white silkscreen on the front (F.Silkscreen) of the green board, even though both components mount on the back!

Figure 3: PCBWay bench photo (silkscreen.png) showing MCU1 silkscreen graphics stranded on F.Silkscreen and overlapping the upper switch row.

When we originally flipped MCU1 to the back layer in KiCad, several child graphical primitives inside the footprint remained explicitly bound to F.Silkscreen and F.Fab. We wrote Hardware/fix_silkscreen.py to iterate through every graphical item and standalone text callout, migrating them to B.Silkscreen and B.Fab with proper mirroring.

docs.title: 3. Cleaning Up Tactile Switch Jumper Connections
docs.text:
The most subtle issue involved how the 43 tactile switches (SW_TACT_ALPS_SKQGABE010) were wired into the \(8 \times 6\) keypad matrix.

A standard 4-terminal SMD tactile switch has two internally bridged pairs of legs (legs 1–1' form one continuous metal bar inside the switch body, and legs 2–2' form the switched bar). Many community KiCad footprints assign duplicate pad numbers (1, 1 and 2, 2) with (duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers yes), allowing the router to pass a row or column bus through the switch's internal metal frame instead of routing a continuous copper trace on the PCB.

During DFM review and rework around the MCU1 / SOFT6 overlap zone, relying on implicit switch-body jumpers and ambiguous 4-pad assignments created confusion about which pads required active electrical jumpering versus mechanical anchoring:

Figure 4: Updated KiCad layout (kicad.png) with (duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers no), explicit active pads (1 and 2), isolated NC anchor pads, and continuous copper bus routing.

To make the schematic-to-board netlist 100% explicit for both the pick-and-place line and our rework instructions: * We set (duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers no) across every tactile switch footprint on the board. * We designated the left-side pair as active electrical pads 1 (row net) and 2 (column net), and explicitly marked the opposite mechanical stabilizing pads as NC. * We rerouted the row and column buses (P0–P21) as continuous \(0.25\text{ mm}\) copper segments on F.Cu and B.Cu, eliminating any dependency on internal switch jumpers to carry matrix continuity downstream.

docs.title: 4. Exporting dummy_pcb.stl from pcbnew for 3D-Printed Enclosure Test-Fitting
docs.text:
While resolving the electronic DFM items with PCBWay, we also needed to verify that our 4-part screwless sliding enclosure (chassis, unified_faceplate, tpu_membrane, and snap-fit top_cap) had zero mechanical interferences with the populated board.

Rather than waiting for physical fiberglass boards to arrive to test our \(0.40\text{ mm}\) lateral PCB rail clearances and \(0.10\text{ mm}\) switch plunger datum, we wrote Hardware/generate_scad.py using KiCad's Python API (pcbnew). Every time make layout runs, it inspects calculator.kicad_pcb and generates two OpenSCAD files: 1. pcb_layout_generated.scad: Extracts the exact \((X, Y)\) centers of all 43 tactile switches, the internal Edge.Cuts LCD FPC ribbon slot, and the rear component sweeps. 2. dummy_pcb.scad \(\rightarrow\) dummy_pcb.stl: A complete 3D-printable plastic replica of the populated PCB—including the \(1.6\text{ mm}\) FR-4 substrate, all 43 switch bodies and actuator stems, the rear MCU1 Pico 2 envelope, the J1 0.5mm ZIF socket, JST1, and the C1–C8 charge-pump capacitors.

By printing dummy_pcb.stl in PLA on our desktop printer, we slid the populated plastic "board" into the chassis rails, verified that all 43 Shore 95A TPU membrane plungers met the switch tops cleanly, and confirmed battery lead clearances before PCBWay finished final assembly.

docs.title: Shipping StackCalc v1.1 on the App Store: A Clean-Room RPN Calculator That Grows With Your Kid (SC-6 to SC-32)
docs.text:
When I trained my own kids to use Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) on a SwissMicros DM41CC, three things became immediately obvious: 1. Kids do not struggle with RPN—they struggle with infix parentheses. Pushing two numbers onto a visible stack and combining them matches the exact order in which children push physical blocks together on a desk. Even better, because there is no hidden infix parser behind an = key, users learn operator-precedence parsing in their own minds in order to decompose and enter expressions onto the stack—appreciating the lessons learned in the past 50 years of computing so they can build the next 50 years. 2. Handing a student a CAS calculator is a trap for exams. Because Computer Algebra System (CAS) calculators are banned on the SAT, ACT, IB, UIL, NCEES FE/PE engineering exams, and university calculus midterms, we purposefully designed StackCalc to be allowed in testing situations (no CAS symbolic manipulation, no QWERTY keyboard, and no wireless transceivers on the hardware). 3. Sending a kid to school with a $250 collector's calculator or a $200 vintage eBay HP-32SII is a terrible idea.

That realization sparked the overarching vision for StackCalc: building a low-cost, kid-friendly RPN calculator and tactile learning ecosystem that grows with a student from first grade through university engineering—starting with our small-batch maker hardware at $89.99 while engineering our production roadmap toward a $29.99 student backpack target.

Today, StackCalc Calculator v1.1 is live on the Apple App Store for iPhone, iPad, and as a 100% standalone Apple Watch app, uniting Visual Learning Mode (StackCalc 6) for Common Core K–6 math with Scientific Mode (StackCalc 32) inside one universal binary.

docs.title: 1. Why the HP-32SII Architecture Over the HP-15C or HP-42S?
docs.text:
As a longtime collector who used an HP-32SII in high school—and currently owns a DM42 (converted to a C47 with custom-printed and cut labels), a DM32, a DM41CC, and a DM15CC—I weighed all three classic HP architectures before designing StackCalc 32:

  • Why not the HP-42S / C47? While powerhouse instruments on an engineer's bench, burying everyday operations inside deep hierarchical softkey menus slows down students and hides what the calculator can do.
  • Why not the HP-15C? The horizontal Voyager form factor and two-digit numeric matrix/label codes are iconic, but less intuitive for a student's first scientific instrument.
  • Why the HP-32SII? The 32SII achieved the ideal ergonomic balance: almost every essential scientific operation sits directly on the primary or shifted keys with zero menu diving, while a clean 1-line context menu handles grouped actions like CLEAR, STAT, SOLVE, and INTG.

docs.title: 2. Not an Emulator: Clean-Room RPNCore Upgrades (H.M., TVM, POLY, PLOT)
docs.text:
Unlike vintage calculator apps that wrap dumped 1980s ROM microcode, StackCalc is powered by RPNCore—a clean-room engine written from scratch in Swift that compiles natively to watchOS, iOS, and bare-metal Raspberry Pi RP2350 silicon (via Embedded Swift).

Writing a clean-room engine allowed us to preserve the classic 4-level stack (X, Y, Z, T), LASTx, and 26 lettered registers (A–Z) while adding the modern capabilities we always wished the original HP-32SII had:

  1. Harmonic Mean (H.M.): Built directly into the STAT analysis suite alongside arithmetic and weighted means for rates, parallel resistance, and physics labs.
  2. Time Value of Money (TVM): Dedicated 5-variable financial solver (N, I%YR, PV, PMT, FV) for personal finance and engineering economics.
  3. Quadratic & Cubic Polynomial Root Solver (POLY): Solves real and complex roots for \(Ax^3 + Bx^2 + Cx + D = 0\) without requiring iterative root-guessing.
  4. Interactive Function & Regression Plotting (PLOT): Renders live function curves, roots, Simpson shaded integrals, and statistical scatter plots directly on the monochrome dot-matrix LCD.

docs.title: 3. StackCalc 6: Common Core K–6 Operations & Pictorial Models
docs.text:
Opening stackcalc://sc6 (or switching modes in the menu) transforms the calculator into StackCalc 6—purpose-built around the operations students need to master in Common Core math up through 6th grade:

  • Step-by-Step Prime Fraction Simplification ([SIMP]): Students enter fractions using quick dot-separated syntax (e.g., .1.2 [ENTER] .1.3 [+] for \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}\)). Instead of reducing \(\frac{12}{18}\) to \(\frac{2}{3}\) inside a black box, pressing [SIMP] in StackCalc 6 factors out one prime divisor per press (displaying the divisor 2 to yield \(\frac{6}{9}\), then 3 to yield \(\frac{2}{3}\)) so students see why fractions simplify.
  • Core K–6 Number Theory Keys: Dedicated one-touch keys for integer division with remainder (÷R), prime factorization ([PRIME]), Greatest Common Divisor ([GCD]), Least Common Multiple ([LCM]), and decimal-to-fraction toggling ([FDISP]).
  • Live Pictorial Dot-Matrix Models: As students calculate on a focused 2-level stack, the \(132 \times 65\) LCD dynamically renders quantities as Ten-Frames (10F), a 20-Bead Rekenrek Number Rack (RACK), a Proportional Number Line (LINE), a Geared Analog Clock (🕒), and a 5-Level Adaptive Fluency Quiz (?).

docs.title: 4. STL-Backed Digital Twin Co-Development
docs.text:
To develop the app and bare-metal RP2350 firmware simultaneously while waiting for PCB fabrication, we connected our OpenSCAD hardware pipeline (generate_scad.py) and laser SVG decal generator (generate_laser_svg.py) directly to our Swift codebase.

By exporting exact switch centers, keycap profiles, and legends into JSON layout registries (layout_data.json), SwiftUI renders a dimensionally exact replica of the physical hardware running the identical \(132 \times 65\) bitmap framebuffer and CoreHaptics tactile key-seam simulation—letting users experience the instrument on iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch today with zero ads and zero subscriptions.

docs.title: Co-Developing an App Store App and Bare-Metal RP2350 Firmware with a Shared Swift Core and STL-Backed Digital Twin
docs.text:
Waiting for PCB fabrication and 3D-printed enclosures usually creates a painful bottleneck in hardware startups: firmware engineers wait for boards to arrive, while app developers build UI mockups that drift away from the physical device.

To build StackCalc—a kid-friendly, exam-legal RPN scientific and educational calculator that grows with learners from StackCalc 6 (Common Core K–6) to StackCalc 32 (AP Calculus and engineering)—we architected our software and mechanical CAD pipelines so the iOS/iPadOS/watchOS App Store app and our bare-metal Raspberry Pi RP2350 firmware share a single Swift codebase (RPNCore) and co-develop against an STL-backed Digital Twin.

docs.title: 1. One Clean-Room Swift Codebase (RPNCore) Across Apple Silicon and Bare-Metal RP2350
docs.text:
Rather than wrapping a vintage 1980s calculator ROM dump in an emulator, we wrote RPNCore from scratch in pure, deterministic Swift with zero external framework dependencies. Because all calculator registers, program steps, statistical accumulators, and solver states live inside value-type structs without dynamic runtime reflection, the exact same Swift package compiles to:

  1. iOS, iPadOS & 100% Standalone watchOS (StackCalc Calculator v1.1):
  2. Scientific Mode (StackCalc 32): Full 4-level RPN stack (X, Y, Z, T), LASTx, 26 lettered storage registers (A–Z), multi-variable equation solver (SOLVE), numerical Simpson integration (∫), Harmonic Mean (H.M.), Time Value of Money (TVM), Quadratic & Cubic Polynomial Root Solver (POLY), and interactive curve/scatter-plot graphing (PLOT).
  3. Visual Learning Mode (StackCalc 6): Focused 2-level K–6 Common Core stack with step-by-step prime fraction simplification ([SIMP]), integer division with remainder (÷R), [PRIME], [GCD], [LCM], and live dot-matrix Ten-Frames (10F), 20-Bead Rekenrek (RACK), Proportional Number Line (LINE), Geared Clock (🕒), and 5-Level Adaptive Quiz (?).
  4. Bare-Metal Raspberry Pi RP2350 Firmware (Embedded Swift):
  5. Compiled for armv8m.main-none-eabi using Embedded Swift and linked against a thin C hardware abstraction layer (hardware_wrapper.c) that scans our 43-key tactile matrix (using active-LOW open-drain column pull-ups for RP2350 Erratum E9 immunity) and drives a \(132 \times 65\) EastRising ERC13265 (ST7567) transflective LCD over 4-wire SPI.

docs.title: 2. Wiring OpenSCAD STLs & Laser Decals Into SwiftUI for 1:1 Co-Development
docs.text:
To guarantee that our firmware UX, key legends, and companion textbooks match the physical calculator down to the tenth of a millimeter before boards even leave the factory, we connected our KiCad and OpenSCAD hardware scripts directly to our Swift workspace:

flowchart LR
    KiCad["KiCad PCB (calculator.kicad_pcb)"] --> ScadGen["generate_scad.py & generate_laser_svg.py"]
    ScadGen --> STLs["Production Enclosures & dummy_pcb.stl"]
    ScadGen --> JSON["layout_data.json & layout_data_sc6.json"]
    JSON --> Replica["SwiftUI HardwareReplicaView + RetroUI (132x65)"]
    Replica --> Tests["40 Hz Differential Fuzzer & Book Screenshot Generator"]
  • CAD-Driven Layout Registries (layout_data.json & layout_data_sc6.json): Whenever we update switch coordinates in KiCad or keycap legends in generate_laser_svg.py, our build pipeline exports the exact physical button geometry, primary/shifted/alpha labels, and bezel dimensions into JSON registries consumed by Swift.
  • Pixel-Exact \(132 \times 65\) Framebuffer (RetroUI.swift & LCDDisplayView.swift): Both the RP2350 firmware and the SwiftUI HardwareReplicaView render into the exact same \(132 \times 65\) monochrome dot-matrix bitmap coordinate space—using custom \(5 \times 7\) and \(6 \times 8\) pixel fonts so every menu bar, fraction stack, and plot curve looks identical on iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and physical transflective glass.
  • Continuous Tactile Field (CoreHaptics): On iOS, sliding a thumb across the replica fires subtle haptic pulses when crossing physical key-seam boundaries and crisp mechanical switch transients on actuation.

docs.title: 3. Verifying Firmware & Textbooks at 40 Hz
docs.text:
Sharing a single Swift core unlocked two automated verification workflows that would be impossible on a traditional split C/Swift codebase: 1. 40 Hz Differential Grammar Fuzzer: Our cross-surface fuzz harness (Tools/fuzz_harness/) generates valid and adversarial postfix token streams (including domain boundaries like 0 ÷, singular matrices, stiffness oscillations in SOLVE, and deep fraction reductions) and executes them across both host RPNCore and the emulated RP2350 firmware loop at 40 Hz, asserting bit-for-bit register and display parity. 2. Compiling 590+ Workbook Problems Like Unit Tests (book_engine.py): Every worked example across our SC-32 Scientific Manual, SC-6 Elementary Manual, 339-Problem SC-32 Casebook, and 253-Problem SC-6 Workbook is extracted from Markdown, executed against RPNCore inside XCTest (TextbookVerificationTests_SC32.swift and TextbookVerificationTests_SC6.swift), and automatically captured as a crisp simulator screenshot.

You can try the universal app today on the Apple App Store (100% offline, zero ads, zero subscriptions) or explore our open-source STLs and hardware build logs on Hackaday.io.

docs.title: From OpenSCAD to the Classroom Desk: 84mm Fraction Towers, Logarithmic Prime Blocks, and Unit-Tested Books
docs.text:
Whenever we tell someone we are manufacturing a new calculator alongside 3D-printed math blocks and printed textbooks, the natural question is: "In a world with smartphones and AI, why does the world need another calculator?"

Because even in the age of AI, students still need to know how to think mathematically. Handing a child an AI chatbot—or a standard school calculator where they type nested parentheses (12 + 8) / (5 - 1) = into a black box—hides every intermediate step of reasoning. By contrast, on a stack-based RPN calculator, students learn operator-precedence parsing themselves because they must break expressions down in the right order of operations to enter them onto the stack, seeing every intermediate result step by step. And unlike CAS (Computer Algebra System) calculators—which are banned on the SAT, ACT, IB, UIL, and college math exams—our calculator is purposefully designed to be allowed in testing situations (zero CAS symbolic manipulation, zero QWERTY keyboard, and zero wireless radios on the hardware).

Our goal with the StackCalc Ecosystem is to make every step of mathematical reasoning visible and physical, connecting 3D-printed classroom manipulatives (manufactured in-house and on Slant3D), unit-test-verified reference books, and our SC-6 / SC-32 calculators.

docs.title: 1. What Our Fraction & Prime Number Blocks Actually Do
docs.text: Every physical kit in the StackCalc Catalog is modeled in parametric OpenSCAD around the \(42\text{ mm}\) Gridfinity standard so the storage box lid turns into an active math stage on the student's desk. Rather than printing generic plastic shapes, each manipulative encodes a specific mathematical invariant that maps \(1:1\) to a key on the calculator:

docs.title: A. Fraction Studio Proportional Towers (\(84\text{ mm}\) Integer Datum)
docs.text:
Standard plastic fraction bars often suffer from awkward decimal thicknesses that drift when stacked. We engineered our Fraction Studio Proportional Towers around an \(84\text{ mm}\) Whole (1/1) height datum—chosen because \(84\) is divisible by \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7,\) and \(12\) into exact integer millimeters (\(42\text{ mm}, 28\text{ mm}, 21\text{ mm}, 14\text{ mm}, 12\text{ mm},\) and \(7\text{ mm}\)), eliminating slicer layer-rounding drift:

  • On the Desk: To compute \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}\), a student drops the \(\frac{1}{2}\) tower (\(42\text{ mm}\)) and \(\frac{1}{3}\) tower (\(28\text{ mm}\)) into the left channel of the Twin Comparator Stage (reaching \(70\text{ mm}\)). In the right channel, they stack \(\frac{1}{6}\) blocks (\(14\text{ mm}\) each) until both columns stand flush at \(5 \times 14\text{ mm} = 70\text{ mm}\) (\(\frac{5}{6}\))—physically discovering why a common denominator is required.
  • On the Calculator (StackCalc 6): The student enters .1.2 [ENTER] .1.3 [+] to see 5/6. And when reducing a fraction like \(\frac{12}{18}\) (.12.18), pressing [SIMP] in StackCalc 6 factors out one prime divisor at a time (showing ÷2 \(\rightarrow \frac{6}{9}\), then ÷3 \(\rightarrow \frac{2}{3}\)) instead of jumping straight to the reduced answer like a black box.

docs.title: B. Prime Factor Studio & Logarithmic Slide Rule Comparator
docs.text:
Factor trees on paper often feel like arbitrary symbol manipulation to 4th–6th graders. Our Prime Factor Studio turns prime factorization, Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), and Least Common Multiple (LCM) into a physical length-matching puzzle:

  • On the Desk: Each prime block (\(2, 3, 5, 7\)) is scaled logarithmically (\(\text{Length} \propto \log(p)\)). Because \(\log(a) + \log(b) = \log(a \times b)\), snapping a 2 block and a 3 block end-to-end inside the comparator trough physically equals the exact length of the 6 marker! When comparing \(12\) (\(2 \times 2 \times 3\)) and \(18\) (\(2 \times 3 \times 3\)) in parallel channels, students physically see the shared prime train (\(2 \times 3 = 6 = \text{GCD}\)) and the combined train needed to make both tracks equal length (\(2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 = 36 = \text{LCM}\)).
  • On the Calculator: Students verify their physical block trains using the dedicated [PRIME], [GCD], [LCM], and [÷R] (integer division with remainder) keys in StackCalc 6 and StackCalc 32.

docs.title: 2. Hybrid Manufacturing (In-House + Slant3D) & 3D-Printed dummy_pcb Checks
docs.text: To bring both the classroom blocks and the calculator enclosures to production simultaneously: * In-House Precision: We print our multi-color silk fraction/prime towers, planetary clock gear trains, and 4-part screwless calculator enclosures on calibrated PEI plates. Using Hardware/generate_scad.py, we also export dummy_pcb.scad \(\rightarrow\) dummy_pcb.stl directly from KiCad's pcbnew API—allowing us to 3D-print an exact plastic replica of the populated PCB (including all 43 switches, the rear Pico 2 envelope, and the 0.5mm ZIF socket) to verify sliding rail clearances and TPU plunger reach before physical boards arrive. * Slant3D Print Farm: We offload the heavy, single-material Gridfinity storage boxes, lids, and trays to Slant3D's automated print farm so our workshop printers stay focused on precision multi-color kits.

docs.title: 3. Compiling Books Like Firmware: A Unit-Tested Publishing Pipeline
docs.text:
Surrounding the hardware and blocks is our library of Official Manuals & Companion Workbooks—including the SC-32 Scientific Manual, SC-6 Elementary Manual, 339-Problem SC-32 Casebook, 253-Problem SC-6 Workbook, and 24 UIL Competition Exams.

To guarantee zero typos or stale screenshots, our build system (Makefile + Tools/book_engine.py) compiles the books just like firmware: 1. Executable Keystroke Macros: Every worked example in the chapters is extracted and executed against RPNCore in TextbookVerificationTests_SC32.swift and TextbookVerificationTests_SC6.swift. If any register state in the prose disagrees with the calculator engine, the build fails. 2. Automated Simulator Screenshots & STL Diagrams: Every LCD dot-matrix screenshot is exported directly from the SwiftUI test runner, and every manipulative diagram is rendered from the production OpenSCAD .stl meshes (blocks_registry.json).

docs.title: StackCalc Curriculum & Standards Guide
docs.text:
PEDAGOGICAL ARCHITECTURE // CRA FRAMEWORK ● CCSS-M • BRIDGES • BIG IDEAS • SINGAPORE DIMENSIONS 📖 Master Guide 🔑 Online Answer Keys 📗 Book 2A: Early Elementary (K–2) 📘 Book 2B: Upper Elementary (3–5) 📙 Book 3: Middle School (6–8) 📕 Book 4: High School & STEM (9–12) 🧑‍🏫 Book 1: Teacher Guide 📝 Worksheets 🎯 Standards Matrix 🏆 UIL Competition

Welcome to the StackCalc Learning Lab Curriculum Hub. At StackCalc, we believe that mathematical comprehension should not begin behind a flat pane of glass or inside abstract parentheses soup.

Our instructional system bridges Jerome Bruner’s Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) framework with the mechanical clarity of Reverse Polish Notation (RPN): 1. Concrete: Students assemble, measure, and verify quantities on physical desk workbench lids. 2. Representational: Students diagram tape models, area grids, and number bonds in structured lab sheets. 3. Abstract: Students formalize the calculation on 4-line live operational stacks (SC-6 Elementary and SC-32 Scientific), where the physical drop and lift of numbers mirror physical reality.

docs.title: Flagship Reference Books & Classroom Companion Manuals
docs.text:
Every curriculum unit, manipulative studio, and station worksheet is anchored by our two comprehensive, engine-verified Bookstore Edition Reference Manuals & Textbooks (836 combined pages, 1,078 verified RPN keystroke sequences, 431 four-register stack tables, plus 592 extended problems in the Companion Workbooks):

docs.title: 1. Concept Labs & Warm-Up Solutions
docs.text:
• Warm-Up A (Core Lab): Place the [4] Digit Block in the Ones column of your Place Value Tray and add 1 Gold [+1] step token. What total quantity do you have now?
  • Verified Answer: 5 ([5] Digit Block; 4 + 1 = 5).
  • Keystrokes: 4 ENTER 1 +
  • Warm-Up B (Extension Lab): Row 1 holds [6] and Row 0 holds [2] on your Place Value Tray. Which row has more, and how many more does it have?
  • Verified Answer: Row 1 has 4 more (6 - 2 = 4).
  • Keystrokes: 6 ENTER 2 -

docs.title: 2. Hands-On Lab Investigations (Investigations 1–4)
docs.text: # Investigation Prompt Expected Solution Calculator Verification Keys 1 Place [3] in the top row and [2] in the bottom row of your Place Value Tray. Combine both groups—what is the total? 5 3 ENTER 2 + 2 You have 5 ones on the tray and take away 2. What Digit Block shows how many ones remain? 3 5 ENTER 2 - 3 You have 3 blocks on the tray and take away all 3. How many blocks are left, and which Digit Block shows an empty tray? 0 (Zero) 3 ENTER 3 - 4 Start with [1] in the Ones socket and add one more [+1] token three times in a row. What count do you reach? 4 1 ENTER 1 + 1 + 1 +

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: The Garden Stepping Stone Trail
docs.text:
Scenario: A landscape gardener designs a walking path with stone markers spaced 1 meter apart. Students calculate steps, distances, and total stones needed.

  • Case Question 1: Start at Stone 4 and lay 3 more stones. What stone number are you on?
  • Expected Result: 7 | Keystrokes: 4 ENTER 1 + 1 + 1 +
  • Case Question 2: A trail has 8 stones. A bird lands on stone 5. How many stones remain to the end?
  • Expected Result: 3 | Keystrokes: 8 ENTER 5 -
  • Case Question 3: Two parallel paths have 4 stones and 5 stones. How many stones total?
  • Expected Result: 9 | Keystrokes: 4 ENTER 5 +
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: Leo says stepping forward 2 stones from 6 gives stone 9. Find the true stone.
  • Expected Result: Stone 8 (6 + 2 = 8, not 9). | Keystrokes: 6 ENTER 2 +

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: The Space Station Cargo Balancing Tray
docs.text:
Scenario: Astronauts balance payloads on the supply shuttle. Each cargo tray holds exactly 10 kg across two compartments (Part 1 and Part 2).

  • Case Question 1: Compartment A holds 6 kg. How many kg fit into Compartment B to make 10 kg?
  • Expected Result: 4 kg | Keystrokes: 10 ENTER 6 -
  • Case Question 2: Compartment A holds 3 kg. What is the missing cargo weight for a 10 kg tray?
  • Expected Result: 7 kg | Keystrokes: 10 ENTER 3 -
  • Case Question 3: Two small containers weigh 4 kg and 5 kg. Can they both fit in a 10 kg tray?
  • Expected Result: Yes, 9 kg total (1 kg space left). | Keystrokes: 4 ENTER 5 +
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: Sam says 10 − 8 = 3. Use the number bond to find the correct missing part.
  • Expected Result: 2 kg (8 + 2 = 10, not 3). | Keystrokes: 10 ENTER 8 -

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: The Farm Fresh Egg Carton Packaging
docs.text:
Scenario: A poultry farm packages organic eggs into cartons of 10. When a carton fills, workers close the lid and pack a new carton.

  • Case Question 1: A basket has 8 brown eggs and 5 white eggs. How many full 10-cartons and loose eggs?
  • Expected Result: 1 full carton of 10 and 3 loose eggs (13 eggs). | Keystrokes: 8 ENTER 5 +
  • Case Question 2: A carton has 7 eggs. How many more eggs are needed to fill the 10-frame carton?
  • Expected Result: 3 eggs | Keystrokes: 10 ENTER 7 -
  • Case Question 3: Two nests have 9 eggs and 6 eggs. What is the total egg harvest?
  • Expected Result: 15 eggs (1 ten and 5 ones). | Keystrokes: 9 ENTER 6 +
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: A student writes 8 + 6 = 15. Count the dots to find the true sum.
  • Expected Result: 14 eggs (8 + 2 = 10, 10 + 4 = 14). | Keystrokes: 8 ENTER 6 +

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: The School Bus Morning Seating Chart
docs.text:
Scenario: A school bus has two identical columns of seats. Children sit in pairs: one on the window side, one on the aisle side.

  • Case Question 1: Row 1 through 7 each have 2 students (7 on left, 7 on right). How many students total?
  • Expected Result: 14 students (7 + 7 = 14). | Keystrokes: 7 ENTER +
  • Case Question 2: 8 students sit on the left and 9 on the right. Use near-doubles to find total passengers.
  • Expected Result: 17 students ((8 + 8) + 1 = 17). | Keystrokes: 8 ENTER + 1 +
  • Case Question 3: 6 boys and 6 girls sit in the front section. How many students in the front section?
  • Expected Result: 12 students | Keystrokes: 6 ENTER +
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: Mia doubles 9 and gets 17. Use the stack to find double 9.
  • Expected Result: 18 (9 [ENTER] [+] = 18). | Keystrokes: 9 ENTER +

docs.text:

docs.title: Unit 06: Fraction Equivalence & Common Denominators
docs.text: Grades: Grade 4 | Instrument: StackCalc SC-6 | Visual / Block Model: Fraction Studio (Comparator Well & Proportional Towers) Key Standards: CCSS.MATH.4.NF.A.1, CCSS.MATH.4.NF.A.2

docs.title: 1. Concept Labs & Warm-Up Solutions
docs.text:
• Warm-Up A (Core Lab): Test 3/6 and 4/8 in the comparator well. What single simplified fraction do both equal?
  • Verified Answer: 1/2 (42.0 mm).
  • Keystrokes: . 3 . 6
  • Warm-Up B (Extension Lab): Find the common denominator and sum of 1/2 + 1/3 on paper, then check on the stack.
  • Verified Answer: 5/6 (3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6).
  • Keystrokes: . 1 . 2 ENTER . 1 . 3 +
  • Hands-On Block Focus (Fraction Multiplication & Division):
  • Multiplication: Scaling one tower by another (e.g., 2/3 of 3/8 = 1/4 matching the 21 mm block).
  • Division (Split & Rebuild 1 Full Tower): To divide 1/2 ÷ 3/4, split the 1/2 block (42 mm) into 3 equal 1/6 blocks (÷ 3 -> 14 mm is 1/4 of the mystery tower), then stack 4 of those 1/6 blocks (× 4 -> 56 mm = 2/3) to prove why ÷(3/4) = ×(4/3)!

docs.text:

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: Gear Train Planetary Mechanism
docs.text:
Scenario: Mechanical engineers design clockwork gear trains using prime tooth counts (2, 3, 5, 7) so wear distributes evenly across every rotation cycle.

  • Case Question 1: Pinion Tooth Decomposition: A 12-tooth brass pinion gear is machined for a clockwork train. Stack your Prime Factor blocks to build 12:
  • Expected Result: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 | Keystrokes: 2 ENTER 2 × 3 ×
  • Case Question 2: Shared Gear Pitch (GCF): An 18-tooth drive gear meshes with a 24-tooth idler gear. Find the largest shared tooth grouping GCF(18, 24):
  • Expected Result: 6 (2 × 3 = 6). | Keystrokes: 18 ENTER 24 GCF
  • Case Question 3: Full Mesh Alignment Cycle (LCM): A 12-tooth gear drives an 18-tooth gear. After how many tooth-meshes do the exact same two marked teeth meet again?
  • Expected Result: 36 | Keystrokes: 12 ENTER 18 LCM
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: An apprentice claims a 9-tooth cog has a prime number of teeth so it cannot share factors. Divide 9 ÷ 3 to prove 9 is composite:
  • Expected Result: 3 (9 = 3 × 3, composite). | Keystrokes: 9 ENTER 3 ÷

docs.text: Grades: Grade 5 | Instrument: StackCalc SC-6 | Visual / Block Model: Fraction Studio (84 mm Proportional Towers) Key Standards: CCSS.MATH.5.NF.B.4, CCSS.MATH.5.NF.B.7

docs.title: 1. Concept Labs & Warm-Up Solutions
docs.text:
• Warm-Up A (Core Lab): Find 2/3 of 3/4 by multiplying (2/3) × (3/4) and simplifying to lowest terms.
  • Verified Answer: 1/2 (6/12 = 1/2, 42.0 mm).
  • Keystrokes: .2.3 ENTER .3.4 ×
  • Warm-Up B (Extension Lab): Use Split & Rebuild to evaluate (3/4) ÷ (3/8) on paper and check on your SC-6.
  • Verified Answer: 2 ((3/4) × (8/3) = 2 wholes).
  • Keystrokes: .3.4 ENTER .3.8 ÷
  • Hands-On Block Focus (Fraction Multiplication & Division):
  • Multiplication: Scaling one tower by another (e.g., 2/3 of 3/8 = 1/4 matching the 21 mm block).
  • Division (Split & Rebuild 1 Full Tower): To divide 1/2 ÷ 3/4, split the 1/2 block (42 mm) into 3 equal 1/6 blocks (÷ 3 -> 14 mm is 1/4 of the mystery tower), then stack 4 of those 1/6 blocks (× 4 -> 56 mm = 2/3) to prove why ÷(3/4) = ×(4/3)!

docs.title: 5. STEM Lab Case Study: Suspension Bridge Tower Cable Geometry
docs.text:
Scenario: Civil engineers calculate tower tension ratios using fraction multiplication and division.

  • Case Question 1: Secondary Suspender Scaling: A main bridge cable carries 3/4 of a kilonewton unit load, and a secondary suspender carries 1/2 of that load (1/2 × 3/4). Find the suspender load:
  • Expected Result: 3/8 meter (31.5 mm). | Keystrokes: . 1 . 2 ENTER . 3 . 4 ×
  • Case Question 2: Three-Strand Load Sharing: A 1/2-meter anchor rod is split equally among 3 steel tie-down brackets (1/2 ÷ 3). What fraction of a meter does each bracket hold?
  • Expected Result: 1/6 (14.0 mm). | Keystrokes: . 1 . 2 ENTER 3 ÷
  • Case Question 3: Full Tower Reconstruction: A 1/2-meter scale test cable represents 3/4 of the design span. Use Split & Rebuild (1/2 ÷ 3/4) to find the full 1-tower design span:
  • Expected Result: 2/3 (56.0 mm tower). | Keystrokes: . 1 . 2 ENTER . 3 . 4 ÷
  • Case Question 4: Error Analysis: A structural intern computed 1/2 ÷ 3/4 = 3/8 by multiplying instead of dividing. Use the 84 mm Split & Rebuild model to explain why 1/2 ÷ 3/4 = 2/3:
  • Expected Result: Dividing by 3/4 scales up by 4/3: 1/2 × 4/3 = 2/3 (56 mm). | Keystrokes: . 1 . 2 ENTER . 3 . 4 ÷

docs.title: 1. Concept Labs & Warm-Up Solutions
docs.text:
• Warm-Up A (Core Lab): Factor x² + 7x + 12 by decomposing 12 with Prime Factor blocks to find the factor pair whose sum is 7, and find both roots of x² + 7x + 12 = 0.
  • Verified Answer: 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7; factored form (x + 3)(x + 4), roots x = -3 and x = -4.
  • Keystrokes: POLY 1 B 7 C 1 2 D XEQ
  • Warm-Up B (Extension Lab): Factor x² - 5x + 6 into two binomials by finding two negative factors of +6 whose sum is -5, and state both roots.
  • Verified Answer: (-2) × (-3) = +6 and (-2) + (-3) = -5; factored form (x - 2)(x - 3), roots x = 2 and x = 3.
  • Keystrokes: POLY 1 B 5 +/- C 6 D XEQ

docs.title: Unit 1: Numerical Expressions & Factors — The Backcountry Trail Crew & Maker Cabin (p. 3)
docs.text:
Big Ideas Math Grade 6 — Chapter 1 — Whole Number Operations, Powers & Exponents, Order of Operations, Prime Factorization, GCF & LCM

📄 Print Unit 1 Chapter Packet PDF (13 Pages: Story Opener + 10 Worksheets + 1-Page Answer Key)
  • Hands-On Block Kits (When Applicable — Place Value Studio (PLACE-01) + Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01)): Place Value Studio (PLACE-01) • Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01)
  • Aligned From Blocks to the Stack Story & Chapter: "Why 24 Is the Champion Packing Number & The 17-Year Cicada Mystery" — SC-6 Ch. 4: Operations & Skip-Counting & Ch. 7: Data, Probability & Primes (Appendix B Lessons 9–12)
  • Target Misconception: Students interpret remainders as meaningless decimal tails (e.g., .875 of a person), read 2^3 as 2×3=6, lose track of PEMDAS parentheses, and confuse GCF (overlap) with LCM (union).
  • Hands-On & Stack Remediation: Have students model division remainders on the Place Value Tray, stack Prime Factor Blocks ([2][2][2] = 2³) for exponents, use the 4-line elevator (Y holds Room 1 while X solves Room 2) instead of rewriting PEMDAS lines, and stand logarithmic Prime Factor Towers side-by-side on the 12-socket lid.

Every summer in the Cascade Mountains, a group of sixth-grade volunteers helps the ranger station prepare backcountry campsites, wildlife observation blinds, and a small maker cabin. Maya signed up to organize the supply crates and battery banks, even though she secretly worried she would mess up the counts and leave a trail crew short on gear miles from the nearest road. Across the cabin, Leo tinkers with mountain bikes, solar signboards, and LEGO robotics prototypes, while Zoe hikes with the field biologists to watch Clark's nutcrackers hide thousands of pine seeds for the winter.

During their first week, guessing got all three of them into trouble. When Maya tried to pack 53 lithium battery cells into 6-cell drone packs, her phone calculator gave her a long decimal that didn't tell her how many real packs she could actually clip into a drone. When 78 campers showed up at the lake for 4-person canoes, Leo wasn't sure whether to round up or down so nobody got left on the dock. And when Sam and Leo added up the cost of a skateboard deck plus four wheels, they got two completely different totals from the exact same numbers.

In the bike and robotics shed, Leo noticed another puzzle: two gears with spiky teeth only mesh smoothly when their tooth counts share common building blocks, and two park shuttles leaving the trailhead on different schedules only meet up at the station when their loop times hit a shared multiple. Even Zoe's field notes on periodical cicadas that emerge every 12 or 15 years followed the exact same pattern.

None of them felt like 'math people' at the start of the summer. But by working out each supply puzzle by hand first and then checking their answers on their SC-6 calculators, they discovered that whole numbers have built-in patterns for leftovers, rapid doubling, grouping rules, and repeating cycles—turning messy real-world guesses into plans they could trust.

docs.title: Section 1.1: Whole Number Operations & Division with Remainders (Workbook pp. 4–5)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 1.1 (Whole Number Operations) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.B.2) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Standard Long Division | Way 2: Partial Quotients | Way 3: Equal-Groups Array Model • Block Kit: PLACE-01 (Place Value Studio)

Key Vocabulary: dividend • divisor • quotient • remainder

In Big Ideas Math, whole-number division splits a dividend into equal groups of the divisor: Dividend = (Quotient × Divisor) + Remainder, where the remainder is always less than the divisor. Modeling the dividend on the Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) physically separates the equal groups (Quotient) from the leftover ones (Remainder).

⚠️ WATCH OUT: A remainder must ALWAYS be smaller than the divisor (Rem < Divisor). Check whether the problem asks for full groups, leftovers, or rounding up!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PLACE-01: Place Value Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Concept: Divide Dividend ÷ Divisor to find the Quotient (full equal groups) and Remainder (leftover < Divisor).
  2. Textbook Check: Always verify division with the Division Algorithm: (Quotient × Divisor) + Remainder = Dividend.
  3. Block Reinforcement (PLACE-01): Group 23 into rows of 4 -> 5 full groups (20) + a [3] Digit Block remainder (5 × 4 + 3 = 23).

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.4) Divide 23 ÷ 4 and check your answer using the Division Algorithm. WAY 1: Standard Long Division: Divide 23 by 4: 4 goes into 23 five times (5 × 4 = 20). Subtract 23 - 20 = 3 -> Quotient 5 R 3. WAY 2: Partial Quotients (Subtract Multiples): Split 23 into friendly multiples of 4: take 3 × 4 = 12 (leaves 11), then 2 × 4 = 8 (leaves 3) -> (3 + 2) = 5 R 3.WAY 3: Equal-Groups Array Model (With Blocks): Arrange 23 tiles into rows of 4: you form 5 full rows of 4 (20 tiles) with 3 leftover tiles -> 5 R 3. (Check: 5×4+3 = 23.) 5 R 3 Practice B (p.5) A robotics tournament has 135 students riding in vans that hold 8 students each. How many vans are needed so every student has a seat? WAY 1: Standard Long Division: Divide 135 ÷ 8: 8 into 13 is 1 (13 - 8 = 5); bring down 5 -> 8 into 55 is 6 (55 - 48 = 7) -> 16 R 7.Textbook Check: 16 × 8 + 7 = 128 + 7 = 135 students (Remainder 7 < Divisor 8). WAY 2: Partial Quotients (10 Vans + 6 Vans): Subtract 10 vans (10 × 8 = 80 students, leaving 55), then 6 vans (6 × 8 = 48, leaving 7) -> 16 full vans + 7 students.Real-Life Rule: Round UP to 17 vans when every person needs a seat; use the quotient 16 when counting full vans.WAY 3: Interpret the Remainder in Context: 16 vans hold 128 students, leaving 7 students waiting. Add 1 more van for the remaining 7 students -> 17 vans total. 17 vans (16 full vans + 1 van with 7 students)

docs.title: How to Use the SC-6 Calculator to Check Your Work
docs.text:
• Practice A Work-Check (p.4): Solve 23 ÷ 4 on paper first. Then check on your SC-6: type 23 [ENTER] 4 [g][÷R]. Read the Remainder (3) on line Y and the Quotient (5) on line X! Press [f][LASTx] [×] [+] to verify 5 × 4 + 3 = 23. (Worked Example Keystrokes: [23] [ENTER] [4] [g] [÷R] → 5 R 3)
  • Practice B Real-Life Work-Check (p.5): Work out 135 ÷ 8 by hand first, then press 135 [ENTER] 8 [g][÷R] on your SC-6. Line X shows 16 full vans and line Y shows 7 leftover students—confirming you must round up to 17 vans! Press [f][LASTx] [×] [+] to check 16 × 8 + 7 = 135. (Worked Example Keystrokes: [135] [ENTER] [8] [g] [÷R] [f] [LASTx] [×] [+] → 17 vans (16 full vans + 1 van with 7 students))

docs.title: Practice B (p. 5): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
At the ranger station, Maya stared at a bin of 53 lithium battery cells and felt her stomach sink. Each drone pack needed 6 cells, and when she typed 53 ÷ 6 into a phone calculator, it spat out 8.8333333—which made no sense at all when you are holding real metal batteries that cannot be cut into pieces. For a moment she worried she wasn't cut out to be supply quartermaster. Then she tried lining the batteries up in rows of 6 on the workbench and realized the messy decimal was hiding a simple whole-number remainder: 8 full rows of 6 use 48 cells, leaving 5 spare cells on the table. And when 78 campers arrived for 4-person canoes that afternoon, she saw that the same remainder meant 19 full canoes wouldn't be enough—they needed a 20th canoe so the last 2 campers wouldn't be left behind.

docs.title: Section 1.2: Powers and Exponents (Workbook pp. 6–7)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 1.2 (Powers and Exponents) (CCSS.MATH.6.EE.A.1) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Multiply Step-by-Step | Way 2: Group Factors in Pairs | Way 3: Square & Cube Array Model • Block Kit: PRIME-01 (Prime Factor Studio)

Key Vocabulary: power • base • exponent • perfect square • perfect cube

A power represents repeated multiplication of the same factor. In bⁿ, the base b is the repeated factor and the exponent n tells how many times the base is used as a factor. In the Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01), stacking n identical prime blocks models bⁿ directly (for example, three [2] blocks build 2³ = 8, and four [2] blocks build 4² = 2⁴ = 16).

⚠️ WATCH OUT: 4³ means 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 — NEVER multiply the base by the exponent (4 × 3 = 12)!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PRIME-01: Prime Factor Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Concept: In bⁿ, the base b is the repeated factor and the exponent n counts how many times b is multiplied.
  2. Textbook Watch-Out: 4² means 4 × 4 = 16 (a 4-by-4 perfect square), NEVER base × exponent (4 × 2 = 8)!
  3. Block Reinforcement (PRIME-01): Stack prime blocks for 4² = 2⁴ = 16 and 4³ = 2⁶ = 64 (or sketch a 4 × 4 square array vs. 4 × 2).

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.6) Write 4² and 4³ as repeated multiplication and find their values. Compare 4² to 4 × 2. WAY 1: Multiply Step-by-Step Left to Right: Write the base 4 as a repeated factor: 4² = 4 × 4 = 16. For 4³: 4 × 4 = 16, then 16 × 4 = 64. WAY 2: Square Area & Cube Volume Model (With Blocks): 4² is the area of a 4 × 4 square (16 square units), and 4³ is the volume of a 4 × 4 × 4 cube (64 cubic units).WAY 3: Decompose into Smaller Powers: Use the previous power: since 4¹ = 4, 4² = 4 × 4¹ = 16, and 4³ = 4 × 4² = 4 × 16 = 64. 4² = 16, 4³ = 64 Practice B (p.7) A video clip is shared by 3 friends in Round 1, and the number of shares triples in each round. How many shares happen in Round 4? WAY 1: Multiply Step-by-Step (Left to Right): Write 3⁴ as four factors of 3: 3 × 3 = 9 -> 9 × 3 = 27 -> 27 × 3 = 81 shares.Textbook Check: Group repeated factors in pairs: (3 × 3) × (3 × 3) = 9 × 9 = 81. WAY 2: Group Factors in Pairs (Associative Property): Pair the four factors of 3 into two squares: (3 × 3) × (3 × 3) = 9 × 9 = 81 shares.Pattern Check: Multiply by the base 3 at each step: 3¹ = 3 -> 3² = 9 -> 3³ = 27 -> 3⁴ = 81.WAY 3: Pattern of Powers Table: Track each round in a table: Round 1 = 3, Round 2 = 9, Round 3 = 27, Round 4 = 81 shares. 81 shares

docs.title: Practice B (p. 7): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
Leo was ready to give up when his biology lab sheet asked how many bacteria there would be after a single cell split in two every hour for 6 hours. He started drawing tiny branching lines on scratch paper, lost count around thirty, and muttered that he always messed up big numbers. Sitting next to him, Maya pointed out that every hour just multiplied the count by 2 again—just like his 8-by-8 LED matrix multiplied 8 × 8 for a square and his 6-by-6-by-6 storage crate multiplied 6 × 6 × 6 for a cube. Once Leo saw that an exponent simply counts how many times a number multiplies by itself (2⁶ = 64), a whole page of messy scribbles shrank into one step he could actually trust.

# Modeling Real Life Application Prompt Tutor Setup & SC-6 Check Final Answer B1 Pixel Art Canvas: A retro game sprite is drawn on an 8-by-8 square grid. Write the total number of pixels as a power and find its value. Setup: 8² | SC-6: 8 [x²] 8² = 64 pixels B2 Cubic Storage Room: You dig a cubic room measuring 6 blocks long, 6 blocks wide, and 6 blocks tall. How many blocks do you mine in all? Setup: 6³ | SC-6: 6 [x³] 6³ = 216 blocks B3 Cell Division Biology Lab: A single bacterium splits into 2 bacteria every hour. How many bacteria are there after 6 hours? Setup: 2^6 | SC-6: 2 [ENTER] 6 [g][yˣ] 2⁶ = 64 bacteria B4 Tournament Bracket: A tennis tournament has 4⁴ players in the opening round. What is the combined area of both squares? Setup: 12² + 5² | SC-6: 12 [x²] 5 [x²] [+] 144 + 25 = 169 ft² B6 Starling Flock Expansion: On call 1, 5 starlings alert 5 neighbors each. Each wave multiplies by 5. How many starlings are alerted on wave 4? Setup: 5^4 | SC-6: 5 [ENTER] 4 [g][yˣ] 5⁴ = 625 starlings B7 Perfect Square Garden: A square community garden has an area of 196 square meters. What is the side length of the garden? Setup: √(196) | SC-6: 196 [f][√x] 14 meters B8 Power Showdown: Which is greater, 2⁵ or 5²? By how much? docs.title: Section 1.3: Order of Operations (Workbook pp. 8–9)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 1.3 (Order of Operations) (CCSS.MATH.6.EE.A.1) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: PEMDAS Step-by-Step Funnel | Way 2: Distributive Property / Fraction-Bar Grouping • Block Kit: PLACE-01 (Place Value Studio)

Key Vocabulary: numerical expression • evaluate • order of operations • grouping symbols

Big Ideas Order of Operations (PEMDAS): (1) Evaluate expressions inside grouping symbols (), [], or fraction bars first; (2) Evaluate powers; (3) Multiply and divide from left to right; (4) Add and subtract from left to right.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Multiply & Divide have EQUAL priority (go Left-to-Right!), and Add & Subtract have EQUAL priority (go Left-to-Right!).

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PLACE-01: Place Value Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Concept (PEMDAS): 1. Grouping Symbols ( ) [ ] 2. Exponents 3. Multiply & Divide (Left -> Right) 4. Add & Subtract (Left -> Right).
  2. Textbook Watch-Out: Multiplication and division have EQUAL priority (go Left to Right); addition and subtraction also go Left to Right!
  3. Test Strategy: Underline the operation to perform on each line and copy the rest of the expression down like a funnel.

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.8) Evaluate (8 + 4) × (9 - 3). WAY 1: Standard Order of Operations (PEMDAS Funnel): Evaluate inside both sets of parentheses first: (8 + 4) = 12 and (9 - 3) = 6. Then multiply: 12 × 6 = 72. WAY 2: Distributive Property Expansion: Simplify (9 - 3) = 6 first, then distribute 6 across (8 + 4): (8 × 6) + (4 × 6) = 48 + 24 = 72. 72 Practice B (p.9) Evaluate 40 - 3 × (2 + 3)² ÷ 5. WAY 1: Standard PEMDAS Funnel (Left-to-Right Multiply/Divide): 1. Parentheses: (2+3) = 5. 2. Exponent: 5² = 25. 3. Multiply then Divide L-to-R: 3 × 25 = 75, then 75 ÷ 5 = 15. 4. Subtract: 40 - 15 = 25.Step-by-Step Funnel: 40 - 3 × 5² ÷ 5 -> 40 - 3 × 25 ÷ 5 -> 40 - 75 ÷ 5 -> 40 - 15 = 25. WAY 2: Write Division as a Fraction Term: Rewrite 3 × 5² ÷ 5 as the fraction (3 × 25) / 5. Divide 25 ÷ 5 = 5 first, multiply 3 × 5 = 15, then subtract: 40 - 15 = 25.Factor Check: Since 25 ÷ 5 = 5, 3 × (25 ÷ 5) = 3 × 5 = 15, and 40 - 15 = 25. 25

docs.title: Practice B (p. 9): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
Sam and Leo both worked out the price of a $45 skateboard deck plus 4 wheels at $7 each, but Sam got $343 while Leo got $73. Sam was ready to crumple up his paper, convinced that math rules like PEMDAS were just made up to trick kids who aren't fast at arithmetic. Then Leo set the actual parts on the counter: one wooden deck and a plastic pack of four $7 wheels. Looking at the table, Sam suddenly saw what had happened—when he added 45 + 4 first and multiplied by 7, he was pretending he bought 49 items at $7 each! Calculating the 4-wheel bundle (4 × $7 = $28) before adding the $45 deck wasn't a random school rule after all; it matched how the parts really sit on the workbench.

# Modeling Real Life Application Prompt Tutor Setup & SC-6 Check Final Answer B1 Movie Night Snack Combo: Four friends each buy a $9 movie ticket and a $5 tub of popcorn. What is your final score? docs.title: Section 1.4: Prime Factorization (Workbook pp. 10–11)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 1.4 (Prime Factorization) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.B.4) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Factor Tree (Pair A) | Way 2: Factor Tree (Pair B) | Way 3: Division Ladder • Block Kit: PRIME-01 (Prime Factor Studio)

Key Vocabulary: factor pair • prime number • composite number • prime factorization • factor tree

In Big Ideas Math, a Factor Tree or Division Ladder splits a composite number until every branch ends at a prime number. In the Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01), block heights are logarithmic, so stacking [2]+[2]+[3]+[5] always reaches the exact 60 mark whether you split 60 as 6 × 10 or 4 × 15.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Keep branching until EVERY bottom leaf is PRIME (do not stop at composite numbers like 4, 6, 8, or 9; and remember 1 is NOT prime).

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PRIME-01: Prime Factor Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Method 1 (Factor Tree): Branch a composite number into any factor pair until every leaf at the bottom is prime.
  2. Textbook Method 2 (Division Ladder): Divide repeatedly by the smallest prime factors (2, 3, 5, ...) until the quotient is prime.
  3. Block Reinforcement (PRIME-01): Stacking prime blocks [2][2][3][5] models why every factor tree of 60 has the exact same prime leaves (2² × 3 × 5).

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.10) Write the prime factorization of 60 using exponents. WAY 1: Factor Tree Starting with 6 × 10: Branch 60 -> 6 × 10. Split 6 -> 2 × 3 and 10 -> 2 × 5. Circle the prime leaves: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 2² × 3 × 5. WAY 2: Factor Tree Starting with 4 × 15: Branch 60 -> 4 × 15. Split 4 -> 2 × 2 and 15 -> 3 × 5. Same prime leaves (and same PRIME-01 blocks): 2² × 3 × 5.WAY 3: Division Ladder (Repeated Prime Division): Divide by smallest primes step-by-step: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 -> 30 ÷ 2 = 15 -> 15 ÷ 3 = 5 (prime) -> 2² × 3 × 5. 60 = 2² × 3 × 5 Practice B (p.11) A marching band has 120 musicians. Write the prime factorization of 120 and find two different rectangular row formations. WAY 1: Factor Tree (12 × 10): Split 120 = 12 × 10 -> (4 × 3) × (2 × 5) -> (2 × 2 × 3) × (2 × 5) = 2³ × 3 × 5.Factor Tree Check: 120 = 12 × 10 = (2 × 2 × 3) × (2 × 5) = 2³ × 3 × 5. WAY 2: Division Ladder by Smallest Primes: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 -> 60 ÷ 2 = 30 -> 30 ÷ 2 = 15 -> 15 ÷ 3 = 5 -> 2³ × 3 × 5.Ladder Check: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 -> ÷ 2 = 30 -> ÷ 2 = 15 -> ÷ 3 = 5 -> 2³ × 3 × 5.WAY 3: Regroup Prime Blocks into Factor Pairs: Group [2][2][2][3][5] in two ways: (2³) × (3 × 5) = 8 rows of 15, or (2 × 5) × (2² × 3) = 10 rows of 12. 2³ × 3 × 5 (e.g., 8 × 15 or 10 × 12)

docs.title: Practice B (p. 11): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
When Maya tried to arrange 48 small solar cells into a neat rectangle on the cabin roof, she kept losing track of which row widths worked evenly and which ones left awkward gaps, while a spare batch of 37 cells wouldn't form any rectangle at all except one long, skinny line. She doubted she could ever find every possible layout without guessing all afternoon. Then Leo showed her how to branch 48 down a factor tree until only prime numbers (2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3) remained at the tips. Even when Maya started her tree with 6 × 8 and Leo started with 4 × 12, both trees ended at the exact same prime building blocks—giving her a foolproof way to see every factor pair inside a number.

docs.title: Section 1.5: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) & Least Common Multiple (LCM) (Workbook pp. 12–13)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Sections 1.5 & 1.6 (GCF and LCM) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.B.4) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: List Factors & Multiples | Way 2: Prime Factorization | Way 3: Prime Factor Venn Diagram • Block Kit: PRIME-01 (Prime Factor Studio)

Key Vocabulary: common factor • greatest common factor (GCF) • common multiple • least common multiple (LCM) • Venn diagram

In Big Ideas Math, a Prime Factor Venn Diagram places shared prime factors in the center overlap and remaining primes in the outer circles: multiplying the center overlap gives the GCF, and multiplying all regions together gives the LCM! Placing Prime Factor Blocks (PRIME-01) into the Venn circles makes the shared overlap and union visible.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: GCF is a factor that divides IN (smaller or equal, Venn overlap); LCM is a multiple they build UP to (larger or equal, all Venn blocks).

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PRIME-01: Prime Factor Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Method 1 (Lists): List all factor pairs to find the Greatest Common Factor (GCF); list multiples to find the Least Common Multiple (LCM).
  2. Textbook Method 2 (Prime Venn Diagram): Overlap primes = GCF; union of all regions (highest power of each prime) = LCM.
  3. Block Reinforcement (PRIME-01): Comparing prime towers for 20 (2²·5) and 50 (2·5²) shows the shared GCF (2·5 = 10) and union LCM (2²·5² = 100).

docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.12) Find the greatest common factor (GCF) and least common multiple (LCM) of 20 and 50. WAY 1: List Factors (for GCF) & Multiples (for LCM): Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20; of 50: 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50 -> GCF = 10. Multiples: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 & 50, 100 -> LCM = 100. WAY 2: Prime Factorization Powers: 20 = 2² × 5 and 50 = 2 × 5². Shared prime factors = 2 × 5 = 10 (GCF). Highest power of each prime = 2² × 5² = 100 (LCM).WAY 3: Prime Factor Venn Diagram (With Blocks): Left circle only: [2]. Center overlap: [2] and [5] -> GCF = 2×5 = 10. Right circle only: [5]. All regions: 2×10×5 = 100 (LCM). GCF = 10, LCM = 100 Practice B (p.13) You have 18 pretzel bags and 24 fruit bars to make identical snack packs with none left over. What is the greatest number of packs you can make? WAY 1: List All Factors of 18 and 24: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Greatest common factor = 6 packs.Venn Diagram Check: 18 = 2 · 3² and 24 = 2³ · 3 -> shared overlap = 2 · 3 = 6 identical packs. WAY 2: Prime Factor Venn Diagram: 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 and 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3. Center overlap has [2] and [3] -> GCF = 2 × 3 = 6 packs (left has 3 pretzels; right has 4 bars).Distributive Check: 18 + 24 = 6(3 + 4) -> 6 packs with 3 pretzels and 4 granola bars per pack.WAY 3: Common Prime Division Ladder: Divide (18, 24) by 2 -> (9, 12); divide by 3 -> (3, 4). Product of side divisors = 2 × 3 = 6 packs (with 3 and 4 inside). 6 packs (3 pretzels and 4 fruit bars per pack)

docs.title: Practice B (p. 13): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
Leo used to dread word problems with GCF and LCM because the two three-letter names sounded almost identical, and he always guessed the wrong one on quizzes. While helping pack 28 bandages and 42 antiseptic wipes into identical trail first-aid kits, he paused and asked himself what the physical objects were actually doing. Splitting supplies into smaller equal bags with zero leftovers meant dividing IN to find the biggest shared building block—the Greatest Common Factor (14 kits). Later, watching two camp shuttles on 18-minute and 24-minute loops and two meshing 14-tooth and 21-tooth LEGO gears, he realized repeating cycles build UP into the future until they meet at the Least Common Multiple.

docs.title: Unit 2: Fractions & Decimals — The Kitchen Bakery, the Avian Lab & the 3D Print Shop (p. 14)
docs.text:
Big Ideas Math Grade 6 — Chapter 2 — Equivalent Fractions, Multiplying & Dividing Fractions, and All Four Decimal Operations

📄 Print Unit 2 Chapter Packet PDF (13 Pages: Story Opener + 10 Worksheets + 1-Page Answer Key)
  • Hands-On Block Kits (When Applicable — Fraction Studio (FRAC-01) + Place Value Studio (PLACE-01)): 84mm Fraction Comparator Studio (FRAC-01) • Place Value Studio (PLACE-01)
  • Aligned From Blocks to the Stack Story & Chapter: "The Pharaoh's Bakery, 84mm Fraction Towers & Simon Stevin's Decimals" — SC-6 Ch. 5: Fractions, Decimals & Ratios (Appendix B Lessons 15–19)
  • Target Misconception: Students treat fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals as unrelated rules, expect multiplication to always make numbers bigger, forget which fraction to flip in division, and misalign decimal columns.
  • Hands-On & Stack Remediation: Use the 84.0 mm Fraction Studio towers so equivalence and common denominators are physical millimeter height matches. Use [f] [1/x] on Floor 1 (X) so students see only the divisor flip, and use [f] [IP] / [g] [FP] to split whole dollars from decimal cents.

If you spend an afternoon helping Elena in her family's bakery kitchen, volunteering with Zoe at the bird-rehab aviary, or watching Marcus run the school's desktop 3D printer, you quickly run into an annoying truth: real measurements almost never land on whole numbers. Elena's measuring scoops are stamped in halves, thirds, quarters, and eighths, and she used to dread fractions because every rule felt backward—why did a bigger number on the bottom mean a smaller scoop?

Next door at the wildlife center, Zoe watches New Caledonian crows bend hooked twigs to pull grubs out of logs and drop pebbles into water tubes, raising the water level by tiny fractions of a centimeter with each splash until a floating treat rises within reach. To know how many pebbles a crow needs, Zoe has to figure out how many 3/8-centimeter splashes fit inside a 4 1/2-centimeter rise.

Meanwhile, in the maker room, Marcus deals with decimals every time he prints a part: the 3D printer's 'slicer' software chops a 14.4-millimeter bracket into paper-thin horizontal layers, each just 0.20 millimeters thick, and melts corn-based plastic one layer at a time. Out on the track, the stopwatch times 100-meter sprints to the hundredth of a second, where 0.55 seconds is the gap between first and second place.

At first, Elena, Zoe, and Marcus all second-guessed themselves whenever fractions or decimals showed up. Across these lessons, they learn how to trade unequal fraction slices for matching pieces, why taking a 'part of a part' shrinks a fraction, how dividing fractions counts how many scoops fit inside a whole, and how to verify every fraction and decimal step on the SC-6 calculator.

docs.title: Section 2.1: Equivalent Fractions, Mixed Numbers & LCD Addition (Workbook pp. 15–16)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 2.1 Prep (Equivalence, Mixed Numbers & Like/Unlike Fractions) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.A.1) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Divide Once by GCF / Use LCD | Way 2: Step-by-Step Common Factors | Way 3: Fraction Strips Model • Block Kit: FRAC-01 (84mm Fraction Studio)

Key Vocabulary: equivalent fractions • simplest form • least common denominator (LCD) • mixed number • improper fraction

In Big Ideas Math, divide the numerator and denominator by their GCF to write a fraction in simplest form, and rewrite unlike fractions using their Least Common Denominator (LCD) to add or subtract. With Fraction Strips (FRAC-01, 1 Whole = 84 mm), equivalent fractions match in length, and trading 1/3 + 1/4 for twelfths shows 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Never add denominators directly (1/3 + 1/4 ≠ 2/7)! Rewrite with the Least Common Denominator (LCD) first, then add only the numerators.

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (FRAC-01: 84mm Fraction Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Concept: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCF to simplify; use LCD = LCM of denominators to add or subtract fractions.
  2. Textbook Mixed Numbers: Multiply Whole × Denominator + Numerator for improper fractions (a b/c = (ac+b)/c); divide to convert back.
  3. Block Reinforcement (FRAC-01): Line up fraction strips to see that 12/18 = 2/3, and trade 1/3 + 1/4 for twelfths (4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12).

docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.15) Write 12/18 in simplest form. WAY 1: Divide by the GCF in One Step: Find GCF(12, 18) = 6. Divide numerator and denominator by 6: (12 ÷ 6) / (18 ÷ 6) = 2/3. WAY 2: Divide Step-by-Step by Small Prime Factors: Divide top and bottom of 12/18 by 2 first -> 6/9. Then divide top and bottom by 3 -> 2/3.WAY 3: Prime Factor Cancellation / Fraction Strips: Write 12/18 = (2 × 2 × 3) / (2 × 3 × 3). Cancel the shared (2 × 3) -> 2/3. 2/3 Practice B (p.16) A hiker walks a 1 2/3-mile ridge trail and a 1 1/4-mile creek trail. How many miles does the hiker walk in all? WAY 1: Add Whole Numbers & LCD Fractions Separately: LCD(3, 4) = 12. Rename: 1 8/12 + 1 3/12. Add wholes (1 + 1 = 2) and twelfths (8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12) -> 2 11/12 miles.LCD Check: Rewrite 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/4 = 3/12 -> 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12 of the garden. WAY 2: Convert Both to Improper Fractions First: 1 2/3 = 5/3 = 20/12 and 1 1/4 = 5/4 = 15/12. Add: 20/12 + 15/12 = 35/12 = 2 11/12 miles.Inverse Subtraction Check: 7/12 - 1/4 = 7/12 - 3/12 = 4/12 = 1/3 (verified!).WAY 3: Fraction Strips Trade (Twelfths): Combine 2 whole bars, trade two 1/3 bars for eight 1/12 bars, and trade one 1/4 bar for three 1/12 bars -> 2 11/12 miles. 2 11/12 miles (35/12 miles)

docs.title: Practice B (p. 16): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
In the bakery kitchen, Elena poured 3/8 cup of blueberries and 1/4 cup of strawberries into a blender and froze when she tried to write down the total. Part of her wanted to just add across the top and bottom to get 4/12, even though she had a nagging feeling that wasn't right—how could adding berries together give her less than she started with? Picking up the clear glass measuring cup, she looked closely at the etched lines and noticed that every 1/4-cup mark was the exact same height as two 1/8-cup marks. Once she traded 1/4 for 2/8 so all the scoops were the same size (eighths), adding 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 cup finally made complete sense.

docs.title: Section 2.2: Multiplying Fractions and Mixed Numbers (Workbook pp. 17–18)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Section 2.1 (Multiplying Fractions) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.A.1) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Multiply Straight Across | Way 2: Cross-Cancel Common Factors First | Way 3: Area Model / Distributive Split • Block Kit: FRAC-01 (84mm Fraction Studio)

Key Vocabulary: product of fractions • area model • cross-canceling (dividing out common factors) • improper fraction

In Big Ideas Math, multiply fractions by multiplying the numerators and multiplying the denominators: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac)/(bd). For mixed numbers, write each mixed number as an improper fraction first, and divide out common factors before multiplying. Partitioning a 3/4 Fraction Strip (FRAC-01) in half visually shows why 1/2 of 3/4 is 3/8.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: For mixed numbers, ALWAYS convert to improper fractions (a b/c = (ac+b)/c) BEFORE multiplying!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (FRAC-01: 84mm Fraction Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Concept: Multiply numerators and multiply denominators: (a/b) × (c/d) = (a·c)/(b·d). Write mixed numbers as improper fractions first.
  2. Textbook Shortcut (Cross-Canceling): Divide out common factors between any numerator and denominator BEFORE multiplying.
  3. Block Reinforcement (FRAC-01): Partitioning a 3/4 fraction strip in half (or shading a 2 × 4 area grid) visually shows 1/2 of 3/4 = 3/8.

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.17) Find 1/2 × 3/4. WAY 1: Multiply Numerators & Multiply Denominators: Multiply numerators across (1 × 3 = 3) and denominators across (2 × 4 = 8) -> (1 × 3) / (2 × 4) = 3/8. WAY 2: 2D Area Model Grid (Shaded Overlap): Draw a 4-column by 2-row grid (8 eighths). Shade 3 columns (3/4) and 1 row (1/2); the overlap is 3 of 8 boxes = 3/8.WAY 3: Partition Fraction Strips (FRAC-01): Trade three 1/4 strips for six 1/8 strips, then take half of those six strips -> three 1/8 strips = 3/8. 3/8 Practice B (p.18) A batch of granola uses 1 1/2 cups of oats. You make 2 2/3 batches. How many cups of oats do you need? WAY 1: Improper Fractions & Multiply Straight Across: Write 1 1/2 = 3/2 and 2 2/3 = 8/3. Multiply across: (3 × 8) / (2 × 3) = 24 / 6 = 4 cups.Improper Fraction Step: 2 2/3 × 1 1/2 = (8/3) × (3/2) = 24/6 = 4 cups. WAY 2: Divide Out (Cross-Cancel) Common Factors First: In (3/2) × (8/3), divide both 3s by 3 (-> 1) and divide 8 and 2 by 2 (-> 4 and 1): (1/1) × (4/1) = 4 cups.Cross-Cancel Check: Divide 8 and 2 by 2 (-> 4) and 3 and 3 by 3 (-> 1): 4 × 1 = 4 cups.WAY 3: Distributive Property (2 Batches + 2/3 Batch): 2 batches use 2 × 1 1/2 = 3 cups. Two-thirds of a batch uses (2/3) × (3/2) = 1 cup. Total = 3 + 1 = 4 cups. 4 cups

docs.title: Practice B (p. 18): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
Elena always assumed multiplying had to make a number get bigger, so when her phone battery was at 4/5 charge and a game used 1/2 of that charge, she was sure she needed to divide—and got a bigger number that made no sense. Discouraged, she sketched a bar split into fifths, shaded 4 of them, and sliced that shaded part in half. Seeing only 2/5 of the whole bar left, she realized that taking a 'fraction of a fraction' shrinks the piece because you are taking part of a part. Better yet, when scaling a 1 3/4-cup pancake recipe by 2 1/2 batches, dividing out matching factors on the diagonal kept the numbers small enough to multiply without getting lost.

docs.title: Section 2.3: Dividing Fractions and Mixed Numbers (Workbook pp. 19–20)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Sections 2.2 & 2.3 (Dividing Fractions and Mixed Numbers) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.A.1) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Multiply by the Reciprocal | Way 2: Common-Denominator Division | Way 3: Fraction Strip / Number-Line Model • Block Kit: FRAC-01 (84mm Fraction Studio)

Key Vocabulary: reciprocals • multiplicative inverses • common-denominator division • measurement division

In Big Ideas Math, you can divide fractions in two ways: (1) Multiply by the Reciprocal of the divisor: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c), or (2) Rewrite both fractions with a Common Denominator and divide their numerators! Placing 1/8 Fraction Strips (FRAC-01) alongside a 3/4 strip shows why six 1/8s fit inside 3/4.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Keep the FIRST fraction as-is and flip ONLY the SECOND fraction (the divisor): a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c.

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (FRAC-01: 84mm Fraction Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Method 1 (Multiply by the Reciprocal): Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the divisor: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
  2. Textbook Method 2 (Common Denominators): Rewrite both fractions with the LCD and divide their numerators: (a/d) ÷ (b/d) = a ÷ b.
  3. Block Reinforcement (FRAC-01): Placing 1/8 strips alongside a 3/4 strip (6/8) shows that six 1/8 strips fit inside 3/4 (3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6).

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.19) Find 3/4 ÷ 1/8. WAY 1: Multiply by the Reciprocal: Keep 3/4, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/8 to its reciprocal 8/1: (3/4) × (8/1) = 24/4 = 6. WAY 2: Common Denominator Method: Rewrite both fractions with LCD = 8: 6/8 ÷ 1/8. Divide the numerators: 6 eighths ÷ 1 eighth = 6 ÷ 1 = 6.WAY 3: Fraction Strips / Number-Line Jumps (With Blocks): Mark 0 to 3/4 (6/8) on a number line or FRAC-01 tray and count jumps of 1/8: it takes 6 jumps of 1/8 to reach 3/4. 6 Practice B (p.20) A carpenter cuts a 6 3/4-foot cedar board into shelves that are each 1 1/8 feet long. How many shelves can be cut? WAY 1: Improper Fractions & Multiply by the Reciprocal: Write 6 3/4 = 27/4 and 1 1/8 = 9/8. Multiply by the reciprocal: (27/4) × (8/9) = (3/1) × (2/1) = 6 shelves.Reciprocal Step: 4 1/2 ÷ 3/4 = (9/2) × (4/3) = 36/6 = 6 bookshelves. WAY 2: Common Denominator (Eighths): Rewrite both in eighths: 6 3/4 = 54/8 and 1 1/8 = 9/8. Divide the numerators: 54 eighths ÷ 9 eighths = 54 ÷ 9 = 6 shelves.Common Denominator Check: 18/4 ÷ 3/4 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 bookshelves.WAY 3: Repeated Subtraction / Grouping: Two shelves use 2 × 1 1/8 = 2 1/4 ft; four shelves use 4 1/2 ft; six shelves use 6 3/4 ft -> 6 shelves. 6 shelves

docs.title: Practice B (p. 20): Modeling Real Life & Multi-Method Applications (10 Exercises)
docs.text:
Whenever a teacher said 'keep, change, flip' for dividing fractions, Zoe followed the steps like a robot but secretly hated that she had no idea why flipping the second fraction worked. At the bird-rehab center, she watched a crow drop pebbles into a clear tube where each pebble pushed the water up by 3/8 centimeter until the water rose 4 1/2 centimeters. She asked herself a simpler question first: how many 3/8-cm splashes does it take to raise the water 1 full centimeter? Since 1 centimeter is 8/8, it takes 8/3 pebbles per centimeter—which is the flipped fraction (the reciprocal)! Multiplying 4 1/2 centimeters by 8/3 pebbles per centimeter gave 12 pebbles, and for the first time the flip rule wasn't magic anymore.

docs.title: Section 2.4: Adding, Subtracting, and Multiplying Decimals (Workbook pp. 21–22)
docs.text:
Textbook Alignment: Big Ideas Grade 6, Sections 2.4 & 2.5 (Adding, Subtracting, and Multiplying Decimals) (CCSS.MATH.6.NS.B.3) • Big Ideas Methods: Way 1: Vertical Place-Value Algorithm | Way 2: Convert to Fractions/Hundredths | Way 3: Place-Value Split / Area Model • Block Kit: PLACE-01 (Place Value Studio)

Key Vocabulary: tenths • hundredths • thousandths • place-value alignment • trailing zeros • estimation

To add or subtract decimals, line up the decimal points vertically so ones, tenths, and hundredths align, and annex trailing zeros as needed. To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers and count the total number of decimal places in the factors—always checking with a whole-number front-end estimate.

⚠️ WATCH OUT: Line up decimal points for + and - (annex trailing 0s), but for × count the TOTAL decimal places in both factors!

docs.title: Textbook Concepts & Hands-On Reinforcement (PLACE-01: Place Value Studio)
docs.text:
1. Textbook Addition/Subtraction: Line up the decimal points vertically and annex trailing zeros so both numbers have the same place values.
  2. Textbook Multiplication: Multiply as whole numbers, then count the total decimal places in both factors to place the decimal point.
  3. Test Strategy: Always estimate with whole numbers first (e.g., 15 + 4 = 19) to verify your decimal point is in the reasonable place!

docs.title: Authentic Textbook Worked Examples (Learn & Solve by Hand First in 1 Way +10 pts or 2 Ways +20 pts)
docs.text: Worksheet Problem Way 1 Way 2 (& Way 3 Where Applicable) Final Answer Practice A (p.21) Find 14.6 + 3.85 and check by subtracting. WAY 1: Line Up Decimal Points Vertically: Annex a zero to write 14.6 as 14.60. Add hundredths (0+5=5), tenths (6+8=14, carry 1), and ones (14+3+1=18) -> 18.45. WAY 2: Decompose by Place Value (Wholes + Hundredths): Add whole numbers (14 + 3 = 17) and decimals (0.60 + 0.85 = 1.45) separately, then combine: 17 + 1.45 = 18.45.WAY 3: Add as Mixed Numbers (Hundredths): 14 60/100 + 3 85/100 = 17 145/100 = 18 45/100 = 18.45. 18.45 Practice B (p.22) You buy 3.6 pounds of trail mix at $2.25 per pound. What is the total cost of the trail mix? WAY 1: Multiply Whole Numbers & Count Decimal Places: Multiply 225 × 36 = 8,100. Count decimal places (1 place in 3.6 + 2 places in 2.25 = 3 places) -> 8.100 = $8.10.Decimal Places Check: 4.5 (1 place) × 1.80 (2 places) = 8.100 (3 places) = $8.10. WAY 2: Distributive Split (3 lb + 0.6 lb): 3 lb × $2.25 = $6.75, and 0.6 lb × $2.25 = $1.35. Add the partial products: $6.75 + $1.35 = \(8.10.<br>*Distributive Check: 4(\)1.80) + 0.5($1.80) = $7.20 + $0.90 = $8.10.WAY 3: Multiply as Fractions / Mixed Numbers:* 3.6 = 18/5 and 2.25 = 9/4. Multiply: (18/5) × (9/4) = 162/20 = 81/10 = $8.10. $8.10
