Keystrokes: 6.328 [E] 7 [+/-] [ENTER] 1.80 [×] 2.5 [E] 4 [+/-] [÷] 1000 [×]\(\to \mathbf{4.55616\text{ mm}}\).

In Thomas Young's double-slit interferometer, constructive interference maxima occur where the optical path difference \(d\sin\theta = m\lambda\); in the paraxial far-field regime (\(\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta = y/L\)), adjacent bright fringes are spaced uniformly by \(\Delta y = \lambda L / d\). Evaluating the He-Ne laser diffraction product \(\lambda L\) (6.328 [E] 7 [+/-] [ENTER] 1.80 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.1390 \times 10^{-6}\)), dividing by slit pitch \(d = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}\) (2.5 [E] 4 [+/-] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0046\)), and scaling to millimeters (1000 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 4.5562\)) resolves fringe spacing \(\Delta y \approx \mathbf{4.56\text{ mm}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.7: Vector Sum of Three Concurrent Forces via [Σ+]
docs.text:
Three coplanar cable forces on a gusset plate: * \(F_1 = 50.0\text{ kN}\) at \(\theta_1 = 30.0^\circ\) * \(F_2 = 75.0\text{ kN}\) at \(\theta_2 = 110.0^\circ\) * \(F_3 = 60.0\text{ kN}\) at \(\theta_3 = 225.0^\circ\)

Keystrokes: 1. Clear stats: [CLΣ] 2. Vector 1: 30 [ENTER] 50 [↱] [▸y,x] [Σ+] 3. Vector 2: 110 [ENTER] 75 [↱] [▸y,x] [Σ+] 4. Vector 3: 225 [ENTER] 60 [↱] [▸y,x] [Σ+] 5. Recall sums and resolve: [↱] [SUMS] [Σy] \(\to \Sigma y = 53.0506\text{ kN}\) [↱] [SUMS] [Σx] \(\to \Sigma x = -24.7731\text{ kN}\) (lifts \(\Sigma y\) to Register \(Y\)) [↰] [▸θ,r]

This workflow is one of the crowning architectural idioms of the SC-32: because [↱] [▸y,x] deposits \((Y: r\sin\theta, X: r\cos\theta)\) and [Σ+] simultaneously accumulates Register \(X\) into \(\Sigma x\) and Register \(Y\) into \(\Sigma y\), you can sum an arbitrary number of 2D vectors without consuming the 4-level stack! Clearing statistical registers ([CLΣ]) and piping each polar cable force through [↱] [▸y,x] [Σ+] accumulates the three gusset loads into hardware memory; recalling the Cartesian totals via the single-scalar SUMS softkeys ([↱] [SUMS] [Σy] \(= 53.0506\text{ kN}\), then [↱] [SUMS] [Σx] \(= -24.7731\text{ kN}\) which lifts \(\Sigma y\) to Register \(Y\)) and converting back to polar ([↰] [▸θ,r], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 115.01^\circ, X: 58.5444\text{ kN}\)) delivers resultant magnitude \(R = \mathbf{58.54\text{ kN}}\) at bearing \(\theta = \mathbf{115.01^\circ}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.8: Solar Zenith Angle and Air Mass Coefficient
docs.text:
Sun at elevation \(\alpha = 42.0^\circ\). Solar zenith angle \(\theta_z = 90^\circ - 42^\circ = 48.0^\circ\).

\[\text{Air Mass } AM = \frac{1}{\cos\theta_z}\]

Keystrokes: 48 [COS] [1/x]\(\to \mathbf{1.4945} \approx AM\,1.5\).

Solar photovoltaic modules are rated worldwide under the ASTM G173 AM1.5 terrestrial spectrum—the optical path length of sunlight through a planar atmosphere when the sun sits at zenith angle \(\theta_z = 48.19^\circ\) (\(\sec 48.19^\circ = 1.50\)). Evaluating the zenith cosine (48 [COS], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.6691\)) and inverting in place ([1/x], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.4945\)) yields the secant optical path \(\text{AM} \approx \mathbf{1.49}\), confirming nearly exact AM1.5 standard irradiance conditions.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.9: Catenary Hanging Cable Tension at Support Tower
docs.text:
Cable unit weight \(w = 12.5\text{ N/m}\), parameter \(a = 600.0\text{ m}\), span \(L = 400.0\text{ m}\) (half-span \(x = 200.0\text{ m}\)).

\[T_0 = w \cdot a = 12.5 \times 600 = 7500.0\text{ N}$$ $$T = T_0 \cosh\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) = 7500 \cosh\left(\frac{200}{600}\right) = 7500 \cosh(0.333333)\]

Keystrokes: 200 [ENTER] 600 [÷] [↰] [HYP] [COS] 7500 [×]\(\to \mathbf{7921.28\text{ N}} \approx 7.92\text{ kN}\).

Unlike a suspension bridge cable loaded by a flat horizontal roadway (which hangs in a parabola), an unencumbered power line supporting its own distributed weight \(w\) hangs in a hyperbolic cosine catenary \(y = a\cosh(x/a)\), where horizontal tension \(T_0 = wa\) is constant and total tension grows as \(T(x) = T_0 \cosh(x/a) = T_0 + w s_{\text{sag}}\). Forming the dimensionless half-span ratio \(x/a\) (200 [ENTER] 600 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.3333\)), evaluating the hyperbolic cosine ([↰] [HYP] [COS], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.0561\)), and scaling by \(T_0 = 7,500\text{ N}\) (7500 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7920.5390\)) yields tower anchor tension \(T \approx \mathbf{7,920.54\text{ N}}\) (\(7.92\text{ kN}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.10: Polar Conic Equation for Elliptical Satellite Orbit
docs.text:
Semi-latus rectum \(p = 7,200.0\text{ km}\), orbital eccentricity \(e = 0.150\). Find orbital radius at true anomaly \(\theta = 60.0^\circ\).

\[r = \frac{p}{1 + e \cos\theta}\]

Keystrokes: 60 [COS] 0.150 [×] 1 [+] 7200 [x⇄y] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{6697.67\text{ km}}\).

Kepler's first law expresses every bound two-body trajectory as a polar conic section \(r(\theta) = p / (1 + e\cos\theta)\) measured from perigee (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)). Evaluating the denominator modulation (60 [COS] 0.150 [×] 1 [+], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.0750\)), loading semi-latus rectum \(p = 7,200\text{ km}\), and dividing via 7200 [x⇄y] [÷] (or [1/x] 7200 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 6697.6744\)) determines the instantaneous geocentric radius \(r = \mathbf{6,697.67\text{ km}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.11: Nautical Waypoint Bearing and Distance
docs.text:
Course from Station A (\(x_1=0, y_1=0\)) to Station B (\(\Delta x = 45.2\text{ nmi}\) East, \(\Delta y = 78.5\text{ nmi}\) North).

Keystrokes: 78.5 [ENTER] 45.2 [↰] [▸θ,r] \(\rightarrow\) 90.583055811

Notice the elegant duality between Cartesian math angles (measured counter-clockwise from East, \(\theta_{\text{math}} = \text{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x)\)) and nautical compass bearings (measured clockwise from True North, \(\text{Az} = \text{atan2}(\Delta x, \Delta y)\)). Loading northing \(\Delta y = 78.5\) into \(Y\) and easting \(\Delta x = 45.2\) into \(X\) and pressing [↰] [▸θ,r] (78.5 [ENTER] 45.2 [↰] [▸θ,r], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 60.0668^\circ, X: 90.5831\text{ nmi}\)) delivers rhumb-line distance \(r = \mathbf{90.58\text{ nmi}}\) in \(X\) and Cartesian angle \(60.07^\circ\) in \(Y\) (nautical bearing \(90^\circ - 60.07^\circ = \mathbf{029.93^\circ}\))—and if you instead enter Easting into \(Y\) and Northing into \(X\) (45.2 [ENTER] 78.5 [↰] [▸θ,r]), Register \(Y\) outputs the true compass azimuth \(\mathbf{029.93^\circ}\) directly!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.12: Circular Arch Chord Length and Segment Arc Length
docs.text:
Circular arch of radius \(R = 25.0\text{ m}\) spanning central angle \(\theta = 70.0^\circ\).

\[\text{Chord } c = 2 R \sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right), \quad \text{Arc } s = R \frac{\theta \pi}{180}\]

Keystrokes for Chord: 25 [ENTER] 2 [×] 35 [SIN] [×]\(\to \mathbf{28.6788\text{ m}}\)

Historically, ancient astronomers tabulated the chord function \(\text{crd}(\theta) = 2R\sin(\theta/2)\) before Indian mathematicians introduced the half-chord jyā-ardha (\(\sin(\theta/2)\)). Computing the arch diameter (25 [ENTER] 2 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 50.0000\)) and multiplying by the half-angle sine (35 [SIN] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 28.6788\)) resolves the horizontal abutment span \(c \approx \mathbf{28.68\text{ m}}\), while the curved masonry extrados arc \(s = 25 \times 70\pi/180 = 30.54\text{ m}\) exceeds the chord by \(1.86\text{ m}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.13: Brewster's Angle of Polarization
docs.text:
Laser beam incident on crown glass window (\(n = 1.520\) in air).

\[\theta_B = \arctan(n)\]

Keystrokes: 1.520 [↰] [ATAN]\(\to \mathbf{56.6593^\circ}\).

At Brewster's angle \(\theta_B + \theta_2 = 90^\circ\), the oscillating dipole electrons inside the dielectric glass point directly along the reflected ray vector; because Hertzian dipoles cannot radiate along their own oscillation axis, \(p\)-polarized reflection vanishes completely (\(R_p = 0\)). Since Snell's law gives \(n\sin\theta_B = \sin(90^\circ - \theta_B) = \cos\theta_B\), entering \(n = 1.520\) and pressing [↰] [ATAN] (\(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 56.6593\)) directly yields the lossless laser-window incidence angle \(\theta_B \approx \mathbf{56.66^\circ}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.14: Aircraft Coordinated Turn Radius and G-Load
docs.text:
Aircraft turning at \(v = 150.0\text{ kts} = 77.1667\text{ m/s}\) at bank angle \(\phi = 45.0^\circ\) (\(g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2\)).

\[R = \frac{v^2}{g \tan\phi}, \quad \text{Load Factor } n = \frac{1}{\cos\phi}\]

Keystrokes for Radius: 77.1667 [↰] [x²] 9.80665 [ENTER] 45 [TAN] [×] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{607.21\text{ meters}}\)

In a coordinated level turn, aerodynamic lift \(L\) must tilt by bank angle \(\phi\) so that \(L\cos\phi = mg\) supports aircraft weight while \(L\sin\phi = mv^2/R\) turns the flight path vector. Squaring true airspeed (77.1667 [↰] [x²], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 5954.6996\)) and dividing by \(g\tan(45^\circ)\) (9.80665 [ENTER] 45 [TAN] [×] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 607.2104\)) yields turn radius \(R \approx \mathbf{607.21\text{ m}}\), while the structural load factor \(n = L/(mg) = \sec(45^\circ) = \sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{1.41\,G}\) increases stall speed by \(\sqrt{n} \approx 19\%\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.15: Roof Truss Member Forces via Method of Joints
docs.text:
Ridge joint with vertical downward roof load \(P = 15.0\text{ kN}\) balanced by two symmetrical rafters inclined at \(\theta = 30.0^\circ\) to horizontal.

\[2 F_{\text{rafter}} \sin\theta = P \implies F_{\text{rafter}} = \frac{P}{2 \sin\theta}\]

Keystrokes: 15 [ENTER] 2 [ENTER] 30 [SIN] [×] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{15.0000\text{ kN}}\) compression.

At a symmetrical gable ridge pin, each rafter carries half the vertical snow load \(P/2 = F_{\text{rafter}}\sin\theta\); because \(\sin(30^\circ) = 0.5000\), the vertical projection factor \(2\sin(30^\circ)\) equals unity! Loading the ridge point load \(P = 15.0\text{ kN}\) (15 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 15.0000, X: 15.0000\)) and dividing by \(2\sin(30^\circ)\) (2 [ENTER] 30 [SIN] [×] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 15.0000\)) confirms axial rafter compression \(F_{\text{rafter}} = \mathbf{15.00\text{ kN}}\) (and keying 30 [COS] [×] immediately gives the \(12.99\text{ kN}\) horizontal collar-tie tension).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.16: Helical Compression Spring Wahl Stress Factor
docs.text:
Spring index \(C = D / d = 7.50\).

\[K_W = \frac{4C - 1}{4C - 4} + \frac{0.615}{C}\]

Keystrokes: 4 [ENTER] 7.5 [×] 1 [-] 4 [ENTER] 7.5 [×] 4 [-] [÷] 0.615 [ENTER] 7.5 [÷] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 1.1973846154

In a coiled helical spring, the inner wire fibers have a shorter radius of curvature than the coil centerline and carry both torsional shear and direct transverse shear, elevating inner-wall shear stress by A. M. Wahl's correction factor \(K_W\). Computing the curvature numerator \(4C - 1 = 29.0\) (4 [ENTER] 7.5 [×] 1 [-], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 29.0000\)), dividing by \((4C - 4) = 26.0\) (4 [ENTER] 7.5 [×] 4 [-] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.1154\)), and adding the transverse shear term \(0.615/C\) (0.615 [ENTER] 7.5 [÷] [+], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.1974\)) establishes \(K_W = \mathbf{1.1974}\) (nearly \(20\%\) higher stress than straight-bar torsion).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.17: Coriolis Acceleration Vector on Artillery Projectile
docs.text:
Projectile traveling North at \(v = 820.0\text{ m/s}\) at latitude \(\phi = 42.0^\circ\text{ N}\). Earth's angular rotation rate \(\Omega = 7.2921 \times 10^{-5}\text{ rad/s}\): $\(a_{\text{coriolis}} = 2 \cdot v \cdot \Omega \cdot \sin\phi\)$

Keystrokes: 2 [ENTER] 820 [×] 7.2921 [E] 5 [+/-] [×] 42 [SIN] [×] \(\to \mathbf{0.0800216236\text{ m/s}^2}\) Eastward.

In a rotating planetary reference frame, a projectile moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) experiences apparent Coriolis acceleration \(\vec{a}_c = -2(\vec{\Omega} \times \vec{v})\), where the local vertical component of Earth's spin vector \(\Omega\sin\phi\) deflects Northern Hemisphere trajectories to the right. Forming \(2v\) (2 [ENTER] 820 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1640.0000\)), multiplying by sidereal spin rate \(\Omega\) (7.2921 [E] 5 [+/-] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.1196\)), and scaling by \(\sin(42^\circ)\) (42 [SIN] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0800\)) yields \(a_{\text{coriolis}} \approx \mathbf{0.0800\text{ m/s}^2}\) Eastward—enough to deflect a \(30\text{-second}\) artillery shell by \(\frac{1}{2}a_c t^2 = 36\text{ meters}\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.18: Involute Gear Tooth Base Pitch and Pressure Angle
docs.text:
Module \(m = 4.0\text{ mm}\), tooth count \(N = 28\), standard pressure angle \(\phi = 20.0^\circ\). Calculate pitch circle diameter \(D\), base circle diameter \(D_b\), and circular base pitch \(p_b\): $\(D = m \cdot N, \quad D_b = D \cos\phi, \quad p_b = \pi \cdot m \cos\phi\)$

Keystrokes: 4 [ENTER] 28 [×]\(\to D = \mathbf{112.00\text{ mm}}\)

By the fundamental law of conjugate gear-tooth action, the common normal at the contact point of two involute profiles always lies tangent to both base circles \(D_b = D\cos\phi\) at constant pressure angle \(\phi = 20.0^\circ\). Multiplying module by tooth count (\(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 112.0000\)) yields pitch diameter \(D = \mathbf{112.00\text{ mm}}\); scaling by 20 [COS] [×] gives the involute generating base circle \(D_b = \mathbf{105.25\text{ mm}}\), and dividing by 28 [÷] [↱] [π] [×] yields base pitch \(p_b = \mathbf{11.81\text{ mm}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.19: Supersonic Oblique Shock Wave Angle
docs.text:
Supersonic flight at Mach \(M_1 = 2.50\) over a compression wedge with deflection angle \(\theta = 15.0^\circ\). Determine shock angle \(\beta\) (approximate weak shock solution \(\beta \approx 36.94^\circ\)): $\(\tan\theta = 2 \cot\beta \left[\frac{M_1^2 \sin^2\beta - 1}{M_1^2 (\gamma + \cos(2\beta)) + 2}\right]\)$

Across an oblique shock inclined at wave angle \(\beta\), tangential velocity is conserved while the normal Mach component \(M_{n1} = M_1 \sin\beta\) must exceed unity (\(M_{n1} > 1\)) to compress the flow. Evaluating the normal Mach number for \(\beta = 36.94^\circ\) (2.50 [ENTER] 36.94 [SIN] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.5024\)) and forming the excess normal kinetic energy factor \(M_{n1}^2 - 1\) ([↰] [x²] 1 [-], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.2573\)) yields the \(\theta\)-\(\beta\)-\(M\) numerator delta \(1.2573\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.20: Wind Turbine Blade Angle of Attack and Relative Velocity
docs.text:
Blade station radius \(r = 32.0\text{ m}\), rotational speed \(\Omega = 1.80\text{ rad/s}\) (\(u_{\text{rot}} = \Omega r = 57.6\text{ m/s}\)), free-stream wind speed \(v_{\text{wind}} = 11.5\text{ m/s}\) with axial induction factor \(a = 0.30\) (\(v_{\text{axial}} = 11.5(1 - 0.30) = 8.05\text{ m/s}\)): $\(W_{\text{rel}} = \sqrt{u_{\text{rot}}^2 + v_{\text{axial}}^2}, \quad \phi_{\text{flow}} = \arctan\left(\frac{v_{\text{axial}}}{u_{\text{rot}}}\right)\)$

Keystrokes: 8.05 [ENTER] 57.6 [↰] [▸θ,r] \(\rightarrow\) 58.15980141

In blade-element momentum (BEM) theory, an airfoil section at radius \(r = 32\text{ m}\) sees the vector sum of the Betz-decelerated axial wind \(v_{\text{axial}} = 8.05\text{ m/s}\) and the much faster tangential sweep velocity \(u_{\text{rot}} = \Omega r = 57.6\text{ m/s}\). Loading \((Y: v_{\text{axial}}, X: u_{\text{rot}})\) and pressing [↰] [▸θ,r] (8.05 [ENTER] 57.6 [↰] [▸θ,r], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 7.9560^\circ, X: 58.1598\text{ m/s}\)) resolves both the relative aerodynamic inflow speed \(W_{\text{rel}} \approx \mathbf{58.16\text{ m/s}}\) and the inflow pitch angle \(\phi_{\text{flow}} \approx \mathbf{7.96^\circ}\) in a single keystroke.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.21: Surveying Triangulation Intersection from Two Stations
docs.text:
Baseline between Stations \(A\) and \(B\) is \(b = 1,250.0\text{ m}\). Angles observed to unknown landmark \(P\): \(\angle A = 58.4^\circ\), \(\angle B = 71.2^\circ\). Angle at \(P\): \(\angle P = 180^\circ - (58.4^\circ + 71.2^\circ) = 50.4^\circ\): $\(\text{Distance } AP = b \frac{\sin B}{\sin P} = 1250 \frac{\sin(71.2^\circ)}{\sin(50.4^\circ)}\)$

Keystrokes: 1250 [ENTER] 71.2 [SIN] [×] 50.4 [SIN] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{1535.84\text{ meters}}\).

Before electronic distance measurement, continental geodetic networks were extended across mountain ranges by measuring a single taped baseline \(b\) in a flat valley and sighting horizontal theodolite angles to distant peaks. Scaling baseline \(b = 1,250\text{ m}\) by the opposing angle sine (1250 [ENTER] 71.2 [SIN] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1183.3116\)) and dividing by the vertex parallax sine \(\sin(50.4^\circ)\) (50.4 [SIN] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1535.7446\)) resolves range \(AP \approx \mathbf{1,535.74\text{ m}}\)—and if you also need range \(BP\), 1250 [ENTER] 58.4 [SIN] [×] 50.4 [SIN] [÷] completes the fix.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.22: Celestial Coordinate Conversion (RA/Dec to Alt/Az)
docs.text:
Observer at latitude \(\phi = 38.0^\circ\text{ N}\). Star with declination \(\delta = 22.5^\circ\) and local hour angle \(H = 40.0^\circ\).

\[\sin a = \sin\phi \sin\delta + \cos\phi \cos\delta \cos H\]

Keystrokes: 38 [SIN] 22.5 [SIN] [×] 38 [COS] 22.5 [COS] [×] 40 [COS] [×] [+] [↰] [ASIN]

Transforming equatorial star catalog coordinates \((\delta, H)\) into local horizon altitude \(a\) for an alt-azimuth telescope mount solves the same spherical cosine law used in marine sextant sight reduction. Computing the polar sine product (38 [SIN] 22.5 [SIN] [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.2356\)), adding the meridian hour-angle cosine term (38 [COS] 22.5 [COS] [×] 40 [COS] [×] [+], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.7933\)), and extracting the inverse sine ([↰] [ASIN], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 52.4954\)) yields horizon altitude \(a \approx \mathbf{52.50^\circ}\) (zenith distance \(z = 90^\circ - a = 37.50^\circ\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.23: Gyroscopic Precession Angular Rate
docs.text:
Rotor mass moment of inertia \(I_s = 0.0125\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\), spin speed \(\omega_s = 24,000\text{ rpm} = 2513.27\text{ rad/s}\). Applied disturbance torque \(\tau = 0.450\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\): $\(\Omega_p = \frac{\tau}{I_s \cdot \omega_s}\)$

Keystrokes: 0.450 [ENTER] 0.0125 [ENTER] 24000 [ENTER] 2 [×] [↱] [π] [×] 60 [÷] [×] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{0.014324\text{ rad/s}} = 0.8207^\circ/\text{s}\).

Because torque equals the time rate of change of angular momentum (\(\vec{\tau} = d\vec{L}/dt = \vec{\Omega}_p \times \vec{L}\)), a high-speed gyroscope rotor responds to an orthogonal torque \(\tau\) by precessing perpendicular to both the spin and torque axes at rate \(\Omega_p = \tau / (I_s \omega_s)\). Loading disturbance torque (0.450 [ENTER], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.4500, X: 0.4500\)) and dividing by the spin angular momentum \(L = I_s \omega_s = 31.4159\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}\) (0.0125 [ENTER] 24000 [ENTER] 2 [×] [↱] [π] [×] 60 [÷] [×] [÷], \(T: 0.4500, Z: 0.4500, Y: 0.4500, X: 0.0143\)) yields precession rate \(\Omega_p \approx \mathbf{0.0143\text{ rad/s}}\) (\(0.82^\circ/\text{s}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.24: Quarter-Wave Plate Retardance and Jones Matrix
docs.text:
Ellipticity angle \(\chi\) produced by linear polarizer at angle \(\theta = 22.5^\circ\) through quarter-wave plate.

$\(\sin(2\chi) = \sin(2\theta) \sin\delta\)$ For a quarter-wave plate (\(\delta = 90.0^\circ\)), \(\sin\delta = 1.0\): $\(\chi = \frac{1}{2} \arcsin(\sin(45^\circ)) = \frac{45^\circ}{2} = \mathbf{22.50^\circ}\)$.

On the Poincaré polarization sphere, a birefringent retarder with phase delay \(\delta\) rotates the Stokes polarization vector about the fast-axis equator by angle \(\delta\), mapping azimuth \(2\theta\) to latitude \(2\chi\) via \(\sin(2\chi) = \sin(2\theta)\sin\delta\). Doubling the incident polarizer angle (22.5 [ENTER] 2 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 45.0000\)), applying the quarter-wave round-trip ([SIN] [↰] [ASIN], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 45.0000\)), and halving (2 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 22.5000\)) confirms ellipticity angle \(\chi = \mathbf{22.50^\circ}\) (\(\tan\chi = 0.4142\) minor-to-major field ratio).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.25: Acoustic Directivity Index of Circular Piston Speaker
docs.text:
Loudspeaker piston radius \(a = 0.10\text{ m}\) radiating at frequency \(f = 2,500\text{ Hz}\) in air (\(c = 343\text{ m/s}\)):

\[k = \frac{2\pi f}{c} = \frac{2\pi(2500)}{343} \approx 45.7958\text{ m}^{-1}$$ $$k a = 45.7958 \times 0.10 = 4.5796$$ Directivity index for $k a \gg 1$: $$D_I \approx 10 \log_{10}(ka)^2 = 20 \log_{10}(ka)\]

Keystrokes: 4.5796 [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]\(\to \mathbf{13.2168\text{ dB}}\).

When the acoustic Helmholtz number \(ka = 2\pi a/\lambda\) exceeds unity, a baffled circular loudspeaker cone transitions from an omnidirectional monopole into a directional Airy-Bessel beam whose on-axis intensity gain scales as \((ka)^2\). Entering \(ka = 4.5796\), taking the common logarithm, and scaling by \(20\) (\(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 13.2166\)) yields an on-axis directivity index \(D_I \approx \mathbf{13.22\text{ dB}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.26: Ballistic Reentry Trajectory Flight Path Angle
docs.text:
Atmospheric entry interface velocity \(v_E = 7,800\text{ m/s}\), radial velocity \(v_r = -210\text{ m/s}\), tangential speed \(v_\theta = \sqrt{7800^2 - 210^2} \approx 7797.17\text{ m/s}\). Find flight path entry angle \(\gamma\): $\(\sin\gamma = \frac{v_r}{v_E} \implies \gamma = \arcsin\left(\frac{-210}{7800}\right)\)$

Keystrokes: 210 [+/-] [ENTER] 7800 [÷] [↰] [ASIN]\(\to \mathbf{-1.5428^\circ}\).

Spacecraft atmospheric entry at \(120\text{ km}\) altitude requires threading a narrow flight-path corridor: too shallow and the capsule skips back into space; too steep and peak deceleration exceeds crew structural limits. Forming the sink-rate ratio \(v_r/v_E\) (210 [+/-] [ENTER] 7800 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -0.0269\)) and extracting the arcsine ([↰] [ASIN], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -1.5428\)) establishes the shallow reentry corridor angle \(\gamma \approx \mathbf{-1.54^\circ}\) below the local horizontal.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.27: Circular Roadway Curve Sight Distance
docs.text:
Curve radius \(R = 250.0\text{ m}\), obstacle setback distance from centerline \(m = 8.5\text{ m}\). Calculate available stopping sight distance \(S\):

\[m = R \left(1 - \cos\left(\frac{28.65^\circ S}{R}\right)\right) \implies S = \frac{R}{28.65^\circ} \arccos\left(1 - \frac{m}{R}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 8.5 [ENTER] 250 [÷] [+/-] 1 [+] [↰] [ACOS] 250 [×] 28.65 [÷]\(\to \mathbf{130.74299272\text{ meters}}\).

In highway geometric design, trees or bridge abutments on the inside of a horizontal curve limit the driver's line-of-sight chord; the middle ordinate setback \(m = R(1 - \cos\frac{\theta}{2})\) is the classical versine of the half-central angle, where \(28.65^\circ \approx \frac{90^\circ}{\pi}\) converts radians to half-angle degrees. Evaluating the inverse-versine argument \(1 - m/R\) and taking its arccosine (8.5 [ENTER] 250 [÷] [+/-] 1 [+] [↰] [ACOS], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 14.9836\)), then scaling by \(R/28.65^\circ\) (250 [×] 28.65 [÷]—or recalling \(R = 250\) from LASTX earlier—\(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 130.7467\)) determines stopping sight distance \(S \approx \mathbf{130.75\text{ m}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.28: Resection Surveying Point Fix (Kaestner Method)
docs.text:
Two known landmarks \(L_1 (0, 1000)\) and \(L_2 (800, 600)\). Measured subtended angle \(\alpha = 42.0^\circ\). Baseline length \(b\):

\[b = \sqrt{800^2 + (1000 - 600)^2} = \sqrt{640000 + 160000} = \sqrt{800000} = 894.4272\text{ m}$$ Radius of circumscribing position circle: $$R_{\text{circ}} = \frac{b}{2 \sin\alpha} = \frac{894.4272}{2 \sin(42^\circ)}\]

Keystrokes: 800000 [√x] 2 [÷] 42 [SIN] [÷]\(\to \mathbf{668.35\text{ meters}}\).

By Euclid's inscribed angle theorem, all observer positions that sight a fixed subtended angle \(\alpha\) between two landmarks \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) lie on a circular arc of radius \(R_{\text{circ}} = b / (2\sin\alpha)\) (the Collins auxiliary circle used in three-point resection). Computing the half-baseline chord \(b/2\) (800000 [√x] 2 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 447.2136\)) and dividing by \(\sin(42^\circ)\) (42 [SIN] [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 668.3502\)) resolves the position-circle radius \(R_{\text{circ}} \approx \mathbf{668.35\text{ m}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.29: Elliptical Polarization Axial Ratio from Phasors
docs.text:
Major ellipse axis \(E_{\max} = 12.4\text{ V/m}\), minor axis \(E_{\min} = 4.2\text{ V/m}\). Calculate axial ratio in decibels:

\[\text{AR}_{\text{dB}} = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{E_{\max}}{E_{\min}}\right)\]

Keystrokes: 12.4 [ENTER] 4.2 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]\(\to \mathbf{9.4036\text{ dB}}\).

Satellite communication antennas rely on circular polarization (\(\text{AR} = 0\text{ dB}\)) to prevent Faraday rotation fading through the ionosphere; any cross-polar mismatch elongates the polarization locus into an ellipse quantified by the voltage axial ratio \(E_{\max}/E_{\min}\). Forming the semi-axis ratio (12.4 [ENTER] 4.2 [÷], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.9524\)), taking the base-10 logarithm, and scaling by \(20\) ([↰] [LOG] 20 [×], \(T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 9.4034\)) yields \(\text{AR}_{\text{dB}} \approx \mathbf{9.40\text{ dB}}\).

docs.title: Chapter 05: Complex Numbers, AC Phasors & Euler's Identity — Extended Engineering & Competition Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 05 of Thinking in the Stack (21 Worked Engineering Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.1: Principal Value of Natural Logarithm of Negative Real: \(\ln(-5)\)
docs.text:
In complex analysis, \(\ln(z) = \ln|z| + i \operatorname{Arg}(z)\). For \(z = -5 + 0i\), \(|z| = 5\) and \(\operatorname{Arg}(z) = \pi\):

\[\ln(-5) = \ln(5) + i\pi \approx 1.609438 + 3.141593i\]

While the real-valued logarithm [LN] halts on negative inputs, extending \(\ln(z)\) to the complex Riemann surface reveals that a negative real number \(-5 = 5 e^{i\pi}\) has log-modulus \(\ln(5)\) as its real part and the half-turn phase angle \(\pi\) radians as its imaginary part. Load \(z = -5 + 0i\) into \((Y, X)\) and evaluate the principal complex logarithm via 5 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [LN] \(\rightarrow\) 3.1415926536, transitioning the stack to \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 1.609438, X: 3.141593)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.2: Complex Reciprocal of High-Q Inductor Admittance
docs.text:
An RF inductor has impedance \(\mathbf{Z}_L = 0.5 + 120.0i\,\Omega\). Calculate its complex admittance \(\mathbf{Y} = 1/\mathbf{Z}\):

\[\mathbf{Y} = \frac{1}{0.5 + 120i} = \frac{0.5 - 120i}{0.5^2 + 120^2} = \frac{0.5 - 120i}{0.25 + 14400} = 3.4722 \times 10^{-5} - 8.3333 \times 10^{-3}i\,\text{S}\]

Keystrokes: 0.5 [ENTER] 120 [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] \(\rightarrow\) -0.008333189

In parallel RF tank circuits, series resistance \(R_s = 0.5\,\Omega\) and reactance \(X_L = +120\,\Omega\) (\(Q = 240\)) cannot be inverted term-by-term; complex inversion [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] automatically divides the conjugate \(R - jX\) by \(|Z|^2 = R^2 + X^2\) using overflow-safe Smith scaling. Load the inductor impedance via 0.5 [ENTER] 120, establishing \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0.5, X: 120)\). Press [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] to invert the complex phasor into admittance \(\mathbf{Y} = G + jB\) in Siemens, arriving at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 3.4722 \times 10^{-5}, X: -8.3333 \times 10^{-3})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.3: Series RLC Circuit Total Impedance
docs.text:
At angular frequency \(\omega = 1,000\text{ rad/s}\), a series circuit has \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 80\text{ mH}\) (\(X_L = \omega L = 80\,\Omega\)), and \(C = 20\,\mu\text{F}\) (\(X_C = 1/(\omega C) = 50\,\Omega\)): $\(\mathbf{Z} = R + j(X_L - X_C) = 50 + j(80 - 50) = 50 + 30i\,\Omega\)$

Keystrokes: 50 [ENTER] 80 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 50 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 30

In a series RLC branch, inductive reactance \(+j\omega L\) (where voltage leads current by \(90^\circ\)) and capacitive reactance \(-j/(\omega C)\) (where voltage lags current by \(90^\circ\)) directly oppose one another along the imaginary axis. Load the RL branch \(\mathbf{Z}_1 = 50 + 80i\) with 50 [ENTER] 80 [ENTER], then key the capacitor \(\mathbf{Z}_2 = 0 - 50i\) with 0 [ENTER] 50 [+/-], priming the 4-level stack to \((T: 50, Z: 80, Y: 0, X: -50)\). Tap [↰] [CMPLX] [+] to execute dyadic phasor addition, leaving \((T: 50, Z: 50, Y: 50.0000, X: 30.0000)\), confirming net inductive impedance \(50.0 + 30.0i\,\Omega\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.4: RLC Circuit Current Phasor via Ohm's Law
docs.text:
The circuit from Workbook Problem 5.3 (\(\mathbf{Z} = 50 + 30i\,\Omega\)) is driven by voltage \(\mathbf{V} = 120 + 0i\text{ V}\). Find current phasor \(\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{V} / \mathbf{Z}\): $\(\mathbf{I} = \frac{120}{50 + 30i} = \frac{120(50 - 30i)}{2500 + 900} = \frac{6000 - 3600i}{3400} = 1.7647 - 1.0588i\text{ A}\)$

Keystrokes: 120 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 50 [ENTER] 30 [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) -1.0588235294

If you are continuing directly from Workbook Problem 5.3 with \(\mathbf{Z} = 50 + 30i\) already sitting in \((Y, X)\), you can invert and scale without re-entering \(\mathbf{Z}\): key [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x] 120 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [×]! Or starting fresh, enter numerator \(\mathbf{V}\) via 120 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] followed by denominator \(\mathbf{Z}\) via 50 [ENTER] 30, giving \((T: 120, Z: 0, Y: 50, X: 30)\). Press [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] to evaluate complex Ohm's law, yielding lagging current phasor \((T: 120, Z: 120, Y: 1.764706, X: -1.058824)\), confirming \(1.7647 - 1.0588i\text{ Amperes}\) (\(|\mathbf{I}| = 2.058\text{ A}\angle -30.96^\circ\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.5: AC Apparent, Real, and Reactive Power Complex Vector
docs.text:
Complex apparent power is \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{I}^*\). For \(\mathbf{V} = 120 + 0i\text{ V}\) and \(\mathbf{I} = 1.7647 - 1.0588i\text{ A} \implies \mathbf{I}^* = 1.7647 + 1.0588i\text{ A}\): $\(\mathbf{S} = 120 \times (1.7647 + 1.0588i) = 211.7647 + 127.0560i\text{ VA}\)$ Real power \(P = 211.76\text{ Watts}\), Reactive power \(Q = 127.06\text{ VAR}\).

Keystrokes: 120 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 1.764706 [ENTER] 1.058824 [↰] [CMPLX] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 127.05888

Why does AC power engineering define complex power as \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}^*\) rather than \(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{I}\)? Conjugating the current phasor ensures that the phase difference \(\theta_v - \theta_i\) is time-invariant, making \(+Q = |\mathbf{V}||\mathbf{I}|\sin(\theta_v - \theta_i) > 0\) positive for lagging inductive loads. Continuing directly from Workbook Problem 5.4 where \(\mathbf{I}\) sits in \((Y, X)\), simply press [+/-] to conjugate \(\mathbf{I} \to \mathbf{I}^*\) in place and multiply by \(\mathbf{V}\)! From scratch, enter voltage \(\mathbf{V}\) via 120 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] and conjugate current \(\mathbf{I}^*\) via 1.764706 [ENTER] 1.058824, loading \((T: 120, Z: 0, Y: 1.764706, X: 1.058824)\). Press [↰] [CMPLX] [×] to evaluate \(\mathbf{S} = P + jQ\), resulting in \((T: 120, Z: 120, Y: 211.7647, X: 127.0589)\), confirming \(P = 211.76\text{ W}, Q = 127.06\text{ VAR}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.6: Power Factor from Complex Apparent Power
docs.text:
For complex power \(\mathbf{S} = 211.7647 + 127.0589i\text{ VA}\) (in radian mode), compute magnitude \(|\mathbf{S}|\) and power factor \(\cos\theta\):

\[|\mathbf{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} \approx 247.0\text{ VA}, \quad \text{PF} = \frac{P}{|\mathbf{S}|} = \frac{211.7647}{247.0588} \approx 0.8572\]

Keystrokes: 211.7647 [ENTER] 127.0589 [x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r] [x⇄y] [COS] \(\rightarrow\) 0.8571673007

Bridging [↰] [CMPLX] rectangular registers \((Y: \text{Real}, X: \text{Imag})\) to the 2D polar converter [↰] [▸θ,r] \((Y: y, X: x)\) requires a single [x⇄y] swap before pressing [↰] [▸θ,r]. Key 211.7647 [ENTER] 127.0589 into \((Y, X)\) (or continue directly from Workbook Problem 5.5's stack!), swap to Euclidean \((Y=Q, X=P)\), and convert to polar form via [x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0.540420, X: 247.0588)\), revealing phase angle \(\theta = 0.5404\text{ rad}\) in \(Y\) and apparent power \(|\mathbf{S}| = 247.06\text{ VA}\) in \(X\). Tap [x⇄y] [COS] to extract the lagging power factor, ending with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 247.0588, X: 0.857167)\), confirming \(\text{PF} = 0.8572\text{ (lagging)}\) with \(|\mathbf{S}|\) preserved in Register \(Y\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.7: Second Root of Unity from de Moivre
docs.text:
From Textbook Showcase Problem 5.5, the real root is \(z_1 = -2.0 + 0.0i\), and the third root is \(z_2 = 1.0 - 1.732051i\). Confirm \(z_1^3\): Keystrokes: 2 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 3 [ENTER] 0 [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ]\(\implies\) \(-8.0000 + 0.0000i\).

By de Moivre's theorem, the three cube roots of \(-8\) sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle \(|z| = 2\) at angles \(\theta_k = \frac{\pi + 2\pi k}{3} \in \{60^\circ, 180^\circ, 300^\circ\}\). Enter the real root \(z_1 = 2 e^{i\pi} = -2.0 + 0.0i\) into \((T, Z)\) and the power \(3.0 + 0.0i\) into \((Y, X)\) via 2 [+/-] [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 3 [ENTER] 0, creating \((T: -2, Z: 0, Y: 3, X: 0)\). Executing [↰] [CMPLX] [yˣ] confirms \((-2+0i)^3 = -8.0 + 0.0i\), leaving \((T: -2, Z: -2, Y: -8.0000, X: 0.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.8: Smith Chart Bilinear Transformation
docs.text:
Compute normalized load \(z = r + jx\) from reflection coefficient \(\Gamma = 0.2 + 0.4i\):

\[z = \frac{1 + \Gamma}{1 - \Gamma} = \frac{1 + 0.2 + 0.4i}{1 - 0.2 - 0.4i} = \frac{1.2 + 0.4i}{0.8 - 0.4i}\]

Keystrokes: 1.2 [ENTER] 0.4 [ENTER] 0.8 [ENTER] 0.4 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1

Phillip H. Smith's 1939 transmission-line chart is a conformal Möbius transformation \(z = (1+\Gamma)/(1-\Gamma)\) that maps the right-half impedance plane \(\text{Re}(z) \ge 0\) onto the interior of the unit reflection disk \(|\Gamma| \le 1\), turning circles of constant resistance and reactance into orthogonal families of circles. Load numerator \(1 + \Gamma = 1.2 + 0.4i\) via 1.2 [ENTER] 0.4 [ENTER] and denominator \(1 - \Gamma = 0.8 - 0.4i\) via 0.8 [ENTER] 0.4 [+/-], loading \((T: 1.2, Z: 0.4, Y: 0.8, X: -0.4)\). Striking [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] evaluates the inverse bilinear mapping to \(z = 1.0 + 1.0i\), with the stack resting at \((T: 1.2, Z: 1.2, Y: 1.000000, X: 1.000000)\) (a matched real resistance \(R = Z_0\) in series with inductive reactance \(X = +Z_0\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.9: Acoustic Wave Impedance at Boundary
docs.text:
Characteristic impedance of air \(Z_1 = 415\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s/m}\), porous fiberglass absorber \(Z_2 = 600 - 450i\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s/m}\). Find acoustic reflection coefficient: $\(\Gamma_a = \frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1} = \frac{(600 - 415) - 450i}{(600 + 415) - 450i} = \frac{185 - 450i}{1015 - 450i}\)$

Keystrokes: 185 [ENTER] 450 [+/-] [ENTER] 1015 [ENTER] 450 [+/-] [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) -0.302987

Plane sound waves striking an architectural fiberglass treatment obey the exact same Fresnel reflection equation \(\Gamma_a = (Z_2 - Z_1)/(Z_2 + Z_1)\) as electromagnetic waves on a transmission line, where the porous absorber's compliance introduces a negative (capacitive) acoustic reactance \(-450i\text{ Rayls}\). Key numerator differential impedance \((Z_2 - Z_1) = 185 - 450i\) with 185 [ENTER] 450 [+/-] [ENTER] and denominator \((Z_2 + Z_1) = 1015 - 450i\) with 1015 [ENTER] 450 [+/-], yielding \((T: 185, Z: -450, Y: 1015, X: -450)\). Press [↰] [CMPLX] [÷] to resolve the complex pressure reflection coefficient \((T: 185, Z: 185, Y: 0.316595, X: -0.302987)\)—and keying [x⇄y] [↰] [▸θ,r] [↰] [x²] 1 [x⇄y] [-] immediately computes the Sabine normal-incidence sound absorption coefficient \(\alpha = 1 - |\Gamma_a|^2 = \mathbf{0.8080}\) (\(80.8\%\) of acoustic energy absorbed!).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.10: Mutual Inductive Coupling in Transformer
docs.text:
Primary inductance \(L_1 = 50\,\mu\text{H}\), secondary \(L_2 = 20\,\mu\text{H}\), coupling factor \(k = 0.8\). Mutual inductance \(M = k\sqrt{L_1 L_2}\):

$\(M = 0.8 \sqrt{50 \times 20} = 0.8 \sqrt{1000} \approx 25.2982\,\mu\text{H}\)$ Keystrokes: 50 [ENTER] 20 [×] [√x] 0.8 [×]\(\implies\) \(25.2982\,\mu\text{H}\).

In coupled-coil RF transformers, magnetic flux leakage limits the mutual inductance \(M\) to the fraction \(k \in [0, 1]\) of the geometric mean \(\sqrt{L_1 L_2}\), introducing a mutual transfer impedance \(Z_m = j\omega M\) between primary and secondary mesh equations. Enter 50 [ENTER] 20 [×] to form the inductive product \(1000\,\mu\text{H}^2\) in \(X\) \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1000)\), take the geometric mean with [√x] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 31.6228)\), and scale by coupling coefficient with 0.8 [×], resolving \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 25.2982)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.11: Waveguide Attenuation and Propagation Constant (\(\gamma\))
docs.text:
Propagation constant \(\gamma = \alpha + j\beta\). In cutoff band: \(\alpha = 14.5\text{ Np/m}, \beta = 0\text{ rad/m}\). Attenuation in decibels per meter:

\[\text{Atten} = 20 \log_{10}(e) \times \alpha = 8.68589 \times 14.5 = \mathbf{125.945\text{ dB/m}}\]

Below a rectangular waveguide's cutoff frequency \(f_c\), the propagation constant \(\gamma = \sqrt{k_c^2 - k^2} = \alpha + j0\) becomes purely real: rather than propagating as a traveling wave, the field decays evanescently as \(e^{-\alpha z}\) at \(20\log_{10}(e) \approx 8.68589\text{ dB}\) per Neper (the basis of waveguide-below-cutoff precision attenuators). Key 1 [eˣ] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] to generate the exact Nepers-to-dB constant (\(8.685890\text{ dB/Np}\)) on the stack \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8.685890)\), then multiply by \(\alpha = 14.5\text{ Np/m}\) with 14.5 [×], resolving total attenuation \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 125.945405)\), confirming \(125.945\text{ dB/m}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.12: Complex Impedance of Parallel RLC Tank at Resonance
docs.text:
Tank circuit with \(R = 10\text{ k}\Omega, L = 10\,\mu\text{H}, C = 100\text{ pF}\). Resonant frequency \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC} = 31.6228\text{ Mrad/s}\). At resonance, reactive admittances cancel (\(j\omega C + 1/(j\omega L) = 0\)), leaving pure resistance: $\(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{tank}} = R = 10,000.0 + 0.0i\,\Omega\)$

In a parallel RLC bandpass resonator at \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\), energy sloshes losslessly between the magnetic field of the inductor and the electric field of the capacitor with equal and opposite susceptances (\(\pm j\sqrt{C/L} = \pm j\,3.1623\text{ mS}\)), so the parallel tank presents a maximum, purely resistive impedance \(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{tank}} = R\) to the driving RF stage. Evaluate the reactive product with 10 [E] 6 [+/-] [ENTER] 100 [E] 12 [+/-] [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1.0 \times 10^{-15})\), extract the resonant angular frequency with [√x] [1/x] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 3.1623 \times 10^7)\), then load the resonant tank impedance 10000 [ENTER] 0 across \((Y, X)\), confirming purely resistive impedance \((T: 0, Z: 3.1623 \times 10^7, Y: 10000.0000, X: 0.0000)\) of \(10,000.0 + 0.0i\,\Omega\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.13: Complex Root Extraction via de Moivre (\(z^4 = -16\))
docs.text:
Roots of \(z^4 = -16 = 16 e^{i\pi}\): \(r = 16^{1/4} = 2.0\). First root \(\theta = \pi/4 = 45^\circ\):

$\(z_0 = 2(\cos 45^\circ + i\sin 45^\circ) = \sqrt{2} + i\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414214 + 1.414214i\)$ Keystrokes: 45 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [▸y,x]\(\implies\) \(1.414214\) in \(X\) and \(Y\).

The four fourth roots of \(-16\) form the \(45^\circ\)-rotated square vertices \(2 e^{i(\pi/4 + k\pi/2)}\)—the exact pole pattern of a 2nd-order Butterworth filter! Key the polar angle and radial modulus 45 [ENTER] 2 into \((Y, X)\) \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 45, X: 2)\), then convert from polar to rectangular via [↱] [▸y,x], extracting principal root \(z_0 = 1.414214 + 1.414214i\) across \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 1.414214, X: 1.414214)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.14: Skin Effect in Solid Copper Conductor
docs.text:
Skin depth \(\delta = \sqrt{2/(\omega \mu \sigma)}\). For copper (\(\sigma = 5.8 \times 10^7\text{ S/m}\)) at \(f = 10\text{ MHz}\) (\(\omega = 6.283185 \times 10^7\text{ rad/s}\)): $\(\delta = \sqrt{\frac{2}{6.283185\cdot 10^7 \times 4\pi\cdot 10^{-7} \times 5.8\cdot 10^7}} \approx 2.089 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m} = \mathbf{20.89\,\mu\text{m}}\)$

At radio frequencies, alternating magnetic flux inside a conductor induces eddy currents that oppose current flow in the core and crowd the current density \(J(r) = J_0 e^{-(1+j)d/\delta}\) into a thin surface annulus of thickness \(\delta\). Form free-space permeability \(\mu_0\) with 4 [↱] [π] [×] 1 [E] 7 [+/-] [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1.2566 \times 10^{-6})\), multiply by angular frequency and conductivity 6.283185 [E] 7 [×] 5.8 [E] 7 [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4.5795 \times 10^9)\), invert into ratio \(2/(\omega\mu\sigma)\) with 2 [x⇄y] [÷] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4.3639 \times 10^{-10})\), and take the square root [√x], arriving at skin depth \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 2.0890 \times 10^{-5})\), confirming \(\delta = 20.89\,\mu\text{m}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.15: Dispersion Relation in Fiber Optics (Group Velocity Dispersion)
docs.text:
Complex propagation constant \(\beta(\omega) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\omega - \omega_0) + \frac{1}{2}\beta_2(\omega - \omega_0)^2\). Pulse dispersion parameter \(D = -2\pi c \beta_2 / \lambda^2\). For \(\beta_2 = -20\text{ ps}^2/\text{km}\) at \(\lambda = 1.55\,\mu\text{m}\): $\(D = \frac{-2\pi(3\cdot 10^8)(-20\cdot 10^{-27})}{(1.55\cdot 10^{-6})^2} \approx \mathbf{15.68\text{ ps/(nm}\cdot\text{km)}}\)$

In single-mode silica telecom fiber operating in the \(1550\text{ nm}\) C-band, negative group-velocity dispersion (\(\beta_2 = -20\text{ ps}^2/\text{km}\), the anomalous dispersion regime where optical solitons form) causes shorter-wavelength blue spectral components to travel faster than red components by \(D \approx 15.68\text{ ps}\) per nanometer of spectral width per kilometer. Compute numerator \(2\pi c |\beta_2|\) with 2 [↱] [π] [×] 3 [E] 8 [×] 20 [E] 27 [+/-] [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 3.7699 \times 10^{-17})\), square wavelength with 1.55 [E] 6 [+/-] [↰] [x²] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 3.7699 \times 10^{-17}, X: 2.4025 \times 10^{-12})\), and divide and scale via [÷] 1 [E] 6 [×], arriving at dispersion parameter \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 15.6841)\), confirming \(15.68\text{ ps/(nm}\cdot\text{km)}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.16: Fractional Pole Filter: \(s^{0.5}\) Fractional Calculus Impedance
docs.text:
Warburg impedance in electrochemistry: \(\mathbf{Z}_W = \frac{A_W}{\sqrt{\omega}} (1 - j)\). For \(A_W = 200\,\Omega\cdot\text{s}^{-1/2}\) at \(\omega = 100\text{ rad/s}\): $\(\mathbf{Z}_W = \frac{200}{10} (1 - j) = \mathbf{20.0000 - 20.0000i\,\Omega}\)$

In electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of lithium-ion battery electrodes, semi-infinite Fickian ion diffusion obeys a half-order fractional differential equation whose Laplace transform \((j\omega)^{-1/2} = \frac{1-j}{\sqrt{2\omega}}\) produces a constant \(-45^\circ\) phase line on a Nyquist plot (the Warburg element). Evaluate \(\sqrt{\omega}\) with 100 [√x] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 10)\), compute scale factor \(A_W/\sqrt{\omega} = 20\,\Omega\) with 200 [x⇄y] [÷] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20)\), and duplicate and negate ([ENTER] [+/-] or 20 [ENTER] 20 [+/-]), confirming Warburg impedance \((T: 20.0000, Z: -20.0000, Y: 20.0000, X: -20.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.17: Complex Poynting Vector & Electromagnetic Radiation Density
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{S}_{\text{cpx}} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}^*\). For \(\mathbf{E} = 10.0 + 5.0i\text{ V/m}\) and \(\mathbf{H} = 0.02 + 0.01i\text{ A/m}\): $\(\mathbf{H}^* = 0.02 - 0.01i \implies \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{H}^* = (10+5i)(0.02-0.01i) = (0.2 + 0.05) + (-0.1 + 0.1)i = 0.25 + 0i\)$ Average radiated power: \(\text{Re}(\mathbf{S}_{\text{cpx}}) = 0.5 \times 0.25 = \mathbf{0.125\text{ W/m}^2}\).

The complex Poynting theorem separates electromagnetic energy flux into time-averaged radiated power density \(\text{Re}(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}^*)\) and reactive near-field stored energy density \(\text{Im}(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H}^*)\). Because \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{H}\) here share the exact same phase angle \(\arctan(0.5) = 26.57^\circ\) (with wave impedance \(E/H = 500\,\Omega\)), their cross-product \(\mathbf{E}\mathbf{H}^*\) is purely real! Load electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) via 10 [ENTER] 5 [ENTER] and conjugate magnetic field \(\mathbf{H}^*\) via 0.02 [ENTER] 0.01 [+/-], placing \((T: 10, Z: 5, Y: 0.02, X: -0.01)\). Execute [↰] [CMPLX] [×] to obtain \(0.25 + 0i\) \((T: 10, Z: 10, Y: 0.25, X: 0)\), swap the real part into Register \(X\), and divide by 2 with [x⇄y] 2 [÷], giving average radiation density \((T: 10, Z: 10, Y: 0, X: 0.1250)\), confirming \(0.125\text{ W/m}^2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.18: Sagnac Ring Interferometer Phase Shift
docs.text:
Fiber optic gyroscope: \(\Delta\Phi = \frac{8\pi A N}{c \lambda} \Omega\). For coil area \(A = 0.01\text{ m}^2\), \(N = 1000\text{ turns}\), \(\lambda = 1.31\,\mu\text{m}\), rotation rate \(\Omega = 1.0\text{ rad/s}\): $\(\Delta\Phi = \frac{8\pi(0.01)(1000)}{(3\cdot 10^8)(1.31\cdot 10^{-6})} \approx \mathbf{0.6395\text{ radians}}\)$

In Georges Sagnac's relativistic ring interferometer, counter-propagating laser beams traversing a rotating fiber coil of total enclosed area \(N A = 10\text{ m}^2\) experience a non-reciprocal transit-time difference \(\Delta t = 4AN\Omega/c^2\), shifting their interference phasor \(e^{i\Delta\Phi}\) by \(\Delta\Phi = \frac{8\pi AN}{c\lambda}\Omega\). Form the optical area-turns product with 8 [↱] [π] [×] 0.01 [×] 1000 [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 251.3274)\), compute \(c\lambda\) with 3 [E] 8 [ENTER] 1.31 [E] 6 [+/-] [×] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 251.3274, X: 393.0000)\), and divide with [÷], resolving Sagnac phase shift \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.6395)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.19: Transformer T-Model Core Loss Branch
docs.text:
Parallel magnetizing branch: \(R_c = 50\text{ k}\Omega \parallel X_m = 15\text{ k}\Omega\). Total complex excitation admittance:

$\(\mathbf{Y}_m = \frac{1}{50000} - j\frac{1}{15000} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} - 6.6667 \times 10^{-5}i\,\text{S}\)$ Impedance: \(\mathbf{Z}_m = 1/\mathbf{Y}_m = \mathbf{4,128.44 + 13,761.47i\,\Omega}\).

In a power transformer's Steinmetz equivalent circuit, eddy-current/hysteresis core loss is modeled by shunt resistance \(R_c = 50\text{ k}\Omega\) in parallel with magnetizing reactance \(+j X_m = +j\,15\text{ k}\Omega\). Converting this parallel excitation branch into its equivalent series impedance \(\mathbf{Z}_m = R_s + j X_s\) is effortless on the stack: key core conductance 50000 [1/x] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 2.0 \times 10^{-5})\) and inductive susceptance 15000 [1/x] [+/-] \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 2.0 \times 10^{-5}, X: -6.6667 \times 10^{-5})\), then take the complex reciprocal with [↰] [CMPLX] [1/x], arriving at equivalent branch impedance \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 4128.4404, X: 13761.4679)\), confirming \(4,128.44 + 13,761.47i\,\Omega\) (or use 50000 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 0 [ENTER] 15000 [↰] [CMPLX] [x∥y] directly!).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 5.20: Elliptical Polarization Axial Ratio from Orthogonal E-Phasors

\[\text{AR} = \frac{10.0}{6.0} = 1.6667 \implies \text{AR}_{\text{dB}} = 20 \log_{10}(1.6667) = \mathbf{4.4370\text{ dB}}\]

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.1: Elliptical Pressure Vessel Manway Area & Perimeter
docs.text:
A vessel inspection hatch is elliptical with semimajor axis \(a = 250.0\text{ mm}\) and semiminor axis \(b = 150.0\text{ mm}\). 1. Area \(A = \pi a b = \pi \times 250 \times 150 = 37,500\pi \approx \mathbf{117,809.72\text{ mm}^2}\) 2. Ramanujan's approximate perimeter \(P \approx \pi [3(a+b) - \sqrt{(3a+b)(a+3b)}]\): \(h = \frac{(a-b)^2}{(a+b)^2} = \frac{100^2}{400^2} = 0.0625 \implies P \approx \pi(a+b)(1 + \frac{3h}{10 + \sqrt{4 - 3h}}) \approx \mathbf{1,276.26\text{ mm}}\)

Keystrokes (Area): 250 [ENTER] 150 [×] [↱] [π] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 117,809.7245

Boiler inspection manways are made elliptical so the cover plate can be rotated \(90^\circ\), slipped edgewise through its own opening, and seated against the inside rim so internal boiler pressure seals the gasket automatically! While the area \(A = \pi ab\) is an exact affine scaling of a circle, the perimeter requires a complete elliptic integral of the second kind (approximated to \(10^{-9}\) accuracy by Srinivasa Ramanujan's rational \(h\)-formula). Push semimajor axis \(a = 250\) via 250 [ENTER], multiply by semiminor axis \(b = 150\) via 150 [×] to obtain planar product \(37,500.0\), and apply [↱] [π] [×] to resolve exact manway opening area at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 117809.7245)\), confirming \(117,809.72\text{ mm}^2\) (\(1,178.10\text{ cm}^2\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.2: Torus Volume and Surface Area (Hydraulic O-Ring)
docs.text:
An elastomer O-ring has major mean radius \(R = 45.0\text{ mm}\) and cross-sectional circular radius \(r = 3.5\text{ mm}\). 1. Volume \(V = 2\pi^2 R r^2 = 2 \pi^2 (45) (3.5^2) = 2 \pi^2 (45) (12.25) \approx \mathbf{10,880.89\text{ mm}^3}\) 2. Surface Area \(A = 4\pi^2 R r = 4 \pi^2 (45) (3.5) \approx \mathbf{6,217.85\text{ mm}^2}\)

Keystrokes (Volume): [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 2 [×] 45 [×] 3.5 [↰] [x²] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 10,881.23885

By Pappus's centroid theorems, sweeping a circle of area \(\pi r^2\) and circumference \(2\pi r\) along a circular centerline of length \(2\pi R\) generates volume \(V = (\pi r^2)(2\pi R) = 2\pi^2 R r^2\) and surface area \(A = (2\pi r)(2\pi R) = 4\pi^2 R r\)—exactly the same as an unwrapped cylinder of length \(2\pi R\)! Evaluate \(2\pi^2\) via [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 2 [×], scale by major centerline radius \(R = 45\text{ mm}\) via 45 [×], and multiply by cross-sectional radius squared \(r^2 = 3.5^2\) via 3.5 [↰] [x²] [×], establishing torus body volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 10880.8872)\).

Keystrokes (Surface Area): [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 4 [×] 45 [×] 3.5 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 6217.6500

Notice that \(A / V = 2 / r\): if you already have \(V = 10,880.89\text{ mm}^3\) in Register \(X\), keying 2 [×] 3.5 [÷] yields \(A = 6,217.85\text{ mm}^2\) in three keystrokes! Or from scratch, compute the \(4\pi^2\) envelope constant via [↱] [π] [↰] [x²] 4 [×], then chain major and minor radii via 45 [×] 3.5 [×] to yield total contact surface area at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 6217.8508)\), confirming \(V = 10,880.89\text{ mm}^3\), \(A = 6,217.85\text{ mm}^2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.3: Truncated Pyramidal Monument Volume
docs.text:
A stone pedestal is a truncated square pyramid: lower base side \(a = 3.20\text{ m}\), upper base side \(b = 1.80\text{ m}\), height \(h = 4.50\text{ m}\). Base areas: \(A_1 = 3.2^2 = 10.24\text{ m}^2\), \(A_2 = 1.8^2 = 3.24\text{ m}^2\): $\(V = \frac{h}{3} (A_1 + A_2 + \sqrt{A_1 A_2}) = \frac{4.5}{3} (10.24 + 3.24 + \sqrt{33.1776}) = 1.5 \times (13.48 + 5.76) = 1.5 \times 19.24 = \mathbf{28.86\text{ m}^3}\)$

Keystrokes: 3.2 [↰] [x²] [STO] 1 1.8 [↰] [x²] [STO] 2 [+] [RCL] 1 [RCL] 2 [×] [√x] [+] 4.5 [×] 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 28.86

Recorded in the 1850 BCE Egyptian Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (Problem 14), the truncated square pyramid formula \(V = \frac{h}{3}(a^2 + ab + b^2) = \frac{h}{3}(A_1 + A_2 + \sqrt{A_1 A_2})\) is one of the oldest jewels of solid geometry. Store lower base \(A_1 = 10.24\) into Register 1 via 3.2 [↰] [x²] [STO] 1, and upper base \(A_2 = 3.24\) into Register 2 via 1.8 [↰] [x²] [STO] 2. Add them via [+] for sum \(13.48\). Compute geometric mean \(\sqrt{A_1 A_2} = 5.76\) via [RCL] 1 [RCL] 2 [×] [√x], sum with base areas via [+], and multiply by \(h/3\) via 4.5 [×] 3 [÷], yielding pedestal volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 28.8600)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.4: Regular Icosahedron Dice Volume and Area
docs.text:
A 20-sided gaming die has edge length \(a = 18.0\text{ mm}\). 1. Surface Area \(A = 5\sqrt{3} a^2 = 5 \sqrt{3} (18^2) = 5\sqrt{3}(324) \approx \mathbf{2,805.9223\text{ mm}^2}\) 2. Volume \(V = \frac{5(3 + \sqrt{5})}{12} a^3 = \frac{5(5.236068)}{12} (5832) \approx \mathbf{12,723.65\text{ mm}^3}\)

Keystrokes (Volume): 5 [√x] 3 [+] 5 [×] 12 [÷] 18 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 12,723.64519

The vertices of a regular icosahedron lie on three mutually orthogonal golden rectangles of aspect ratio \(\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2\), so its volume constant \(\frac{5(3+\sqrt{5})}{12} = \frac{5\varphi^2}{6}\) is governed directly by the square of the golden ratio! Evaluate icosahedral volume factor \(\frac{5(3+\sqrt{5})}{12} \approx 2.181695\) via 5 [√x] 3 [+] 5 [×] 12 [÷]. Cube die edge \(a = 18\text{ mm}\) via 18 [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] and multiply via [×], arriving at total polyhedron volume at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 12723.6452)\), confirming \(V = 12,723.65\text{ mm}^3\), \(A = 2,805.92\text{ mm}^2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 6.5: Regular Dodecahedron Volume
docs.text:
12-sided solid with edge \(a = 12.0\text{ mm}\):

\[V = \frac{15 + 7\sqrt{5}}{4} a^3 \approx \frac{15 + 15.652476}{4} (1728) = 7.663119 \times 1728 = \mathbf{13,241.87\text{ mm}^3}\]
