docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.1: Torricelli Efflux Tank Draining Velocity
docs.text:
A cylindrical fluid storage tank maintains an open liquid column height \(h = 5.0\text{ meters}\). Standard acceleration of gravity \(g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2\). Determine the efflux velocity \(v\): $\(v = \sqrt{2 g h} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.80665 \times 5.0} = \sqrt{98.0665} \approx \mathbf{9.90285\text{ m/s}}\)$

Keystrokes: 2 [ENTER] 9.80665 [×] 5 [×] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 9.9028531242.

Evangelista Torricelli's 1643 efflux theorem—a direct specialization of Daniel Bernoulli's streamline energy balance \(\rho g h = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2\)—states that liquid jets exit a bottom orifice at the free-fall speed acquired across head height \(h\): evaluating 2 [ENTER] 9.80665 [×] 5 [×] (\(2gh = 98.0665\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 98.0665)\)) and extracting the square root via [√x] determines the discharge velocity \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{9.9029}\text{ m/s})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.2: Darcy-Weisbach Friction Head Loss in Piping
docs.text:
Water at \(20^\circ\text{C}\) flows at velocity \(v = 2.40\text{ m/s}\) through a commercial steel pipe with length \(L = 85.0\text{ m}\) and inner diameter \(D = 0.15\text{ m}\). Darcy friction factor \(f = 0.0192\): $\(h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2g} = 0.0192 \times \frac{85.0}{0.15} \times \frac{2.40^2}{2 \times 9.80665} \approx \mathbf{3.1952\text{ meters}}\)$

In Julius Weisbach and Henry Darcy's pipe-friction formulation, viscous boundary-layer shear dissipates mechanical energy in proportion to the dimensionless resistance coefficient \(f(L/D)\) times the velocity head \(v^2/(2g)\): evaluating .0192 [ENTER] 85 [×] .15 [÷] (\(f L/D = 10.8800\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 10.8800)\)) and chaining 2.4 [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷] 9.80665 [÷] resolves the viscous head loss \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{3.1952}\text{ m})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.3: Infill Grid Volume Integration & Spool Consumption
docs.text:
A rectangular drone chassis housing has outer bounding box dimensions \(140\text{ mm} \times 90\text{ mm} \times 35\text{ mm}\). The part is sliced with 3 solid perimeter walls (\(2.0\text{ mm}\) thick) consuming \(85,000\text{ mm}^3\), while the internal cavity (\(355,000\text{ mm}^3\)) is filled with a \(25\%\) gyroid infill density (\(\rho_{\text{infill}} = 0.25\)). Technical polymer density is \(\rho = 1.25\text{ g/cm}^3\) (\(0.00125\text{ g/mm}^3\)): $\(V_{\text{total}} = V_{\text{walls}} + \rho_{\text{infill}} \times V_{\text{cavity}} = 85,000 + (0.25 \times 355,000) = 85,000 + 88,750 = \mathbf{173,750\text{ mm}^3}\)$ $\(M_{\text{part}} = V_{\text{total}} \times \rho = 173,750 \times 0.00125 \approx \mathbf{217.19\text{ grams}}\)$

Triply periodic minimal surfaces such as Alan Schoen's gyroid partition internal core cavities into isotropic structural lattices at a fraction of solid mass: weighting the cavity volume by the infill fraction and adding the solid shell (355000 [ENTER] .25 [×] 85000 [+] \(\rightarrow V_{\text{total}} = 173,750\text{ mm}^3\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 173750.0)\)) before scaling by .00125 [×] determines the exact spool mass budget \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{217.1875}\text{ g})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.4: Ideal Brayton Gas Turbine Cycle Thermal Efficiency
docs.text:
An industrial gas turbine operates on the ideal Brayton cycle with compressor pressure ratio \(r_p = 14.5\) and air specific heat ratio \(\gamma = 1.40\):

\[\eta_{\text{Brayton}} = 1 - \frac{1}{r_p^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}} = 1 - \frac{1}{(14.5)^{(0.40/1.40)}} \approx \mathbf{53.41\%}\]

In George Brayton's open gas-turbine cycle, isentropic compression across pressure ratio \(r_p\) raises absolute air temperature by the Poisson factor \(T_2/T_1 = r_p^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\): evaluating 14.5 [ENTER] .40 [ENTER] 1.40 [÷] [yˣ] (\(2.1465\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.1465)\)) and chaining [1/x] 1 [x⇄y] [-] determines the ideal Brayton thermal efficiency \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.5341}\), or \(53.41\%)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.5: Composite Wall Conduction Heat Flux
docs.text:
A furnace wall consists of \(L_1 = 0.15\text{ m}\) firebrick (\(k_1 = 1.2\text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}\)) and \(L_2 = 0.05\text{ m}\) insulating mineral wool (\(k_2 = 0.04\text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}\)). Inner temperature \(T_{\text{in}} = 850^\circ\text{C}\), outer temperature \(T_{\text{out}} = 50^\circ\text{C}\): $\(R_{\text{total}} = \frac{L_1}{k_1} + \frac{L_2}{k_2} = \frac{0.15}{1.2} + \frac{0.05}{0.04} = 0.125 + 1.250 = \mathbf{1.375\text{ m}^2\text{K/W}}\)$ $\(q'' = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{850 - 50}{1.375} = \frac{800}{1.375} \approx \mathbf{581.82\text{ W/m}^2}\)$

By Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier's law of heat conduction across series planar layers, thermal resistances \(R_i = L_i/k_i\) add directly like series electrical resistors: summing the firebrick and mineral-wool resistances via .15 [ENTER] 1.2 [÷] .05 [ENTER] .04 [÷] [+] (\(R_{\text{total}} = 1.3750\text{ m}^2\text{K/W}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.3750)\)) and dividing into the overall thermal drop 850 [ENTER] 50 [-] [x⇄y] [÷] determines the steady-state heat flux \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{581.8182}\text{ W/m}^2)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.6: Rankine Steam Power Cycle Thermal Efficiency
docs.text:
In a subcritical Rankine steam cycle, high-pressure steam enters the turbine at enthalpy \(h_1 = 3,450.0\text{ kJ/kg}\) and expands to condenser pressure with enthalpy \(h_2 = 2,180.0\text{ kJ/kg}\). The feedwater pump consumes work \(w_p = 15.0\text{ kJ/kg}\) to pressurize liquid from \(h_3 = 190.0\text{ kJ/kg}\) to boiler inlet state \(h_4 = 205.0\text{ kJ/kg}\). 1. Net turbine work output: $\(w_{\text{net}} = (h_1 - h_2) - w_p = (3450.0 - 2180.0) - 15.0 = 1270.0 - 15.0 = \mathbf{1,255.0\text{ kJ/kg}}\)$ 2. Heat input supplied by the boiler: $\(q_{\text{in}} = h_1 - h_4 = 3450.0 - 205.0 = \mathbf{3,245.0\text{ kJ/kg}}\)$ 3. Thermal efficiency: $\(\eta_{\text{Rankine}} = \frac{w_{\text{net}}}{q_{\text{in}}} = \frac{1255.0}{3245.0} \approx \mathbf{38.67\%}\)$

Evaluating net shaft work 3450 [ENTER] 2180 [-] 15 [-] (\(w_{\text{net}} = 1,255.0\text{ kJ/kg}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1255.0000)\)), computing boiler enthalpy addition 3450 [ENTER] 205 [-] (\(q_{\text{in}} = 3,245.0\text{ kJ/kg}\) in \(X\) while \(w_{\text{net}}\) waits in \(Y\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 1255.0000, X: 3245.0000)\)), and dividing via [÷] 100 [×] resolves the Rankine cycle efficiency \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{38.6749}\%)\)—or by duplicating throttle enthalpy \(h_1 = 3450\) upfront (3450 [ENTER] [ENTER] 2180 [-] 15 [-] [x⇄y] 205 [-] [÷] 100 [×]), 3450 is entered only once!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.7: Otto Cycle Internal Combustion Efficiency vs. Compression Ratio
docs.text:
The theoretical thermal efficiency of an internal combustion Otto cycle engine depends solely on compression ratio \(r = V_{\max} / V_{\min}\) and air specific heat ratio \(\gamma = 1.40\): $\(\eta_{\text{Otto}} = 1 - \frac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}}\)$ For a high-performance racing engine with compression ratio \(r = 11.5\): $\(\eta_{\text{Otto}} = 1 - \frac{1}{11.5^{0.40}} = 1 - \frac{1}{2.65839} = 1 - 0.376167 = \mathbf{62.35\%}\)$

In Nikolaus Otto's four-stroke spark-ignition cycle, isentropic compression across volume ratio \(r = 11.5\) elevates the cycle temperature ratio to \(r^{\gamma-1}\): keying 11.5 [ENTER] .40 [yˣ] (\(11.5^{0.40} \approx 2.6563\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.6563)\)) and chaining [1/x] 1 [x⇄y] [-] determines the air-standard Otto efficiency \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.6235}\), or \(62.35\%)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.8: 2nd-Order Butterworth Crossover Filters
docs.text:
Crossover frequency \(f_c = 2500\text{ Hz}\), driver nominal impedance \(R = 8.0\,\Omega\):

\[L = \frac{R \sqrt{2}}{2\pi f_c} = \frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{2\pi \times 2500} \approx \mathbf{0.720253\text{ mH}}$$ $$C = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{2} R f_c} = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{2} \times 8 \times 2500} \approx \mathbf{5.62698\text{ }\mu\text{F}}\]

Stephen Butterworth's maximally flat second-order crossover (\(Q = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.7071\)) requires reactive impedance \(X_L = \sqrt{2}R\) and capacitive reactance \(X_C = R/\sqrt{2}\) at the crossover frequency \(f_c\): evaluating 8 [ENTER] 2 [√x] [×] 2 [÷] [↱] [π] [÷] 2500 [÷] determines the series woofer inductance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{7.2025 \times 10^{-4}}\text{ H}\), or \(0.7203\text{ mH})\), and evaluating 2 [↱] [π] [×] 2 [√x] [×] 8 [×] 2500 [×] [1/x] determines the shunt tweeter capacitance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 7.2025 \times 10^{-4}, X: \mathbf{5.6270 \times 10^{-6}}\text{ F}\), or \(5.63\,\mu\text{F})\)—or even faster, since \(C = \frac{L}{2 R^2} = \frac{L}{128}\), simply dividing \(L\) by 128 [÷] directly on the stack yields \(C = \mathbf{5.6270\,\mu\text{F}}\) in a single division!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.9: 4th-Order Linkwitz-Riley Crossover (\(24\text{ dB/octave}\))
docs.text:
For \(f_c = 2500\text{ Hz}, R = 8.0\,\Omega\):

\[L_{LR4} = \frac{R}{\pi f_c} = \frac{8.0}{\pi \times 2500} \approx \mathbf{1.01859\text{ mH}}$$ $$C_{LR4} = \frac{1}{4\pi R f_c} = \frac{1}{4\pi \times 8.0 \times 2500} \approx \mathbf{3.97887\text{ }\mu\text{F}}\]

Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley demonstrated in 1976 that cascading two Butterworth filters produces \(-6\text{ dB}\) acoustic amplitude and zero phase difference at \(f_c\), summing to a flat unity acoustic wavefront: keying 8.0 [↱] [π] [÷] 2500 [÷] resolves the LR4 series inductance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{1.0186 \times 10^{-3}}\text{ H}\), or \(1.019\text{ mH})\), and keying 4 [↱] [π] [×] 8 [×] 2500 [×] [1/x] (or dividing \(L_{LR4}\) by \(4R^2 = 256\,\Omega^2\) via 256 [÷]!) resolves the shunt capacitance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0010, X: \mathbf{3.9789 \times 10^{-6}}\text{ F}\), or \(3.98\,\mu\text{F})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.10: Complex AC Impedance Addition via [↰] [CMPLX]
docs.text:
Branch 1 impedance \(Z_1 = 8 + 4i\,\Omega\) (\(Y = 8, X = 4\)). Branch 2 impedance \(Z_2 = 4 - 8i\,\Omega\) (\(Y = 4, X = -8\)). Total series impedance: \(Z_{\text{total}} = (8 + 4i) + (4 - 8i) = \mathbf{12 - 4i\,\Omega}\).

In Charles Proteus Steinmetz's AC phasor calculus, series impedances combine vectorially across real resistance and imaginary reactance: staging \(Z_2 = 4 - 8i\) and \(Z_1 = 8 + 4i\) across the four registers via 4 [ENTER] 8 [+/-] [ENTER] 8 [ENTER] 4 \((T: 4.0000, Z: -8.0000, Y: 8.0000, X: 4.0000)\) and executing [↰] [CMPLX] [+] sums the real parts \((T + Y)\) into \(Y\) and imaginary parts \((Z + X)\) into \(X\) in a single cycle \((T: 4.0000, Z: 4.0000, Y: \mathbf{12.0000}, X: \mathbf{-4.0000})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.11: Zobel Network Dynamic Impedance Equalizer
docs.text:
Dynamic loudspeaker voice coils exhibit rising inductive impedance at high frequencies (\(Z(f) = R_e + j\omega L_e\)). A Zobel network placed in parallel with the driver flattens the impedance back to pure resistance \(R_e\): $\(R_z = 1.25 \times R_e, \quad C_z = \frac{L_e}{R_z^2}\)$ For a woofer with DC voice coil resistance \(R_e = 6.4\,\Omega\) and voice coil inductance \(L_e = 0.85\text{ mH}\) (\(0.00085\text{ H}\)): 1. Zobel resistor: \(R_z = 1.25 \times 6.4 = \mathbf{8.00\,\Omega}\). 2. Zobel capacitor: $\(C_z = \frac{0.00085}{8.0^2} = \frac{0.00085}{64.0} \approx \mathbf{13.281\text{ }\mu\text{F}}\)$

Otto Zobel's constant-resistance Boucherot cell neutralizes voice-coil inductive rise so passive crossovers see a resistive termination: computing 6.4 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] establishes the damping resistor \(R_z\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{8.0000}\,\Omega)\), squaring in place via [↰] [x²] (\(R_z^2 = 64.0\,\Omega^2\)), and chaining .00085 [x⇄y] [÷] 1 [E] 6 [×] determines the conjugate Zobel capacitance \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{13.2813}\,\mu\text{F})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.12: Snell's Law & Total Internal Reflection Critical Angle
docs.text:
Light propagates from optical glass (\(n_1 = 1.52\)) into air (\(n_2 = 1.00\)). Determine the critical angle \(\theta_c\):

\[\theta_c = \arcsin\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right) = \arcsin\left(\frac{1.00}{1.52}\right) = \arcsin(0.657895) \approx \mathbf{41.14^\circ}\]

By Willebrord Snellius's refraction law \(n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2\), total internal reflection commences when the transmitted ray grazes the interface at \(\theta_2 = 90^\circ\) (\(\sin\theta_2 = 1\)): dividing the refractive indices 1 [ENTER] 1.52 [÷] (\(\sin\theta_c \approx 0.6579\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.6579)\)) and pressing [↰] [ASIN] in Degrees mode determines the critical angle \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{41.1395}^\circ)\)—or in just two operations via 1.52 [1/x] [↰] [ASIN]!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.13: Numerical Aperture & Light Acceptance Angle of Optical Fiber
docs.text:
A multi-mode step-index silica optical fiber has core refractive index \(n_{\text{core}} = 1.482\) and cladding refractive index \(n_{\text{clad}} = 1.460\): 1. Numerical Aperture (\(NA\)): $\(NA = \sqrt{n_{\text{core}}^2 - n_{\text{clad}}^2} = \sqrt{1.482^2 - 1.460^2} = \sqrt{2.196324 - 2.131600} = \sqrt{0.064724} \approx \mathbf{0.2544}\)$ 2. Maximum acceptance half-angle in air (\(\theta_{\max}\)): $\(\theta_{\max} = \arcsin(NA) = \arcsin(0.254409) \approx \mathbf{14.74^\circ}\)$

Ernst Abbe's numerical aperture \(NA = \sqrt{n_{\text{core}}^2 - n_{\text{clad}}^2}\) governs both the light-gathering cone and modal dispersion of a step-index waveguide: evaluating 1.482 [↰] [x²] 1.460 [↰] [x²] [-] [√x] determines \(NA = \mathbf{0.2544}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.2544})\), and pressing [↰] [ASIN] in Degrees mode resolves the acceptance half-cone \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{14.7389}^\circ)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.14: Thick Lens Equivalent Focal Length (Gullstrand Formula)
docs.text:
A thick biconvex crown glass lens has front radius \(R_1 = 50.0\text{ mm}\), rear radius \(R_2 = -80.0\text{ mm}\), center thickness \(d = 12.0\text{ mm}\), and refractive index \(n = 1.520\). Gullstrand's lens maker formula states: $\(\frac{1}{f} = (n - 1) \left[ \frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{(n - 1) d}{n R_1 R_2} \right]\)$ 1. Front surface power: \((n - 1) / R_1 = 0.520 / 50 = 0.010400\text{ mm}^{-1}\). 2. Rear surface power: \(-(n - 1) / R_2 = -0.520 / (-80) = 0.006500\text{ mm}^{-1}\). 3. Thickness coupling term: $\(\frac{(n - 1)^2 d}{n R_1 R_2} = \frac{0.520^2 \times 12.0}{1.520 \times 50.0 \times (-80.0)} = \frac{3.2448}{-6080.0} = -0.00053368\text{ mm}^{-1}\)$ 4. Total optical power: \(P = 0.010400 + 0.006500 - 0.00053368 = 0.01636632\text{ mm}^{-1}\). 5. Equivalent focal length: \(f = 1 / P \approx \mathbf{61.10\text{ mm}}\).

Allvar Gullstrand's paraxial thick-lens equation accounts for principal-plane separation across axial thickness \(d = 12.0\text{ mm}\): summing the two surface dioptric powers .520 [ENTER] 50 [÷] .520 [ENTER] 80 [÷] [+] (\(0.016900\text{ mm}^{-1}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0169)\)), deducting the thickness coupling term .520 [↰] [x²] 12 [×] 1.52 [ENTER] 50 [×] 80 [×] [÷] [-] (\(P = 0.016366\text{ mm}^{-1}\), \((T: 0.0169, Z: 0.0169, Y: 0.0169, X: 0.0164)\)), and inverting via [1/x] yields the equivalent focal length \((T: 0.0169, Z: 0.0169, Y: 0.0169, X: \mathbf{61.1011}\text{ mm})\)—and by noting that \(\frac{1}{50} + \frac{1}{80} = (50 \parallel 80)^{-1}\), you can evaluate the bracketed geometry via 50 [ENTER] 80 [x∥y] [1/x]!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.15: Hohmann Transfer Orbit \(\Delta v\) (LEO to GEO)
docs.text:

Target GEO radius \(r_2 = 4.2164 \times 10^7\text{ m}\) (\(h = 35,786\text{ km}\)). Transfer semi-major axis \(a = (r_1 + r_2)/2 = 2.4421 \times 10^7\text{ m}\). 1. docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.16: Rocket Motor Burnout Velocity via Romberg Quadrature
docs.text:
Integrate thrust acceleration \(a(t) = 4t^2 - 0.5t^3\) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 6.0\text{ seconds}\):

$\(\Delta v = \int_0^6 (4t^2 - 0.5t^3) dt = \left[ \frac{4}{3}t^3 - \frac{1}{8}t^4 \right]_0^6 = \frac{4}{3}(216) - \frac{1}{8}(1296) = 288 - 162 = \mathbf{126.0\text{ m/s}}\)$ Executed in [↱] [EQN] via [↱] [∫]: engine converges to exactly 126.0000 m/s.

When solid-propellant grain regression causes thrust acceleration \(a(t) = 4t^2 - 0.5t^3\) to vary non-linearly over the burn duration, integrating \(a(t)\) in [↱] [EQN] (4 T [↰] [x²] [×] 0.5 T 3 [yˣ] [×] [-]) across the burn window 0 [ENTER] 6 \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 6.0000)\) via [↱] [∫] T applies Richardson extrapolation to resolve the exact burnout velocity increment \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{126.0000}\text{ m/s})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.17: Gravitational Escape Velocity from Earth and Mars
docs.text:
Planetary surface escape velocity is given by \(v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{r}}\): 1. Earth (\(\mu = 3.986004 \times 10^{14}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}^2, r = 6.378 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)): $\(v_{\text{esc},\oplus} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 3.986004 \times 10^{14}}{6.378 \times 10^6}} \approx \mathbf{11,180.00\text{ m/s}} \quad (\mathbf{11.18\text{ km/s}})\)$ 2. Mars (\(\mu_{\text{Mars}} = 4.282837 \times 10^{13}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}^2, r_{\text{Mars}} = 3.3895 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)): $\(v_{\text{esc,Mars}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 4.282837 \times 10^{13}}{3.3895 \times 10^6}} \approx \mathbf{5,026.91\text{ m/s}} \quad (\mathbf{5.03\text{ km/s}})\)$

Setting total specific mechanical energy \(\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{\mu}{r} = 0\) on a parabolic escape trajectory yields \(v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2\mu/r} = \sqrt{2}\,v_{\text{circ}}\): evaluating 2 [ENTER] 3.986004 [E] 14 [×] 6.378 [E] 6 [÷] (\(2\mu/r \approx 1.2500 \times 10^8\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.2500 \times 10^8)\)) and extracting the square root via [√x] determines Earth's surface escape velocity \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{11180.00}\text{ m/s}\), or \(11.18\text{ km/s})\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.18: Meridian Convergence & True vs. Magnetic Azimuth
docs.text:
A geodetic survey line in a mid-latitude UTM zone has a measured magnetic azimuth \(\alpha_{\text{mag}} = 142.35^\circ\). The local magnetic declination is \(\delta = 4.12^\circ\text{ E}\) (East declination is added), and grid convergence angle is \(\gamma = -1.25^\circ\): $\(\alpha_{\text{true}} = \alpha_{\text{mag}} + \delta = 142.35^\circ + 4.12^\circ = \mathbf{146.47^\circ}\)$ $\(\alpha_{\text{grid}} = \alpha_{\text{true}} - \gamma = 146.47^\circ - (-1.25^\circ) = \mathbf{147.72^\circ}\)$

Reducing a field compass bearing to a State Plane Lambert conformal conic grid azimuth requires two sequential angular rotations: staging the magnetic azimuth 142.35 [ENTER] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 142.3500, X: 142.3500)\), adding easterly geomagnetic declination 4.12 [+] to obtain geodetic true north azimuth \(\alpha_{\text{true}} = \mathbf{146.47^\circ}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 146.4700)\), and subtracting meridian convergence 1.25 [+/-] [-] to establish grid azimuth \(\alpha_{\text{grid}} = \mathbf{147.72^\circ}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 147.7200)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.19: Bowditch Compass Rule Linear Misclosure Balancing
docs.text:
A field traverse leg has raw measured length \(L_1 = 250.0\text{ ft}\) along a total perimeter \(L_{\text{total}} = 1,250.0\text{ ft}\). The total survey departure misclosure is \(E_x = +0.15\text{ ft}\). Calculate the Bowditch proportional departure correction \(C_{x1}\): $\(C_{x1} = - E_x \times \left( \frac{L_1}{L_{\text{total}}} \right) = -0.15 \times \left( \frac{250.0}{1250.0} \right) = -0.15 \times 0.20 = \mathbf{-0.030\text{ ft}}\)$

Nathaniel Bowditch's 1807 Compass Rule distributes linear traverse misclosure in proportion to each leg's fraction of total perimeter length: negating the departure misclosure .15 [+/-] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -0.1500)\), weighting by leg length 250 [×] (\(-37.50\text{ ft}^2\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -37.5000)\)), and dividing by total traverse perimeter 1250 [÷] determines the leg departure adjustment \(C_{x1} = \mathbf{-0.030\text{ ft}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -0.0300)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.20: Uniform Distributed Load Maximum Bending Moment
docs.text:
A simply supported floor girder spans \(L = 8.0\text{ meters}\) supporting a combined dead and live distributed load \(w = 24.5\text{ kN/m}\) (\(24,500\text{ N/m}\)). Calculate the maximum bending moment \(M_{\max}\) at midspan: $\(M_{\max} = \frac{w L^2}{8} = \frac{24500 \times 8.0^2}{8} = 24500 \times 8 = \mathbf{196,000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}} \quad (\mathbf{196.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}})\)$

Integrating the linear shear diagram \(V(x) = w(L/2 - x)\) from the support to midspan \(x = L/2\) yields the parabolic bending-moment maximum \(M_{\max} = \frac{wL^2}{8}\): staging the distributed load 24500 [ENTER] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 24500.0000, X: 24500.0000)\), multiplying by squared span 8 [↰] [x²] [×] (\(1,568,000.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1568000.0000)\)), and dividing by 8 [÷] resolves the peak midspan moment \(M_{\max} = \mathbf{196,000\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}\) (\(196.0\text{ kN}\cdot\text{m}\)) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 196000.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.21: Cantilever Beam Maximum Tip Deflection Under Uniform Load
docs.text:
A balcony cantilever beam of length \(L = 2.5\text{ m}\) carries uniform distributed load \(w = 3,200\text{ N/m}\). The beam is structural steel with \(E = 200.0\text{ GPa}\) (\(200 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}\)) and second moment of area \(I = 1.65 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^4\). Maximum tip deflection is: $\(\delta_{\max} = \frac{w L^4}{8 E I} = \frac{3200 \times 2.5^4}{8 \times (200 \times 10^9) \times (1.65 \times 10^{-5})} = \frac{3200 \times 39.0625}{26,400,000} \approx \mathbf{0.004735\text{ m}} \quad (\mathbf{4.74\text{ mm}})\)$

Because cantilever tip deflection under uniform loading scales with the fourth power of overhang length (\(L^4\)), small span increases produce dramatic compliance penalties: raising the span 2.5 [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] (\(39.0625\text{ m}^4\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 39.0625)\)), scaling by 3200 [×] (\(125,000.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^3\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 125000.0000)\)), and dividing sequentially by 8 [÷] 200 [E] 9 [÷] (\(7.8125 \times 10^{-11}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.8125 \times 10^{-11})\)) and 1.65 [E] 5 [+/-] [÷] determines the free-end deflection \(\delta_{\max} = \mathbf{0.004735\text{ m}}\) (\(4.74\text{ mm}\)) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0047)\)—note that 2.5 [↰] [x²] [↰] [x²] computes \(2.5^4\) in two single-cycle squarings!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.22: Standard Gibbs Free Energy & Equilibrium Constant
docs.text:
For the chemical synthesis of ammonia (\(\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3\)) at temperature \(T = 298.15\text{ K}\), the thermodynamic equilibrium constant is \(K_p = 5.8 \times 10^5\). Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G^\circ\): $\(\Delta G^\circ = - R T \ln K_p = - 8.314462 \times 298.15 \times \ln(5.8 \times 10^5) \approx \mathbf{-32,897.4\text{ J/mol}} \quad (\mathbf{-32.90\text{ kJ/mol}})\)$

J. Willard Gibbs's chemical-potential isotherm \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K_p\) links macroscopic reaction equilibrium to standard molar free energy: taking the natural logarithm 5.8 [E] 5 [LN] (\(13.2708\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 13.2708)\)), scaling by thermal energy 8.314462 [×] 298.15 [×] (\(32,897.70\text{ J/mol}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 32897.7010)\)), and negating/converting to kilojoules via [+/-] 1000 [÷] confirms a strongly exergonic Haber-Bosch synthesis at \(298.15\text{ K}\): \(\Delta G^\circ = \mathbf{-32.90\text{ kJ/mol}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -32.8977)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.23: Nernst Electrochemical Cell Potential
docs.text:
A galvanic Daniell cell (\(\text{Zn} + \text{Cu}^{2+} \rightleftharpoons \text{Zn}^{2+} + \text{Cu}\)) has standard cell potential \(E^\circ = 1.100\text{ V}\) with \(n = 2\text{ electrons transferred}\) at \(T = 298.15\text{ K}\). Faraday constant \(F = 96,485.33\text{ C/mol}\). The electrolyte concentrations are \([\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 0.50\text{ M}\) and \([\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 0.010\text{ M}\) (reaction quotient \(Q = 0.50 / 0.010 = 50.0\)): $\(E = E^\circ - \frac{R T}{n F} \ln Q = 1.100 - \frac{8.314462 \times 298.15}{2 \times 96485.33} \ln(50.0) = 1.100 - (0.012845 \times 3.912023) \approx \mathbf{1.0497\text{ V}}\)$

Walther Nernst's electromotive equation quantifies how product ion accumulation (\(Q = [\text{Zn}^{2+}]/[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 50.0\)) depresses galvanic cell voltage below the standard potential \(E^\circ\): evaluating the molar free-energy shift 50 [LN] 8.314462 [×] 298.15 [×] (\(RT\ln Q = 9,697.74\text{ J/mol}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 9697.7358)\)), dividing by charge transfer \(nF\) via 2 [÷] 96485.3 [÷] (\(\Delta E = 0.050255\text{ V}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 0.0503)\)), and subtracting from \(E^\circ\) via 1.100 [x⇄y] [-] determines the terminal cell electromotive force \(E = \mathbf{1.0497\text{ V}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.0497)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.24: Carbon-14 Archeological Radiocarbon Dating
docs.text:
Living plant tissue maintains a steady Carbon-14 activity of \(A_0 = 15.3\text{ disintegrations/min}\cdot\text{g of carbon}\). An ancient timber specimen excavated from a ceremonial structure exhibits an activity of \(A(t) = 9.4\text{ dpm/g}\). Using the true physical Cambridge \(^{14}\text{C}\) half-life \(t_{1/2} = 5,730\text{ years}\) (\(\lambda = \ln 2 / 5730 \approx 0.00012097\text{ yr}^{-1}\); note that uncalibrated archaeological laboratory reports use the conventional \(5,568\text{-year}\) Libby half-life prior to IntCal20 calibration): $\(t = - \frac{1}{\lambda} \ln\left(\frac{A(t)}{A_0}\right) = - \frac{5730}{\ln 2} \ln\left(\frac{9.4}{15.3}\right) = -8266.64 \times (-0.487144) \approx \mathbf{4,027.0\text{ years}}\)$

Willard Libby's radiocarbon chronometer measures the time elapsed since an organism ceased exchanging atmospheric \(^{14}\text{CO}_2\): evaluating the logarithmic activity depletion 9.4 [ENTER] 15.3 [÷] [LN] (\(\ln(9.4/15.3) = -0.487144\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -0.4871)\)), scaling by the mean lifetime \(\tau = t_{1/2}/\ln 2\) via 5730 [×] 2 [LN] [÷] (\(-4,027.014\text{ yr}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -4027.0141)\)), and reversing sign with [+/-] dates the timber specimen to \(t = \mathbf{4,027.0\text{ years}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 4027.0141)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.25: Gamma Ray Shielding & Lead Half-Value Layer (HVL)
docs.text:
Cobalt-60 emits energetic gamma photons (\(1.17\text{ MeV}\) and \(1.33\text{ MeV}\)) with linear attenuation coefficient \(\mu = 0.650\text{ cm}^{-1}\) in lead shielding. 1. Half-Value Layer thickness: $\(\text{HVL} = \frac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \frac{0.693147}{0.650} \approx \mathbf{1.0664\text{ cm}}\)$ 2. Required thickness \(x\) to reduce radiation intensity by a factor of 100 (\(I / I_0 = 0.01\)): $\(x = - \frac{\ln(0.01)}{\mu} = \frac{4.605170}{0.650} \approx \mathbf{7.0849\text{ cm}}\)$

By the Beer-Lambert exponential attenuation law \(I(x) = I_0 e^{-\mu x}\), attenuating a narrow gamma beam to \(1\%\) transmission (\(I/I_0 = 0.01\), or two Tenth-Value Layers) requires optical depth \(\mu x = -\ln(0.01) = 4.605170\): keying .01 [LN] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -4.6052)\), dividing by the linear attenuation coefficient .650 [÷] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: -7.0849)\), and pressing [+/-] specifies a lead shield thickness of \(x = \mathbf{7.0849\text{ cm}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 7.0849)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.26: Decibel Addition of Incoherent Environmental Noise Sources
docs.text:
An industrial shop floor operates three loud machines with sound pressure levels: Machine 1: \(L_1 = 88.0\text{ dBA}\), Machine 2: \(L_2 = 91.0\text{ dBA}\), Machine 3: \(L_3 = 85.0\text{ dBA}\). Determine the combined acoustic noise level \(L_{\Sigma}\): $\(L_{\Sigma} = 10 \log_{10} \left( 10^{88/10} + 10^{91/10} + 10^{85/10} \right) = 10 \log_{10}(6.3096 \times 10^8 + 1.2589 \times 10^9 + 3.1623 \times 10^8) \approx \mathbf{93.43\text{ dBA}}\)$

Because uncorrelated machinery noise sources sum in acoustic intensity (\(W/\text{m}^2\)) rather than decibels, antilogging each bel level (\(L_i/10\)) via 8.8 [↰] [10ˣ] 9.1 [↰] [10ˣ] [+] (\(1.8899 \times 10^9\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 1.8899 \times 10^9)\)) plus 8.5 [↰] [10ˣ] [+] (\(2.2061 \times 10^9\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.2061 \times 10^9)\)) and re-compressing to decibels via [↰] [LOG] 10 [×] determines the composite shop-floor exposure \(L_{\Sigma} = \mathbf{93.44\text{ dBA}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 93.4363)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.27: Inverse Square Law Acoustic Attenuation with Distance
docs.text:
An outdoor emergency warning siren emits sound level \(L_1 = 105.0\text{ dB}\) measured at distance \(r_1 = 10.0\text{ meters}\). Assuming spherical propagation without ground reflections, determine sound pressure level \(L_2\) at distance \(r_2 = 120.0\text{ meters}\): $\(L_2 = L_1 - 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right) = 105.0 - 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{120.0}{10.0}\right) = 105.0 - 20 \log_{10}(12.0) = 105.0 - 21.5836 \approx \mathbf{83.42\text{ dB}}\)$

In free-field spherical spreading, acoustic intensity falls off as \(1/r^2\) (\(-6.02\text{ dB}\) per distance doubling): evaluating the divergence loss 120 [ENTER] 10 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×] (\(21.5836\text{ dB}\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 21.5836)\)) and deducting it from the reference level via 105 [x⇄y] [-] determines the far-field sound pressure level \(L_2 = \mathbf{83.42\text{ dB}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 83.4164)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 13.28: Cross-Discipline Isomorphism of the Parallel Key ([x∥y])
docs.text:
Because the SC-32 elevates \(x \parallel y = \frac{1}{1/x + 1/y} = \frac{xy}{x+y}\) to a primary function key, a practicing engineer solves five distinct physical domains with the exact same 3-keystroke gesture: 1. Staging \(C_1 = 47.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) via 47 [ENTER] \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 47.0000, X: 47.0000)\) and combining with \(C_2 = 22.0\text{ }\mu\text{F}\) via 22 [x∥y] executes the harmonic product-over-sum operation \(\frac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\) in a single hardware cycle to resolve the series equivalent capacitance \(C_{\text{eq}} = \mathbf{14.99\text{ }\mu\text{F}}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 14.9855)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 14.17: Gravitational Potential Energy Shift

\(\Delta U = G M m \left( \frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} \right)\) where \(G M m = 4.0 \times 10^{14}, R_1 = 6.4 \times 10^6, R_2 = 6.8 \times 10^6\).

docs.text:

docs.title: Workbook Problem 14.27: Cubic Polynomial Brent's Solver Extraction
docs.text:
Find the real root of \(x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0\).

With the cubic residual \(f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5\) programmed in [↱] [EQN] mode (X 3 [yˣ] 2 X [×] [-] 5 [-]), typing 2 [ENTER] 3 loads initial physical bracketing interval \([2.0, 3.0]\) across registers \((Y, X)\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: -5.0000, Y: 2.0000, X: 3.0000)\). Executing [↱] [SOLVE] X contracts the bracket via Brent's hybrid algorithm until \(|f(x)| < 10^{-12}\), depositing the converged real root \(x = \mathbf{2.0946}\) into Register \(X\) \((T: -5.0000, Z: 2.0000, Y: 3.0000, X: 2.0946)\) (3-sig-fig target: 2.09, full mantissa \(2.094551481\)).

(Tournament Closed-Form Alternative): In sprint contests, you can also solve \(x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0\) instantaneously with Cardano's exact polynomial engine [↱] [POLY]. Because unentered coefficients default to \(0.0\), quadratic coefficient \(B\) can be skipped entirely: key 1 [A] 2 [+/-] [C] 5 [+/-] [D] [XEQ] [RCL] 1 to extract \(2.094551\) in \(<5\text{ ms}\)!

Convert three dimension measurements given in inches to millimeters using the exact conversion constant \(25.4\text{ mm/in}\): \(2.0\text{ in}, 5.0\text{ in}, 10.0\text{ in}\). Target Answers: - \(2.0\text{ in}\): 50.8 \(\text{mm}\) - \(5.0\text{ in}\): 127 \(\text{mm}\) - \(10.0\text{ in}\): 254 \(\text{mm}\)

Loading the SI conversion factor across all four stack tiers via 25.4 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] \((T: 25.4000, Z: 25.4000, Y: 25.4000, X: 25.4000)\) turns Register \(T\) into a non-depleting constant source: 2 [×] resolves 50.8000 mm \((T: 25.4000, Z: 25.4000, Y: 25.4000, X: 50.8000)\), [CLx] 5 [×] resolves 127.0000 mm \((T: 25.4000, Z: 25.4000, Y: 25.4000, X: 127.0000)\), and [CLx] 10 [×] resolves 254.0000 mm \((T: 25.4000, Z: 25.4000, Y: 25.4000, X: 254.0000)\) without re-entering 25.4.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 14.39: Infix Operator Precedence vs Native RPN Stack Equivalence
docs.text:
Compare algebraic infix parsing requiring nested parentheses with natural RPN execution for two standard tournament expressions: 1. \((12 - 4) \times (6 + 2) \div 4 = \mathbf{16.0}\) 2. \(3 + 4 \times 5 = \mathbf{23.0}\)

RPN Keystrokes: - Expression 1: 12 [ENTER] 4 [-] 6 [ENTER] 2 [+] [×] 4 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 16.0 (Evaluates intermediate differences and sums directly on the stack without a single parenthesis) - Expression 2: 3 [ENTER] 4 [ENTER] 5 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 23.0 (Multiplying 4 and 5 first, then adding 3, completely mirrors operator precedence without requiring parentheses).

In Jan Łukasiewicz's postfix logic, operator position alone encodes tree topology without delimiters: evaluating 12 [ENTER] 4 [-] (\(8.0000\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 8.0000)\)), 6 [ENTER] 2 [+] (\(8.0000\) in \(X\) with \(8.0000\) lifted to \(Y\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 8.0000, X: 8.0000)\)), and [×] 4 [÷] yields \(\mathbf{16.0000}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 16.0000)\), while 4 [ENTER] 5 [×] 3 [+] evaluates \(\mathbf{23.0000}\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 16.0000, X: 23.0000)\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 14.40: Nested Horner's Method for Cubic Polynomials
docs.text:
Evaluate \(P(x) = 3x^3 - 5x^2 + 4x - 7\) at \(x = 2.5\). Speed Optimization Insight: Evaluating polynomials term-by-term with powers (\(x^3, x^2\)) wastes time and invites syntax errors. Rewriting in nested Horner form \(((3x - 5)x + 4)x - 7\) allows continuous left-to-right streaming on the stack with zero parentheses: Keystrokes: 3 [ENTER] 2.5 [×] 5 [-] 2.5 [×] 4 [+] 2.5 [×] 7 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 18.625 (3-sig-fig target: 18.6 (Full mantissa: 18.625)).

William George Horner's 1819 nested synthetic division reduces a degree-\(n\) polynomial to \(n\) multiply-add pairs: evaluating 3 [ENTER] 2.5 [×] 5 [-] (\(3x - 5 = 2.5000\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 2.5000)\)), chaining 2.5 [×] 4 [+] (\((3x - 5)x + 4 = 10.2500\), \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 10.2500)\)), and finishing with 2.5 [×] 7 [-] resolves \(P(2.5) = \mathbf{18.6250}\) (\(18.6\)) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 18.6250)\)—and by pre-filling the stack with \(x = 2.5\) (2.5 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] 3 [×] 5 [-] [×] 4 [+] [×] 7 [-]), Register \(T\) feeds \(2.5\) into every Horner stage automatically so 2.5 is typed only once!

docs.title: Chapter 02: How Stack Math Works: Stacking Numbers Just Like Blocks — Extended Worked Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 02 of From Blocks to the Stack (21 Worked Practice Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.1: The Three-Day Gravel Mountain
docs.text:
To fill the fossil-dig sandbox, your crew wheels loads of washed pea gravel from the supply pile: 4 wheelbarrows on Monday, 5 on Tuesday, and 6 on Wednesday. How many total wheelbarrows of gravel did you pour in? Stack 4 unit cubes on your desk, add 5 cubes (making 9), and then add 6 more cubes to form a tower of 15 cubes.

Watch how the stack chains all three days without clearing: 4 [ENTER] 5 [+] 6 [+] \(\to\) 15 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 15). Why didn't you need to press [ENTER] before typing 6? Because automatic stack lift pushed Tuesday's running total (\(9\)) upstairs to Floor \(Y\) the instant your finger tapped 6!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.2: Stepping Stones Across the Ten-Bridge
docs.text:
Your crew is laying round sensory stepping stones along a winding garden path: 8 smooth slate stones in the morning, and 7 sparkling granite stones in the afternoon. How many stepping stones lead to the climbing tower? Place [8] in Row 1 and [7] in Row 0 of your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Take 2 from 7 to complete a full 10 (snapping a Gold [+1] carry token into the Tens column), leaving [5] in the Ones column (\(10 + 5 = 15\)).

Fuse the morning and afternoon stone deliveries on the stack: 8 [ENTER] 7 [+] \(\to\) 15 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 15), bridging cleanly past ten to reach 15 stepping stones.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.3: Climbing-Dome Steel Bolts
docs.text:
A hardware box holds 10 heavy steel bolts for the geodesic climbing dome. Your crew bolts 6 of them into the main arch. How many bolts are left in the box for the balance-beam brackets? On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), start with 10 ([1] in Tens, [0] in Ones) and subtract [6]—finding the complement [4] in the Ones column.

Verify the ten-partner on your stack: 10 [ENTER] 6 [-] \(\to\) 4 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4), leaving 4 bolts ready in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.4: The Zero-Flag Mystery (Additive Identity)
docs.text:
Your crew stakes 7 bright orange flags along the zip-line landing zone. The safety inspector checks the tape measure and says zero extra flags are needed (\(+0\)). How many flags stand along the runway? Place 7 counting tiles on your desk and add nothing to them—you still have 7 tiles!

Test the Zero Addition Rule on the stack: 7 [ENTER] 0 [+] \(\to\) 7 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 7), proving that adding \(0\) leaves any number unchanged (\(a + 0 = a\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.5: Zipline Carabiners on the Rack
docs.text:
The gear chest has 8 climbing carabiners clipped to the rack. Because the zip-line cable is still being tensioned, zero carabiners are removed this morning (\(-0\)). How many carabiners stay clipped to the rack? Set out 8 counting tiles and take away zero—all 8 tiles stay right where they are.

Confirm on the keypad: 8 [ENTER] 0 [-] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8), showing that subtracting zero leaves your starting number intact (\(a - 0 = a\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.6: Clearing the Tire-Swing Chains
docs.text:
Six heavy link chains are uncoiled on the grass for the three playground tire swings. Your crew hoists and bolts all 6 chains onto the overhead beam. How many unbolted chains are left on the grass? Place 6 counting tiles on the desk, then sweep all 6 away into your hand—zero remain (\(6 - 6 = 0\)).

Run the self-subtraction on your calculator: 6 [ENTER] 6 [-] \(\to\) 0 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0). Whenever a number subtracts itself, the ground shelf drops cleanly to zero!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.7: The Twin-Pod Explorer Doubler
docs.text: A glass sky-elevator carries 16 young space-camp explorers up from the lobby. At the sky-bridge level, a twin pod docks and an equal team of 16 more explorers steps aboard! How many explorers are riding together now? Why type 16 twice when [ENTER] clones whatever is on Floor \(X\)? Watch how 16 [ENTER] [+] doubles a number in two clicks: 16 [ENTER] [+] \(\to\) 32 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 32). Pressing [ENTER] copies 16 onto Floor \(Y\) while keeping 16 on Floor \(X\), so [+] doubles it to 32 without re-keying!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.8: Starlight Observation Deck Countdown
docs.text:
The glass-floored Starlight Observation Deck holds at most 100 visitors at a time. If a group of 43 stargazers steps out onto the glass floor, how many more visitors can join them before the deck is full? Picture a 100-flat grid: taking away 4 full rows of ten (\(40\)) leaves \(60\), and taking away 3 more units leaves \(57\) (\(43 + 57 = 100\)).

Verify the open spots on the stack: 100 [ENTER] 43 [-] \(\to\) 57 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 57), confirming 57 open stargazer spots.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.9: Express 10-Floor Beacon Test
docs.text:
The tower flight engineer tests the altitude beacons every 10 floors starting from the underground launch bay (Floor 0) up to Floor 50. Line up 5 ten-rods end-to-end on your desk (\(10, 20, 30, 40, 50\)). Seed the initial 10-floor step on your SC-6: 10 [ENTER] 0 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 10 (and in 2-LV mode—or after pressing [g] [REP] on 10 in 4-stack mode—four more taps of [+] climb straight through Floors 20, 30, 40, and 50).

Keying 10 [ENTER] 0 [+] sets the first 10-floor beacon at (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 10, X: 10) in 2-LV mode so each tap of [+] steps up another 10 stories!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.10: Hover-Drone Charging Bays
docs.text:
The Sky-Tower's drone hangar has 4 launch decks, and each deck has 6 magnetic wireless charging pads. How many drone charging pads are in the hangar altogether? Snap together all 24 counting tiles from your studio kit into a \(4 \times 6\) rectangle—your fingers can feel that 4 rows of 6 make a solid rectangle of 24!

Multiply the 4 decks by 6 pads per deck: 4 [ENTER] 6 [×] \(\to\) 24 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 24), giving 24 charging bays.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.11: Robotic Window-Climbing Gecko Bots
docs.text: To polish the solar-glass windows on the outside of the tower, robotic suction-cup "Gecko Bots" clean 7 giant window panels on each of 8 upper floors. How many window panels do the robots polish on this run? Build a small \(3 \times 4\) tile array (\(12\)) and spin it \(90^\circ\) to see why \(7 \times 8\) and \(8 \times 7\) cover the exact same area. Then multiply 7 panels across 8 floors: 7 [ENTER] 8 [×] \(\to\) 56 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 56), totaling 56 gleaming solar windows!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.12: Sky-Lab Weather Sensor Deployment
docs.text: The chief meteorologist unpacked 56 wind-speed sensors and mounted an equal number on each of 7 sky-bridge levels. How many sensors guard each sky-bridge? Just as \(7 \times 8 = 56\) in Workbook Problem 2.11, dividing \(56\) into \(7\) equal groups reveals the missing partner side of the rectangle (\(56 \div 7 = 8\)): 56 [ENTER] 7 [÷] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8), placing 8 wind sensors on each sky-bridge.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.13: Maker Fair Backpack Swaps
docs.text:
You walk into the Maker Fair with 14 3D-printed badges in your backpack. You win 5 more badges at the robotics booth, then trade 3 badges to a friend. How many badges are in your backpack now? Place 14 counting tiles on your desk, slide 5 more in (\(19\)), and slide 3 away (\(16\)).

Track the live running balance on the stack: 14 [ENTER] 5 [+] 3 [-] \(\to\) 16 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 16). Because the subtotal \(19\) automatically lifts to Floor \(Y\) when you type \(3\), you never press [ENTER] a second time!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.14: Battle-Bot Arena Bumper Railings
docs.text: The Maker Fair's rectangular Battle-Bot arena measures 12 feet long and 8 feet wide. How many feet of polycarbonate bumper railing are needed to wrap all the way around the arena? Why add \(12 + 8 + 12 + 8\) four times when a rectangle has two equal L-shaped half-perimeters? Add one length and one width (\(12 + 8 = 20\text{ ft}\)), then double it: 12 [ENTER] 8 [+] 2 [×] \(\to\) 40 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 40), giving 40 feet of arena bumper railing!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.15: Sailboat Pennant Triangle Area
docs.text: A triangular racing pennant for a model RC sailboat has a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm. What is the area of the pennant? Form a \(4 \times 3\) rectangle of 12 tiles and slice it diagonally in half (\(12 \div 2 = 6\)). Every triangle is exactly half of its surrounding rectangle! Multiply base by height and divide by 2 (\(10 \times 6 \div 2 = 30\text{ cm}^2\)): 10 [ENTER] 6 [×] 2 [÷] \(\to\) 30 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 30), giving a \(30\text{ cm}^2\) pennant area.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.16: The \(\$50\) Market Pouch Countdown
docs.text:
You bring a crisp \(\$50\) bill to the weekend market. You spend \(\$18\) on a crystal-growing kit and \(\$12\) on fresh berries. How much cash is left in your pouch? Start with 5 ten-rods (\(50\)), remove 18 (leaving 32), and remove 12 (leaving 20). (Mental Math Shortcut: Notice that \(\$18 + \$12 = \$30\) spent in all, and \(\$50 - \$30 = \$20\)!)

Deduct both purchases in a continuous chain on the stack: 50 [ENTER] 18 [-] 12 [-] \(\to\) 20 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20), leaving \(\$20.00\) in your pouch.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.17: Splitting the Giant Nacho Platter
docs.text:
Four friends split a giant stadium nacho platter costing \(\$17.50\). Using Quotient & Remainder ([g] [÷R]), find how many whole one-dollar bills each friend pays and how much coin change is left to split! Deal out 17 dollar tiles among 4 friends: each friend puts in 4 whole dollars (\(\$16.00\)), leaving \(\$1.50\) to cover with quarters!

Split \(\$17.50\) across 4 friends with [g] [÷R]: 17.50 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R] \(\to\) 4 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 1.5, X: 4), showing \(X = \$4.00\) whole dollars each and \(Y = \$1.50\) remaining coin change.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.18: Rescuing a Number from the Top Floor
docs.text:
Suppose you parked the number 10 way up on the top shelf (\(T = 10\)) while 20, 30, and 40 sit below it. How many clicks of [f] [R↓] bring the top shelf (\(T\)) down to the active ground shelf (\(X\))? Three clicks ([f] [R↓] [f] [R↓] [f] [R↓]) rotate \(T \to Z \to Y \to X\): 10 [ENTER] 20 [ENTER] 30 [ENTER] 40 [f] [R↓] [f] [R↓] [f] [R↓] \(\rightarrow\) 10.

Loading all four shelves and rotating three times lands at (T: 20, Z: 30, Y: 40, X: 10), bringing 10 cleanly into Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.19: Crushing the Giant Fraction Bar
docs.text: Look at this intimidating fraction bar: $\(\frac{48 - (4 \times 6)}{3 + (2 \times 4.5)}\)$ On a normal calculator, you would need four sets of parentheses! On your SC-6, work from the inside out: compute the top (\(48 - 24 = 24\)), compute the bottom (\(3 + 9 = 12\)) while \(24\) waits upstairs, and press [÷]: 48 [ENTER] 4 [ENTER] 6 [×] [-] 2 [ENTER] 4.5 [×] 3 [+] [÷] \(\to\) 2 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 2), resolving the entire fraction bar to \(2.0\) with zero parentheses!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.20: The Treehouse Zip-Line Shortcut (Pythagorean Theorem)
docs.text: Your backyard treehouse sits \(6\text{ meters}\) north and \(8\text{ meters}\) east of the porch post, forming a right triangle with legs of 6 and 8. How long is the diagonal zip-line cable \(c = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2}\) connecting them? Square both legs ([x²]), add them together ([+]), and tap Square Root ([f] [√x]): 6 [x²] 8 [x²] [+] [f] [√x] \(\to\) 10 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 10), finding a \(10.0\text{ m}\) zip-line in 7 keystrokes with zero scratch paper!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 2.21: Weather Station Thermometer Code (\(^\circ\text{F} \to ^\circ\text{C}\))
docs.text: Your school weather station reads \(68^\circ\text{F}\). Convert it to Celsius using the inside-out formula \(C = (F - 32) \times 5 \div 9\): 68 [ENTER] 32 [-] 5 [×] 9 [÷] \(\to\) 20 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20), landing cleanly on \(20.0^\circ\text{C}\).

docs.title: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio — Extended Worked Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 03 of From Blocks to the Stack (24 Worked Practice Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.1: Bioluminescent Jellyfish Pods
docs.text:
A marine tank holds 8 neon-blue comb jellies in Pod A and 7 glowing moon jellies in Pod B. How many bioluminescent jellyfish are swimming in the tank? On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), [8] needs 2 more to complete 10—telling you right away to split 7 into \(2 + 5\) and snap a Gold [+1] carry token into the Tens column!

Bridge to ten on the stack: 8 [ENTER] 2 [+] 5 [+] \(\to\) 15 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 15), filling the first ten-group with 2 moon jellies before placing the remaining 5 into Frame 2's top row. \(X = 15\) (1 full ten-group plus 1 full five-row).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.2: Completing the Double-Frame Solar Array
docs.text:
Your nature dome's rooftop charger has 16 mini solar tiles wired across two 10-slot mounting frames. How many more solar tiles do you need to snap in so both ten-groups are completely full at 20? On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), 16 has [1] in the Tens column and [6] in the Ones column—needing 4 more ones to regroup to 20.

Snap the 4 remaining solar tiles into the second tray: 16 [ENTER] 4 [+] \(\to\) 20 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20). Both frames are now 100% full at \(X = 20\) because \(6 + 4\) are ten-group partners!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.3: Combining Lunar Sample Canisters
docs.text:
Inside the clean-room airlock, Rover Tray A holds 9 sealed lunar dust canisters and Rover Tray B holds 8 canisters. How many canisters are ready for analysis? Because 9 is just 1 away from 10, borrow 1 canister from the 8 (splitting 8 into \(1 + 7\)) to complete the first ten-group!

Total the two canister trays: 9 [ENTER] 1 [+] 7 [+] \(\to\) 17 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 17), completing Frame 1 at 10 and leaving 7 in Frame 2 (\(X = 17\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.4: Five-Anchor Addition on the Bottom Wire
docs.text:
Your underwater docking bay already holds 12 waterproof camera drones (10 on Rail 1, and 2 red beads on Rail 2). A surface boat lowers 5 more camera drones down the cable. How many drones are in the bay now? On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), place 12 ([1] in Tens, [2] in Ones) in Row 1 and [5] in Row 0 of the Ones column to combine the ones (\(2 + 5 = 7\), giving 17)!

Add the 5 new drones to the bay tally: 12 [ENTER] 5 [+] \(\to\) 17 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 17), combining the two groups into 17 without ever touching the top rail of 10 (\(X = 17\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.5: Decomposing Teen Numbers on the Place Value Tray
docs.text:
A reef diver carries a mesh bag with 18 biodegradable coral-reef temperature tags (10 on Rail 1, and 8 on Rail 2: 5 red + 3 white). Along the outer reef wall, the diver clips 5 tags onto brain corals. How many tags are left in the mesh bag? On Rail 2, slide a whole group of 5 beads back to the right in one motion, leaving 3 beads on Rail 2 and all 10 on Rail 1!

Subtract the 5 attached reef tags: 18 [ENTER] 5 [-] \(\to\) 13 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 13), leaving 10 on Wire 1 and 3 on Wire 2 (\(X = 13\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.6: Splitting a Teen Number into Ten and Ones
docs.text:
A sea-floor basket holds 15 titanium diving weights. To store 10 weights in the main ballast locker and keep the rest on the workbench, how many single weights stay on the bench? On the Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), 15 is [1] in the Tens socket and [5] in the Ones socket.

Subtract the full bundle of 10 to isolate the ones: 15 [ENTER] 10 [-] \(\to\) 5 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 5), proving that taking 10 away from 15 leaves the 5 red beads on Wire 2!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.7: Clearing the Bottom Rail in One Sweep
docs.text:
A deep-sea sample rack holds 19 glowing hydrothermal vent tubes (10 on Rail 1, and 9 on Rail 2). Scientists transfer 8 of those tubes into the lab freezer. How many vent tubes remain in the sample rack? On Rail 2, sliding 8 beads back to the right leaves just 1 lonely red bead on the bottom wire alongside the full 10 on the top wire.

Subtract the 8 transferred tubes: 19 [ENTER] 8 [-] \(\to\) 11 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 11), leaving 10 on Wire 1 and 1 on Wire 2 (\(X = 11\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.8: Subtracting from a Full Twenty-Rack
docs.text:
A scuba gear locker holds a full rack of 20 compressed-air tanks across two rows of 10. A dive team checks out 7 tanks for an afternoon kelp-forest survey. How many tanks remain in the locker? On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), start with 20 ([2] Tens, [0] Ones) and regroup 1 ten into 10 ones so you can subtract 7 (\(10 - 7 = 3\), leaving 13).

Find the remaining scuba tanks on the rack: 20 [ENTER] 7 [-] \(\to\) 13 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 13). Even without counting, you know \(10 - 7 = 3\) on the bottom wire, plus the untouched 10 on the top wire gives \(X = 13\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.9: Measuring the Gap Between Desert Landmarks
docs.text:
On your trail map, the Ghost Gum tree stands at kilometer marker 15, and Red Sand Gap stands at kilometer marker 42. How far apart are these two landmarks? Remember that subtraction doesn't just mean "taking away"—on a number line, it measures the distance gap between two points! Mentally hop from 15 to 20 (\(+5\)), from 20 to 40 (\(+20\)), and from 40 to 42 (\(+2\)).

Calculate the exact gap on the stack: 42 [ENTER] 15 [-] \(\to\) 27 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 27), confirming the \(5 + 20 + 2 = 27\text{ km}\) trail interval (\(X = 27\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.10: Solar Rover Odometer Leap
docs.text:
Your solar-powered desert rover drives 35 kilometers across a dry salt flat in the morning, then rolls another 18 kilometers through red dunes in the afternoon. What does the odometer read at camp? On your Open Number Line, start at 35, use 5 of the 18 kilometers to reach round milestone 40, and leap the remaining 13 kilometers to 53!

Log the rover's full-day distance: 35 [ENTER] 18 [+] \(\to\) 53 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 53), bridging across decades 40 and 50 to land at \(X = 53\text{ km}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.11: Camp Water Tank Countdown
docs.text:
Your desert camp starts with a 50-liter solar water tank. Over two hot days on the trail, the crew drinks and cooks with 24 liters of water. How many liters remain in the tank? On your Open Number Line, start at 50, leap back 20 units to hit 30, and step back 4 more units to land on 26.

Subtract the 24 liters used on the trail: 50 [ENTER] 24 [-] \(\to\) 26 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 26), leaving \(X = 26\text{ liters}\) in the tank.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.12: Double-Zone Outback Tree Survey
docs.text:
A wildlife botanist counts 28 river red gums along the northern creek bed and 36 ghost gums across the southern gorge. How many native trees are mapped in all? On your Open Number Line, start at 28, hop \(+2\) to land on round decade 30, and then leap the remaining \(+34\) in one clean bound!

Combine the two tree surveys: 28 [ENTER] 36 [+] \(\to\) 64 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 64), landing squarely on \(X = 64\) native trees.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.13: Solar Viewer Nickel Tokens Ladder
docs.text:
At the solar telescope viewing deck, student astronomers count 5-cent tokens up to 50 cents. In 2-Stack mode, each tap of [+] drops another 5-cent group onto the stack: 5 [ENTER] 5 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 10.

In 2-Stack mode, run this sequence \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 5, X: 10). Successive taps of [+] step by 5s on the Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), advancing through 15, 20, 25, up to 50 cents (10 nickels = 50 cents).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.14: Planetarium Dime-Rod Ladder
docs.text:
To buy a new lunar filter, the astronomy club stacks 10-cent dimes up to 100 cents (one full dollar). In 2-Stack mode, each press of [+] adds another ten-rod until 10 rods snap together into a 100-flat: 10 [ENTER] 10 [+] \(\to\) 20.

In 2-Stack mode, run this sequence \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 10, X: 20). Successive taps of [+] advance by 10s until 10 rods assemble into a complete 100-flat (\(X = 100\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.15: Seven-Day Star-Watch Schedule with [g] [REP]
docs.text:
Observatory sky-surveys are planned in 7-day weekly cycles. In 4-Stack mode, fill the stack with 7 using [g] [REP] and step through 7 weeks of star-watch nights by tapping 7 [g] [REP] [+] [+].

In 4-Stack mode, tap 7 [g] [REP] [+] \(\to\) (T: 7, Z: 7, Y: 7, X: 14). Five more taps of [+] pull constant 7 from the top of the stack, climbing through 21, 28, 35, 42, to 49 days (7 weeks = 49 days).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.16: The Mystery of the Silent Zero Placeholders
docs.text:
A deep-space radio dish records a burst of 8 thousands and 4 tens of signal pulses—with 0 in the HUNDREDS socket and 0 in the ONES socket of your Place Value Studio (PV-01) Whole Numbers Tray. When you add \(8,000\) and \(40\) on the stack, why doesn't the number squash together into \(84\)?

Add the thousands and tens directly: 8000 [ENTER] 40 [+] \(\to\) 8040 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8040). The two 0 digit miniblocks act like placeholders holding the HUNDREDS and ONES sockets open so the 8 stays in the THOUSANDS column and the 4 stays in the TENS column!

Results: Thousands (\(1000\)): \(8\), Hundreds (\(100\)): \(0\), Tens (\(10\)): \(4\), Ones (\(1\)): \(0\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.17: Zooming Inside a Single Millimeter
docs.text:
Place value doesn't stop at the ONES socket! Switch to your Decimal Place Value Tray (PV-01: 1 • 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.001): moving right past the raised decimal point (•), each column divides by 10 into tenths (\(0.1\)), hundredths (\(0.01\)), and thousandths (\(0.001\)). A laser micrometer measures a telescope mirror thickness of \(345\) whole millimeters, plus \(6\) tenths (\(0.6\)) and \(7\) hundredths (\(0.07\)).

Sum the whole millimeters, tenths, and hundredths: 345 [ENTER] 0.6 [+] 0.07 [+] \(\to\) 345.67 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 345.67), assembling whole units, tenths, and hundredths into \(345.67\text{ mm}\).

Tenths place \(= 6\), Hundredths place \(= 7\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.18: Dimes and Pennies as Decimal Blocks
docs.text:
In the observatory gift shop, a glow-in-the-dark Saturn sticker costs 4 dimes (\(0.40\)) and 7 pennies (\(0.07\)). Because a dime is \(\frac{1}{10}\) of a dollar and a penny is \(\frac{1}{100}\) of a dollar, pocket change is a real-life decimal place-value kit!

Add the dimes and pennies together: 0.40 [ENTER] 0.07 [+] \(\to\) 0.47 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.47), combining 4 dimes and 7 pennies into \(\$0.47\).

Results: Dimes (Tenths) \(= 4\), Pennies (Hundredths) \(= 7\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.19: Combining Planetarium Seating Bowls
docs.text:
The science center's outdoor star-amphitheater seats \(10,000\) sky-watchers, and the indoor laser-dome seats \(2,500\) more. Combine these two large place-value blocks on the stack to find the total seating capacity.

Total the outdoor and indoor seating capacities: 10000 [ENTER] 2500 [+] \(\to\) 12500 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 12500), combining both venues into \(12,500\) seats.

Results: Ten-thousands \(= 1\), Thousands \(= 2\), Hundreds \(= 5\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.20: Eclipse Watchers Across Three Cities
docs.text:
During a total solar eclipse, three neighboring towns log \(400,000\), \(50,000\), and \(200\) sky-watchers wearing eclipse glasses. Combine the three place-value tiers on the stack and notice which columns stay at zero!

Combine the three sky-watcher tiers: 400000 [ENTER] 50000 [+] 200 [+] \(\to\) 450200 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 450200), building \(450,200\) with zero thousands, zero tens, and zero ones.

Results: Hundred-thousands \(= 4\), Ten-thousands \(= 5\), Hundreds \(= 2\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.21: Human Heartbeats in a Full Decade
docs.text:
At a steady resting pulse of 80 beats per minute, your heart beats about \(42,048,000\) times in a single year! What happens to every digit's place-value column when you multiply by \(10\text{ years}\) to find your heartbeats across a full decade?

Multiply the annual heartbeat count by 10 years: 42048000 [ENTER] 10 [×] \(\to\) 420480000 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 420480000), shifting every digit one column to the left to reach \(420,480,000\) beats!

Decompose Hundred-Millions: [ENTER] 100000000 [PV] \(\longrightarrow X = \mathbf{4}\) (4 hundred-million heartbeats).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.22: Counting Water Drops in an Olympic Pool
docs.text:
An Olympic-sized swimming pool holds \(2,500,000\text{ liters}\) of water, and every single liter holds about \(20,000\text{ water drops}\). Multiply those two giant numbers on the stack to discover how many drops fill the pool, then spotlight the ten-billions digit!

Multiply the liters by drops per liter: 2500000 [ENTER] 20000 [×] \(\to\) 50000000000 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 50000000000), revealing an astonishing \(50,000,000,000\) (\(50\text{ billion}\)) water drops!

Decompose Ten-Billions: [ENTER] 10000000000 [PV] \(\longrightarrow X = \mathbf{5}\) (5 ten-billion drops).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.23: Spotlight on Saturn's Giant Rings
docs.text:
Through the observatory's main telescope, Saturn's glittering ring system spans \(282,000\text{ kilometers}\) from edge to edge—wide enough to line up more than 22 Earths side by side! Use [PV] to spotlight the hundred-thousands, ten-thousands, and thousands digits: 282000 [ENTER] 100000 [PV] 10000 [PV] 1000 [PV] \(\rightarrow\) 2.

Place Value Spotlight: Park 282,000 in Register \(Y\) with 282000 [ENTER]. Because [PV] never erases Register \(Y\), you can inspect each column in a chain: 100000 [PV] yields 2 hundred-thousands, 10000 [PV] yields 8 ten-thousands, and 1000 [PV] yields 2 thousands (Y: 282000, X: 2).

Results: Hundred-Thousands \(= 2\), Ten-Thousands \(= 8\), Thousands \(= 2\) (a palindrome pattern: \(2\text{-}8\text{-}2\)!).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 3.24: Sharing Nearly a Million Library Books
docs.text:
A city library network holds \(875,420\) adventure and science books shared equally across 12 branch libraries. First, spotlight the ten-thousands digit (875420 [ENTER] 10000 [PV] \(\longrightarrow X = \mathbf{7}\)). Then calculate the average number of books per branch: 875420 [ENTER] 12 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 72,951.66667.

This sequence yields an average branch collection of \(\mathbf{72,951.67\text{ books}}\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 72951.66667).

docs.title: Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations & Skip-Counting Ladders — Extended Worked Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 04 of From Blocks to the Stack (30 Worked Practice Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.1: Remapping the Twenty-Four Tiles into Four Rows
docs.text:
Can those exact same 24 tiles form a chunkier rectangle without any leftovers? Rearrange your Cobalt Blue and White tiles into 4 rows with 6 tiles in each row to model a 4-by-6 arcade button grid.

Find the total button count on the stack: 4 [ENTER] 6 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 24. This sequence lifts the 4 rows into Register \(Y\), multiplies by 6 buttons per row, and displays \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 24)\) buttons (\(X = 24\)). Pause and notice: \(3 \times 8\) and \(4 \times 6\) look like completely different rectangles, yet both hold the exact same 24 tiles!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.2: The Five-Column Pixel Sprite Matrix
docs.text:
In your game studio, you design a glowing treasure-map icon made of 7 rows with 5 Radiant Gold pixel tiles in each row. Because every row is a friendly Five-Anchor, you can count by fives (\(5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35\)) or multiply the rectangle in one strike!

Multiply the 7 rows by 5 pixels per row: 7 [ENTER] 5 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 35. This sequence holds the 7 rows in Register \(Y\), multiplies by 5 pixels per row, and evaluates directly to \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 35)\) pixels (\(X = 35\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.3: Six-Row Geode Display Case
docs.text:
A rock-and-mineral collector builds a wooden wall case with 6 shelves and 9 glowing crystal compartments on each shelf. On your desk mat, build a smaller \(2 \times 9 = 18\)-tile starter section first, then imagine stacking three of those \(2 \times 9\) sections together!

Scale the calculation to all 6 shelves on the stack: 6 [ENTER] 9 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 54. This sequence loads 6 shelves into Register \(Y\) and multiplies by 9 compartments, yielding \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 54)\) crystals (\(X = 54\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.4: The Classic Eight-by-Eight Chessboard Square
docs.text:
Why is \(64\) called a square number? Because when a rectangle has the exact same number of rows and columns (\(8\) rows of \(8\) tiles), it forms a geometric square! Build a \(4 \times 4 = 16\)-tile checkerboard corner using alternating white and slate tiles on your desk mat, then scale up to a full \(8 \times 8\) chessboard on the SC-6.

Compute the full \(8 \times 8\) board area: 8 [ENTER] 8 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 64. This sequence lifts 8 into Register \(Y\) and multiplies by 8 to drop the stack to \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 64)\) squares (\(X = 64\)). (Shortcut tip: Since both factors are 8, you can also just type 8 [ENTER] [×] to square 8 in three taps!)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.5: Hydroponic Space-Garden Tower
docs.text:
Inside a lunar habitat greenhouse, a vertical hydroponic rack holds 12 columns with 4 lettuce pods in each column. Snap together 3 columns of 4 tiles (\(12\) tiles) on your desk mat—then notice that 12 columns is just four of those \(3 \times 4\) blocks side by side!

Find the pod capacity across all 12 columns: 12 [ENTER] 4 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 48. This sequence parks the 12 columns in Register \(Y\) and multiplies by 4 pods per column, leaving \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 48)\) plants thriving in the lunar greenhouse (\(X = 48\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.6: Granite Cliff Anchor Ropes by Fours
docs.text:
To reach a ledge high on a granite cliff, a rescue climber clips an anchor bolt every 4 vertical meters. Build 4 four-tile rungs (\(16\) tiles) on your desk mat and slide your finger up the rungs: 4, 8, 12, 16 meters.

Find the total rope height at the 9th anchor bolt: 4 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 36. Pressing 4 [g] [REP] loads the 4-meter step across the entire stack, and 8 rhythmic taps of [+] climb to \((T: 4, Z: 4, Y: 4, X: 36)\) meters (\(X = 36\text{ meters}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.7: High-Altitude Shelter Packs by Sixes
docs.text:
Eight mountain huts are stocked with 6 emergency solar blankets each. On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), place [6] in Row 1 and [6] in Row 0 (\(6 + 6 = 12\), regrouping a Gold [+1] carry token to Tens) to see the first two huts.

Step through all 8 mountain huts with Constant Repeat: 6 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 48. Seeding the stack with 6 [g] [REP] keeps 6 locked in Register \(T\), while 7 steady taps of [+] climb to \((T: 6, Z: 6, Y: 6, X: 48)\) solar blankets (\(X = 48\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.8: Glacier Rope-Bridge Carabiners by Eights
docs.text:
To cross a crevasse field, the rescue team rigs 8 rope-bridge spans, using 8 locking steel carabiners on every span. Assemble 2 rows of 8 counting tiles (\(16\) tiles) on your desk mat to see the first two spans.

Climb the 8s ladder across all 8 spans: 8 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 64. Replicating 8 with 8 [g] [REP] and tapping [+] 7 times marches through the 8s table (\(16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56\)) to \((T: 8, Z: 8, Y: 8, X: 64)\) carabiners (\(X = 64\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.9: Summit Radio Beacons and the Magic Nine-Pattern
docs.text:
Nine mountain summits each broadcast 9 emergency weather pulses per minute. On your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), compare adding [9] to adding [1] Ten and stepping the Ones digit back by 1 (\(9 + 9 = 18\))!

Climb all 9 summits with Constant Repeat: 9 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 81. Priming all four registers with 9 [g] [REP] and tapping [+] 8 times reaches \((T: 9, Z: 9, Y: 9, X: 81)\) pulses (\(X = 81\)). Watch the screen as you climb (\(09, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81\)): the tens digit climbs up by 1 while the ones digit steps down by 1, so the two digits always add up to 9!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.10: Helicopter Dozens Ladder to One Gross
docs.text:
A rescue helicopter drops a supply crate holding 12 boxes of hand-warmers, with 12 warmers in every box (a dozen dozens, called 1 gross!). Snap together a 12-tile strip on your desk and add a second 12-tile strip to reach 24.

Step through all twelve dozens on the stack: key in 12 [g] [REP] to seed all four registers \((T: 12, Z: 12, Y: 12, X: 12)\), followed by 11 rhythmic taps of [+]. The stack advances through every dozen (\(24, 36, 48 \dots 132\)) until reaching 144 warming packets (\(X = 144\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.11: Five-Stage Compound Pulley Doubler
docs.text:
A cliff-rescue winch starts with a \(3\text{ kN}\) pulling force. Every time you clip on another compound pulley block, the pulling force doubles! Start with 3 tiles on your desk and double them to 6, 12, and 24 tiles.

Double 3 through 5 pulley stages ([ENTER] [+]): 3 [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 96. Tapping [ENTER] [+] five times rockets through \(6 \to 12 \to 24 \to 48 \to 96\), leaving \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 96)\text{ kN}\) on the screen (\(X = 96\text{ kN}\))—32 times stronger than the bare rope!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.12: Trail Mix Energy Bars in Eight-Packs
docs.text:
Your expedition kitchen bakes 75 oat-and-honey trail bars and seals them into waterproof pouches holding 8 bars each. How many full 8-packs can you seal, and how many bars are left over for the cooks to snack on?

Pack all 75 bars into pouches of 8: 75 [ENTER] 8 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 9. Integer division loads quotient 9 into Register \(X\) and remainder 3 into Register \(Y\) with inline trace \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 3, X: 9)\) (\(Q = 9\text{ pouches}\), \(R = 3\text{ leftover bars}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.13: The Four-Person Wilderness Tent Dilemma
docs.text:
Twenty-nine student explorers hike up to base camp for an overnight star-watch, and each expedition tent sleeps 4 campers. When you divide 29 by 4, why isn't the answer just the quotient?

Find the tent count on the stack: 29 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 7. The stack drops into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 1, X: 7)\). Seven tents hold 28 campers, leaving \(Y = 1\) camper still standing outside! Because you can't leave a friend out in the cold, any remainder \(> 0\) means you must pitch \(7 + 1 = \mathbf{8\text{ tents}}\) (\(Q = 7\text{ full tents}\), \(R = 1\text{ camper}\), total \(= 8\text{ tents}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.14: Cutting Parachute Cord from a Master Spool
docs.text:
To rig model recovery parachutes, you cut \(35\text{ cm}\) shroud lines from a \(250\text{ cm}\) spool of braided nylon cord. How many full \(35\text{ cm}\) lines can you cut, and how many centimeters of cord are left on the spool?

Divide the \(250\text{ cm}\) spool into \(35\text{ cm}\) lines: 250 [ENTER] 35 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 7. Tapping [g] [÷R] yields \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 5, X: 7)\), giving 7 full parachute lines with a \(5\text{ cm}\) scrap left over (\(Q = 7\text{ lines}\), \(R = 5\text{ cm leftover}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.15: Nine-Grid Meteorite Display Trays
docs.text:
The planetarium curator sorts 115 iron meteorite fragments into \(3 \times 3\) display boxes that hold 9 fragments each. How many complete 9-fragment boxes can be filled?

Package all 115 meteorites into 9-slot boxes: 115 [ENTER] 9 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 12. The display resolves into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 7, X: 12)\), filling 12 complete display boxes with 7 fragments left over for the touch-table (\(Q = 12\text{ boxes}\), \(R = 7\text{ fragments}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.16: Whitewater River Rafting Boats
docs.text:
Forty-six adventure campers arrive at the river dock, and each inflatable whitewater raft holds 7 paddlers. How many rafts get completely filled, and how many rafts must launch so everyone gets down the river?

Divide all 46 campers across the 7-passenger rafts: 46 [ENTER] 7 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 6. Integer division drops the registers to \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 4, X: 6)\); since the 4 remaining campers in Register \(Y\) need a boat too, the river guides launch \(6 + 1 = \mathbf{7\text{ rafts}}\) (\(Q = 6\text{ full rafts}\), \(R = 4\text{ campers}\), total \(= 7\text{ rafts}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.17: Building Four-Wheel All-Terrain Rovers
docs.text:
The robotics workshop bin holds 78 knobby rubber tires for 4-wheeled mini-rovers. Unlike tents or rafts (where leftover people need an extra vehicle), can 2 leftover tires build a whole 4-wheel rover on their own?

Sort all 78 tires into 4-wheel sets: 78 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 19. The stack drops into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 2, X: 19)\), proving you can build 19 complete 4-wheel rovers with 2 spare tires left in the parts bin (\(Q = 19\text{ rovers}\), \(R = 2\text{ spare tires}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.18: Weather-Station Four-Battery Packs
docs.text:
Each automated forest weather station runs on a 4-battery pack, and your field kit has 42 fresh rechargeable AA batteries. How many stations can you power up completely?

Check how many 4-battery packs 42 batteries can fill: 42 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 10. Integer division leaves \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 2, X: 10)\) on the screen: 10 weather stations get full 4-battery packs, leaving 2 spare batteries in your backpack (\(Q = 10\text{ packs}\), \(R = 2\text{ batteries}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.19: Eight-Pack Glow-Stick Bundles for Cave Explorers
docs.text:
Before entering a limestone cavern, the expedition leader bundles 175 chem-light glow-sticks into team packs of 8 sticks each. How many full 8-packs are ready, and how many extra glow-sticks go to the lead guide?

Divide all 175 glow-sticks into packs of 8: 175 [ENTER] 8 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 21. The operational stack separates \(175 \div 8\) into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 7, X: 21)\), making 21 full team packs with 7 extra sticks (\(Q = 21\text{ packs}\), \(R = 7\text{ glow-sticks}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.20: Claw-Bot Servos & Bumper Sensors
docs.text:
Your grabbing claw-bot needs 5 high-torque digital servos at \(\$12\) each and 4 bumper touch-sensors at \(\$8\) each. How much does the whole sensor-and-servo upgrade cost?

Combine the servo and sensor subtotals on the stack: 5 [ENTER] 12 [×] 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 92. Multiplying \(5 \times 12\) stores \(\$60\) while \(4 \times 8 = \$32\) evaluates in Register \(X\); tapping [+] fuses both subtotals into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 92)\), giving \(\mathbf{\$92}\) (\(X = 92\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.21: 3D-Printed Mini-Drone Frame Fundraiser
docs.text:
For the school maker fair, your club 3D-prints 45 mini-drone frames that sell for \(\$2\) each, and you spend \(\$28\) on spools of neon PLA filament. What is your club's net profit after paying for the filament?

Find the net fundraiser profit on the stack: 45 [ENTER] 2 [×] 28 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 62. Evaluating \(45 \times 2 = \$90\) and immediately subtracting the \(\$28\) filament cost leaves \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 62)\), earning \(\mathbf{\$62}\) for the club (\(X = 62\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.22: Electric Go-Kart Frame Rails & Corner Brackets
docs.text:
To build a solar go-kart frame, your team orders 40 feet of aluminum frame tubing at \(\$6\) per foot, plus 5 heavy-duty corner-bracket packs at \(\$14\) per pack. Chain both products and add them on the stack!

Calculate the combined go-kart frame order: 40 [ENTER] 6 [×] 5 [ENTER] 14 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 310. Multiplying \(40 \times 6 = \$240\) lifts automatically to Register \(Z\) while you compute \(5 \times 14 = \$70\), and the final [+] drops the stack into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 310)\) (\(X = \$310\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.23: The Robot Pit-Crew Bolt Bin Tracker
docs.text:
Your team's pit-crew organizer bin starts tournament morning with 850 hex bolts. During round-one builds, 145 bolts are used on new bumpers, and then 88 spare bolts from a retired practice bot are recycled back into the bin. How many hex bolts are in the bin now?

Track the bolt bin on the stack: 850 [ENTER] 145 [-] 88 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 793. Subtracting 145 leaves 705 bolts, and adding the 88 recycled bolts leaves \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 793)\) bolts ready for the finals (\(X = 793\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.24: Three-Part Arcade Cabinet Wiring Kit
docs.text:
To wire a custom classroom arcade cabinet, you buy three batches of parts: 120 LED jumper wires at \(\$3\) per pack, 85 arcade micro-switches at \(\$2\) each, and 40 braided USB cables at \(\$4\) each. Watch the stack accumulate all three products in a chain!

Sum all three arcade wiring batches on the stack: 120 [ENTER] 3 [×] 85 [ENTER] 2 [×] [+] 40 [ENTER] 4 [×] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 690. The stack evaluates jumper wires (\(120 \times 3 = \$360\)), adds switches (\(85 \times 2 = \$170 \to \$530\)), and adds cables (\(40 \times 4 = \$160\)) to finish at \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 690)\) (\(X = \$690\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.25: Packaging Brass Standoffs for Robot Brains
docs.text:
Four maker tables each build 24 microcontroller boards, and every board needs 2 brass standoff posts. If standoffs come in bags of 15, how many full bags do you empty, and how many extra standoffs do you need from one more bag?

Chain the multiplication and remainder division on the stack: 4 [ENTER] 24 [×] 2 [×] 15 [g] [÷R] \(\rightarrow\) 12. Chaining \(4 \times 24 \times 2\) produces 192 standoffs, and tapping 15 [g] [÷R] drops the stack into \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 12, X: 12)\): 12 full bags are used, plus 12 standoffs from a 13th bag (\(Q = 12\text{ bags}\), \(R = 12\text{ standoffs}\), open 13 bags).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.26: The Ninety-Nine Overshoot Shortcut
docs.text:
When a tournament timer flashes \(45 \times 99\), don't do long multiplication! Ninety-nine groups of 45 is just 100 groups of 45 minus 1 group of 45 (\(45 \times 100 - 45\)).

Run the \(100\times\) minus \(1\times\) shortcut on the stack: 45 [ENTER] 100 [×] 45 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 4455. Keying 45 [ENTER] 100 [×] gives \(4,500\), and subtracting one group of 45 [-] immediately lands on \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4455)\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.27: Young Gauss's Staircase Pairing Trick
docs.text:
What is the sum of every whole number from \(1\) to \(20\) (\(1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + 20\))? Build a 4-step staircase with 10 counting tiles (\(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\)), build a second identical 10-tile staircase, flip it upside down, and snap the two staircases together! They form a solid \(4 \times 5 = 20\) rectangle—and half of that rectangle is \(10\)! For \(1\) to \(20\), two staircases snap into a \(20 \times 21\) rectangle, and half of that area is the sum!

Evaluate Gauss's pairing rectangle for \(1\) through \(20\): 20 [ENTER] 21 [×] 2 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 210. Entering 20 [ENTER] 21 [×] builds the \(420\) double-staircase rectangle, and pressing 2 [÷] cuts it in half to \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 210)\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 4.28: The Secret of Squaring Numbers Ending in Five
docs.text:
Here is a mental-math party trick that looks like wizardry: to square any two-digit number ending in 5 (like \(35^2\)), take the tens digit (\(3\)), multiply it by the next whole number up (\(3 \times 4 = 12\)), and stick \(25\) on the end: \(1,225\)! Why does it work? Because \((30 + 5) \times (30 + 5) = 30 \times 30 + 2 \times (30 \times 5) + 25 = 30 \times 40 + 25 = 1,200 + 25\)!

Verify \(35^2\) on the stack: 35 [ENTER] 35 [×] \(\rightarrow\) 1225. Keying 35 [ENTER] 35 [×] (or simply 35 [ENTER] [×] without re-typing 35!) yields \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1225)\). Now try \(65^2\) in your head (\(6 \times 7 = 42 \to 4,225\)) and check it with 65 [ENTER] [×]!
