docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.1: Compound Coin Toss: Three Consecutive Heads
docs.text:
Triple Coin Toss Tournament Tiebreaker: A match tiebreaker requires flipping three consecutive heads with a balanced coin (\(P = (1/2)^3\)). Determine the compound probability of three consecutive heads. Arrange a 3-tier binary tree using two-color counters. Out of 8 possible paths (\(\text{HHH}, \text{HHT}, \dots, \text{TTT}\)), exactly 1 path yields three consecutive heads.

Cube the single-flip probability (\(0.5^3\)) on the SC-6: 0.5 [ENTER] [3] [g] [yˣ] \(\to\) 0.125 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.125). Every flip cuts your surviving branch in half (\(1/2 \to 1/4 \to 1/8\)), leaving a \(\mathbf{0.1250}\) (\(12.5\%\)) chance of three heads in a row.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.2: Sum of Two Dice: Rolling an 11 or 12
docs.text:
High-Rollers Two-Dice Roll: Two dice are rolled simultaneously in the final round. The sum is 11 for two combinations (\((5,6), (6,5)\)) and 12 for one combination (\((6,6)\)). Find the probability of rolling an 11 or 12. Map the \(6 \times 6\) grid of 36 equally likely outcomes. Highlight the 3 winning combinations in the top-right corner.

Find the decimal odds for those 3 corner cells out of 36: [3] [ENTER] 36 [÷] \(\to\) 0.0833333333 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.0833). Notice why 11 is twice as likely as 12—rolling \((5,6)\) or \((6,5)\) gives you two ways to make 11, while \((6,6)\) is the lone path to 12 (\(3/36 = 1/12 \approx \mathbf{8.33\%}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.3: Complementary Probability
docs.text:
Complementary Event Probability: The championship venue weather report indicates a \(35\%\) probability of rain (\(P = 0.35\)). Determine the complementary probability of fair weather (\(P' = 1 - P\)). On the 10-sector probability spinner, \(3.5\) sectors represent rain while \(6.5\) sectors represent fair weather, illustrating the complement rule \(1 - P\).

Subtract the rain chance from the whole certainty of \(1\): [1] [ENTER] 0.35 [-] \(\to\) 0.65 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.65). Because rain and dry skies partition 100% of the possibilities, the complementary chance of fair weather is \(\mathbf{0.6500}\) (\(65\%\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.4: Prime Fortress Barbican Trap Door: Primality of 91
docs.text:
The fortress barbican is guarded by a deceptive trap door set to trigger on composite impostor codes. Evaluate candidate code 91. Take 21 tiles (\(7 \times 3\)) and arrange them into 3 rows of 7 with zero gaps to demonstrate composite grouping. Now test 91 on your SC-6 against prime factor 7 (\(91 \div 7 = 13\)), exposing 91 as composite.

Unmask the famous prime impostor 91 on your SC-6: 91 [PRIME] \(\to\) 91 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 91). Even though 91 looks odd and dodges 2, 3, and 5, it is secretly \(7 \times 13\) (\(70 + 21\))—so the status line flashes COMPOSITE while preserving \(\mathbf{91}\) in Register \(X\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.5: Prime Fortress Moat Portcullis: Primality of 143
docs.text:
The iron portcullis over the fortress moat evaluates candidate 143. Determine if the credential is prime or composite. Take 22 tiles (\(11 \times 2\)) to see how groups of 11 assemble into neat rectangles. For 143, note that \(143 \div 11 = 13\), confirming factor pairs beyond 1 and itself.

Test 143 on the SC-6: 143 [PRIME] \(\to\) 143 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 143). Notice the middle digit of 143 is the sum of its outer digits (\(1 + 3 = 4\)), the classic hallmark of a multiple of 11 (\(11 \times 13 = 143\))—flashing COMPOSITE and keeping \(\mathbf{143}\) in Register \(X\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.6: Prime Fortress Armory Key: Prime Factorization of 72
docs.text:
The fortress armory lock requires the exact prime decomposition string of tumbler code 72. Decompose 72 into prime factors. Take three Blue 2-blocks (\(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\)) and two Amber 3-blocks (\(3 \times 3 = 9\)). Stack them vertically on the Prime Factor Studio stage: their combined height (\(3 \times 12.64\text{ mm} + 2 \times 20.04\text{ mm} = 78.00\text{ mm}\)) aligns squarely with the 72 mark on the comparator wall (\(8 \times 9 = 72\)).

Reveal the prime building blocks of 72 with [g] [FACT]: 72 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 72 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 72). The screen displays 2³ × 3², matching your three Blue 2-blocks and two Amber 3-blocks (\(8 \times 9 = 72\)) to disengage the armory lock!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.7: Prime Fortress Citadel Key: Prime Factorization of 210
docs.text:
The inner citadel vault is sealed with master product code 210. Find its complete prime factor decomposition. Select one 2-block, one 3-block, one 5-block, and one 7-block. Stacking these four distinct prime towers models the square-free product \(2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 210\).

Factor 210 on the SC-6 display: 210 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 210 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 210). The screen displays 2 × 3 × 5 × 7—the product of the first four prime numbers (called a primorial)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.8: Prime Fortress High Tower Vault Key: Prime Factorization of 504
docs.text:
The high observatory tower is protected by an astronomical key code of 504. Determine its prime factor components. Factor 504 using prime blocks: three 2-blocks (\(2^3 = 8\)), two 3-blocks (\(3^2 = 9\)), and one 7-block (\(7\)). Product: \(8 \times 9 \times 7 = 504\).

Extract the prime factor tree for 504: 504 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 504 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 504). The display reveals 2³ × 3² × 7, showing that 504 is simply the armory code 72 (\(2^3 \times 3^2\)) multiplied by one Red 7-block!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.9: Fortress Twin Bastions Gear Synchronization: \(\gcd(48, 72)\)
docs.text:
Twin drawbridge drive winches with 48 teeth and 72 teeth must mesh via a common drive gear. Find the greatest common factor \(\gcd(48, 72)\). Model \(48 = 2^4 \times 3\) and \(72 = 2^3 \times 3^2\). Place shared prime blocks into the central intersection well: three 2-blocks and one 3-block \(\implies 2^3 \times 3 = 24\).

Find the largest shared gear step on the stack: 48 [ENTER] 72 [GCF] \(\to\) 24 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 24). A drive gear with \(\mathbf{24\text{ teeth}}\) turns the 48-tooth winch in exactly 2 rotations and the 72-tooth winch in 3 rotations without slipping a single tooth.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.10: Fortress Water Gate Sluice Synchronization: \(\gcd(84, 140)\)
docs.text:
Two hydraulic sluice floodgates operate on cycles of 84 seconds and 140 seconds. Find the greatest common synchronization interval \(\gcd(84, 140)\). Factor \(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(140 = 2^2 \times 5 \times 7\). Shared intersection: two 2-blocks and one 7-block \(\implies 2^2 \times 7 = 28\).

Compute \(\gcd(84, 140)\) using the [GCF] key: 84 [ENTER] 140 [GCF] \(\to\) 28 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 28). Both floodgate timers divide cleanly into \(\mathbf{28\text{-second}}\) beats (\(84 = 3 \times 28\) and \(140 = 5 \times 28\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.11: Fortress Sentry Patrol Synchronization: \(\operatorname{lcm}(15, 20)\)
docs.text:
Two rampart sentry patrols cycle every 15 minutes and 20 minutes respectively. Find the least common multiple \(\operatorname{lcm}(15, 20)\) when both sentries meet at the gate. Model \(15 = 3 \times 5\) and \(20 = 2^2 \times 5\). The union takes maximum powers: two 2-blocks, one 3-block, and one 5-block \(\implies 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60\). Stacking blocks aligns with mark 60.

Evaluate the patrol meeting interval with [f] [LCM]: 15 [ENTER] 20 [f] [LCM] \(\to\) 60 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 60). After 4 laps for the 15-minute sentry and 3 laps for the 20-minute sentry, both guards meet at the gate every \(\mathbf{60\text{ minutes}}\) (\(1\text{ hour}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.12: Fortress Signal Beacon Cycle: \(\operatorname{lcm}(12, 18)\)
docs.text:
Two optical signal beacons on the fortress bastions flash at intervals of 12 seconds and 18 seconds. Find the least common interval \(\operatorname{lcm}(12, 18)\) when both flash in unison. Decompose \(12 = 2^2 \times 3\) and \(18 = 2 \times 3^2\). The union of prime blocks takes two 2-blocks and two 3-blocks \(\implies 4 \times 9 = 36\).

Calculate the synchronized flash cycle on the stack: 12 [ENTER] 18 [f] [LCM] \(\to\) 36 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 36). Beacon A flashes 3 times and Beacon B flashes 2 times to light up the night sky together every \(\mathbf{36\text{ seconds}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.13: Fortress Supply Depot Allocation: Euclidean Division \(148 \div 32\)
docs.text:
In the fortress provisions depot, 148 ration packs are organized into standard field cases holding 32 packs each. Find the number of full cases packed and remaining loose packs using [g] [÷R]. Docking 1, 4, and 8 on your Place Value Tray (PV-01) (or modeling a smaller proportional batch like \(14 \div 3 = 4\text{ R }2\) with your 24 Counting Tiles first), grouping 148 into sets of 32 fills 4 cases (\(4 \times 32 = 128\)) and leaves 20 packs remaining.

Compute the quotient and remainder in a single tap: 148 [ENTER] 32 [g] [÷R] \(\to\) 4 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 20, X: 4). Instead of a messy decimal (\(4.625\)), Register \(X\) gives you 4 full cases while Register \(Y\) hands you the 20 leftover packs directly!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.14: Fortress Treasury Safe Cipher Wheel: \(\gcd(24, 36)\)
docs.text:
The fortress treasury safe wheel requires identifying the greatest shared factor of 24 and 36 to engage the master locking tumblers. List all divisors: for 24: \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24\}\); for 36: \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36\}\). The shared common factor set is \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12\}\), with greatest factor 12.

Confirm the greatest common factor on the SC-6: 24 [ENTER] 36 [GCF] \(\to\) 12 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 12). The largest locking step shared by both safe wheels is 12.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.15: Median of an Even Dataset
docs.text:
Environmental Temperature Monitoring: Six ambient temperatures are recorded: \(68, 72, 74, 76, 80, 84^\circ\text{F}\). Find the median temperature (average of two central elements 74 and 76). Line up six Counting Tiles in ascending order. Because \(n = 6\) is even, there is no single middle tile; average the middle pair (74 and 76) to find their midpoint: \(\frac{74+76}{2} = 75^\circ\text{F}\).

Evaluate the even-sample median on your SC-6: [g] [CLΣ] 68 [Σ+] 72 [Σ+] 74 [Σ+] 76 [Σ+] 80 [Σ+] 84 [Σ+] [f] [MED] \(\to\) 75 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 6, X: 75). The SC-6 automatically sorts all \(n=6\) readings and averages the middle pair (\(74\) and \(76\)) to report \(\mathbf{75.00^\circ\text{F}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.16: Mode of a Shoe Size Survey
docs.text:
Footwear Inventory Survey: Shoe sizes collected from 8 customers: \(6, 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10\). Find the statistical mode (most frequent size). Stack Counting Tiles for each shoe size. Size 7 forms the tallest column with 3 tiles, visually standing out as the statistical mode.

Extract the mode from the statistical registers: [g] [CLΣ] [6] [Σ+] [7] [Σ+] [7] [Σ+] [7] [Σ+] [8] [Σ+] [8] [Σ+] [9] [Σ+] 10 [Σ+] [g] [MODE] \(\to\) 7 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 8, X: 7). For a shoe store manager, the mode (size 7) is more useful than the mean because you can't stock a fractional shoe size!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.17: Range of High Temperatures
docs.text:
Weather Station Spread Analysis: Weekly maximum temperatures: \(62, 65, 78, 81, 74, 69, 85^\circ\text{F}\). Calculate the temperature range (\(\max - \min = 85 - 62\)). Mark the minimum temperature (\(62^\circ\)) and maximum temperature (\(85^\circ\)) on a number line. The span between the two extremes measures \(23^\circ\).

Calculate the weekly spread using [RNG]: [g] [CLΣ] 62 [Σ+] 65 [Σ+] 78 [Σ+] 81 [Σ+] 74 [Σ+] 69 [Σ+] 85 [Σ+] [RNG] \(\to\) 23 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 23). Even though the temperatures were entered out of order, the SC-6 finds the coolest (\(62^\circ\)) and warmest (\(85^\circ\)) days to report a \(\mathbf{23.00^\circ\text{F}}\) range.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.18: Interquartile Range of Daily Rainfall
docs.text:
Precipitation Spread: Weekly rainfall measurements: \(0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.5\text{ inches}\). Find the interquartile range (\(Q_3 - Q_1\)). Using the SC-6 exclusive-median quartile method (matching Big Ideas Math), excluding the median (\(0.6\)) leaves the lower half (\(0.1, 0.2, 0.4\)) with midpoint \(Q_1 = 0.20\) and the upper half (\(0.9, 1.2, 1.5\)) with midpoint \(Q_3 = 1.20\), giving \(\text{IQR} = 1.20 - 0.20 = 1.00\text{ inch}\).

Compute the middle-50% spread directly with [IQR]: [g] [CLΣ] 0.1 [Σ+] 0.2 [Σ+] 0.4 [Σ+] 0.6 [Σ+] 0.9 [Σ+] 1.2 [Σ+] 1.5 [Σ+] [IQR] \(\to\) 1 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1). Unlike the full range, the interquartile range (\(\mathbf{1.00\text{ inch}}\)) ignores the driest and stormiest outlier days to show how typical rainfall varies.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.19: Mean Absolute Deviation of a 5-Point Dataset
docs.text:
Sensor Error Analysis: A 5-point dataset: \(10, 15, 20, 25, 30\) has mean \(\bar{x} = 20.0\). Deviations from mean are \(|-10|, |-5|, |0|, |+5|, |+10|\). Sum of deviations \(= 30\). Find the Mean Absolute Deviation (\(\text{MAD} = 30 / 5 = 6.0\)). Lay out the points on a number line. Measure the distance from each point to the center mark 20: \(10 + 5 + 0 + 5 + 10 = 30\). Dividing by 5 yields the average distance from center.

Find the Mean Absolute Deviation on the SC-6: [g] [CLΣ] 10 [Σ+] 15 [Σ+] 20 [Σ+] 25 [Σ+] 30 [Σ+] [g] [MAD] \(\to\) 6 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 6). On average, each sensor reading sits 6 units away from the balance point of 20.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.20: Frequency of Score 85
docs.text:
Scorecard Frequency Binning: In survey dataset \(70, 75, 80, 80, 85, 85, 85, 90, 90, 95\), accumulate observation 85 and inspect active sample counter. Place a Counting Tile into the score 85 column as the calculator logs the entry into the statistical registers.

Log the observation into [Σ+]: 85 [Σ+] \(\to\) 1 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1). Every time you press [Σ+], Register \(X\) shows the updated sample count \(n\) so you never lose your place in a long list of numbers.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.21: Subtracting a Negative Number
docs.text:
Evaluate \(12 - (-18)\). Try a tabletop example with two-color counters by placing positive yellow counters and introducing zero pairs (1 yellow \(+1\) paired with 1 crimson \(-1\)). Removing the negative crimson counters leaves both sets of positive yellow counters (\(12 + 18 = 30\)).

Key in \(12 - (-18)\) using [+/-] and [-]: 12 [ENTER] 18 [+/-] [-] \(\to\) 30 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 30). Taking away an 18-point penalty has the exact same effect as awarding 18 bonus points (\(12 + 18 = \mathbf{30}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.22: Multiplying Signed Numbers (Negative times Negative)
docs.text:
Evaluate \((-7) \times (-8)\). On a number line, facing the negative direction and walking backward reverses your orientation \(180^\circ\) twice, moving you forward into positive territory to \(+56\).

Multiply the two negative factors on the stack: [7] [+/-] [ENTER] [8] [+/-] [×] \(\to\) 56 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 56). Removing 7 debts of \(\$8\) each leaves you \(\$56\) richer!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.23: Dividing Signed Numbers (Negative divided by Positive)
docs.text:
Evaluate \((-72) \div (+9)\). Partitioning a total debt of \(-72\) evenly across 9 equal groups places a debt of \(-8\) into each group.

Divide \(-72\) by \(9\) on the SC-6: 72 [+/-] [ENTER] [9] [÷] \(\to\) -8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -8). Splitting a 72-meter submarine dive into 9 equal stages means descending \(-8\text{ meters}\) per stage.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.24: Absolute Value of Negative Integer
docs.text:
Evaluate \(|-125|\). Locate \(-125\) on a number line. Regardless of direction from the origin, geometric distance from 0 to \(-125\) is strictly non-negative: 125 units.

Measure the distance from zero using [ABS]: 125 [+/-] [ABS] \(\to\) 125 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 125). Whether you walk 125 steps east or 125 steps west, your pedometer logs 125 steps of distance.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.25: Absolute Value Expression: \(|-18| + |+12|\)
docs.text:
Evaluate \(|-18| + |12|\). On a number line, the distance from \(-18\) to 0 is 18 units and the distance from 0 to \(+12\) is 12 units, giving a combined distance of 30 units.

Add the two magnitudes on the stack: 18 [+/-] [ABS] 12 [ABS] [+] \(\to\) 30 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 30). Because [ABS] acts immediately on Register \(X\), you never need vertical-bar brackets around each term to find the total distance of 30 units.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.26: Number Line Distance: Between \(-12\) and \(+15\)
docs.text:
Find distance between \(-12\) and \(+15\) on the real line: \(|15 - (-12)|\). Mark \(-12\) and \(+15\) on a number line and count the unit intervals between them: 12 units to reach zero, plus 15 units past zero, totaling 27 units.

Compute the span with subtraction and [ABS]: 15 [ENTER] 12 [+/-] [-] [ABS] \(\to\) 27 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 27). Subtracting the two coordinates and tapping [ABS] always gives the positive distance (27 units), no matter which endpoint you enter first!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.27: Square of Negative Number: \((-9)^2\)
docs.text:
Evaluate \((-9)^2\). Take 9 tiles from your kit and assemble a \(3 \times 3\) grid (\((-3)^2 = +9\)) to see that squaring a negative value yields a positive result. Scaling up to \((-9)^2\) produces \(+81\).

Square \(-9\) in place on the SC-6: [9] [+/-] [x²] \(\to\) 81 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 81). On an algebraic calculator, typing -9² without parentheses gives -81 because it squares 9 before negating; on the SC-6, -9 is already a signed number in Register \(X\), so [x²] multiplies \((-9) \times (-9) = \mathbf{81}\) cleanly!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.28: Geometric Square Root: \(\sqrt{289}\)
docs.text:
A square plaza has area \(289\text{ m}^2\). Find side length. Model the square root concept on a small scale with your Counting Tiles: assemble a \(4 \times 4\) square using 16 tiles to see that edge length is \(\sqrt{16} = 4\). For the \(289\text{ m}^2\) plaza, taking the square root extracts the side length directly.

Extract the side length with [f] [√x]: 289 [f] [√x] \(\to\) 17 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 17). Because \(17\) is a prime number, a 289-tile plaza can only be arranged as a \(\mathbf{17\text{ m}} \times 17\text{ m}\) square (or a \(1 \times 289\) strip)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.29: Geometric Square Root: \(\sqrt{625}\)
docs.text:
A square chessboard has area \(625\text{ cm}^2\). Find side length. Using your Place Value flats and rods, notice that \(25 \times 25 = 625\), so each edge of the square board measures 25 cm.

Confirm \(\sqrt{625}\) on the SC-6: 625 [f] [√x] \(\to\) 25 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 25). Every edge of the chessboard measures \(\mathbf{25\text{ cm}}\) (\(5^2\text{ cm}\)), since \(625 = 5^4\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.30: Random Number in Range 10 to 50
docs.text:
Generate a random integer between 10 and 50 using [g] [t…x]. Just as spinning the 10-sector Probability Spinner generates uniform random digits, the [g] [t…x] key samples every whole number from the lower bound in Register \(Y\) (\(10\)) to the upper bound in Register \(X\) (\(50\)) with equal likelihood.

Sample the bounded range [10, 50] on the stack: 10 [ENTER] 50 [g] [t…x] \(\to\) 28 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 10, X: 28). Each of the 41 integers from 10 through 50 has an identical \(1/41\) chance of landing in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.31: Divisibility by 9 Check via Remainder
docs.text:
Check if 1,557 is divisible by 9 using Euclidean division ([g] [÷R]). First, try a small example with your Place Value kit: test divisibility by 9 on 18 (1 ten-bar and 8 unit cubes), grouping into 2 sets of 9 with zero remainder (\(18 \div 9 = 2\text{ R }0\)). Now check 1,557 on the stack without needing 1,557 blocks:

Divide 1,557 by 9 with [g] [÷R]: 1557 [ENTER] [9] [g] [÷R] \(\to\) 173 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 173). Notice why the remainder in Register \(Y\) is \(0\): the digits of \(1,557\) add up to \(1 + 5 + 5 + 7 = 18\), which is a multiple of 9 (\(173 \times 9 = 1,557\))!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.32: LCD of Three Denominators: \(\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{1}{10}\)
docs.text:
Model common multiples with your kit tiles by aligning 4-tile and 6-tile rows until their edges meet flush at 12 tiles (\(\operatorname{lcm}(4,6)=12\)), and then use your SC-6 to include a third denominator of 10: [4] [ENTER] [6] [f] [LCM] 10 [f] [LCM] \(\rightarrow\) 60.

This sequence finishes with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 60)\), chaining the two LCM operations directly on the stack (\(\operatorname{lcm}(4,6) = 12\), then \(\operatorname{lcm}(12,10) = 60\)) to find the three-way Least Common Denominator of 60.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.33: Temperature Range Across a Sub-Zero Week
docs.text:
Lowest temperature was \(-22^\circ\text{F}\), highest was \(+14^\circ\text{F}\). Find total temperature swing. On a vertical thermometer scale, mark \(-22\) below zero and \(+14\) above zero. Trace the rise from \(-22\) to 0 (22 degrees) and from 0 to \(+14\) (14 degrees), measuring the total thermal swing of 36 degrees.

Subtract \(-22\) from \(14\) on the stack: 14 [ENTER] 22 [+/-] [-] \(\to\) 36 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 36). Climbing \(22^\circ\) up to zero and another \(14^\circ\) above zero produces a total weather swing of \(\mathbf{36^\circ\text{F}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.34: Rolling Double Sixes with Two Dice
docs.text:
What is the probability of rolling double sixes with two fair six-sided dice (\(1\) favorable outcome out of \(36\))? Examine a \(6 \times 6\) grid of dice pairings (36 cells). Only one cell represents \((6,6)\). Compute the decimal share of that single cell.

Divide 1 by 36 on the SC-6: [1] [ENTER] 36 [÷] \(\to\) 0.0277777778 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.0278). Out of all 36 cells in the two-dice matrix, "boxcars" \((6,6)\) occupies just a single corner cell (\(\approx \mathbf{2.78\%}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.35: Probability of Not Rolling a 6 on a Die
docs.text:
Five faces are not 6. Compute \(5/6\). Inspect the 6 faces on a physical die from your kit: \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\). Excluding the 6-face leaves 5 faces for the complement event (\(E'\)).

Evaluate \(5 \div 6\) on the stack: [5] [ENTER] [6] [÷] \(\to\) 0.8333333333 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.8333). Five of the six faces dodge the number 6, giving an \(\mathbf{83.33\%}\) chance of rolling 1 through 5.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.36: Prime Factor Decomposition of 1,001
docs.text:
Decompose 1,001 into prime factors (a classic number-theory product). Take 12 unit cubes from your Place Value kit and build a \(2 \times 2 \times 3\) prism to see how three prime dimensions multiply into a single 3D volume. Now factor 1,001 on your SC-6 to discover its three prime dimensions \(7 \times 11 \times 13\):

Factor 1,001 with [g] [FACT]: 1001 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 1001 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1001). Known as the "Arabian Nights number," \(1,001\) factors into three consecutive primes: 7 × 11 × 13! (Try multiplying any 3-digit number like \(452 \times 1,001 = 452,452\)—dividing it by 7, 11, and 13 brings your secret number right back!)

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.37: Prime Factor Decomposition of 1,729 (Hardy-Ramanujan Number)
docs.text:
Decompose 1,729 into prime factors. Known as the Hardy-Ramanujan taxicab number, 1,729 is the smallest positive integer expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways (\(1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3\)). Use your SC-6 to reveal its three prime factors:

Decompose 1,729 on the display: 1729 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 1729 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1729). When the mathematician G. H. Hardy visited Srinivasa Ramanujan in the hospital and called cab #1729 "a rather dull number," Ramanujan immediately replied that it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two ways—and on your SC-6, [g] [FACT] shows it also splits into three primes spaced 6 units apart: 7 × 13 × 19!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.38: Weighted Mean of Classroom Grades
docs.text:
A grading syllabus weights homework (average 90, weight 2), quizzes (average 82, weight 3), and exams (average 88, weight 5) for a total weight of 10. Accumulate the weighted points directly on the stack: 90 [ENTER] [2] [×] 82 [ENTER] [3] [×] [+] 88 [ENTER] [5] [×] [+] 10 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 86.6.

This sequence finishes with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 86.6)\), computing the weighted grade average of \(86.6\%\) without scratch paper or order-of-operations ambiguity.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.39: School Book Fair & Robotics Club Treasury Across Four Seasons
docs.text:
The district student council tracks its combined STEM Club & Book Fair treasury across four school seasons: Fall Book Fair brings in \(+\$14,500\), Winter 3D-printer filament and kit restocking spends \(-\$3,200\), Spring Maker Market earns \(+\$8,900\), and Summer camp bus chartering spends \(-\$1,400\). Try a small tabletop test with yellow credit and crimson debit counters to see how expenses cancel part of each fundraiser, then combine the four seasonal cash flows on the stack: 14500 [ENTER] 3200 [-] 8900 [+] 1400 [-] \(\rightarrow\) 18800.

This sequence finishes with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 18800)\), yielding a net year-end student club treasury balance of \(\$18,800.00\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.40: Drawing Consecutive Matching Socks
docs.text:
A drawer holds 6 black socks and 4 blue socks (10 total). The probability of drawing a first black sock is \(6/10\), and drawing a second black sock without replacement is \(5/9\). Evaluate the dependent pair probability on the stack: [6] [ENTER] 10 [÷] [5] [ENTER] [9] [÷] [×] \(\rightarrow\) 0.3333333333.

This sequence finishes with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.3333333333)\), proving an exact \(1/3\) (\(33.33\%\)) chance of pulling two black socks in the dark.

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.41: Prime Factorization of 3,600
docs.text:
Decompose 3,600 into prime factors (\(3600 = 60^2\)). Constructing a factor tree shows \(3600 = 36 \times 100 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5^2\).

Verify the prime factor decomposition on your SC-6: 3600 [g] [FACT] \(\to\) 3600 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 3600). Look at the exponents in 2⁴ × 3² × 5²: every single exponent is an even number (\(4, 2, 2\)), which is why \(3,600\) is a perfect square (\(60^2\))—and why there are \(3,600\) seconds in an hour!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.42: GCD and LCM of 45 and 75
docs.text:
Decomposing \(45 = 3^2 \times 5\) and \(75 = 3 \times 5^2\) reveals their prime intersection \(3 \times 5 = 15\) (\(\gcd\)) and prime union \(3^2 \times 5^2 = 225\) (\(\operatorname{lcm}\)). Compute both dual parameters on the stack: 45 [ENTER] 75 [GCF] 45 [ENTER] 75 [f] [LCM] \(\rightarrow\) 225.

This sequence finishes with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 15, X: 225)\), displaying \(\text{LCM} = 225\) in Register \(X\) while preserving \(\text{GCF} = 15\) in Register \(Y\) (\(15 \times 225 = 3,375 = 45 \times 75\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.43: Synchronized Municipal Traffic Signal Cycles
docs.text:
Signal A cycles every \(45\text{ seconds}\), Signal B cycles every \(60\text{ seconds}\). Find the synchronized cycle time: \(\operatorname{lcm}(45, 60)\). Listing multiples of 45 (\(45, 90, 135, 180\dots\)) and multiples of 60 (\(60, 120, 180\dots\)) shows that their first shared multiple is 180 seconds.

Find \(\operatorname{lcm}(45, 60)\) using [f] [LCM]: 45 [ENTER] 60 [f] [LCM] \(\to\) 180 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 180). Both traffic lights turn green together every 180 seconds (\(3\text{ minutes}\)).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.44: Euclidean Division Ladder for \(\gcd(546, 210)\)
docs.text:
Compute Euclidean steps for \(546\) and \(210\): \(546 \div 210 = 2\text{ R }126\); \(210 \div 126 = 1\text{ R }84\); \(126 \div 84 = 1\text{ R }42\); \(84 \div 42 = 2\text{ R }0\). Each remainder becomes the new divisor for the next step until the remainder reaches zero, leaving 42 as the last non-zero remainder.

Verify the Euclidean ladder endpoint on the SC-6: 546 [ENTER] 210 [GCF] \(\to\) 42 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 42). In one keystroke, the hardware [GCF] engine zips down all four rungs of Euclid's ladder to reveal \(\gcd(546, 210) = \mathbf{42}\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.45: Mean Absolute Deviation of a 7-Element Dataset
docs.text:
Dataset: \(12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 24\) (Mean = 17.0). Deviations: \(5, 3, 2, 1, 1, 3, 7\). Sum = 22. MAD = \(22/7\). Plot the 7 points on a dot plot and mark the mean at 17. Measuring the distance from each dot to 17 gives \(5 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 7 = 22\), and dividing among the 7 data points gives \(22/7 \approx 3.1429\).

Evaluate the Mean Absolute Deviation with [g] [MAD]: [g] [CLΣ] 12 [Σ+] 14 [Σ+] 15 [Σ+] 16 [Σ+] 18 [Σ+] 20 [Σ+] 24 [Σ+] [g] [MAD] \(\to\) 3.1428571429 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 3.1428571429). Look closely at the decimal \(3.142857\dots\) in Register \(X\): because the sum of deviations is \(22\) across \(n=7\) points, the MAD is the famous fraction \(22/7\) (Archimedes' classic approximation for \(\pi\))!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.46: Interquartile Range Across Grade 6 Science Scores
docs.text:
Scores: \(65, 72, 75, 80, 84, 88, 92, 96\). Find IQR (\(Q_3 - Q_1 = 90 - 73.5 = 16.5\)). Line up 8 Counting Tiles to mark the 8 sorted scores, splitting them into a lower half (\(65, 72, 75, 80\)) with midpoint \(Q_1 = 73.5\) and an upper half (\(84, 88, 92, 96\)) with midpoint \(Q_3 = 90\). The spread between the quartiles is \(90 - 73.5 = 16.5\).

Compute the interquartile range on the stack: [g] [CLΣ] 65 [Σ+] 72 [Σ+] 75 [Σ+] 80 [Σ+] 84 [Σ+] 88 [Σ+] 92 [Σ+] 96 [Σ+] [IQR] \(\to\) 16.5 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 16.5). Across the \(n=8\) students, the middle 50% of the class spans 16.5 points in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.47: Chemical Freezing Point Depression
docs.text:
Pure water freezes at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). Adding rock salt lowers the freezing point by \(-7.8^\circ\text{C}\). Adding calcium chloride drops it an additional \(-6.4^\circ\text{C}\). Find final freezing point. On a vertical thermometer scale, move down \(7.8^\circ\) below zero and then \(6.4^\circ\) further below zero for a combined drop of \(14.2^\circ\), reaching \(-14.2^\circ\text{C}\).

Sum the two negative temperature drops on the SC-6: 7.8 [+/-] [ENTER] 6.4 [+/-] [+] \(\to\) -14.2 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -14.2). That is why road crews spread de-icing salts before a winter storm: water won't freeze into ice until the thermometer plunges to \(-14.2^\circ\text{C}\)!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.48: Product of Three Signed Integers
docs.text:
Evaluate \((-4) \times (-5) \times (-6)\). On a number line, multiplying negative by negative reverses direction twice into positive territory: \((-4) \times (-5) = +20\). Multiplying by a third negative factor reverses direction back into negative territory: \(+20 \times (-6) = -120\). Multiply all three signed integers on the stack: [4] [+/-] [ENTER] [5] [+/-] [×] [6] [+/-] [×] \(\rightarrow\) -120.

Tap 4 [+/-] [ENTER] 5 [+/-] [×] \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20). The first pair of negative factors flips positive (\(+20\)). Tap 6 [+/-] [×] \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -120). Multiplying by the third negative factor flips the sign back to \(-120\)—showing why any odd number of negative factors produces a negative product!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.49: Order of Operations with Negative Numbers
docs.text:
Evaluate \((-18) \times 4 - (-36) \div (-9) = -72 - 4 = -76\). Model the two terms separately: Term 1 is 4 groups of \(-18\) (\(-72\)), and Term 2 is \((-36) \div (-9) = +4\). Subtracting \(+4\) from \(-72\) moves 4 units further into negative territory to \(-76\). Evaluate both terms without parentheses on the SC-6: 18 [+/-] [ENTER] [4] [×] 36 [+/-] [ENTER] [9] [+/-] [÷] [-] \(\rightarrow\) -76.

Tap 18 [+/-] [ENTER] 4 [×] \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -72) to lock the first term (\(-72\)) on the stack. Tap 36 [+/-] [ENTER] 9 [+/-] [÷] \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: -72, X: 4) so the second quotient (\(+4\)) sits in \(X\) while \(-72\) waits safely in \(Y\). Tap [-] \(\to\) (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: -76) to subtract \(-72 - 4 = \mathbf{-76}\) with zero parentheses!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.50: Geometric Square Root of a Square Ranch
docs.text:
A square ranch has an area of \(4,096\text{ m}^2\). Find side length. Because \(60^2 = 3,600\) and \(70^2 = 4,900\), the side length of the square ranch must lie between 60 m and 70 m, with \(64 \times 64 = 4,096\).

Find the exact side length using [f] [√x]: 4096 [f] [√x] \(\to\) 64 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 64). Fun computer-science bonus: \(4,096\) is \(2^{12}\), so its square root is \(2^6 = \mathbf{64\text{ m}}\) per side!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.51: Divisibility by 11 Verification
docs.text:
Test if 2,596 is divisible by 11 using Euclidean division ([g] [÷R]). Apply the alternating digit sum divisibility rule for 11: \((2 + 9) - (5 + 6) = 11 - 11 = 0\). Since the alternating difference is a multiple of 11, the number is divisible with zero remainder.

Confirm exact divisibility on the stack: 2596 [ENTER] 11 [g] [÷R] \(\to\) 236 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 236). Register \(X\) shows the exact quotient 236 and Register \(Y\) shows remainder 0, proving that the alternating-digit trick (\(2 - 5 + 9 - 6 = 0\)) spotted a true multiple of 11!

docs.title: Workbook Problem 7.52: Mersenne Number Primality Check: \(2^5 - 1 = 31\)
docs.text:
Compute \(2^5 - 1\) and check if the result is prime. Just as 7 or 13 tiles from your Counting Tile kit can only form a single \(1 \times p\) row, evaluating \(2^5 - 1 = 31\) on your SC-6 confirms that 31 has no rectangular factors.

Compute \(2^5 - 1\) and test primality on the SC-6: [2] [ENTER] [5] [g] [yˣ] [1] [-] [PRIME] \(\to\) Flashes (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 31). Named after the French monk Marin Mersenne, primes of the form \(2^p - 1\) hold the world record for the largest known prime numbers ever discovered—and \(M_5 = 2^5 - 1 = \mathbf{31}\) flashes PRIME right in your hand!

docs.title: Chapter 08: The Gamified Math Quiz Engine — Extended Worked Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 08 of From Blocks to the Stack (29 Worked Practice Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.1 (Level 1): \(6 + 3 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Start with the larger benchmark group of 6 (a full row of 5 plus 1 dot), then count on 3 quick hops: 7, 8, 9 (\(6 + 3 = 9\)). When 6 3 + = ? appears in Quiz Mode, key in 9 [≠] in under \(< 2.0\text{ seconds}\).

On the stack, 6 [ENTER] 3 [+] \(\to\) 9 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 9). Watch 6 lift to Floor \(Y\) on [ENTER] before [+] drops it onto 3 to land on 9.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.2 (Level 1): \(8 - 0 = ?\)
docs.text:
In your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), set out 8 counters (5 on top, 3 on bottom). Subtracting zero means taking away zero blocks—all 8 counters stay locked in position (\(8 - 0 = 8\)). For 8 0 - = ? in Quiz Mode, press 8 [≠] on the keypad (target time: \(< 1.0\text{ seconds}\)).

Testing 8 [ENTER] 0 [-] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8) shows that subtracting 0 in Register \(X\) leaves 8 completely unchanged!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.3 (Level 1): \(3 + 7 = ?\)
docs.text:
Look at your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Place 3 blue counters in the first row. The 7 empty pockets show its exact 10-partner—together they fill all 10 pockets of the tray (\(3 + 7 = 10\)). When 3 7 + = ? (or Missing-Value Puzzle 3 ? + = 10) shows up in Quiz Mode, tap 10 [≠] (aim for under \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\)).

Stack verification: 3 [ENTER] 7 [+] \(\to\) 10 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 10). Just like Textbook Drill 2 in reverse, 3 and 7 snap together on the stack to form a complete 10.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.4 (Level 1): \(9 - 5 = ?\)
docs.text:
With your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01), a group of 9 fills the top row of 5 plus 4 on the bottom row. When you lift off the full top row of 5, the 4 bottom counters remain (\(9 - 5 = 4\)). For the Quiz Mode prompt 9 5 - = ?, enter 4 [≠] within \(< 1.8\text{ seconds}\).

Keying 9 [ENTER] 5 [-] \(\to\) 4 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4) takes the benchmark 5 away from 9 in Register \(Y\) and drops the difference 4 into Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.5 (Level 1): \(4 + 4 = ?\)
docs.text:
Place matching [4] digit blocks in Row 1 and Row 0 of your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Both halves show identical \(2 \times 2\) square clusters (\(4 + 4 = 8\)); doubling 4 clicks together like twin booster rockets! When you see 4 4 + = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 8 [≠] in under \(< 1.0\text{ seconds}\).

On your SC-6, 4 [ENTER] 4 [+] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8). Pro Tip: Because [ENTER] copies 4 into both \(Y\) and \(X\), you can even test 4 [ENTER] [+] to double a number in three taps!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.6 (Level 1): \(10 - 2 = ?\)
docs.text:
Start with a full 10 in your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Pop out the 2 end counters from the bottom row: you see a full row of 5 plus 3 on the bottom, giving 8 counters (\(10 - 2 = 8\)). For 10 2 - = ? (or Missing-Value Puzzle 10 ? - = 8) in Quiz Mode, press 8 [≠] (target time: \(< 1.2\text{ seconds}\)).

Stack trace: 10 [ENTER] 2 [-] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8). Counting back 2 from 10 on the stack lands cleanly on 8.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.7 (Level 2): \(34 + 12 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your two Place Value Tray (PLACE-01): in the left tray, model the tens (\(3 + 1 = 4\text{ tens} = 40\)); in the right tray, model the ones (\(4 + 2 = 6\text{ ones}\)). Put them together for \(46\). When 34 12 + = ? is shown in Quiz Mode, key in 46 [≠] in under \(< 2.5\text{ seconds}\).

Checking 34 [ENTER] 12 [+] \(\to\) 46 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 46) shows how both tens and ones add without regrouping, landing on 46 in Register \(X\).

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.8 (Level 2): \(67 - 25 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your two Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) as a Tens Tray and a Ones Tray: subtract the tens (\(6 - 2 = 4\text{ tens} = 40\)) and subtract the ones (\(7 - 5 = 2\text{ ones}\)) to get \(42\). On 67 25 - = ? in Quiz Mode, press 42 [≠] (target time: \(< 2.8\text{ seconds}\)).

In [NUM] mode, 67 [ENTER] 25 [-] \(\to\) 42 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 42). Keeping 67 in Register \(Y\) and subtracting 25 in Register \(X\) confirms 42.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.9 (Level 2): \(47 + 38 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use the Make-a-Round-Number Trick with your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01)! Notice that 38 is just 2 shy of 40 (a nearly full 10-group with 8 counters). Add 40 to 47 first (\(47 + 40 = 87\)), then step back 2 counters to land on \(85\). For 47 38 + = ? in Quiz Mode, tap 85 [≠] (aim for under \(< 3.5\text{ seconds}\)).

Stack check: 47 [ENTER] 38 [+] \(\to\) 85 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 85). Or see how the ones regroup: \(7 + 8 = 15\) (1 ten and 5 ones) plus \(40 + 30 = 70\) gives 85.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.10 (Level 2): \(72 - 45 = ?\)
docs.text:
Count Up to Subtract! Use your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) to bridge the gap from 45 to 72: add 5 counters to 45 to reach the friendly multiple of ten (\(50\)), then add 22 more (\(2\text{ tens} + 2\text{ ones}\)) to reach \(72\). Your total jump is \(5 + 22 = 27\). When 72 45 - = ? (or Missing-Value Puzzle 72 ? - = 27) appears in Quiz Mode, enter 27 [≠] within \(< 3.5\text{ seconds}\).

Keying 72 [ENTER] 45 [-] \(\to\) 27 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 27) confirms the difference—counting up from the smaller number to the larger number turns borrowing into easy addition!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.11 (Level 2): \(56 + 19 = ?\)
docs.text:
Model 19 on your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01)—it fills all 20 pockets except 1. Add 20 to 56 first (\(56 + 20 = 76\)), then take back that 1 empty pocket (\(76 - 1 = 75\)). For 56 19 + = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 75 [≠] in under \(< 2.8\text{ seconds}\).

Verify on the stack: 56 [ENTER] 19 [+] \(\to\) 75 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 75). Anytime you add 19, 29, or 39, jump up by the next ten and step back 1.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.12 (Level 2): \(91 - 38 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use Overshoot & Give Back! Since 38 is 2 less than 40, subtract 40 from 91 first (\(91 - 40 = 51\)). Because you took away 2 too many, pop 2 counters back into your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) to finish at \(51 + 2 = 53\). On 91 38 - = ? in Quiz Mode, press 53 [≠] (target time: \(< 3.5\text{ seconds}\)).

Stack verification: 91 [ENTER] 38 [-] \(\to\) 53 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 53). Overshooting by 40 and giving back 2 beats crossing out digits every time.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.13 (Level 3): \(6 \times 9 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) to see the "10 Minus 1" Rule! Nine is \(10 - 1\), so 6 groups of 9 is 6 groups of 10 (\(60\)) minus 6 single counters (\(60 - 6 = 54\)). For 6 9 × = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 54 [≠] in under \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

Stack trace: 6 [ENTER] 9 [×] \(\to\) 54 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 54). Notice that in 54, the tens digit is \(6 - 1 = 5\) and the digits add up to \(5 + 4 = 9\).

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.14 (Level 3): \(48 \div 6 = ?\)
docs.text:
Model Half with Your Kit \(\to\) Double It! Take all 24 Array Tiles from your kit and arrange them into 6 equal rows: you get 6 rows of 4 (\(24 \div 6 = 4\)). Since 48 is double 24, double the row length from 4 to 8 (\(48 \div 6 = 8\)). On 48 6 ÷ = ? (or Missing-Value Puzzle 48 ? ÷ = 8) in Quiz Mode, press 8 [≠] (target time: \(< 1.8\text{ seconds}\)).

Keying 48 [ENTER] 6 [÷] \(\to\) 8 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 8) confirms 8. Halving 48 to 24 turns a big division fact into one you can build right on your desk.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.15 (Level 3): \(12 \times 7 = ?\)
docs.text:
Split 12 into \(10 + 2\). Use 14 of your 24 Array Tiles to build the \(2 \times 7 = 14\) rectangle on your desk, then add the easy \(10 \times 7 = 70\) mental block: \(70 + 14 = 84\). When 12 7 × = ? flashes in Quiz Mode, tap 84 [≠] (aim for under \(< 2.2\text{ seconds}\)).

On the stack, 12 [ENTER] 7 [×] \(\to\) 84 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 84). Every \(12 \times N\) fact is just \(10N + 2N\)!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.16 (Level 3): \(9 \times 9 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) to picture 9 groups of 10 (\(90\)) and pull off 1 counter from each of the 9 groups (\(90 - 9 = 81\)). For 9 9 × = ? in Quiz Mode, enter 81 [≠] within \(< 1.2\text{ seconds}\).

Testing 9 [ENTER] 9 [×] \(\to\) 81 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 81) confirms 81—or press 9 [x²] in [NUM] mode to square 9 in a single operation!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.17 (Level 3): \(84 \div 12 = ?\)
docs.text:
Take all 24 Array Tiles and group them into dozens (\(24 \div 12 = 2\text{ dozens}\)). Now scale up to 84: since \(70 + 14 = 84\), it takes 7 dozens to make 84 (\(84 \div 12 = 7\)). When 84 12 ÷ = ? (or Missing-Value Puzzle 84 ? ÷ = 7) appears in Quiz Mode, key in 7 [≠] in under \(< 2.0\text{ seconds}\).

Stack check: 84 [ENTER] 12 [÷] \(\to\) 7 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 7). Recognizing 84 from Workbook Drill 8.15 (\(12 \times 7 = 84\)) gives you the inverse division fact for free!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.18 (Level 3): \(11 \times 11 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use the 11s Split Trick! Model \(2 \times 11 = 22\) with 22 of your 24 Array Tiles. For \(11 \times 11\), split the digits 1 and 1 apart and put their sum (\(1 + 1 = 2\)) right in the middle: 121. For 11 11 × = ? in Quiz Mode, press 121 [≠] (target time: \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\)).

In [NUM] mode, 11 [ENTER] 11 [×] \(\to\) 121 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 121). \(10 \times 11 = 110\), plus one more \(11\) equals 121.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.19 (Level 4): \(3/4 - 2/5 = ?\)
docs.text:
Compare three \(1/4\) pieces (\(3/4\)) against two \(1/5\) pieces (\(2/5\)) in your Fraction Towers comparator well, then find their shared common denominator of 20: \(3/4 = 15/20\) and \(2/5 = 8/20\), so the height difference is \(15/20 - 8/20 = 7/20\). When 3/4 2/5 - = ? appears in Quiz Mode, tap [.] 7 [.] 20 [≠] (aim for under \(< 4.5\text{ seconds}\)).

In [NUM] mode, . 3 . 4 [ENTER] . 2 . 5 [-] \(\to\) 7/20 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 7/20). Two-Dot entry ([.] 3 [.] 4 and [.] 2 [.] 5) automatically finds the common denominator of 20 on the stack!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.20 (Level 4): \(38 \div 6 \to Q=?, R=?\)
docs.text:
Take 14 of your 24 Array Tiles and make groups of 6 (2 full groups of 6 with 2 left over). Now scale up to 38: 6 full groups of 6 use \(36\) tiles and leave \(2\) tiles left over (\(Q=6, R=2\)). For 38 6 ÷R = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 6 [≠] in under \(< 3.0\text{ seconds}\).

On the stack, 38 [ENTER] 6 [g] [÷R] \(\to\) 6 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 2, X: 6). [g] [÷R] puts the whole quotient 6 in Register \(X\) and the remainder 2 right above it in Register \(Y\)!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.21 (Level 5): \(0.25 \times 80 = ?\)
docs.text:
Connect decimals to your Fraction Towers! The decimal \(0.25\) is stamped right on the \(1/4\) tower (\(0.25 = 1/4\)). Taking one fourth of 80 is just \(80 \div 4 = 20\). For 0.25 80 × = ? in Quiz Mode, enter 20 [≠] within \(< 2.0\text{ seconds}\).

On the stack, 0.25 [ENTER] 80 [×] \(\to\) 20 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 20). Multiplying by 0.25 is always the same as dividing by 4.

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.22 (Level 5): \(0.5 \times 48 = ?\)
docs.text:
Check the \(1/2\) piece in your Fraction Towers kit: \(0.5\) is one half! Splitting 48 in half (\(48 \div 2 = 24\)) leaves exactly 24—the full count of your 24 Array Tiles! For 0.5 48 × = ? in Quiz Mode, enter 24 [≠] within \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

Keying 0.5 [ENTER] 48 [×] \(\to\) 24 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 24) confirms 24. Multiplying any even number by 0.5 is as fast as cutting both digits in half (\(4 \to 2\), \(8 \to 4 \implies 24\)).

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.23 (Level 5): \(10\%\text{ of } 250 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) to see why \(10\%\) means 1 counter out of 10 (\(\frac{1}{10}\)). To find one tenth of 250, simply divide by 10 (shift the decimal point one place left): \(250 \div 10 = 25\). On 250 10 % = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 25 [≠] in under \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

Stack check: 250 [ENTER] 10 [%] \(\to\) 25 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 250, X: 25). Notice how [%] keeps the base 250 in Register \(Y\) while placing \(10\%\) (25) in Register \(X\)!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.24 (Level 6): \(35^2 = ?\)
docs.text:
For any number ending in 5, multiply the tens digit \(3\) by the next whole number \(4\) using 12 of your 24 Array Tiles (\(3 \times 4 = 12\text{ hundreds} = 1,200\)), then snap on \(5^2 = 25\) at the end: \(1,225\). When 35 x² = ? flashes in Quiz Mode, tap 1225 [≠] (aim for under \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\)).

In [NUM] mode, 35 [x²] \(\to\) 1225 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1225). The unary [x²] key squares 35 right inside Register \(X\) without even needing [ENTER]!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.25 (Level 6): \(43 \times 11 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use the 11s Middle-Sum Shortcut! Model \(4 + 3 = 7\) in your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01). Now spread the digits 4 and 3 apart and drop their sum 7 right into the middle tens place: 473. For 43 11 × = ? in Quiz Mode, enter 473 [≠] within \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

On the stack, 43 [ENTER] 11 [×] \(\to\) 473 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 473). Why does it work? Because \(43 \times 10 = 430\), and \(430 + 43 = 473\).

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.26 (Level 6): \(65^2 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use the Ends-in-5 Squaring Rule! Multiply the tens digit \(6\) by the next integer \(7\) (\(6 \times 7 = 42\text{ hundreds} = 4,200\)), then attach \(5^2 = 25\) to the last two digits: \(4,225\). On 65 x² = ? in Quiz Mode, key in 4225 [≠] in under \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\).

Checking 65 [x²] \(\to\) 4225 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 4225) confirms 4225—once you know \(6 \times 7 = 42\), you can type 4225 faster than anyone using an algebraic calculator!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.27 (Level 6): \(75^2 = ?\)
docs.text:
Recall \(7 \times 8 = 56\) from Textbook Drill 5. Multiply the tens digit \(7\) by the next integer \(8\) (\(56\text{ hundreds} = 5,600\)) and tack on \(25\): \(5,625\). For 75 x² = ? in Quiz Mode, press 5625 [≠] (target time: \(< 1.5\text{ seconds}\)).

Keying 75 [x²] \(\to\) 5625 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 5625) confirms your mental square 5625 in Register \(X\) with a single tap of [x²].

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.28 (Level 6): \(67 \times 11 = ?\)
docs.text:
Use the 11s Shortcut with a Carry! Model \(6 + 7 = 13\) across your two Place Value Tray (PLACE-01) (1 full ten and 3 ones). Put the 3 in the middle tens slot and carry the 1 ten-group over to the hundreds digit (\(6 + 1 = 7\)), giving 737. When 67 11 × = ? appears in Quiz Mode, tap 737 [≠] (aim for under \(< 1.8\text{ seconds}\)).

Stack verification: 67 [ENTER] 11 [×] \(\to\) 737 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 737). Whenever the two digits add to 10 or more, carry 1 to the left digit!

docs.title: Workbook Drill 8.29 (Level 6): \(15\%\text{ of } 80 = ?\)
docs.text:
Split \(15\%\) into \(10\% + 5\%\) using your Place Value Tray (PLACE-01)! \(10\%\) of 80 is \(8\) counters, and \(5\%\) is half of that (\(4\) counters). Add them together in your tray: \(8 + 4 = 12\). For 80 15 % = ? in Quiz Mode, enter 12 [≠] within \(< 1.8\text{ seconds}\).

Testing 80 [ENTER] 15 [%] \(\to\) 12 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 80, X: 12) shows 80 waiting in Register \(Y\) and 12 in Register \(X\)—so pressing [+] next would even give you \(80 + 15\% = 92\).

docs.title: Chapter 09: Applied Elementary STEM & Maker Labs — Extended Worked Problems
docs.text: Accompanies Chapter 09 of From Blocks to the Stack (26 Worked Practice Problems)

docs.title: Workbook Challenge 9.1: Kitchen Model Mass from Density (\(\rho = 1.24\text{ g/cm}^3\))
docs.text:
With the funnel volume established at \(28.86\text{ cm}^3\), you must convert that cubic volume into mass in grams so you can verify the finished print on your kitchen gram scale. Placing a \(1\text{ cm} \times 1\text{ cm} \times 1\text{ cm}\) solid PLA calibration cube on your digital balance yields \(1.24\text{ grams}\), establishing the density \(\rho = 1.24\text{ g/cm}^3\).

Calculate the total part mass using 28.86 [ENTER] 1.24 [×] \(\to\) 35.79 g (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 35.7864). Multiplying volume by polymer density (\(m = V \times \rho\)) shows that the finished bioplastic funnel will weigh approximately \(\mathbf{35.79\text{ grams}}\).

docs.title: Workbook Challenge 9.2: Spool Material Cost for Kitchen Print (\(\$0.02/\text{g}\))
docs.text:
Your maker space purchased a \(1,000\text{ gram}\) spool of corn-based PLA for \(\$20.00\), establishing an exact material cost ratio of \(\$0.02\) per gram. Setting two shiny copper pennies next to each \(1\text{ gram}\) calibration weight on your scale pan provides a concrete visual of this unit cost before committing the print job.

Compute the fabrication expense with 35.79 [ENTER] .02 [×] [$] \(\to\) $0.72 (T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 0.7158). Formatting the result in two-decimal currency mode confirms that fabricating the custom spice funnel costs just \(\mathbf{\$0.72}\) in raw bioplastic.

docs.text:

Integrating physical manipulatives and calculators into a busy classroom—or a home study table—works best when every tool serves a clear mathematical purpose. Because no one wakes up searching for an "RPN calculator curriculum"—ours is the first ever built—every book in the StackCalc Learning Lab has a separate print cover and begins in standard book order with a Title Page (Page i), Copyright & Library Colophon Page (Page ii), Table of Contents (Page iii), and Educator / Student Preface (Page iv+) that introduce our ecosystem from zero assumptions:

  1. The Mathematical Concept (Grounded in the Stack): When you solve math by hand on paper, you hold your first quantity on a top Waiting Line (Y), write your second quantity below it on an active Workbench (X), and then apply the operation (+, -, ×, ÷). Every lesson begins with this inside-out mathematical structure—never with mechanical button-pushing.
  2. The Three Published Physical Block Studios: Where concrete geometry clarifies Place Value, Fractions, or Prime Factors, students build the structure first using one of our three Published Block Studios—Place Value Studio (PLACE-01) (0–9 digit blocks & Gold [+1] carry tokens on a 2-row tray mirroring Y and X), Fraction Studio (FRAC-01) (84.0 mm proportional towers where common denominators stand dead-flush), or Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01) (logarithmic prime blocks 2, 3, 5, 7 scaled to \(h(p) = 7.0 \cdot \log_2(p)\text{ mm}\) where equal products stand equal in height)—before solving by hand in their workbook.
  3. The Four-Line Stack Calculators (SC-6 Elementary & SC-32 Scientific): Because there is no [=] key and no parentheses keys, the calculator is never a "black box." Students predict the result by hand first, then verify step-by-step across four visible stack registers (T, Z, Y, X).

Companion Illustrated Storybooks & State/District Curriculum Integration: Pairs with our illustrated history-of-math trade books—From Blocks to the Stack (Grades K–6 / SC-6) and Thinking in the Stack (Grades 7–12 / SC-32)—and plugs directly into state-mandated standards (Common Core CCSS, Texas TEKS, Florida B.E.S.T., Virginia SOL, AP) and district basal textbooks (Eureka Math / EngageNY, Illustrative Mathematics, enVision Mathematics, Big Ideas Math, HMH Into Math, Bridges in Mathematics, and Dimensions Math) without changing a teacher's pacing calendar.

docs.title: 💡 For the Reluctant Teacher: Why There Is No [=] Key (And Why You Already Teach Stack Math Every Day)
docs.text:
Almost every educator grew up using a standard algebraic calculator where you type 8 + 5 =. When teachers first see a calculator with an [ENTER] key and no [=] button, their natural reaction is hesitation: "Why is the plus sign at the end? I have state standards to cover—I don't have time to learn or teach an unfamiliar calculator notation!"

Here is the reassuring truth: Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) is not a new way to do math—it is the exact order in which you already teach math with physical blocks and on the whiteboard every day.

docs.title: 1. The "Noun, Noun, Verb" Principle: Physical Blocks & Vertical Paper Math Are Already Stack-Based
docs.text: How You Teach with Physical Blocks How You Teach Vertical Paper Math How the 4-Line Stack Calculator Works 1. "Place the [8] block on the tray."2. "Now place the [5] block below it."3. "Now combine them (+)!"Notice: You cannot combine two quantities before the second quantity is on the desk. 1. Write 8 on the top line (Line Y).2. Write 5 on the line below (Line X).3. Draw the line and add (+ \(\rightarrow\) 13).Notice: Both numbers exist on the paper before the operation happens. 1. Type [8] [ENTER] \(\rightarrow\) 8 sits on Line Y.2. Type [5] \(\rightarrow\) 5 sits on Line X.3. Press [+] \(\rightarrow\) adds Y + X = 13.Line Y is the Waiting Shelf; Line X is the Workbench. Both operands are visible before you act.

docs.title: 2. How the Stack Solves Order-of-Operations Confusion
docs.text:
Consider what happens when a middle school student evaluates \(\frac{8 + 4}{9 - 3}\):

  • On a 1-Line Infix ([=]) Calculator: A student who types 8 + 4 ÷ 9 - 3 = left-to-right gets 5.444... because the calculator divides 4 ÷ 9 first, or must wrap both parts in nested parentheses ((8 + 4) / (9 - 3)). Because a 1-line screen erases each number when an operator is pressed, it is difficult to see where an entry error occurred.
  • On the 4-Line Stack Calculator: Because there are no parentheses keys, the student must apply Order of Operations (PEMDAS) and work from the inside out:
  • Numerator (8 + 4): Type [8] [ENTER] [4] [+] \(\rightarrow\) 12 waits visibly on Line Y.
  • Denominator (9 - 3): Type [9] [ENTER] [3] [-] \(\rightarrow\) 6 sits visibly on Line X.
  • Divide (12 ÷ 6): Both 12 and 6 are visible on screen together. Press [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 2.

docs.title: 3. Answering the Three Biggest Teacher Questions
docs.text:
• Question 1: "Will this confuse my students when they take state tests with a standard calculator?" No—it builds stronger order-of-operations habits: Because the stack has no parentheses keys, students practice identifying which inner sub-expression must be evaluated first. When handed a basic four-function calculator on a state test, they already know to compute the numerator and denominator before dividing rather than typing left-to-right.
  • Question 2: "What if a student gets stuck mid-problem and asks me for help?" A 2-Second Visual Check: All 4 registers (T, Z, Y, X) remain visible on screen—you can immediately see their first quantity sitting on Line Y and their second quantity on Line X.
  • Question 3: "How long does it take to feel comfortable teaching with it?" About 3 minutes. Follow the 3 Golden Rules and try the 4 exercises below (also printed on Pages iii–iv of Book 1: Master Teacher's Guide).

docs.title: 4. The 3-Minute Teacher Hands-On Primer & Day 1 Classroom Script
docs.text:
• Golden Rule 1 ([ENTER] = "Put It on the Waiting Shelf"): Press [ENTER] only to separate two numbers you type back-to-back.
  • Golden Rule 2 (Action Keys Work Immediately): Press [+], [-], [×], or [÷] after both numbers are in place—never press [ENTER] after an operator.
  • Golden Rule 3 (Automatic Stack Lift): When you type a new number after an operation finishes, your previous result automatically lifts up to Line Y so you can build the next part on Line X.
45-Second Teacher Try-It Exercise Exact Keys to Press What You See on the 4-Line Screen (Y and X) Try-It 1: Basic Addition (8 + 5 = 13) [8] [ENTER] [5] [+] [8] [ENTER] lifts 8 onto Shelf Y. Typing [5] puts 5 on Workbench X. Pressing [+] adds Y + X -> 13. Try-It 2: Two-Group PEMDAS ((8 + 4) × (9 - 3) = 72) [8] [ENTER] [4] [+] [9] [ENTER] [3] [-] [×] First group gives 12. When you type 9, 12 lifts automatically to Y while 9 - 3 = 6 forms on X. Press [×] \(\rightarrow\) 72. Try-It 3: Two-Dot Fractions (1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12) [.] [1] [.] [3] [ENTER] [.] [1] [.] [4] [+] Pressing [.] twice on the SC-6 enters a fraction (0.1.3 = 1/3). Press [+] \(\rightarrow\) displays 7/12 as an exact fraction. Try-It 4: Fixing Reversed Numbers (20 ÷ 4 = 5) [4] [ENTER] [2] [0] [x⇄y] [÷] Typed 4 then 20 when you meant 20 ÷ 4? Press Swap ([x⇄y] / [⇅]) to flip Y and X, then press [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 5.

[!TIP] Your 60-Second Day 1 Script, Stack Hand-Signals & Partner Protocols "Class, look at your calculator—notice there is no equals sign and no parentheses. That is because this calculator works just like the blocks on your desk. The bottom line, Line X, is your Workbench where you type a number. The line right above it, Line Y, is your Waiting Shelf. When we want to add 8 + 5, we first type 8 and press [ENTER] to push 8 up onto the Waiting Shelf. Then we type 5 on our Workbench, and press [+] to combine them. Put the two numbers on the shelves first, then press the operation key."

  • 4 Physical Stack Hand-Signals: Hands flat on desk = Register X (Workbench) • Hands at chest height = Register Y (Waiting Shelf) • Hands at shoulder height = Register Z • Hands overhead = Top Shelf T.
  • Partner Roles & The Two-Token Rule: Pair students as Partner A (The Architect, builds the physical block model first for a +10 token) and Partner B (The Stack Navigator, verifies on the keypad for a +10 token), swapping roles every 3 problems so no student skips the concrete blocks. End every lab with the 60-Second Gridfinity Socket Count-In (84.0 mm flush waterline check).
  • SC-6 Pedagogical Superpower Keys & Classroom [FLAGS] ([g] [FLAGS]):
  • [SIMP] (Step-by-Step Fraction Reduction, Flag 8): Shows the true unreduced product first (e.g., 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 matching the 12-part area grid) and steps down factor by factor to LOWEST TERMS when the student presses [SIMP].
  • [LASTX] ([g] [LSTx] — 2-Tap Inverse Detective Check): Recalls the last number consumed by an operation so students can check division with multiplication or subtraction with addition in two taps.
  • Classroom Flags ([g] [FLAGS]): Flag 6 toggles Classroom Silent Mode; Flag 7 switches between 2-Shelf Beginner Mode (2-LVL, K–2) and 4-Shelf Full Stack (4-LVL); Flag 8 toggles Manual [SIMP] vs. Auto-Simplify.

docs.title: 🎲 Classroom Games & Orthographic Teacher Checks (The 3 Published Block Studios)
docs.text:
When thirty students are building with blocks at their desks, you shouldn't have to count tiny pieces to know if a student understands the lesson. Our three published classroom block kits—Place Value Studio (PLACE-01), Fraction Studio (FRAC-01), and Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01)—use self-verifying physical geometry so you can check any desk in 2 seconds during a walk-by.

Below are the step-by-step orthographic checks and 9 lesson-linked classroom games (printed on Pages vi–viii of Book 1: Master Teacher's Guide).

docs.title: 1. Place Value Studio (PLACE-01): Regrouping Games & Orthographic Column Check (Units 01–05, 12 & MS Unit 03)
docs.text: Classroom Game (10–12 Min Partner Activity) How Students Play with the Trays & Blocks How to Check Students Are Right + SC-6 Keys Game 1: "Race to 1,000 Carry Relay"(Units 03 & 05 • Grades 2–5) Partners start at 000 on the 6×2 Whole Number Tray. Take turns rolling two dice (or spinning 0–9) to form a 2- or 3-digit addend in Row 0 (100 / 10 / 1) and add it to the running total in Row 1. Whenever a column sum reaches 10+, the student calls "Regroup!", leaves the ones remainder digit in Row 0, and snaps a Gold [+1] Carry Token one column left. First pair to click [1] into THOUSANDS (1000) wins. Walk-By Check: Every active Row 0 socket holds one single digit (0–9), and Gold [+1] tokens sit in Row 1 above the columns that received a carry.SC-6 Keys (147 + 285 = 432):[1] [4] [7] [ENTER] [2] [8] [5] [+] [PV] Game 2: "The Decimal Point Shifter (×10 & ÷10 Slide)"(Unit 05 & MS Unit 03 • Grades 4–6) Dock the Whole Number Tray (100,000 to 1) and Decimal Tray (0.1 to 0.000001) side-by-side at the raised tactile decimal point (•). Call out a decimal (e.g., 4.75) and a power-of-10 action (× 10, × 100, or ÷ 10). Students physically slide every digit block one or two columns left (for ×10/×100) or right (for ÷10) across the stationary decimal point—seeing why digits shift columns rather than the decimal point moving. Walk-By Check: The digits [4] [7] [5] stay in the same relative order (4–7–5) shifted one socket left across the tactile • separator.SC-6 Keys (4.75 × 10 = 47.5):[4] [.] [7] [5] [ENTER] [1] [0] [×] [PV] Game 3: "The Borrowing Bank Vault (Zero-Placeholder Regrouping)"(Unit 05 • Grades 3–6) Set a "Vault Target" containing zeros in Row 1 (e.g., 502) and a subtraction code in Row 0 (e.g., 168). Because Ones (2 - 8) and Tens (0 - 6) cannot subtract directly, the "Banker" partner must un-group 1 Hundred ([5] \(\rightarrow\) [4]), trade across the zero Tens ([0] \(\rightarrow\) [9]), and snap the Gold [+1] regrouping token onto the Ones column (12 - 8 = 4) to unlock 334. Walk-By Check: Tens socket holds [9] (not [10]) after passing +1 to the Ones column.SC-6 Keys (502 - 168 = 334):[5] [0] [2] [ENTER] [1] [6] [8] [-] [PV]

docs.title: 2. Fraction Studio (FRAC-01): Equivalence Games & Orthographic Flush Ridge Check (Unit 06 & MS Units 02, 04)
docs.text: Classroom Game (10–12 Min Partner Activity) How Students Play with the 84.0 mm Towers & Comparator Lid How to Check Students Are Right + SC-6 Keys Game 1: "The 84 mm Flush Tower Challenge (Make 1 Whole)"(Unit 06 • Grades 3–5) Stand the Gold 1 Whole (84.0 mm) reference tower in Col 0 of the 12-Socket Comparator Lid. Call out a challenge—e.g., "Build 1 Whole in Col 1 using 4 blocks from at least 3 different denominator colors" (e.g., 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12 = 42 + 21 + 14 + 7 = 84.0 mm). Students swipe a finger across the top ridge to verify a 0.0 mm step, then check on the SC-6. Walk-By Check: Even a 1/12 error creates a 7.0 mm stair-step. If Col 1 stands flush with the 84.0 mm Gold 1 Whole block, it is exact.SC-6 Keys:[.] 1 [.] 2 [ENTER] [.] 1 [.] 4 [+] [.] 1 [.] 6 [+] [.] 1 [.] 12 [+] Game 2: "Two-Dot Common Denominator Duel (1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12)"(Unit 06 & MS Unit 02 • Grades 4–6) Partner A stacks two unlike fractions in Col 2 (e.g., 1/3 [28 mm] + 1/4 [21 mm] = 49.0 mm). Partner B must find a single-color block family (twelfths, 7.0 mm each) and stack enough identical blocks in Col 3 (seven 1/12 blocks = 49.0 mm) to stand flush with Partner A's tower. Both partners key the sum on the SC-6 and press [d/c] to inspect proper/improper forms. Walk-By Check: Col 2 (1/3 + 1/4) and Col 3 (7/12) stand flush at 49.0 mm, and Col 3 uses one uniform block size.SC-6 Keys (1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12):[.] [1] [.] [3] [ENTER] [.] [1] [.] [4] [+] [d/c] Game 3: "Mystery Tower Blind Fingertip Check & 4-Face Spin"(Unit 06 & MS Unit 04 • Grades 3–6) Student A builds a target fraction tower (e.g., three 1/4 blocks = 3/4 = 63.0 mm) and challenges Student B to build an equal-height tower using no fourths (e.g., 1/2 + 1/4, or four 1/6 + one 1/12 = 63.0 mm). Student A closes their eyes and runs one fingertip across both tops to judge if they are flush, then both rotate a block \(90^\circ\) at a time to read Fraction (1/4), Decimal (0.25), Percent (25%), and RPN Key (.1.4). Walk-By Check: Zero ridge step (0.0 mm) between the two towers; all 12 caddy columns sit flush at the 84.0 mm waterline at cleanup.SC-6 Keys (4/6 + 1/12 = 3/4):[.] [4] [.] [6] [ENTER] [.] [1] [.] [1] [2] [+]

docs.title: 3. Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01): Factor Tree, GCF/LCM Games & Logarithmic Flush Check (Units 07, 10 & MS Unit 01)
docs.text: Classroom Game (10–12 Min Partner Activity) How Students Play with the Logarithmic Prime Blocks (\(h(p) = 7.0 \cdot \log_2(p)\text{ mm}\)) How to Check Students Are Right + SC-6 Keys Game 1: "The Commutative Skyscraper Race (2 × 3 × 5 = 30)"(Units 07 & 10 • Grades 3–6) Call out a composite number (e.g., 12, 30, or 42). Partner A factors it using one factor tree (e.g., 30 = 6 × 5 \(\rightarrow\) [2] + [3] + [5]) and stacks the prime blocks in Col 2. Partner B uses a different factor tree (30 = 10 × 3 \(\rightarrow\) [5] + [2] + [3]) in Col 3. Because block height follows \(h(p) = 7.0 \cdot \log_2(p)\text{ mm}\) ([2] = 7.0 mm = 1U, [3] = 11.09 mm, [5] = 16.25 mm), both towers stand flush (34.35 mm)—demonstrating commutativity and unique factorization physically. Walk-By Check: Both factor trees stand flush (0.000 mm step) regardless of stacking order ([2][3][5] vs [5][3][2]).SC-6 Keys (30 = 2 × 3 × 5):[3] [0] [ENTER] [FACT] Game 2: "Impossible Impostor (Fundamental Theorem Challenge)"(Units 07, 10 & MS Unit 01 • Grades 5–8) Student A builds a prime tower (e.g., 12 = [2] + [2] + [3] = 25.10 mm) and challenges Student B to match its exact height using different prime blocks (e.g., trying [5] + [2] = 10 = 23.25 mm or [2] + [7] = 14 = 26.65 mm). Students see immediately that no other combination of primes will ever stand flush—experiencing the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in their hands. Walk-By Check: Any wrong prime factor creates an immediate height step (like the red 2×3×7 = 42 tower stepping above 30 in Step 3 above).SC-6 Keys:[1] [2] [FACT] vs [1] [4] [FACT] Game 3: "Side-by-Side GCF Overlap & LCM Union Duel"(Units 07, 10 & MS Unit 01 • Grades 5–8) Given A = 20 and B = 50, students stack Tower A ([2]+[2]+[5]) in Col 1 and Tower B ([2]+[5]+[5]) in Col 2. To build GCF(20,50) = 10 in Col 0, they copy only the shared prime blocks present in both towers ([2]+[5]). To build LCM(20,50) = 100 in Col 3, they stack the tallest count of each prime ([2]+[2]+[5]+[5]), then verify [FACT], [GCF], and [LCM] on the SC-6. Walk-By Check: Col 0 (GCF) is the shortest tower, Col 3 (LCM) is the tallest tower, and h(GCF) + h(LCM) = h(A) + h(B).SC-6 Keys:[2] [0] [ENTER] [5] [0] [GCF] (10) & [LCM] (100)

docs.text:
Most public, charter, and private school teachers do not choose their district's textbook—they are bound to state standards (Common Core CCSS, Texas TEKS, Florida B.E.S.T., Virginia SOL) and an adopted basal series (Eureka Math / EngageNY, Illustrative Mathematics, enVision Mathematics, Big Ideas Math, HMH Into Math, or Bridges in Mathematics). docs.title: 📚 Complete 12-Unit K–12 Teacher Curriculum (Concept → Blocks → Calculator, Units 01–12)
docs.text: Each unit below follows the 1. Mathematical Concept (Stack Approach) → 2. Physical Blocks (When Applicable) → 3. Calculator Execution progression so teachers can lead conceptual discussion first, transition to physical blocks where appropriate, and verify on the 4-level stack:

docs.title: Unit 01: Counting, Cardinality & The One-More Step Counter
docs.text: Grade Band: Pre-K – Kindergarten  |  Calculator: SC-6 Elementary (Grades K–6)  |  Published Block Kit (When Applicable): Place Value Studio (PLACE-01) (Place Value Studio (Digit Blocks 0–9 & Gold [+1] Step Tokens)) Standards: CCSS.MATH.K.CC.A.1, CCSS.MATH.K.CC.B.4, CCSS.MATH.K.CC.B.5, CCSS.MATH.K.OA.A.1  |  Curricular Alignment: Bridges in Mathematics (Kindergarten Unit 1) • Singapore Math (Earlybird Kindergarten) 📄 Printable 4-Page Unit Packet: Download Unit 01 PDF (Concept, Blocks, Stack Trace, Student Lab Sheet & Answer Key)  |  📖 Companion Textbook: From Blocks to the Stack (SC-6 Manual) — Ch. 3: Counting, Subitizing & Place Value + Appendix B: Station F.1

docs.title: 1. Core Mathematical Rules & Stack Mapping (How Counting Maps to the Calculator)
docs.text:
• Every Gold [+1] step token added on the Place Value Tray matches one count on the calculator screen.
  • A [0] block in the Ones socket represents zero [0]. Press [C] to start a fresh count.
  • To step count by 1: press [1] [ENTER] [1] [+], then press [1] [+] as you step your Ones digit block from [1] to [2], [3], [4]...
  • Numbers show quantity (cardinality): the digit block in the Ones socket matches the total count on Line X.
  • Canonical Stack Pattern: [1] [ENTER] [1] [+] = 2, then [1] [+] = 3, [1] [+] = 4...

docs.title: 2. Primary Core Lesson — 1-to-1 Correspondence: The Concrete Step Counter (Bridges in Mathematics: Kindergarten, Unit 1 • CCSS.MATH.K.CC.B.4)
docs.text:
• Lesson Objective: Establish one-to-one correspondence between physical digit blocks and step tokens on the Place Value Tray and calculator screen increments.
  • Step 1 — The Mathematical Concept & Stack-Based Approach: Counting by ones is repeated addition of the unit 1 (n -> n + 1). In a stack-based approach, the current total waits on Shelf Y while the unit step (1) enters Workbench X; pressing [+] combines them into the new total.
  • Step 2 — Modeling with Physical Blocks (When Applicable) & Student Prediction (PLACE-01):
  • Hands-On Setup: Place the [1] Digit Block into the Ones socket of the Place Value Tray. Keep Gold [+1] step tokens ready beside the tray.
  • Student Prediction (Before Pressing Keys): When we place 1 Gold [+1] step token and step the Ones block up by 1, what digit block replaces [1]? (Prediction: [2])
  • Teacher Coaching ("Say This, Not That"): Say: ""Place 1 Gold [+1] step token on the tray first, then press [1] [+] to match the count you just touched.""  |  Avoid: ""Just press 1 + 1 + 1 as fast as you can until the screen says 5.""
  • Step 3 — Calculator Execution & 4-Level Stack Trace (T, Z, Y, X):
Key Pressed Screen (X) Internal 4-Level Stack Effect (T, Z, Y, X) 1 1 First count placed: 1 enters register X enter 1 1 copied to register Y: holds the current count 1 1 Gold [+1] step token added: 1 enters register X plus 2 Press [+]: 1 + 1 = 2! Swap Ones block to [2] 1 1 Next Gold [+1] step token added: 1 enters X plus 3 Press [+]: 2 + 1 = 3! Tray [3] and screen match perfectly
  • Step 4 — Story Context & Guided Classroom Investigation:
  • Historical & Real-World Hook ("How Ten Fingers & an Empty Shell Created Place Value & The 1-to-10 Staircase"): Long before paper or keyboards existed, ancient shepherds counted flocks with clay pebbles ('calculi' in Latin—the root of 'calculator'!) and Maya astronomers drew a shell for zero so an empty socket had its own symbol. Stepping 1 token at a time on the Place Value Tray while pressing [1] [+] builds the exact 1-to-10 Staircase from Chapter 3 of From Blocks to the Stack.
  • 60-Second Bell-Ringer Prompt: Close your eyes and clap slowly 4 times. Before opening your eyes, which Digit Block belongs in the Ones socket of your Place Value Tray and what number waits on Line X?
  • Guided Classroom Investigation: Place the [4] Digit Block in the Ones column of your Place Value Tray. Add 1 Gold [+1] step token. Write the keystrokes to show 4 + 1 on the calculator. Worked Solution & Keystrokes: 5 ([5] Digit Block). Keystrokes: [4] [ENTER] [1] [+]

docs.title: 3. Follow-Up Extension Lesson — More, Less & Zero: Finding Differences (Singapore Math: Kindergarten, Book A • CCSS.MATH.K.CC.C.6)
docs.text:
• Extension Objective: Compare two quantities on the two rows of the Place Value Tray and find the difference using subtraction.
  • Step 1 — The Mathematical Concept & Stack-Based Approach: Comparison subtraction finds the difference ('how many more?') between two quantities. In stack order, the larger reference quantity sits on Waiting Shelf Y while the smaller quantity enters Workbench X before pressing [-].
  • Step 2 — Modeling with Physical Blocks (When Applicable) & Hypothesis (PLACE-01):
  • Setup: Place the [5] Digit Block in Row 1 (top row) and the [2] Digit Block in Row 0 (bottom row) of the Ones column on the Place Value Tray.
  • Student Hypothesis: Look at the two rows on the tray. Which row has the larger quantity? How many more is 5 than 2?
  • Step 3 — Calculator Execution & 4-Level Stack Trace (T, Z, Y, X):
Key Pressed Screen (X) Internal 4-Level Stack Effect (T, Z, Y, X) 5 5 Row 1 quantity (5) enters register X enter 5 5 lifted to register Y (first set) 2 2 Row 0 quantity (2) enters register X minus 3 Minus subtracts X from Y: Row 1 has 3 more!
  • Extension Investigation: Row 1 holds [6] and Row 0 holds [2] on your Place Value Tray. How many more is in Row 1? Write the keystrokes. Worked Solution & Keystrokes: 4 more. Keystrokes: [6] [ENTER] [2] [-]

docs.title: 4. Target Misconceptions & 30-Second Teacher Remediations
docs.text:
• Misconception: Reciting number names faster than placing physical step tokens (losing 1-to-1 correspondence). 30-Second Teacher Remediation: Have the student place 1 Gold [+1] token on the Place Value Tray and step the Ones Digit Block first, say the number aloud, and only then press [1] [+] so the tray and Register X stay locked in step.
  • Misconception: Confusing the action of adding 1 more with the total quantity on the tray (cardinality). 30-Second Teacher Remediation: Ask the student to point to the Digit Block in the Ones socket of the Place Value Tray and verify that its numeral matches Register X on the screen.

docs.title: 5. Student Lab Worksheet Problems (P1–P4) & Answer Key
docs.text: Problem Student Lab Investigation Prompt StackCalc Check Keystrokes Expected Answer P1 Place [3] in Row 1 and [2] in Row 0 of the Ones column. Write the keystrokes to find the total.
