docs.title: The Four Most Common Student Traps & Quick Verbal Cues
Trap 1: The "Where is the Equals Key?" Reflex
docs.text:
• What Happens: The student enters 3 [ENTER] 5 [+] and then sits looking at the keypad, asking why the calculator hasn't calculated the answer yet.
  • The Cause: Conditioning on standard algebraic keyboards where nothing happens until = is pressed.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "When you combine a [3] block and a [5] block on your tray, do you have to press an equals button after combining them? No—combining them IS the operation! The [+] button combined Waiting Shelf Y and Workbench X. Look at Line X: 8 is already there."

docs.title: Trap 2: The "Double Enter" Accidental Stack Lift
docs.text:
• What Happens: The student wants to calculate \(4 + 7\). They type 4 [ENTER] 7 [ENTER] [+] and get 14 instead of 11.
  • The Cause: The student treats [ENTER] like a comma after every number. The second [ENTER] duplicated 7 into Register Y, pushing 4 up to Register Z. When they pressed [+], the calculator evaluated \(7 + 7 = 14\).
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Look at the 4 stack lines on your screen. [ENTER] is the elevator that lifts your first number onto Waiting Shelf Y so you have room to type the second number on Workbench X. You only press [ENTER] between two numbers typed back-to-back: 4 [ENTER] 7 [+] (11)."

docs.title: Trap 3: The "Larger Denominator Means Bigger Fraction" Fallacy
docs.text:
• What Happens: When comparing \(\frac{1}{8}\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\), the student asserts that \(\frac{1}{8}\) is larger because \(8 > 3\).
  • The Cause: Treating the denominator as a whole-number count rather than the number of equal partitions of a 1 Whole (84.0 mm) unit.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Pick up the \(\frac{1}{8}\) block (10.5 mm) in your left hand and the \(\frac{1}{3}\) block (28.0 mm) in your right hand from the Fraction Studio (FRAC-01). Stand them side-by-side in the comparator well and run your index finger across the top. Cutting the 84.0 mm whole into 8 pieces makes each piece smaller than cutting it into 3 pieces."

docs.title: Trap 4: The "Factor Addition vs. Multiplicative Height" Trap
docs.text:
• What Happens: When working with Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01), a student stacks a [2] block and a [3] block and expects the tower height to represent \(2 + 3 = 5\) rather than \(2 \times 3 = 6\).
  • The Cause: Confusing additive place-value/fraction heights with logarithmic prime factor blocks (h = k·log10(p)), where stacking adds logarithms and therefore multiplies prime factors.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "In Prime Factor Studio, stacking blocks multiplies their factors: a [2] block plus a [3] block builds \(2 \times 3 = 6\) (the exact same height as [3] plus [2]). Press 6 [g] [FACT] on your SC-6 to verify the prime factorization \(2 \times 3\) on the screen."

docs.title: Core Stack Teaching Techniques: 5 Classroom Routines on the 4-Level XYZT Display
docs.text:
The StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator and SC-32 Scientific Calculator display all four operational stack registers (T, Z, Y, X) simultaneously. Rather than hiding intermediate quantities behind a single-line display or nested parentheses, the 4-level stack keeps both operands visible on Waiting Shelf Y and Workbench X.

[!TIP] Focused 2-Stack Mode (\(Y, X\)) for Early Elementary Learners: Kindergarten and Grade 1–2 teachers can optionally set the SC-6 into a simplified 2-Stack Mode (\(Y, X\)) across all operations so early learners focus solely on the Waiting Shelf (Y) and Workbench (X): press [↱] [FLAGS] → [5] (5:DEP) → [C].

For additional elementary routines, see the RPN Elementary Power Guide →. Below are five practical classroom routines:

docs.title: Routine 1: Constant-Step Skip-Counting & Multiplication Ladders ([REP])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups (\(7 \times 4 = 7 + 7 + 7 + 7\)).
  • How It Works on the Stack:
  • Enter the step size: 7 [g] [REP]. All 4 stack levels (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) fill with 7.
  • Press [+] repeatedly: 14, 21, 28, 35, 42...
  • Why It Works: Because the top register (\(T\)) replicates downward whenever the stack drops, 7 stays loaded as a constant increment in \(Y, Z, T\) while the running multiple accumulates in \(X\).
  • Teacher Cue:

    "With every press of [+], read the multiple aloud: '2 sevens are 14, 3 sevens are 21, 4 sevens are 28...' so students connect skip-counting to multiplication facts."

docs.title: Routine 2: Whole-Number Division with Remainders ([÷R])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Division in Grades 3–5 is fair-sharing with whole-number leftovers (\(23 \div 4 = 5 \text{ R } 3\)) before converting remainders into fractions or decimals.
  • How It Works on the Stack:
  • Enter dividend and divisor: 23 [ENTER] 4.
  • Press [↱] [÷R] (full sequence: 23 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R]).
  • Read the two bottom lines together:
    • Line X: 5 (Whole Quotient \(Q\))
    • Line Y: 3 (Remainder \(R\))
  • Teacher Cue:

    "Look at your two bottom lines: Line X shows how many full groups of 4 we made (5), and Line Y shows the leftover units (3) waiting to be shared."

docs.title: Routine 3: Inverse-Operation Self-Checking with [LASTX] ([↰] [LASTX])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Verifying calculations using inverse operations (\(A + B = C \implies C - B = A\), and \(Q \times D + R = \text{Dividend}\)).
  • How It Works on the Stack:
  • Calculate \(48 + 37\): 48 [ENTER] 37 [+] → 85.
  • Press [↰] [LASTX]: recalls the last X operand (37) into Register \(X\), automatically lifting 85 to Register \(Y\).
  • Press [-] (full sequence: 48 [ENTER] 37 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-]): returns to the starting value 48.
  • Division Proof (\(Q \times D + R = \text{Dividend}\)):
  • After \(79 \div 8\) with [÷R] (X: 9, Y: 7), press [↰] [LASTX] (retrieves Divisor 8) [×] [+] → 79.
  • Teacher Cue:

    "Before asking if your answer is right, press [LASTX] and the inverse operation key. If your starting number comes back on Line X, you have proved your own work."

docs.title: Routine 4: Inside-Out Sub-Expression Evaluation Without Parentheses
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Evaluating multi-step expressions like \((4 \times 8) + (15 \div 3)\) by identifying and solving the inner products/quotients before combining terms.
  • How It Works on the Stack:
  • Evaluate the first term: 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] → 32 in \(X\).
  • Evaluate the second term: 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] → 5 in \(X\), while 32 automatically lifts to Waiting Shelf \(Y\).
  • Combine both terms (4 [ENTER] 8 [×] 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [+]): [+] → 37 in \(X\).
  • Teacher Cue:

    "Notice how Waiting Shelf Y holds your first result (32) while you compute the second part (5) on Workbench X. Once both parts are visible on Y and X, press [+] to combine them."

docs.title: Routine 5: Two-Method Verification & Tutorial Mode ([↰] [C])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Encouraging students to connect paper/block reasoning with stack verification rather than relying on a single rote procedure.
  • How It Works in Practice:
  • Method 1 (+10 pts): Solve the problem by hand in the workbook (and build with PLACE-01, FRAC-01, or PRIME-01 on Place Value, Fraction, or Prime Factor units), and record the predicted answer.
  • Method 2 (+20 pts): Verify the exact same problem on the 4-level stack (or using SC-6 Tutorial Mode ([↰] [C])) and check that the stack registers match the intermediate steps of the paper/block solution.

docs.title: Classroom Storage & Desk Management (3 Published Block Kits)
docs.text: Our three published manipulative kits—Place Value Studio (PLACE-01), Fraction Studio (FRAC-01), and Prime Factor Studio (PRIME-01)—are built on the 42.0 mm Gridfinity modular standard: * The Lid Doubles as the Desk Workbench: Students do not dump loose pieces across the desk. The indexed comparator or place-value tray keeps digit blocks, fraction towers, and prime factor blocks organized in vertical columns during the lesson. * Self-Checking Waterline Pack-Up Routine: Before the bell rings, announce: "Towers in their columns, lids flush!" In Fraction Studio and Prime Factor Studio, every column packs to a uniform flush height (84.0 mm in Fraction Studio), and in Place Value Studio, every 0–9 digit slot is indexed so any missing block is visible at a glance.

docs.title: Turnkey Classroom Pacing Guides
Pacing Option A: The Hands-On Math Station (1 Period / Week)
docs.text: Ideal for classrooms rotating a small-group set of Place Value, Fraction, or Prime Factor blocks and calculators through three 20-minute stations: * Minutes 0–10: Whole-group concept introduction (Concept & Stack Approach). * Minutes 10–35: Three rotating small-group stations: * Station 1 (Blocks & Stack Verification): Students work in pairs modeling the concept with PLACE-01, FRAC-01, or PRIME-01 and verifying on the SC-6/SC-32 stack. * Station 2 (Representational Sketching): Independent practice drawing place-value tables, fraction bars, factor trees, or stack register traces. * Station 3 (Teacher Guided Group): Targeted misconception diagnostics and "Say This, Not That" verbal coaching. * Minutes 35–45: Whole-group synthesis and exit ticket check.

docs.title: Pacing Option B: The 3-Week Foundational Intervention Sprint
docs.text: Designed for math recovery and small-group intervention using the three published block kits: * Week 1 (Place Value Studio PLACE-01): Units 01–05 (Counting, Number Bonds, Make-10 Regrouping with Gold [+1] Carry Tokens, and Multi-Step Stack Evaluation). * Week 2 (Fraction Studio FRAC-01): Unit 06 & MS Units 02, 04 (84.0 mm Tower Equivalence, Common Denominators, and Two-Dot Fraction Arithmetic). * Week 3 (Prime Factor Studio PRIME-01): Units 07 & 10 & MS Unit 01 (Logarithmic Prime Factor Towers, [FACT], [GCF], [LCM], and Inside-Out Order of Operations).

docs.title: Pacing Option C: Full-Year K–12 Vertical Progression
docs.text: A 36-week vertical progression across the 12 Concept Domains: * Q1 (Units 01–04): Early Number Sense, Place Value Trays, Complements to 10 & Equal Groups (PLACE-01 + SC-6). * Q2 (Units 05–07): 4-Register Stack Operations, 84 mm Fraction Towers (FRAC-01), Prime Factorization (PRIME-01) & Postfix Order of Operations. * Q3 (Units 08–09): Base-\(x\) Polynomial Structure, Quadratic Roots ([POLY]), Right-Triangle Ratio Towers & Polar/Rectangular Vectors (SC-32). * Q4 (Units 10–12): Logarithmic Scaling (PRIME-01), Exponential Growth ([eˣ] / [LN]), Combinatorics & Statistical Accumulation ([Σ+]), and Base-\(N\) Computer Arithmetic ([BASE]).

docs.title: The Tournament Keystroke Race: Texas UIL Problem 14
docs.text:
In Texas UIL and TMSCA Calculator Applications, competitors have exactly 30 minutes to complete 70 rigorous problems. At an average pace of 25.7 seconds per problem, typing speed, finger rhythm, and error prevention dictate tournament medalists. Missing a single closing parenthesis triggers a fatal syntax error or silently corrupts algebraic operator precedence, costing \(-4\) penalty points per missed question.

Here is an authentic tournament benchmark: evaluating a multi-stage rational expression typical of UIL High School Problem 14:

\[ \text{Problem 14: } \frac{4.82 \times 10^3 - 195}{\sqrt{84.6} + 12.7^2} \]

docs.title: Contest Coaching & Sprint Pacing Strategies
docs.text: Coaches training calculator teams can apply these proven pacing milestones to maximize score yields:

docs.title: 1. The Page 1–2 Baseline Sprint (Minutes 0:00 – 7:00)
docs.text: Pages 1 and 2 consist of straightforward numerical calculations. Contestants should complete all 20 problems in under 7 minutes. Because RPN eliminates parentheses, keystroke cadence should be fluid and rhythmic. Aim for \(100\%\) accuracy here, yielding \(+100\) baseline points.

docs.title: 2. The Word Problem Filter (Minutes 7:00 – 16:00)
docs.text: Pages 3 and 4 introduce stated word problems and first-tier geometry (triangles, rectangles). Contestants should read the word problem, extract the required formula, execute the RPN chain, and write down the 3-sig-fig answer immediately without writing scratch equations.

docs.title: 3. The Geometry Vector Sweep (Minutes 16:00 – 24:00)
docs.text: Page 5 contains geometric figures (frustums, circular sectors). Train competitors to solve from the inside out: compute radius subtractions first, stack the result, multiply by slant height, and terminate with [↱] [π] and [×].

docs.title: 4. The Final Push & Strategic Stopping (Minutes 24:00 – 30:00)
docs.text: Under UIL scoring rules, an unattempted question incurs zero penalty, while an incorrect guess costs \(-4\) points. In the final 2 minutes, competitors should never make blind guesses. Once they reach their peak problem, they should stop cleanly to avoid negative deductions.

docs.title: Pedagogical Guiding Principles
1. Authentic Math Problem Solving (No Calculator Write-In Cells)
docs.text: Students are learning mathematics, not calculator operation. Practice problems feature spacious drawing canvases for tape diagrams, bar models, number bonds, or area matrices. Students solve with physical blocks and paper first. There are strictly zero calculator button fill-in blanks.

docs.title: 2. Student Self-Check Rule (No Cheating)
docs.text: A clear instructional banner enforces that the calculator is strictly a self-checking device. When a student enters their solution into the StackCalc 4-line LCD screen, any discrepancy immediately prompts them to re-inspect their physical bench model or regrouping, turning mistakes into productive struggle without requiring teacher intervention.

docs.title: 3. Exact Continuous Squircle App Buttons
docs.text: All buttons in keystroke sequences and LCD traces are rendered with millimeter-precision touch squircles featuring dark trench bezels matching the StackCalc iOS/macOS production app (HardwareReplicaKeyCap.swift).

docs.title: 4. Step-by-Step LCD Stack Trace
docs.text: Zone 1 (Right Panel) illustrates worked-out examples with the stack after each keypress: explicitly starting with the Mode Key ([PV], [FDISP], [🕒], [POLY], [DEG]), followed by operands, automatic stack lift (Y: val | X: val), and operator stack drop transitions (X: result).

docs.text:
// HACKADAY.IO PROJECT · BUILD LOG ARCHIVE

Project Page: https://hackaday.io/project/206743-stackcalc32-a-tactile-rpn-calculator Status: Mechanical Prototype Verified · Custom RP2350 PCB in Fabrication

docs.title: 1. Project Overview
docs.text:
Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) eliminated parentheses in the golden age of scientific computing, yet modern students are still forced into nested syntax traps. StackCalc32 redesigns the RPN calculator from the ground up: starting with an ultra-constrained Apple Watch UI, extending to a shared clean-room Swift core (RPNCore), and culminating in an open-hardware pocket calculator powered by the Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller.

The mechanical enclosure uses a novel tool-free 4-part sliding rail system. The custom 4-layer PCB is currently in fabrication at the board house; visible hardware photos represent unpowered 3D-printed mechanical prototypes used for ergonomic and tolerance validation.

docs.title: 2. Current Prototype & Evidence Boundaries
docs.text: We hold our documentation to a strict standard of engineering truthfulness: - Board Design Status: The 4-layer custom KiCad RP2350 PCB design is complete and currently in fabrication at the factory. There is no powered physical board on the desk yet. - Physical Photos: All hardware photos in this project show the 3D-printed tool-free mechanical prototype (chassis_award, unified_faceplate_award, tpu_membrane_award, top_cap_award). These parts are unpowered and evaluate rail sliding tolerances, membrane fit, and snap closure. - Firmware Verification: The firmware logic, display driver, and keyboard matrix scanner are tested and verified via a native WebAssembly and RP2350 software emulator subjected to 40 Hz differential grammar fuzzing. - Companion Apps: Full v1.1 versions of StackCalc are available on the Apple App Store for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch.

docs.title: Board Arrival Evidence Protocol & Checklist
docs.text:
// HARDWARE BRING-UP · GATED EVIDENCE PROTOCOL

Hardware Gate Constraint: A booted screen does not prove keypad reliability or battery endurance. Each physical property must be inspected and recorded as an independent test observation before making public hardware claims.

docs.title: The Seven Verification Stages
docs.text: Stage Inspection Target Verification Method Acceptance Threshold Failure Condition & Triage 1. Seating Plane PCB fit into chassis rails Slide board into chassis_award guide channels. Measure perimeter gap. Board seats flush on internal shelf; zero lateral rocking; \(\le 0.20\text{ mm}\) gap. Rail binding -> Measure caliper width of PCB routing edge. Sand or adjust CAD. 2. Display Alignment 2.5" ST7567 LCD centering Mount LCD in faceplate cowl. Inspect viewing window margins with backlit test pattern. Active display area centered within \(\pm 0.3\text{ mm}\); zero pixel cutoff by bezel cowl. Misaligned window -> Adjust faceplate aperture in unified_faceplate_award.scad. 3. Connector Clearance 0.5 mm ZIF ribbon loop Insert FFC into bottom-contact ZIF socket. Slide assembly closed. Ribbon maintains natural \(\ge 1.5\text{ mm}\) radius bend; zero pinching against chassis rib. Creased ribbon -> Immediate stop; deepen chassis relief notch. 4. Matrix / Switch Reach Key actuator contact Depress each of the 37 keys through TPU membrane. Inspect switch plunger contact. Every key achieves tactile dome click with \(\le 1.8\text{ mm}\) travel; zero key binds against aperture. Switch not engaging -> Check actuator stem height on tpu_membrane_award.scad. 5. Cap Closure & Retention Snap-retention top cap Slide top_cap_award into place. Measure retention force with pull gauge. Audible dual-snap engagement; withstands \(\ge 15\text{ N}\) pull force without popping open. Loose cap -> Increase detent engagement lip by \(+0.15\text{ mm}\). 6. Powered Boot & Current USB-C power-up & quiescent draw Connect current-limited DC bench supply (3.3V, 100mA limit). Flash UF2 test image. Boot banner appears; quiescent current \(\le 18\text{ mA}\) at 133 MHz; zero thermal runaway. Short circuit / high current -> Immediate power cut; inspect for soldering bridges. 7. First Calculation Operational stack execution Execute standard golden keystroke sequence: 2 [ENTER] 3 [+] and verify screen. Screen displays exact integer 5 in X register; stack lifts cleanly; zero debounce ghosting. Calculation error or ghost keys -> Check matrix diode orientation and software debounce timer.

Title: StackCalc 32: Why I Built a Kid-Friendly, Clean-Room HP-32SII Successor (and Ecosystem) After Training My Kids on a DM41CC

Body: 

Hello everyone,

I have been lurking here for years and wanted to share a project that grew directly out of teaching my own kids RPN—and invite feedback from this community.

First, a bit of personal background: I fell in love with RPN on an HP-32SII in high school and was heartbroken when I no longer had it. Over the years I bought a few vintage HP-32SII units off eBay, but the aging switch feel and build quality were disappointing. Like many of you, I turned to SwissMicros: I own a DM42 (which I converted to a C47, including printing and cutting the overlays), a DM32, a DM41CC, and a DM15CC.

I actually trained my kids on my DM41CC. They picked up the stack effortlessly—which proved to me that kids don't struggle with RPN; they struggle with infix parentheses! Better yet, because a postfix stack has no hidden infix parser, **students actually learn operator-precedence parsing in their own minds** to enter expressions onto the stack, seeing every intermediate result step by step. And unlike CAS calculators (which are banned on the SAT, ACT, IB, and university/FE exams), our hardware is purposefully designed to be allowed in testing situations (no CAS, no QWERTY keyboard, and no wireless radios). But there was no way I was going to send a child to school every day with a $250 boutique calculator or a $200 vintage eBay antique in their backpack. Our long-term goal is a durable, kid-friendly RPN calculator at a $29.99 classroom price point (we are launching our first small maker batch at $89.99 while we scale up volume).

### Why the HP-32SII Architecture Instead of the HP-15C or HP-42S?
When designing StackCalc 32 (`SC-32`), I thought hard about whether to model the workflow on the 15C, 42S, or 32SII:
- Why not the HP-42S / C47? As much as I love my C47 and 42S on the bench, burying everyday functions inside multi-layer softkey menus slows down learners and hides what the instrument can do.
- Why not the HP-15C? The landscape form factor and memorized numeric matrix/label codes are iconic, but less approachable for a student's first scientific instrument.
- Why the HP-32SII? The 32SII hit the ergonomics sweet spot: almost every essential scientific operation lives directly on the primary or shifted keys (zero menu diving for daily math), while a single-line context menu cleanly handles `CLEAR`, `STAT`, `SOLVE`, and `INTG`.

### Not an Emulator: A Clean-Room Engine (`RPNCore`) with Deliberate Upgrades
StackCalc 32 is not a ROM emulator or microcode wrapper. It is a clean-room engine written from scratch in Swift (`RPNCore`) that compiles both to our iPhone/iPad/standalone Apple Watch app and to bare-metal silicon on the Raspberry Pi RP2350. Writing our own engine let us keep the classic 4-level stack (`X, Y, Z, T`), `LASTx`, and 26 lettered registers (`A–Z`) while adding features I always wished the 32SII had:
1. Harmonic Mean (`H.M.`) alongside arithmetic and weighted means in `STAT`.
2. Built-in Time Value of Money (`TVM`) solver (`N`, `I%YR`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`).
3. Dedicated Quadratic & Cubic Polynomial Root Solver (`POLY`) with complex root support.
4. Interactive Function & Scatter-Plot Graphing (`PLOT`) on the app and 132×65 graphic LCD.

### Growing With the Student: `StackCalc 6` (Common Core K–6) & The Tactile Ecosystem
To help kids start before high school, our app and firmware also include `StackCalc 6` (`SC-6`)—an elementary RPN mode covering every key operation in Common Core math up through 6th grade:
- Whole-number integer division with remainder (`÷R`), prime factorization (`[PRIME]`), `GCD`/`LCM`, ratio tables, and elapsed clock time.
- Step-by-Step Fraction Simplification (`[SIMP]`): Instead of silently jumping from `12/18` to `2/3`, pressing `[SIMP]` in `SC-6` factors out one prime divisor per press so a student sees *how* the fraction reduces.
- Live dot-matrix visualizations: Ten-Frames, a 20-bead Rekenrek rack, and proportional Number Lines.

Surrounding the calculator is a complete learning ecosystem:
- Physical 3D-Printed Math Blocks (available free on Printables or pre-printed on Etsy): Fraction Studio Proportional Towers, Prime Factor Studio & Slide Rule, Place Value Regrouping Trays, and Ten-Frames that dock onto 42mm Gridfinity desk lids.
- Unit-Test-Verified Books & Workbooks: Complete SC-32 and SC-6 Owner's Manuals plus 590+ graded problems (339-problem SC-32 Casebook, 253-problem SC-6 Workbook, and 24 UIL speed-calculation exams), compiled with an automated verification pipeline that executes every worked keystroke sequence against the calculator engine in unit tests so there are zero typos.

We just got our first 5 physical RP2350 calculators running on the bench (and wrote a blog post with the factory DFM photos PCBWay sent us when they caught our rear header pins colliding with a front softkey).

Title (Under 80 chars): Show HN: StackCalc – Using AI to build an open RPN calculator and math lab

URL: https://www.stackcalc.io

First Comment to Post Immediately After Submitting: 

Hi HN! I’m a software/AI engineer, and over the past year I used AI coding agents to help me cross into physical hardware engineering—designing a 4-layer RP2350 PCB, parametric OpenSCAD 3D-printed enclosures, 280-run FEA keypad physics simulations, and automated Blender studio renders.

The irony isn't lost on me: I used AI to build a deterministic, 100% offline pocket calculator and physical block set because I strongly believe that **despite the availability of AI, students still need to know math**.

Why build a stack-based RPN calculator for kids instead of just handing them a $20 infix Casio/TI calculator—or a CAS graphing calculator?
- First, an infix calculator hides order-of-operations inside a black box: the student types `(12 + 8) / (5 - 1) =`, sees zero intermediate state, and blindly trusts whatever pops out at the end. On a stack-based postfix calculator, **users have to learn operator-precedence parsing themselves** in order to decompose and enter expressions onto the stack. While the original 1970s motivation for RPN may have been hardware constraints, we want kids to appreciate the lessons learned in the past 50 years of computing (stack machines, AST post-order traversal, Forth/JVM/Wasm) so they can build the next 50 years.
- Second, handing students a CAS calculator doesn't work when **CAS calculators are banned on tests** (now banned on both the SAT and ACT, as well as IB, NCEES FE/PE engineering exams, and university calculus midterms). Our physical calculator is purposefully designed to be **allowed in testing situations**—strictly numeric/scientific with zero CAS symbolic algebra, zero QWERTY keyboard, and zero wireless transceivers. (And for parents who already love RPN, sending a kid to school with a $250 collector's DM41/DM42 isn't practical—so we are launching our small-batch maker units at $89.99 on a hardware roadmap toward a $29.99 student price point.)

Here is how we built the stack and what we’re launching today:

1. One Clean-Room Swift Core (`RPNCore`) + 40 Hz Differential Fuzzer:
We wrote a zero-dependency RPN engine in Swift that compiles to iOS, iPadOS, a 100% standalone watchOS app, and bare-metal Raspberry Pi RP2350 silicon (via Embedded Swift). To guarantee the bare-metal C/Swift firmware never diverges from the host engine, a grammar-based differential fuzzer hammers both surfaces at 40 Hz with random and adversarial postfix sequences.

2. Physics Simulations for the TPU Membrane Buttons & Screwless Enclosure:
Because 3D-printed calculator buttons often feel mushy or bind when pressed on a corner, we modeled our 43-key Shore 95A TPU keypad membrane in parametric OpenSCAD and ran a **280-condition Finite Element Analysis (FEA) physics sweep** (7 off-axis thumb angles up to 15° × 8 compass directions × 5 strike offsets):
- We simulated off-center corner presses to tune our faceplate aperture chamfers and membrane webbing thickness—guaranteeing that even a 15° diagonal thumb strike transmits clean vertical force to the SMD tactile switch plunger underneath without wedging against the wall or causing parasitic cross-talk on neighboring keys: https://www.stackcalc.io/blog/2026/09/24/we-pressed-one-tpu-key-280-ways-before-the-pcb-arrived/
- We also ran structural FEA on our 4-part screwless sliding enclosure to design a zero-preload serpentine top latch (0.0 MPa static stress when closed so PLA never creeps over time) and used KiCad's `pcbnew` Python API to generate a 3D-printable `dummy_pcb.stl` for physical fit checks—which helped us catch a factory floor DFM collision when PCBWay sent us photos of our rear Pico 2 header pins poking between the front SMD pads of a softkey: https://www.stackcalc.io/blog/2026/10/20/pcbway-dfm-photos-and-jumper-fixes/

3. 3D-Printed Math Blocks Engineered Around Mathematical Invariants:
To bridge physical intuition with the calculator's stack (especially in our `StackCalc 6` Common Core K–6 mode), we designed a modular suite of 42mm Gridfinity manipulatives manufactured in-house and on Slant3D (with free STLs on Printables):
- **84mm Datum Fraction Towers:** Standard plastic fraction bars drift when stacked due to decimal thicknesses. We chose an **84mm Whole (`1/1`) height datum** because 84 is divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and 12 into exact integer millimeters (42mm, 28mm, 21mm, 14mm, 12mm, 7mm)—eliminating 0.20mm FDM slicer rounding drift. Students stack `1/2 + 1/3` (70mm) against five `1/6` blocks in a comparator trough, then enter `.1.2 [ENTER] .1.3 [+]` on the calculator (or use `[SIMP]` in `SC-6` to factor out one prime divisor per key press).
- **Logarithmic Prime Factor Slide Rule:** We scaled our prime number blocks (`2, 3, 5, 7`) logarithmically (`Length ∝ log(p)`). Because `log(a) + log(b) = log(a × b)`, snapping a `2` block and a `3` block end-to-end inside the rail physically equals the exact length of the `6` marker—turning prime factorization (`[PRIME]`), `GCD`, and `LCM` into a physical length-matching puzzle.

4. Compiling Textbooks Like Firmware (`book_engine.py`):
We wrote two owner's manuals and 590+ graded workbook problems (covering `SC-6` Common Core K–6 visual math and `SC-32` scientific/calculus). Our `Makefile` extracts every worked keystroke sequence from the Markdown prose, runs it as an `XCTest` unit test against `RPNCore`, and auto-renders the exact 132×65 LCD screenshots and STL orthographic diagrams. If a book example disagrees with the engine, the build fails.

Title: StackCalc: Co-Developing an App Store App and Bare-Metal RP2350 Firmware with a Shared Swift Core and STL-Backed Digital Twin

Body: 

Hi Swift community!

I’d love to share **StackCalc**, a project where we co-developed an iOS/iPadOS/standalone watchOS app and a physical Raspberry Pi RP2350 pocket RPN calculator from a single shared Swift package (`RPNCore`).

### 1. One Swift Codebase Across Apple Silicon and Bare-Metal RP2350
`RPNCore` is architected with zero external dependencies and deterministic value-type state so the exact same Swift code runs on:
- **iOS, iPadOS & Standalone watchOS (`StackCalc v1.1`):** Powering both `StackCalc 32` (4-level scientific RPN, numerical solver, Simpson integration, polynomial root finder, TVM, and curve plotting) and `StackCalc 6` (a K–6 Common Core visual stack that renders live Ten-Frames, Rekenrek bead racks, and number lines).
- **Bare-Metal RP2350 Firmware (Embedded Swift):** Compiled for `armv8m.main-none-eabi` and linked with a thin C hardware layer (`hardware_wrapper.c`) that scans our 43-key tactile switch matrix and drives a 132×65 ST7567 monochrome LCD over SPI.

### 2. Using Our Production STLs and Laser Decals for 1:1 Firmware/Hardware Co-Development
Waiting for PCB fabrication and 3D prints usually slows down firmware UX iteration. To solve this, we wired our hardware CAD pipeline directly into our Swift workspace:
- Our OpenSCAD generator (`generate_scad.py`) and laser decal scripts (`generate_laser_svg.py`) export the exact physical button geometry, keycap travel envelopes, and key legends into JSON layout registries (`layout_data.json` and `layout_data_sc6.json`).
- Inside the app (`HardwareReplicaView.swift` and `LCDDisplayView.swift`), SwiftUI renders an exact dimensional and pixel-level replica of the physical calculator—driving the identical 132×65 dot-matrix framebuffer (`RetroUI.swift`) and simulating physical switch boundaries via `CoreHaptics`.
- Our test suite (`SwiftUIVisualFuzzTests.swift` and our 40 Hz differential grammar fuzzer) runs keystroke sequences across the replica and exports live screenshots directly into our 590-problem companion workbooks and owner's manuals.

### Links & Resources

Title: StackCalc 32: Generating 3D-Printable Dummy PCBs from pcbnew for Test-Fitting + Real PCBWay Assembly Floor DFM Photos

Body: 

Hello KiCad community,

I wanted to share two workflows that saved us a ton of enclosure rework on **StackCalc 32**, our open-hardware RP2350 scientific RPN calculator:

### 1. Exporting `dummy_pcb.scad` from `pcbnew` to 3D-Print Physical Fit-Check Boards
Our calculator uses a 4-part, 100% screwless sliding rail enclosure (`chassis`, `unified_faceplate`, `tpu_membrane`, and snap-fit `top_cap`) with tight clearances ($0.40\text{ mm}$ lateral PCB rail allowance and $0.10\text{ mm}$ front switch datum).

Rather than waiting weeks for fabricated fiberglass boards to discover a mechanical collision, we wrote `Hardware/generate_scad.py` using KiCad's Python API (`pcbnew`). Every time `make layout` runs, it inspects `calculator.kicad_pcb` and generates two OpenSCAD files:
- `pcb_layout_generated.scad`: Exports the exact $(X, Y)$ centers of all 43 tactile switches, the internal `Edge.Cuts` LCD FPC ribbon slot, and the rear component sweeps.
- `dummy_pcb.scad` $\rightarrow$ `dummy_pcb.stl`: A complete 3D-printable plastic replica of the populated PCB—including the $1.6\text{ mm}$ FR-4 substrate, all 43 switch bodies and stems, the rear `MCU1` Pico 2 envelope, the `J1` 0.5mm ZIF socket, `JST1`, and the `C1`–`C8` charge-pump capacitors.

By printing `dummy_pcb.stl` in PLA on our desktop printer, we could slide the populated "board" into the chassis rails, verify that all 43 TPU membrane plungers met the switch tops cleanly, and check top-cap battery wire clearances before ordering a single PCB.

### 2. What Software DRC Missed (Caught by PCBWay's Assembly Line Photos)
Even with zero DRC errors and a perfect `dummy_pcb` fit, our first turnkey PCBA run at PCBWay caught three real-world BOM/footprint traps (documented with factory bench photos in our blog post below):
1. **Rear Header Pins vs. Front Switch `SOFT6`:** Our BOM accidentally called out `SC1632` (Pico 2 with pre-soldered through-hole headers) with PTH pads on `B.Cu`. The pins poked straight through the board between the four SMD pads of front switch `SOFT6`. We wrote `fix_mcu_pads.py` to convert `MCU1` to pure bottom-side castellated SMD pads (`B.Cu`, zero drill) and switched to `SC1631`.
2. **JST Footprint Mismatch & Stranded Silkscreen:** Updated `JST1` from through-hole `S2B-PH-K-S` to SMD `S2B-PH-SM4-TB` and wrote `fix_silkscreen.py` to move stranded `F.Silkscreen` graphics inside flipped footprints to `B.Silkscreen`.
3. **4-Pad Tactile Switch Internal Jumpers:** Disabled implicit pass-through switch jumpers (`(duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers no)`), marked the mechanical anchor pads `NC`, and routed explicit $0.25\text{ mm}$ copper buses across the matrix.

### Links & Files
- **PCBWay DFM Bench Photos & `pcbnew` Scripts Post:** https://www.stackcalc.io/blog/2026/10/20/pcbway-dfm-photos-and-jumper-fixes/
- **Hardware CAD Reference & Free Enclosure STLs:** https://www.stackcalc.io/hardware/

Title: StackCalc 32: From Slapping a Pico 2 on the Back of the PCB (Batch 1) to Bare RP2350A Integration (Batch 2)

Body: 

Hi everyone,

I wanted to share the hardware journey of StackCalc 32—an open-hardware pocket RPN scientific and educational calculator built around the RP2350, paired with 3D-printed Gridfinity math blocks and a companion iOS/watchOS app.

Our long-term goal is a durable, kid-friendly RPN calculator that students can toss in a backpack without their parents worrying about a $200+ calculator—starting at $89.99 for our first maker batch and driving the BOM down toward a $29.99 target.

### Batch 1 (First 5 Units): Slapping a Pico 2 onto the Back of the PCB
To get our first 5 physical calculators built and verified as fast as possible, we designed a 4-layer board where a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 (`MCU1`) solders directly onto the rear (`B.Cu`) behind the LCD area, scanning 43 tactile switches on the front (`F.Cu`) and driving a 2.5" 132×65 EastRising ST7567 transflective LCD over SPI.
- Funny DFM lesson from the factory floor: We initially listed `SC1632` (Pico 2 *with headers*) in our PCBWay BOM with through-hole pads. PCBWay sent us a photo showing the header pins poking straight through the front of the board right between the SMD pads of softkey `SOFT6`! Switching to the bare castellated Pico 2 (`SC1631`) and converting the footprint to pure bottom-side SMD pads solved it cleanly: https://www.stackcalc.io/blog/2026/10/20/pcbway-dfm-photos-and-jumper-fixes/

### Batch 2 (Next 20 Units — Hardware V2 Specification Ready): Full Bare-Silicon Integration
Now that Batch 1 proves out the 43-key matrix, TPU membrane feel, display driver, and our Embedded Swift firmware, our next 20-unit order moves to our **Hardware V2** layout—which keeps the exact same exterior enclosure and switch coordinates while eliminating the Pico 2 carrier board completely:
- **Direct QFN-60 RP2350A + Winbond W25Q32 4MB QSPI Flash + 12MHz Crystal** placed directly on `B.Cu` (dropping the MCU subsystem cost from $9.30 down to $1.22).
- **Direct CR2032 Spring Clip + Microne `ME2188` 3.3V Synchronous Boost (`Iq < 15µA`):** Replaces the wired JST battery harness and complex buck-boost power mux.
- **Strict Two-Zone Partitioning:** 100% of the ICs sit above a 6.13mm dead-band behind the LCD, leaving 100% bare ground copper behind all 43 tactile switches so key presses never flex solder joints.
- **RP2350 Erratum E9 Immunity:** Active-LOW open-drain matrix scanning (`gpio_pull_up()` on columns, High-Z inactive rows) in `hardware_wrapper.c`.

Title: Why the World Needs a Kid-Friendly Calculator That Grows With Them (Plus Our 3D-Printed Fraction & Prime Number Blocks)

Body: 

Hello fellow parents and educators,

Whenever I tell people we built a new calculator, the first question is understandably: "Why does the world need another calculator?"

Here is the problem I ran into with my own kids:
In early elementary school, kids learn math with physical blocks on a desk. If they want to add 2 and 3, they put down 2 blocks, put down 3 blocks, and push them together. That natural order—quantities first, action second—is called Postfix (or Reverse Polish Notation, RPN).

Then around 4th grade, we take away the blocks and hand them an infix school calculator where they type nested parentheses `(12 + 8) / (5 - 1) =` into a black box that hides every intermediate step until they press `=`. With a stack-based RPN calculator, **students actually internalize operator-precedence parsing** because they have to break expressions down in the right order of operations to enter them onto the stack, seeing every intermediate result along the way. And unlike CAS (Computer Algebra System) calculators—which are banned on the SAT, ACT, IB, UIL, and college math exams—our calculator is purposefully designed to be **allowed in testing situations** (no CAS symbolic solver, no QWERTY keyboard, and no Wi-Fi/Bluetooth on the hardware).

We built **StackCalc** as a kid-friendly mathematical instrument that grows with a student from 1st grade (`StackCalc 6` — covering Common Core math through 6th grade) all the way to AP Calculus and engineering (`StackCalc 32`), paired with physical desk blocks and unit-tested workbooks. (Nobody wants to send a kid to school with a $250 collector's RPN calculator or a $200 vintage antique—so our initial small-batch hardware launches at $89.99 while we scale manufacturing toward a $29.99 student target, and our universal iPhone/iPad/Apple Watch app is available today with zero ads and zero subscriptions.)

### How the Physical Blocks and the Calculator Work Together

Every physical kit we manufacture is built around a 42mm Gridfinity storage box whose lid turns into an active math stage on the student's desk:

1. **Fraction Studio Proportional Towers (`1/1` through `1/12`):**
   - **What the blocks do:** Our Whole (`1/1`) tower is exactly 84mm tall—a composite length chosen so that halves (42mm), thirds (28mm), fourths (21mm), sixths (14mm), and twelfths (7mm) all divide into exact integer millimeters. When a child wants to add `1/2 + 1/3`, they drop the `1/2` and `1/3` towers into the left slot of the Twin Comparator Stage (reaching 70mm). In the right slot, they stack `1/6` blocks until the heights match flush at 5 sixths (`5/6`), physically discovering why a common denominator is needed!
   - **What the calculator does:** On StackCalc, the child enters `.1.2 [ENTER] .1.3 [+]` and sees `5/6`. Even better, in `StackCalc 6`, if they have an unreduced fraction like `12/18` (`.12.18`), pressing our `[SIMP]` key does *not* just jump to `2/3` like a black-box calculator—it factors out **one prime divisor at a time** (showing the common factor `2`, reducing to `6/9`, and letting the student press `[SIMP]` again to factor out `3` to reach `2/3`).

2. **Prime Factor Studio & Logarithmic Slide Rule Comparator:**
   - **What the blocks do:** Instead of memorizing factor trees on paper, students snap physical prime-number blocks (`2`, `3`, `5`, `7`) end-to-end inside a dual comparison rail. Because the block lengths are scaled logarithmically, placing a `2` block and a `3` block end-to-end physically equals the length of `6`! To find the **Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)** or **Least Common Multiple (LCM)** of 12 (`2 × 2 × 3`) and 18 (`2 × 3 × 3`), students line up both prime trains side by side and immediately see the shared prime backbone (`2 × 3 = 6`).
   - **What the calculator does:** In `StackCalc 6`, students verify their physical trains directly with dedicated one-touch `[PRIME]` (prime factorization), `[GCD]`, `[LCM]`, and `[÷R]` (integer division with remainder) keys, alongside live on-screen Ten-Frames, a 20-bead Rekenrek rack, a proportional Number Line, and a 5-level Adaptive Mental Math Quiz (`?`).

### Explore the Ecosystem (Free Downloads & Printed Kits)
- **Full Article on Our 84mm Fraction Towers, Prime Blocks & Books:** https://www.stackcalc.io/blog/2026/10/26/manufacturing-math-blocks-and-reference-books/

- **App Store (iPhone, iPad & Standalone Apple Watch — 100% Offline, No Ads/Subs):** https://apps.apple.com/app/id6801788040

I would love to hear what math concepts give your students the most trouble and how we can add more station worksheets to help!

Title: StackCalc Open-Source Tactile Math Lab (Fraction Towers, Logarithmic Prime Slide Rule, & Screwless RPN Calculator Enclosure)

Body: 

### Why We Designed This
Sending a kid to school with a $250 collector's RPN calculator—or replacing an entire $60 classroom manipulative kit when one plastic block goes missing under a desk—makes no sense.

We designed the **StackCalc Tactile Math Lab** in parametric OpenSCAD so teachers, parents, and makers can print replacement blocks for pennies, dock every kit to the **42mm Gridfinity standard**, and pair hands-on blocks with our **StackCalc** RPN calculator (available today on iOS/watchOS, with our RP2350 open-hardware unit launching at $89.99 on the way to a $29.99 student target).

### Engineering Highlights in the STL / 3MF Bundle
1. **84mm Datum Fraction Studio Towers (`1/1` to `1/12`):** Engineered around an 84mm unit height so `1/2`, `1/3`, `1/4`, `1/6`, `1/7`, and `1/12` resolve to exact integer millimeter heights without slicer layer-rounding drift.
2. **Logarithmic Prime Factor Studio & Slide Rule:** Prime blocks (`2, 3, 5, 7`) scaled logarithmically so placing prime factors end-to-end physically multiplies their lengths (`log(a) + log(b) = log(a×b)`).
3. **4-Part Screwless Calculator Mechanical Prototype & Flat-Pack Puzzle Stand:** Uses 0.20mm sliding dovetail rails, a Shore 95A TPU membrane, a zero-preload serpentine snap latch (0.0 MPa static stress while latched so PLA never creeps), and a 6mm flat-packing desk stand.

docs.title: Log 01: The Watch Constraint: Designing an RPN UI for 40mm
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 01 · WEARABLE RPN

Canonical Article: Why We Started with the Apple Watch Topic: UI Architecture & Physical Constraints Artifact: Standalone watchOS Calculator Target & Minimap Navigation Engine

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
When building a modern scientific calculator, the natural temptation is to fill a high-resolution smartphone display with dozens of tiny buttons and nested flyout sheets. That approach masks sloppy ergonomic decisions.

We chose the opposite path: we designed for a 40 mm Apple Watch screen first.

A 40 mm OLED face allows exactly four readable rows of numeric typography and zero room for full alphanumeric button matrices. This extreme constraint forced three foundational architecture choices: 1. The Four-Level Operational Stack as Primary UI: In traditional infix calculators, you need an expression buffer, cursor indicators, and parenthesis counters. In RPN, the stack is the interface. Stacking \(X\) (bottom/active), \(Y\), \(Z\), and \(T\) fits the vertical aspect ratio of a smartwatch display with mathematical perfection. 2. The Rotary Minimap (Digital Crown Scrubbing): Instead of cramming 40 buttons onto a touch screen where fingers cause occlusion errors, the watch uses the physical Digital Crown to smoothly scrub across three functional planes (Arithmetic, Transcendental, and Memory). 3. Discrete Haptic Detents: Physical calculators provide tactile dome snap. On watchOS, we synthesize this with CoreHaptics: sharp .click transients on key contact, followed by inertia detents when rotating through registers.

Figure 1: Standalone watchOS interface displaying the four-level stack with zero phone tethering.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
The state machine decoupling the active display register from touch entry is extracted into our standalone Swift engine: 

// Core Watch Minimap State Transition
public enum MinimapPlane: Int, CaseIterable {
    case basic = 0      // +, -, *, /, ENTER
    case scientific = 1 // sin, cos, tan, ln, log, sqrt
    case memory = 2     // STO, RCL, CLSTK, SWAP
}

docs.title: Log 02: One Core to Rule Them All: Swift Package to Bare-Metal Silicon
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 02 · EMBEDDED SWIFT

Canonical Article: One Calculator Core for Watch, Phone, and RP2350 Topic: Clean-Room Systems Architecture & Embedded Swift Artifact: Shared RPNCore Architectural Model & Target Matrix

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Maintaining separate calculator logic across different platforms is a recipe for divergence: rounding discrepancies, subtle order-of-operation bugs, and stack lift mismatches between app and hardware.

We built a single clean-room engine (RPNCore) that compiles across three radically different execution environments: 1. Darwin Host (iOS, iPadOS, macOS): Rich SwiftUI interfaces, Metal rendering, high-level haptics. 2. watchOS Target: Highly optimized memory constraints, 40 Hz rendering budgets. 3. Bare-Metal RP2350 Microcontroller (Cortex-M33): Zero dynamic heap allocation, zero standard library dependencies, running bare-metal Embedded Swift 6.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           RPNCore (Swift Package)                       |
|           • Four-Level Stack Architecture (X, Y, Z, T)                  |
|           • Arbitrary-Precision Rational Fraction Engine                |
|           • Classic RPN Computing Engine Parity (Clean-Room)           |
+--------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------+
                     │                                │
                     ▼                                ▼
       [Darwin / SwiftUI Runtime]         [Embedded Swift 6 / ARM]
       • iOS & iPadOS (v1.1 Live)         • Bare-metal Cortex-M33
       • watchOS (Standalone)             • WebAssembly Emulator Loop

By decoupling state transitions from UI rendering, the core processes a stream of atomic key tokens (.digit(5), .enter, .operation(.add)) and emits immutable display frame representations.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
The stack lift state machine ensures that entering a number immediately after a binary operation automatically pushes the previous result up the stack, exactly matching Corvallis hardware specifications: 

// Stack Lift State Machine
public mutating func pushDigit(_ d: Int) {
    if stackLiftEnabled {
        t = z
        z = y
        y = x
        x = 0
        stackLiftEnabled = false
    }
    x = (x * 10) + Double(d)
}

docs.title: Log 03: Tool-Free Sliding Assembly: Four 3D-Printed Parts, Zero Screws
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 03 · MECHANICAL ENCLOSURE

Canonical Article: A Tool-Free Calculator Built Around a Sliding Assembly Topic: Mechanical Engineering, CAD & Tolerancing Artifact: 4-Part Mechanical STL Pack (chassis_award.stl, unified_faceplate_award.stl, tpu_membrane_award.stl, top_cap_award.stl)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Most 3D-printed electronics enclosures fail in one of two ways: - They use self-tapping screws driven directly into thermoplastic, which strip out after three battery swaps. - They rely on fragile, non-compliant snap tabs that snap off along print layer lines.

For StackCalc32, we engineered a tool-free sliding rail assembly that requires zero metal fasteners, screws, or heat-set brass inserts.

The architecture separates the enclosure into four distinct components: 1. The Rigid Chassis (chassis_award.stl): Provides structural integrity, houses the battery bay and PCB slide rails, with continuous internal lateral guides. 2. The Unified Faceplate (unified_faceplate_award.stl): Slides along the chassis rails, retaining the 2.5" LCD screen and locking the key matrix into position. 3. The Flexible TPU Membrane (tpu_membrane_award.stl): Acts as the tactile keyboard layer and environmental barrier, trapped between the faceplate and internal board shelf. 4. The Retention Snap-Cap (top_cap_award.stl): Slides over the top perimeter, snapping into dual retention detents to lock all four parts into an unyielding pocket instrument.

Figure 1: The four-part mechanical prototype opened along its continuous sliding rails.

docs.title: 2. Print Settings & Tolerances
docs.text:
• Layer Height: 0.20 mm (Chassis / Faceplate / Cap); 0.15 mm (TPU Membrane).
  • Filament: Prusament PLA / PETG for structural parts; Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95A for membrane.
  • Inter-Part Sliding Clearance: \(0.25\text{ mm}\) nominal clearance on guide rails, allowing smooth sliding while eliminating rattle.
  • Detent Retention Force: Designed for \(15\text{ N}\) thumb release force.

docs.text: To the Hackaday Community: When designing sliding mechanical joints for FDM 3D printers, how do you handle anisotropic layer shrinkage and seam placement along sliding channels? Have you found PETG on PLA to offer lower sliding friction than PLA on PLA? We'd love your maker tips!

docs.title: Log 04: TPU Keypad Membrane: FEA Simulation vs. Printed Actuation
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 04 · FEA & TACTILE KEYPAD

Canonical Article: What the First Printed StackCalc Prototype Can Teach Us Topic: Materials Science, FEA Simulation & Keypad Haptics Artifact: 280-Condition FEA Simulation Sweep & OpenSCAD Parametric Key Model

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Keypad feel makes or breaks a handheld calculator. Early prototypes explored print-in-place cantilevered leaf springs (prototype-print-in-place-springs.jpg), but FDM layer delamination under repetitive fatigue proved unreliable.

We pivoted to an integrated TPU95A elastomer membrane that sits directly over tactile snap-dome switches.

Before printing dozens of variations, we ran an automated 280-condition Finite Element Analysis (FEA) parameter sweep modeling keycap travel under non-ideal real-world loading: - Off-axis Press Angles: \(0^\circ\) (vertical) to \(25^\circ\) (angled thumb press). - Contact Offsets: Center strike vs. edge strike (\(1.5\text{ mm}\) off-center). - Web Wall Geometry: Tapered thickness from \(0.6\text{ mm}\) to \(1.2\text{ mm}\).

Figure 1: FEA simulation mesh illustrating stress concentration along the membrane hinging web under angled actuation.

docs.title: What FEA Taught Us (and What It Didn't)
docs.text:
• What it solved: The simulation identified severe binding when key caps had sharp rectangular corners. Filleting the perimeter to \(r=1.2\text{ mm}\) eliminated edge pinching against the faceplate aperture.
  • The limitation: FEA predicts geometry deformation; it does not measure tactile snap ratio, post-press switch bounce, or real-world fingertip fatigue. Physical testing on the printed specimen remains essential.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
OpenSCAD parametric web definition used to generate the uniform deformation profile: 

module key_hinge_web(w, h, t_web, drop_angle) {
    rotate([drop_angle, 0, 0])
        difference() {
            cylinder(h=h, d=w, $fn=32);
            translate([0,0,-0.1])
                cylinder(h=h+0.2, d=w - (2 * t_web), $fn=32);
        }
}

docs.title: Log 05: Tactile Math: The 3D-Printed Learning Lab & Expression Trees
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 05 · TACTILE MANIPULATIVES

Canonical Articles: - Making the Four-Level Stack Visible - Reading an Expression Tree as a Postfix Program - Teaching Fractions as an RPN Sequence Topic: Educational Hardware, Physical Manipulatives & Binary Trees Artifact: Learning Lab 3D Print Pack & Lesson Plan (Collection 01, rev 0.2.0)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Why do students struggle with Reverse Polish Notation? Because algebraic notation has conditioned them to think of expressions as static text strings wrapped in parentheses.

To make postfix intuition natural and intuitive, we designed The StackCalc Learning Lab: a suite of physical 3D-printed and laser-engraved classroom manipulatives.

docs.title: 1. The Stack Stage (stack_board.stl)
docs.text: A rigid 4-register desktop tray representing registers \(T, Z, Y,\) and \(X\). Blank writable tiles represent numeric values. When students press ENTER, they physically duplicate tile \(X\) into slot \(Y\). When an operator is evaluated, two operand tiles are removed and the calculated result is placed in \(X\).

docs.title: 2. Upright Fraction Towers (fraction_blocks.stl)
docs.text:
Traditional fraction strips lie flat and make comparison clumsy. Our towers have a fixed \(24 \times 24\text{ mm}\) footprint and proportional vertical heights (\(96/n\text{ mm}\)): - Whole (\(n=1\)): \(96\text{ mm}\) - Half (\(n=2\)): \(48\text{ mm}\) - Third (\(n=3\)): \(32\text{ mm}\) - Quarter (\(n=4\)): \(24\text{ mm}\) - Sixth (\(n=6\)): \(16\text{ mm}\) - Eighth (\(n=8\)): \(12\text{ mm}\)

Two halves or four quarters stack to the exact physical height of one whole block. Contact surfaces are completely flat with no embossed text; legends are laser-marked on top faces.

Figure 1: The Fraction Studio tray mapping tactile heights to dot-notation keystroke sequences.

docs.title: 3. Binary Expression Tree Board (tree_board.stl)
docs.text: To evaluate \((a + b) \times (c - d)\), students place tokens into a structured binary tree. Moving from leaves to root in postorder traversal (Left, Right, Node) yields the exact RPN keystroke sequence: $\(\text{Keystrokes: } a \rightarrow b \rightarrow + \rightarrow c \rightarrow d \rightarrow - \rightarrow \times\)$

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: All 13 STL plates containing 79 separate solids and four printable classroom teacher guides are downloadable free from the StackCalc Learning Lab.

docs.title: Log 06: Emulating the RP2350: Cross-Surface Differential Fuzzing at 40 Hz
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 06 · DIFFERENTIAL FUZZING

Canonical Article: Fuzzing the Firmware Path in an RP2350 Emulator Topic: Verification, Emulation & Differential Fuzzing Artifact: 40 Hz Grammar-Guided Differential Fuzz Harness

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Waiting for physical PCBs to arrive before validating firmware is the slowest way to build hardware. But standard unit tests only check the scenarios the engineer remembered to write down.

To ensure mathematical and stack state parity across our Apple Silicon host, watchOS app, and bare-metal RP2350 firmware, we built an automated cross-surface differential fuzzer.

                           +------------------------+
                           | Grammar-Guided Fuzzer  |
                           |  (40 Keystrokes / Sec) |
                           +-----------+------------+
                                       │
                     ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                     ▼                                   ▼
        [Darwin Host Reference]             [Emulated RP2350 Core]
        • 64-bit IEEE 754 Engine            • ARM Cortex-M33 Binary
        • Native Swift 6 Runtime            • Custom Memory Layout
                     │                                   │
                     └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                       ▼
                           [Differential State Checker]
                           • Checksum X, Y, Z, T Registers
                           • Flag Registers & Overflow Flags
                           • Bit-for-Bit Discrepancy Halt

docs.title: The Fuzzing Strategy
docs.text:
1. Grammar Generation: The fuzzer generates valid and degenerate mathematical keystroke streams: mixed fractions, nested square roots, transcendental edge cases, division by zero, stack overflow/underflow, and rapid clear/drop sequences.
  2. Lock-Step Execution: Each keystroke token is dispatched simultaneously to the Darwin reference engine and the RP2350 software emulator.
  3. Automated Shrinking: When a state discrepancy occurs, the harness minimizes the input sequence down to the minimal reproducible bug trace (e.g. 2 [ENTER] 0 [/] [DROP] [ENTER]).

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
Differential assertion check executing inside the test runner: 

def check_parity(darwin_state, rp2350_state, step_idx):
    assert darwin_state.x == rp2350_state.x, f"Mismatch at step {step_idx}: X={darwin_state.x} vs {rp2350_state.x}"
    assert darwin_state.stack == rp2350_state.stack, f"Stack diverged at step {step_idx}"
    assert darwin_state.flags == rp2350_state.flags, f"Flags diverged at step {step_idx}"

docs.title: Log 07: From Folding Cardstock to a 3D-Printed Interlocking Desk Stand
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 07 · KINEMATIC PACKAGING

Canonical Article: From an Origami Box to a Puzzle Stand Topic: Ergonomics, Kinematic Packaging & 3D Printing Artifact: OpenSCAD Puzzle Stand Models (puzzle_stand.scad, puzzle_stand_assembly.scad)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Calculators used lying flat on a workbench suffer from severe room-light glare and poor ergonomic viewing angles. Standard desktop docks, however, are bulky, take up too much desk space, and are awkward to transport in a backpack or pencil pouch.

We wanted a stand that could: 1. Support the calculator securely at two distinct ergonomic angles: Desk Mode (\(22^\circ\) for seated typing) and Shelf/Display Mode (\(58^\circ\) for upright reference viewing). 2. Pack completely flat into a standard pencil pouch. 3. Lock together securely without loose screws, hinges, or rubber bands.

docs.title: The Evolution: Origami Paper to Precision CAD
docs.text:
We began prototyping using heavy 100 lb cardstock and origami scoring techniques. Paper allowed us to iterate on center-of-gravity balance and tip-over angles in minutes.

Once the kinematic pivot lines were verified, we translated the geometry into OpenSCAD, engineering a set of interlocking puzzle joints: - The tabs incorporate a \(0.20\text{ mm}\) interference friction fit. - The base features angled cradles that capture the bottom chamfer of the StackCalc32 chassis. - When disassembled, the pieces nest together into a flat \(6.0\text{ mm}\) thick plate.

Figure 1: The 3D-printed puzzle stand supporting the mechanical calculator prototype in desk viewing mode.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
OpenSCAD puzzle joint interlocking cutouts: 

module puzzle_tenon(w, t, clearance=0.15) {
    difference() {
        cube([w, t, t*2]);
        translate([w/4, -0.1, t/2])
            cube([w/2 + clearance, t + 0.2, t + clearance]);
    }
}

docs.title: Log 08: Designing the Envelope: How PCB Routing Drove the Enclosure Geometry
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 08 · HARDWARE ENVELOPE

Canonical Article: How the PCB Design Shapes a Printed Calculator Before It Arrives Topic: PCB Design, KiCad, High-Density Routing & Mechanical Envelopes Artifact: KiCad Schematic & 4-Layer Board Layout Constraints

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
In textbook product design, the industrial designer creates an enclosure and hands the internal volume to the electrical engineer. In custom handheld hardware, the PCB and the enclosure must co-evolve simultaneously.

Three critical electrical constraints directly dictated the physical geometry of StackCalc32's 3D-printed chassis:

docs.title: 1. The 0.5 mm Pitch ZIF Display Connector
docs.text: We selected an EastRising 2.5" monochrome LCD (\(132 \times 65\) dot-matrix) with an integrated ST7567 controller. Its flexible flat cable (FFC) terminates in a 0.5 mm pitch bottom-contact ZIF socket. - Placing the ZIF socket at the top edge of the board created a severe bend-radius pinch point against the chassis wall. - Moving the socket \(4.2\text{ mm}\) downward provided adequate FFC loop clearance, but required notching the internal structural ribs of the printed faceplate.

docs.title: 2. Key Matrix Switch Clearances
docs.text: The keyboard matrix uses 37 tactile switches arranged in a high-density 5-column by 8-row grid. To prevent the board from bowing under forceful thumb presses, the chassis incorporates three continuous longitudinal support ribs that make contact with bare ground plane zones on the PCB's bottom side.

docs.title: 3. Current Fabrication Status
docs.text:
The complete 4-layer board layout passed all electrical Design Rule Checks (DRC) in KiCad with zero clearance errors. The gerber packages and drill files were submitted to our PCB fabricator and are currently in the production pipeline.

Crucial Note: Until physical boards arrive, are seated into the printed rails, and successfully execute their first powered boot, all hardware claims in this project remain strictly at the CAD, simulation, and mechanical prototype stage.

Figure 1: Exploded view of the four printed mechanical pieces awaiting board arrival.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: Key mechanical envelope specifications: - PCB Dimensions: \(142.0\text{ mm} \times 68.0\text{ mm} \times 1.6\text{ mm}\) - Trace/Space: \(0.15\text{ mm} / 0.15\text{ mm}\) (4-layer stackup: Signal / GND / 3V3 / Signal) - ZIF Loop Clearance: \(1.8\text{ mm}\) vertical clearance above board plane.

How do you prevent display FFC cables from creeping out of ZIF sockets under thermal expansion or drop shocks? Let us know in the comments!

docs.title: Log 09: Notes from the PCBWay Assembly Floor: Header Pins, JST Pads & Switch Jumpers
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 09 · FACTORY DFM & JUMPER ROUTING

Canonical Article: Notes from the PCBWay Assembly Floor: Header Pins, JST Footprints, and Switch Jumper Routing Topic: Turnkey PCBA DFM, Castellated Mounting & Switch Matrix Jumper Routing Artifact: Hardware/calculator.kicad_pcb, fix_mcu_pads.py, & fix_silkscreen.py

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text: Passing a software DRC in KiCad does not guarantee a smooth run on the SMT assembly line. When our first calculator boards reached the PCBWay assembly floor, their engineers paused the line and sent back bench inspection photos highlighting four physical integration issues:

docs.title: 1. Rear MCU1 Through-Hole Header Pins Colliding with Front Switch SOFT6
docs.text:
In our initial BOM (bom.csv), we specified SC1632 (Raspberry Pi Pico 2 with pre-soldered through-hole headers) alongside a PTH footprint on B.Cu. When PCBWay dry-fitted the module from the back, the header pins poked straight through to the front (F.Cu) right between the four SMD pads of tactile switch SOFT6:

Figure 1: PCBWay bench photo (headers.png). The red box shows the rear MCU1 pins protruding directly into the front SOFT6 switch footprint.

The Fix: We updated the BOM to SC1631 (bare castellated Pico 2) and ran fix_mcu_pads.py to convert all 40 MCU1 pads to pure bottom-side PAD_ATTRIB_SMD (B.Cu, B.Paste, B.Mask) with zero drill holes.

docs.title: 2. JST1 Pad Mismatch & Stranded Front Silkscreen
docs.text:
PCBWay's second photo caught a mismatch on JST1 (our right-angle CR2032 battery header): the BOM specified the through-hole S2B-PH-K-S(LF)(SN) while the board had undrilled SMD pads, and both the JST (ON BACK) and MCU1 silkscreen callouts were stranded on F.Silkscreen instead of B.Silkscreen:

Figure 2: PCBWay bench photo (jst.png) showing the through-hole JST header alongside the surface-mount pads.

We updated JST1 to the surface-mount S2B-PH-SM4-TB and ran fix_silkscreen.py to migrate and mirror all rear component silkscreen primitives onto B.Silkscreen.

docs.title: 3. Eliminating Implicit Tactile Switch Jumper Connections
docs.text:
Standard 4-pad SMD tactile switch footprints (SW_TACT_ALPS_SKQGABE010) often set (duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers yes), using the switch's internal metal bars as pass-through jumpers for matrix rows and columns. During DFM rework around the switch pads, relying on internal switch jumpers created ambiguity over which pads needed active electrical jumpering versus mechanical anchoring:

Figure 3: Updated KiCad routing (kicad.png) with (duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers no), explicit 1/2 active pads, NC mechanical pads, and continuous copper traces.

We disabled implicit switch jumpers across all 43 switches ((duplicate_pad_numbers_are_jumpers no)), assigned active row/column nets strictly to pads 1 and 2, marked the opposite anchor pads NC, and routed continuous \(0.25\text{ mm}\) copper buses across the matrix.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
pcbnew script (Hardware/fix_mcu_pads.py) used to convert MCU1 from PTH to bottom-side castellated SMD: 

import pcbnew
board = pcbnew.LoadBoard("calculator.kicad_pcb")
mcu = board.FindFootprintByReference("MCU1")
for pad in mcu.Pads():
    if pad.GetAttribute() == pcbnew.PAD_ATTRIB_PTH:
        pad.SetAttribute(pcbnew.PAD_ATTRIB_SMD)
        lset = pcbnew.LSET()
        lset.AddLayer(pcbnew.B_Cu)
        lset.AddLayer(pcbnew.B_Paste)
        lset.AddLayer(pcbnew.B_Mask)
        pad.SetLayerSet(lset)
        pad.SetDrillSize(pcbnew.VECTOR2I(0, 0))
pcbnew.SaveBoard("calculator.kicad_pcb", board)

docs.title: Log 10: Shipping StackCalc v1.1: A Clean-Room RPN Calculator That Grows With Your Kid (SC-6 to SC-32)
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 10 · SHARED CORE & V1.1 RELEASE

Canonical Article: Shipping StackCalc v1.1 on the App Store: A Clean-Room RPN Calculator That Grows With Your Kid (SC-6 to SC-32) Topic: HP-32SII Ergonomics, Clean-Room RPNCore Upgrades & STL-Backed Digital Twin Artifact: StackCalc Calculator v1.1 (id6801788040 on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text: After training my kids on a SwissMicros DM41CC (and owning a DM42/C47, DM32, DM15CC, and vintage HP-32SIIs), I realized two things: kids learn RPN effortlessly when freed from infix parentheses, and sending a kid to school with a $250 collector's calculator or a $200 vintage eBay antique is a non-starter. Our goal with StackCalc is a kid-friendly RPN ecosystem launching at $89.99 for small-batch maker units on a manufacturing roadmap toward a $29.99 student target.

docs.title: 1. Why the HP-32SII Over the HP-15C or HP-42S?
docs.text: Unlike the HP-42S/C47 (which buries everyday functions inside hierarchical softkey menus) or the HP-15C (landscape form factor with numeric matrix/label codes), the HP-32SII puts almost every essential scientific operation directly on the primary and shifted keys without menu diving, using a clean 1-line context bar for CLEAR, STAT, SOLVE, and INTG.

docs.title: 2. Clean-Room RPNCore Upgrades (Not a ROM Emulator)
docs.text: Written from scratch in Swift (RPNCore) and compiled to both Apple silicon and bare-metal RP2350 (Embedded Swift), StackCalc 32 adds features we always wished the 32SII had: - Harmonic Mean (H.M.), Time Value of Money (TVM), and a Quadratic/Cubic Polynomial Solver (POLY). - Interactive Curve & Scatter-Plot Graphing (PLOT) on the app and \(132 \times 65\) dot-matrix LCD.

docs.title: 3. StackCalc 6 (Common Core K–6) & STL Digital Twin Co-Development
docs.text:
Switching to StackCalc 6 reconfigures the calculator around K–6 Common Core operations—including Step-by-Step Prime Fraction Simplification ([SIMP]) (which factors out one prime divisor per press from dot-entered fractions like .12.18 \(\rightarrow \div 2 \rightarrow\) 6/9 \(\rightarrow \div 3 \rightarrow\) 2/3), ÷R integer remainder division, [PRIME], [GCD], and [LCM]—paired with live dot-matrix Ten-Frames (10F), a 20-Bead Rekenrek (RACK), Number Line (LINE), Geared Clock (🕒), and 5-Level Adaptive Quiz (?). By exporting our OpenSCAD STLs and laser SVG decals into layout_data.json, our SwiftUI HardwareReplicaView runs an exact 1:1 replica of the RP2350 firmware for simultaneous hardware/software co-development.

Figure 1: StackCalc v1.1 unifies Scientific Mode (SC-32) and Visual Learning Mode (SC-6) on a shared dot-matrix engine.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: Clean-room extensions in RPNCore beyond classic HP-32SII parity: - Statistics: Arithmetic mean (\(\bar{x}, \bar{y}\)), weighted mean (\(\bar{x}_w\)), and Harmonic Mean (H.M.). - Solvers: Secant/Brent root finder (SOLVE), Simpson integration (∫), Cubic/Quadratic Polynomial Solver (POLY), and 5-variable TVM. - Number Theory (SC-6 & SC-32): Iterative prime-divisor reduction ([SIMP]), prime factorization ([PRIME]), GCD, LCM, and Euclidean quotient/remainder (÷R).

docs.title: Log 11: 84mm Fraction Towers, Logarithmic Prime Blocks, 3D-Printed Dummy PCBs & Unit-Tested Books
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 11 · BLOCK MANUFACTURING & DOCS PIPELINE

Canonical Article: From OpenSCAD to the Classroom Desk: 84mm Fraction Towers, Logarithmic Prime Blocks, and Unit-Tested Books Topic: Mathematical CAD Invariants, dummy_pcb.stl Fit Checks & Unit-Tested Textbooks Artifact: Hardware/generate_scad.py, Tools/book_engine.py, & TextbookVerificationTests_SC32.swift

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text: Even in the age of AI, students still need to know how to think mathematically. While our first batch of PCBs finishes assembly at PCBWay, we moved our 3D-printed Gridfinity math manipulatives (manufactured in-house and on Slant3D) and our unit-tested reference manuals into production:

docs.title: 1. Mathematical CAD Invariants: 84mm Fraction Towers & Logarithmic Prime Blocks
docs.text:
• Fraction Studio (\(84\text{ mm}\) Whole Datum): Engineered around an \(84\text{ mm}\) unit height so \(\frac{1}{2}\) (\(42\text{ mm}\)), \(\frac{1}{3}\) (\(28\text{ mm}\)), \(\frac{1}{4}\) (\(21\text{ mm}\)), \(\frac{1}{6}\) (\(14\text{ mm}\)), \(\frac{1}{7}\) (\(12\text{ mm}\)), and \(\frac{1}{12}\) (\(7\text{ mm}\)) resolve to exact integer millimeters without slicer layer-rounding drift. Students stack \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}\) (\(70\text{ mm}\)) in the left comparator channel, match it with five \(\frac{1}{6}\) blocks in the right channel, enter .1.2 [ENTER] .1.3 [+] on StackCalc 6, and step through prime reduction one divisor at a time on the SC-6 [SIMP] key.
  • Prime Factor Studio & Logarithmic Slide Rule: Prime blocks (\(2, 3, 5, 7\)) are scaled logarithmically (\(\text{Length} \propto \log(p)\)) so snapping a 2 block and a 3 block end-to-end physically equals the length of 6 (\(\log(2) + \log(3) = \log(6)\)), making GCD and LCM tangible length-matching puzzles.

docs.title: 2. Exporting dummy_pcb.stl from KiCad pcbnew for Physical Fit Checks
docs.text: To verify enclosure tolerances before fiberglass boards arrived, Hardware/generate_scad.py reads calculator.kicad_pcb via pcbnew and generates dummy_pcb.scad \(\rightarrow\) dummy_pcb.stl—an exact 3D-printable plastic replica of the populated PCB (including the \(1.6\text{ mm}\) board, all 43 switches, rear Pico 2 envelope, and ZIF socket) that we printed in PLA to test rail slide clearances and TPU plunger reach.

docs.title: 3. Compiling Textbooks Like Firmware (book_engine.py)
docs.text:
Our Makefile and book_engine.py extract every worked keystroke sequence from the SC-32 Scientific Manual, SC-6 Elementary Manual, and 590+ workbook problems, run them as unit tests against RPNCore, and auto-render simulator screenshots and OpenSCAD STL diagrams.

Figure 1: The physical manipulatives and test-verified reference manuals manufactured alongside the calculator.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
The 5-stage dependency chain in our documentation Makefile: 

# 1. OpenSCAD (.scad) -> STL (.stl) -> Orthographic Block Diagrams & blocks_registry.json
# 2. Swift Layout & SwiftUI Tests (.swift) -> layout_data*.json, sequences_registry.json, & Screenshots
# 3. Manuscript Chapters (.md) + Registries + book_engine.py -> Validated Guides & RPNCore Unit Tests
# 4. Validated Guides + Assets + generate_manual_pdfs.py -> Publication PDFs
# 5. Publication PDFs + mkdocs.yml + Chapters -> Strict MkDocs Site (site/index.html)

docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 12 · SYNCHRONIZED ECOSYSTEM LAUNCH

Canonical Article: Launch Day: Why the World Needs a Kid-Friendly RPN Calculator That Grows With Them Topic: First Batch Hardware Verification, HP-32SII Ergonomics & Ecosystem Launch Artifact: First 5 Batch 001 Units, App Store v1.1, Printables STLs & Unit-Tested Manuals

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
After training my kids on a SwissMicros DM41CC (and owning a DM42 converted to C47, DM32, DM15CC, and vintage HP-32SIIs), it was obvious that kids love postfix stack math. On a postfix stack calculator, users learn operator-precedence parsing themselves to decompose and enter expressions onto the stack—appreciating the lessons learned in the past 50 years of computing so they can build the next 50 years. Furthermore, unlike CAS calculators (which are banned on the SAT, ACT, IB, and NCEES FE/PE exams), StackCalc is purposefully designed to be allowed in testing situations (no CAS symbolic solver, no QWERTY keyboard, and no wireless radios)—and no parent wants a child carrying a $250 boutique calculator or a $200 fragile eBay antique in a school backpack.

Today we are launching the complete StackCalc ecosystem simultaneously across hardware, software, 3D-printed math blocks, and books—starting at $89.99 for our initial maker batch while scaling toward a $29.99 classroom target:

docs.title: 1. Why the HP-32SII Architecture + Clean-Room Upgrades
docs.text: We modeled StackCalc 32 on the HP-32SII rather than the HP-42S (which hides functions inside deep softkey menus) or the HP-15C (landscape numeric matrix codes). Built on our clean-room Swift engine (RPNCore) rather than a ROM emulator, StackCalc 32 adds Harmonic Mean (H.M.), Time Value of Money (TVM), a Quadratic/Cubic Polynomial Solver (POLY), and interactive curve plotting (PLOT)—paired with StackCalc 6 (SC-6) covering Common Core math up through 6th grade (including step-by-step prime fraction simplification [SIMP], ÷R, [PRIME], [GCD], and [LCM]).

docs.title: 2. First 5 Units Verified \(\rightarrow\) Next 20 Units (Hardware V2) Triggered
docs.text:
With our first 5 Batch 001 calculators verified across our 7-Stage Board Arrival Protocol (confirming the 43-key matrix, TPU membrane plunger travel, 132x65 ST7567 LCD contrast, and Embedded Swift firmware), we are releasing the 4 Founder's Batch units and triggering our 20-unit Hardware V2 order (which replaces the rear Pico 2 carrier board with bare QFN-60 RP2350A silicon, W25Q32 QSPI flash, and a ME2188 synchronous boost stage).

Figure 1: The five-pillar StackCalc ecosystem launching together.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: The five synchronized launch surfaces: - Universal App v1.1 (SC-32 + SC-6): Live on iPhone, iPad, and 100% standalone Apple Watch (id6801788040). - Physical Manipulatives & Hardware: Live on Etsy and stackcalc.io/products (84mm Fraction Studio Towers, Logarithmic Prime Slide Rule, Place Value Trays, Ten-Frames). - Free Open-Source STLs & 3MFs: Live in the Download Center and Printables/MakerWorld. - Unit-Tested Reference Manuals & 590+ Problem Workbooks: Verified against RPNCore via book_engine.py.

docs.title: Official Reference Books & Companion Volumes
Official Reference Books & Companion Volumes
docs.text:
Welcome to the StackCalc Books & Reference Hub. Both of our flagship volumes—From Blocks to the Stack (for Grades 3–6 learners, parents, and teachers using the SC-6 Elementary) and Thinking in the Stack (for high school, university, and practicing engineers using the SC-32 Scientific)—are available to read online right here in full, as downloadable typeset PDFs, and as spiral-bound lay-flat print editions ($16.00) built to sit open beside your calculator and 3D-printed math blocks.

Every worked example, story, and 4-register stack trace in both books is verified directly against the StackCalc calculation engine.

Open-Source Curriculum & Printable 3D Studios: While our spiral-bound print books are available for $16.00, all online chapters, the Master Curriculum Guide, Printable Student Station Workbooks, and 3D-Printable Manipulative Studio Files (.stl / .3mf) are 100% free and open-source in our Curriculum Center and Download Center.

docs.title: Choose Your Volume
Volume I: From Blocks to the Stack: Hands-On Math & the SC-6 Stack Calculator (Grades 3–6)
docs.text:
Written directly for curious 3rd–6th graders, parents, and teachers, From Blocks to the Stack begins with a simple observation: before you ever learned to write equations with parentheses and equals signs, your hands already knew how to do math by stacking physical things.
