docs.title: C.3.6 Why "Goldbach's Comet" Has High Ridges and Low Valleys
docs.text:
In Chapter 7, you met Christian Goldbach's famous 1742 letter to Leonhard Euler—observing that every even number greater than \(2\) can be written as the sum of two prime numbers (\(4 = 2 + 2\), \(6 = 3 + 3\), \(8 = 3 + 5\), \(10 = 3 + 7 = 5 + 5\)). When mathematicians plot how many different prime pairs add up to each even number, the dots streak across the page like a glowing comet tail (Goldbach's Comet) split into low valleys and high ridges.

Why do powers of \(2\) like \(8\) (\(1\) pair: \(3 + 5\)), \(16\) (\(2\) pairs: \(3 + 13, 5 + 11\)), \(32\) (\(2\) pairs: \(3 + 29, 13 + 19\)), and \(64\) (\(5\) pairs) sit in the lowest valleys? Because powers of \(2\) have no odd prime factors at all (they are not divisible by \(3, 5,\) or \(7\)), nearly half of the odd primes below them are blocked from pairing up when their partners land on multiples of \(3\) or \(5\)! Conversely, multiples of \(6\) (\(2 \times 3\)) and \(30\) (\(2 \times 3 \times 5\)) like \(18\) (\(2\) pairs), \(30\) (\(3\) pairs), \(42\) (\(4\) pairs), \(60\) (\(6\) pairs), and \(90\) (\(9\) pairs) ride the top ridge of the comet: because multiples of \(6\) already divide evenly by both \(2\) and \(3\), subtracting any prime greater than \(3\) from a multiple of \(6\) is guaranteed never to land on a multiple of \(2\) or \(3\), giving every prime a much higher chance of meeting a prime partner!

You can test any even number on Goldbach's Comet right on your SC-6 by picking a prime candidate with [PRIME], subtracting it from your even number, and tapping [PRIME] on the partner:

Even Number How Many Prime Pairs? All Prime Pairs That Add to This Even Number Why It Sits Low or High on Goldbach's Comet 4 1 pair \(2 + 2\) Only even number that uses the even prime \(2\) 8 1 pair \(3 + 5\) Power of \(2\) (\(2^3\)): only one odd prime pair works 10 2 pairs \(3 + 7,\; 5 + 5\) Includes the twin-center pair \(5 + 5\) 16 2 pairs \(3 + 13,\; 5 + 11\) Power of \(2\) (\(2^4\)): sits on the bottom edge of the comet 24 3 pairs \(5 + 19,\; 7 + 17,\; 11 + 13\) Multiple of \(6\): three symmetric prime pairs around \(12\) 30 3 pairs \(7 + 23,\; 11 + 19,\; 13 + 17\) Primorial (\(2 \times 3 \times 5\)): every non-3, non-5 prime pairs up! 32 2 pairs \(3 + 29,\; 13 + 19\) Power of \(2\) (\(2^5\)): drops back down to just \(2\) pairs 36 4 pairs \(5 + 31,\; 7 + 29,\; 13 + 23,\; 17 + 19\) Square multiple of \(6\): four distinct prime pairs 48 5 pairs \(5 + 43,\; 7 + 41,\; 11 + 37,\; 17 + 31,\; 19 + 29\) Multiple of \(6\): climbs to five prime pairs 60 6 pairs \(7 + 53,\; 13 + 47,\; 17 + 43,\; 19 + 41,\; 23 + 37,\; 29 + 31\) Champion under \(60\) (\(2^2 \times 3 \times 5\)): six distinct prime pairs! 64 5 pairs \(3 + 61,\; 5 + 59,\; 11 + 53,\; 17 + 47,\; 23 + 41\) Power of \(2\) (\(2^6\)): fewer pairs than \(60\) even though \(64 > 60\) 100 6 pairs \(3 + 97,\; 11 + 89,\; 17 + 83,\; 29 + 71,\; 41 + 59,\; 47 + 53\) Six pairs of two-digit primes add to an exact \(100\)

docs.title: C.3.7 Perfect Numbers & Giant Factor Challenges
docs.text:
A Perfect Number is a special whole number whose smaller factors add up to the number itself. Look at the first four perfect numbers:

Perfect Number Prime Recipe Smaller Factors Added Together 6 \(2 \times 3\) \(1 + 2 + 3 = \mathbf{6}\) 28 \(4 \times 7\) \(1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = \mathbf{28}\) 496 \(16 \times 31\) \(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 31 + 62 + 124 + 248 = \mathbf{496}\) 8,128 \(64 \times 127\) \(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64 + 127 + \dots = \mathbf{8,128}\)

You can build the third perfect number (\(496\)) right on the stack by following Euclid's ancient recipe: multiply \(2^4\) (\(16\)) by the prime number \(2^5 - 1\) (\(31\)) to reach \(16 \times 31 = 496\):

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X What Happens on the Stack 2 [ENTER] 0 0 2 2 Enter base 2 and copy onto Shelf \(Y\) 5 [g] [yˣ] 0 0 0 32 Raise \(2^5 = 32\) 1 [-] 0 0 0 31 Subtract 1 for Mersenne candidate \(2^5 - 1 = 31\) [PRIME] 0 0 0 31 Screen flashes PRIME to confirm that \(31\) is a prime number 2 [ENTER] 0 31 2 2 Enter base 2; \(31\) lifts to Shelf \(Z\) 4 [g] [yˣ] 0 0 31 16 Raise \(2^4 = 16\); \(31\) drops to Shelf \(Y\) [×] 0 0 0 496 Multiply \(31 \times 16 =\) 496 (the third perfect number)

The display lands on \(496\), the third perfect number. That same curiosity about giant powers of two led to one of history's most famous division checks: in 1640, Pierre de Fermat guessed that \(2^{32} + 1 = 4,294,967,297\) was a prime number, and for nearly a hundred years no one could factor it—until Leonhard Euler proved in 1732 that \(641\) divides into it evenly with zero remainder: $\(4,294,967,297 = 641 \times 6,700,417\)$ You can test Euler's discovery right on your SC-6 by keying in 4294967297 [ENTER] 641 [÷], which lands cleanly on \(6,700,417.00\) with no decimal remainder.

docs.title: C.4 Everyday Rates, Money & Shopping Word Rules
docs.text:
Whether you are comparing unit prices in a grocery store aisle, computing average speed on a family road trip, or adding sales tax at a register, the SC-6 stack keeps your starting numbers visible at every step:

Everyday Math Task What You Know Word Rule SC-6 Keystroke Pattern Speed (Unit Rate) Distance, Time \(\text{Distance} \div \text{Time}\) [Distance] [ENTER] [Time] [÷] Travel Distance Speed, Time \(\text{Speed} \times \text{Time}\) [Speed] [ENTER] [Time] [×] Travel Time Distance, Speed \(\text{Distance} \div \text{Speed}\) [Distance] [ENTER] [Speed] [÷] Unit Price (Best Buy) Total Cost, Count \(\text{Total Cost} \div \text{Count}\) [Total Cost] [ENTER] [Count] [÷] [$] Density of an Object Mass (g), Volume (\(\text{cm}^3\)) \(\text{Mass} \div \text{Volume}\) [Mass] [ENTER] [Volume] [÷] Percent of a Number Whole, Percent \(\text{Whole} \times (\text{Percent} \div 100)\) [Whole] [ENTER] [Percent] [%] Percent Change Starting, Ending \((\text{Ending} - \text{Starting}) \div \text{Starting} \times 100\) [Starting] [ENTER] [Ending] [g] [%CHG]

docs.title: C.4.1 Why Distance, Unit Price & Density All Share One Rule
docs.text:
Look closely at the first five rows of that table and you will spot a wonderful shortcut: Speed (\(\text{miles} \div \text{hours}\)), Unit Price (\(\text{dollars} \div \text{ounces}\)), and Density (\(\text{grams} \div \text{cm}^3\)) are all the exact same mathematical idea! Every time you see the word "per" in everyday life—miles per hour, dollars per pound, heartbeats per minute, or grams per cubic centimeter—the word "per" simply means "divide the total on Shelf \(Y\) by the number of units on Shelf \(X\)" ([÷]):

  • Finding the Best Buy in the Grocery Store Aisle: Suppose a \(12\text{-ounce}\) box of cereal costs \(\$4.56\), while a giant \(18\text{-ounce}\) family box of the same cereal costs \(\$6.30\). Which box gives you more cereal for each dollar?
  • Key in the first box's price and ounces (4.56 [ENTER] 12 [÷]): Shelf \(X\) shows 0.38 (\(38\text{ cents per ounce}\)).
  • Now key in the family box right on top (6.30 [ENTER] 18 [÷]): Shelf \(X\) shows 0.35 (\(35\text{ cents per ounce}\)), while the first box's 0.38 waits right above it on Shelf \(Y\) so you can compare both unit prices side by side! Subtracting [-] confirms that the family box saves \(3\text{ cents per ounce}\) (\(\$0.54\) saved across the \(18\text{-ounce}\) box).
  • Combining Road-Trip Speed and Clock Time ([g] [▸HMS]): Suppose your family is driving \(210\text{ miles}\) to a state park at a steady highway speed of \(60\text{ miles per hour}\). Dividing 210 [ENTER] 60 [÷] gives 3.5 hours in decimal time—and one tap of [g] [▸HMS] ([g] then [🕒]) translates 3.5 decimal hours directly into 3.3000 (\(3\text{ hours, } 30\text{ minutes}\))!

docs.title: C.4.2 Adding Tax, Tips & Discounts in One Tap
docs.text:
Because [%] on the SC-6 computes the percentage on Ground Shelf \(X\) while keeping your original dollar amount untouched on Shelf \(Y\), you never have to retype a price to add sales tax or subtract a sale discount:

Money Task Word Rule SC-6 Keystroke Pattern Simple Interest Earned \(\text{Starting Money} \times \text{Yearly Rate \%} \times \text{Years}\) [Money] [ENTER] [Rate] [%] [Years] [×] [$] Sales Tax Amount \(\text{Price} \times \text{Tax Rate \%}\) [Price] [ENTER] [Tax Rate] [%] [$] Total Price with Tax \(\text{Price} + \text{Sales Tax}\) [Price] [ENTER] [Tax Rate] [%] [+] [$] Discount Saved \(\text{Regular Price} \times \text{Discount \%}\) [Price] [ENTER] [Discount] [%] [$] Sale Price After Discount \(\text{Regular Price} - \text{Discount}\) [Price] [ENTER] [Discount] [%] [-] [$] Restaurant Tip (\(18\%\)) \(\text{Bill} \times 18\%\) [Bill] [ENTER] 18 [%] [$] Splitting a Bill Equally \((\text{Bill} + \text{Tip}) \div \text{Diners}\) [Bill] [ENTER] 18 [%] [+] [Diners] [÷] [$]

Even two-step store sales—like taking a \(20\%\) coupon off a \(\$45.00\) backpack and then adding \(8\%\) sales tax at the register—flow in one unbroken chain without writing down a single intermediate number: 1. Key in 45 [ENTER] 20 [%] to see the 9.00 discount on Shelf \(X\) while 45 waits on Shelf \(Y\), then tap [-] to land on the 36.00 sale price. 2. Now type 8 [%] (2.88 tax on Shelf \(X\), 36.00 sale price on Shelf \(Y\)), tap [+], and tap [$] to round cleanly to 38.88 at the checkout counter!

When money stays in a savings account for several years, the interest itself starts earning interest! For example, to watch a \(\$500\) savings account grow at \(4\%\) interest compounded yearly for \(3\) years, multiply \(\$500\) by \(1.04\) three times (\(1.04^3 \times 500 = 562.43\) dollars):

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X What Happens on the Stack 1.04 0 0 0 1.04 Enter yearly growth multiplier (\(1 + 0.04 = 1.04\)) [ENTER] 0 0 1.04 1.04 Copy \(1.04\) up onto Shelf \(Y\) 3 0 0 1.04 3 Enter 3 years of compounding [g] [yˣ] 0 0 0 1.124864 Raise \(1.04^3 = 1.124864\) 500 0 0 1.124864 500 Enter starting savings (\(\$500\)); multiplier lifts to \(Y\) [×] 0 0 0 562.43 Multiply by \(\$500\) for $562.43 total savings

After \(3\) years, the account holds \(\$562.43\) total savings (\(\$62.43\) in interest earned).

docs.title: C.5 Annotated Bibliography & Primary Mathematical Sources
docs.text:
Every numbered reference across this volume links to a classic book, historical source, or mathematical study in the Annotated Bibliography below. If a story or puzzle in this book sparked your curiosity, several unforgettable books from our bibliography are waiting for you at your school or public library. For puzzle lovers and aspiring math magicians, Martin Gardner's The Colossal Book of Short Puzzles and Problems (Gardner, 1959) and George Pólya's How to Solve It (Pólya, 1945) show how drawing a picture, testing a smaller case, or working backward can crack seemingly impossible riddles. For young engineers and machine builders, David Macaulay's The Way Things Work Now (Macaulay, 2016) and Randall Munroe's What If? (Munroe, 2014) open up gears, levers, pendulums, and wild physics questions with playful illustrations that pair naturally with Chapter 6 and Chapter 9, while Simon Singh's The Code Book (Singh, 1997) tells the true history of secret ciphers from ancient Rome to modern RSA prime-number internet security.

To explore the history and beauty of everyday math, look for Steven Strogatz's The Joy of x (Strogatz, 2012), Jordan Ellenberg's How Not to Be Wrong (Ellenberg, 2014), and Georges Ifrah's The Universal History of Numbers (Ifrah, 2000), which trace how human beings use place value, fractions, geometry, and probability to understand the natural world. And for parents, teachers, and math coaches, Jerome Bruner's Toward a Theory of Instruction (Bruner, 1966), Liping Ma's Knowing and Teaching Elementary Mathematics (Ma, 1999), and Zoltan Dienes's Building Up Mathematics (Dienes, 1960) explain why building with physical blocks before moving to visual diagrams and symbols builds deep, lasting mathematical confidence.

docs.title: C.5.1 History of Stack Notation & Pocket Calculators
docs.text:
[lukasiewicz1924] Jan Łukasiewicz (1929) — Elementy logiki matematycznej (Elements of Mathematical Logic; parenthesis-free notation devised 1924). Komisja Wydawnicza Koła Matematyczno-Fizycznego Słuchaczów Uniwersytetu Warszawskiego (Warsaw; English trans. Pergamon Press, 1963).

Annotation: Introduces parenthesis-free prefix and postfix notation (devised in 1924 and published in his 1929 Warsaw logic treatise), demonstrating that operator position alone uniquely determines evaluation order without grouping symbols. Cited in Chapters: App C, Ch 02

[burks1954] Arthur W. Burks, Don W. Warren & Jesse B. Wright (1954) — An Analysis of a Logical Machine Using Parenthesis-Free Notation. Mathematical Tables and Other Aids to Computation, Vol. 8, No. 46, pp. 53–57.

Annotation: Formalizes Polish parenthesis-free postfix notation for electronic digital computers, laying the theoretical foundation for hardware-evaluated operational stacks. Cited in Chapters: App B

[hamrick1980] Kathy B. Hamrick (1996) — The History of the Hand-Held Electronic Calculator. The American Mathematical Monthly, Vol. 103, No. 8, pp. 633–639.

Annotation: Traces the historical evolution of Polish notation from abstract Warsaw mathematical logic to Corvallis handheld scientific computing. Cited in Chapters: App B, App C

docs.title: C.5.2 Classic Discoveries in Mathematics & Physics
docs.text:
[napier1614] John Napier (1614) — Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio. Andrew Hart, Edinburgh.

Annotation: The invention of logarithms, transforming laborious multi-digit multiplication into addition and doubling the working lifespan of astronomers. Cited in Chapters: Ch 05

[galilei1638] Galileo Galilei (1638) — Discorsi e Dimostrazioni Matematiche, intorno à due nuoue scienze (Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences). Louis Elsevier, Leiden.

Annotation: Establishes the geometric Square-Cube Law governing surface-area-to-volume scaling in structural mechanics and biological thermoregulation, as well as the isochronous law of the pendulum. Cited in Chapters: Ch 06, Ch 09

[gauss1809] Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809) — Theoria Motus Corporum Coelestium in Sectionibus Conicis Solem Ambientium. Perthes and Besser, Hamburg.

Annotation: Introduces the Method of Least Squares and the Gaussian Normal error distribution, recovering the lost celestial orbit of Ceres. Cited in Chapters: Ch 04, Ch 07

[kahan1979] William M. Kahan (1979) — Personal Calculator Has Key to Solve Any Equation f(x) = 0. Hewlett-Packard Journal, Vol. 30, No. 12, pp. 20–26.

Annotation: Establishes the non-destructive base-preserving percentage invariant and foundational floating-point error bounds for handheld solvers. Cited in Chapters: App B

docs.title: C.5.3 Mathematics, Nature & Popular Nonfiction
docs.text:
[sartorius1856] Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen (1856) — Gauss zum Gedächtniss. S. Hirzel, pp. 12–13, Leipzig.

Annotation: Primary biographical source recording young Carl Friedrich Gauss's arithmetic series solution in J.G. Büttner's Brunswick classroom and his Low German exclamation 'Ligget se!' ('There it lies!'). Cited in Chapters: Ch 04

[gardner1959] Martin Gardner (1959) — The Scientific American Book of Mathematical Puzzles and Diversions. Simon & Schuster, New York.

Annotation: Pioneered popular mathematical recreations, flexagons, hexaflexagons, and spatial puzzles that celebrate mathematical play. Cited in Chapters: App C, Ch 07

[gould1977] Stephen Jay Gould (1977) — Ever Since Darwin: Reflections in Natural History. W. W. Norton & Company, New York.

Annotation: Analyzes the evolutionary biology of 13-year and 17-year periodical cicadas (Magicicada) and prime-number predator avoidance cycles. Cited in Chapters: Ch 07

[singh1997] Simon Singh (1997) — Fermat's Enigma: The Epic Quest to Solve the World's Greatest Mathematical Problem. Walker & Company, New York.

Annotation: Captures the three-century human quest to prove Fermat's Last Theorem, conveying the passion and stakes of mathematical discovery. Cited in Chapters: App C, Ch 07

[ifrah2000] Georges Ifrah (2000) — The Universal History of Numbers: From Prehistory to the Invention of the Computer. John Wiley & Sons, New York.

Annotation: Comprehensive historical account of tally stones, Mesopotamian sexagesimal accounting, Egyptian hieroglyphic numerals, and the independent invention of zero and positional place value in India and Mesoamerica. Cited in Chapters: App C, Ch 03

[webb2001] Glenn F. Webb (2001) — The Prime Number Periodical Cicada Problem. Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems - Series B, Vol. 1, No. 3, pp. 387–399.

Annotation: Mathematical population model proving that 13-year and 17-year prime emergence periods minimize resonance with multi-year predator-prey cycles. Cited in Chapters: Ch 07

[gilbert2006] Caroline Gilbert, Graham Robertson, Yvon Le Maho, Yasuhiko Naito & André Ancel (2006) — Huddling behavior in emperor penguins: Dynamics of huddling. Physiology & Behavior, Vol. 88, No. 4-5, pp. 479–488.

Annotation: Quantifies how Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) reduce exposed windward surface area per bird to survive Antarctic winter blizzards. Cited in Chapters: Ch 06

[strogatz2012] Steven Strogatz (2012) — The Joy of x: A Guided Tour of Math, from One to Infinity. Eamon Dolan / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Boston.

Annotation: Guides the reader through arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and calculus using everyday curiosity and intuitive geometric insight. Cited in Chapters: App C, Ch 06, Foreword

[ellenberg2014] Jordan Ellenberg (2014) — How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking. Penguin Press, New York.

Annotation: Exposes common cognitive biases, non-linear scaling traps, and statistical survivorship fallacies with conversational wit. Cited in Chapters: App C

[munroe2014] Randall Munroe (2014) — What If?: Serious Scientific Answers to Absurd Hypothetical Questions. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Boston.

Annotation: Applies order-of-magnitude dimensional analysis, physics Fermi approximations, and creative mathematical modeling to wild scenarios. Cited in Chapters: App C

docs.title: D.1.4 How the Three Labels on Every Button & Number-Pad Shortcuts Work
docs.text:
Look closely at any button on your SC-6 and you will spot up to three labels—plus a clever spatial pattern hidden across the number pad (1–9). The bold Primary Legend printed on the keycap face runs with a single tap. Tapping [f] once lights the ↰ indicator in the top-left corner of the screen and selects the upper-left [f] label on your next key press; tapping [g] once lights ↱ and selects the upper-right [g] label (and tapping the same shift key a second time cancels it if you change your mind).

docs.title: D.3.3 Continuing Your Mathematical Journey
docs.text: Every time you place a number on Shelf \(Y\) with [ENTER], watch a finished answer lift automatically to Shelf \(Z\), or unfold a 3D box into [Σ+], you are practicing the exact way scientists, architects, and engineers think: breaking big puzzles into small, honest pieces you can see and touch. Keep your math blocks and your SC-6 within reach on your desk—and whenever you are ready for trigonometric waves, orbital mechanics, and numerical calculus, Thinking in the Stack (Volume II: StackCalc SC-32) is waiting for you.

docs.title: StackCalc Domain Calculator Series
When Mathematics Meets the Physical Trades
docs.text: Who this series is for: You already know how algebra, trigonometry, vectors, and logarithms work on paper. But how does an electrician turn right triangles into bent steel pipes thirty feet in the air? How does an artisan baker use percentages where the total is \(197\%\)? Why does an ICU nurse use square roots of height and weight to protect an elderly patient's kidneys? And why does a radio engineer care about waves reflecting backward down a coaxial cable?

docs.title: The Philosophy: Mathematics Grounded in Physical Reality
docs.text:
Pure mathematics is clean, timeless, and abstract. But when math steps out of the lecture hall and onto a job site, it hits the friction of the real world: - Heat dissipates in copper wires. - Measurement errors compound across property lines. - Microprocessors overflow when numbers exceed silicon registers. - Yeast fermentation speeds up when a mixer blade gets warm. - Sound waves collide in echoes and phase cancellations.

For decades, professionals in these fields used specialized pocket slide rules, tables, or legendary instruments like the HP-35, HP-16C, and HP-12C.

The StackCalc Domain Series expands that heritage into nine specialized physical and software instruments. Each calculator takes the timeless power of the 4-level Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) stack and customizes its keys, constants, and display for the natural rhythm of a specific craft.

Every instrument in the series shares five core engineering principles:

  1. Pure Scalar Stack (X, Y:, Z:, T:): Calculations are never blocked by clunky unit-mismatch errors. The numbers are clean, double-precision scalars.
  2. Top-Zero Suppression: Empty stack registers above your active numbers stay silent, keeping the screen uncluttered.
  3. Dedicated Table Inspector (TBL via [g] [+/-]): Lookup tables (AWG wire ampacities, periodic table molar masses, hop yields, and pipe dimensions) are accessible instantly without modifying your working stack.
  4. Physical Row 0 Softkeys: Six dedicated keys align with LCD screen slots for 1-tap parameter workspaces.
  5. Non-Destructive Inspection (SHOW): Transiently displays deep analytical breakdowns (like quadrant bearings, IEEE-754 float bitfields, or kitchen utensil equivalents) and returns to the stack untouched.

docs.title: Chapter 1: SC-35 Geomatics, Land Surveying & Flight Navigation
docs.text: Mapping a World That Refuses to Stand Still - The Core Puzzle: Why do surveyors swap sine and cosine compared to standard math, and why do historic property deeds use quadrant bearings (\(\text{S } 45^\circ \text{ W}\)) instead of \(0\text{--}360^\circ\) angles? - Key Concepts: Sexagesimal \(DDD.MMSS\) angles, Forward and Inverse Coordinate Geometry (COGO), traverse loop closure with Gauss's Shoelace polygon area, and solving aerodynamic crosswind drift.

docs.title: Chapter 2: SC-14 Industrial Trades, Electrical & Mechanical Handbook
docs.text: When Ohm's Law Meets Heavy Copper - The Core Puzzle: Why does a vacuum cleaner dim your living room lamp, and how do electricians use cosecant multipliers to bend rigid steel conduit around ceiling beams? - Key Concepts: Conductor resistance and Circular Mils (\(CM\)), single-phase and 3-phase voltage drop (\(VD = 2KIL/CM\)), the geometric \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\) factor of 3-phase AC power, and CNC surface feet per minute (\(SFM\)).

docs.title: Chapter 3: SC-16 Systems Programming, Embedded & Cyber Operations

docs.title: SC-35 Geomatics, Land Surveying & Flight Navigation
docs.text: Who this is for: Anyone who knows high school trigonometry and vectors, but has ever wondered how a surveyor turns a tripod on a muddy hillside into legal property boundaries, or how an airplane pilot navigates across a continent without drifting off course in the wind.

docs.title: 1. Mapping a World That Refuses to Stand Still
docs.text:
If you took geometry in school, you learned to plot points on a neat Cartesian plane: \(x\) goes to the right, \(y\) goes up, and angles turn counterclockwise starting from the positive \(x\)-axis.

Then you step outside with a tripod, and the real world immediately breaks all three rules: 1. North is up, not East. In land surveying and aviation, \(0^\circ\) points straight toward North. 2. Angles turn clockwise, like a clock face. \(90^\circ\) is East, \(180^\circ\) is South, and \(270^\circ\) is West. 3. The ground is not flat. The earth is a bumpy, curved spheroid, and every measurement you make with a laser, tape, or compass accumulates physical error.

Centuries ago, when young surveyors like George Washington paced out Virginia valley tracts with a 66-foot iron chain, or when sea captains like Nathaniel Bowditch steered sailing ships by the stars, they faced the same fundamental challenge: How do you keep small measurement errors from compounding into legal and physical disasters?

If a boundary line is off by just a quarter of a degree, that error acts like a giant lever arm. Over a half-mile run, a property fence drifts by dozens of feet, overlapping a neighbor's land and sparking bitter legal disputes. In the air, a five-degree wind error over a three-hour flight can put an airplane fifty miles off course over fuel-empty wilderness.

The StackCalc 35 (SC-35) is designed specifically to tame this geometry. Instead of forcing you to balance parentheses or convert sexagesimal degrees in your head while standing in the rain or turbulence, it puts coordinate geometry (COGO), horizontal curve design, differential leveling, and wind-triangle vector calculations directly into a fast, transparent 4-level RPN stack.

docs.title: Why Not Just Use a Phone App?
docs.text:
Modern surveyors have \(\$30{,}000\) robotic total stations, and pilots carry iPad tablets running GPS moving maps. Why does anyone want a dedicated pocket instrument?

  • Sunlight, Rain, and Gloves: Capacitive phone screens wash out in harsh desert glare, register phantom touches in the rain, and refuse to work when you are wearing heavy leather work gloves or flight mittens. The SC-35 uses high-contrast reflective optics and crisp tactile mechanical keys you can feel through a glove.
  • The Legal Reality of Old Deeds: Modern GPS gives coordinates in decimal degrees and \(360^\circ\) azimuths. But real property deeds recorded fifty or a hundred years ago are written in Quadrant Bearings: "Thence South \(42^\circ 15' 30''\) West, \(324.50\text{ feet}\)". Re-tracing a boundary requires typing quadrant angles directly.
  • Licensing Exam Rules: The National Council of Examiners for Engineering and Surveying (NCEES) strictly bans smartphones, cellular tablets, and graphing calculators from Fundamentals of Surveying (FS) exams. Candidates must know how to solve traverse loops on a dedicated, approved instrument.

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts: How Surveyors and Pilots Think
Concept 1: The Compass Clock and Sexagesimal Angles
docs.text:
In high school math, you convert \(125^\circ 30'\) into \(125.5^\circ\) before pressing [SIN]. But in surveying and navigation, angles are always read from optical theodolites, compass circles, and navigation charts in Degrees, Minutes, and Seconds (\(DDD^\circ MM' SS''\)): - \(1^\circ = 60 \text{ arcminutes } (')\) - \(1' = 60 \text{ arcseconds } ('')\)

On the SC-35, you don't need multi-key menu conversions. You enter sexagesimal angles as a single decimal number in canonical DDD.MMSS format: - \(125^\circ 30' 45''\) is entered directly as 125.3045. - \(45^\circ 05' 12''\) is entered as 45.0512.

Softkey 5 (DMS / DEG) toggles the calculator between sexagesimal and decimal degrees instantly.

docs.title: Why the Trig Functions Swap Places
docs.text:
Because surveying azimuths measure clockwise from North (\(+y\)) rather than counterclockwise from East (\(+x\)), the trigonometric coordinate displacements swap roles: - Departure (East displacement): \(\Delta E = \text{Distance} \cdot \sin(\text{Azimuth})\) - Latitude (North displacement): \(\Delta N = \text{Distance} \cdot \cos(\text{Azimuth})\)

If you enter an azimuth of \(90^\circ\) (due East), \(\sin(90^\circ) = 1\) and \(\cos(90^\circ) = 0\), so all your travel becomes East departure with zero North latitude.

                     North (0°)
                         ^
                         |        * Point B (E_B, N_B)
                         |       /
                         |      / Distance (D)
                         |  θ  / 
                         | ^  /   ΔN = D * cos(θ)
                         | | /
                         +----------> East (90°)
                   Point A (0, 0)   ΔE = D * sin(θ)

docs.title: Concept 2: The Two Fundamental Vector Problems (Forward & Inverse COGO)
docs.text:
Every land survey and aerial flight path comes down to two reciprocal questions: 1. Forward COGO: "I am at point A. If I walk \(500\text{ feet}\) along azimuth \(045^\circ\), what are my new coordinates?" $\(E_B = E_A + D\sin\theta, \quad N_B = N_A + D\cos\theta\)$ 2. Inverse COGO: "I have point A and point B on a map. What direction must I head, and how far must I travel to get from A to B?" $\(\Delta E = E_B - E_A, \quad \Delta N = N_B - N_A\)$ $\(\text{Distance} = \sqrt{\Delta E^2 + \Delta N^2}, \quad \text{Azimuth} = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta E, \Delta N)\)$

On the SC-35, pressing [ FWD ] takes coordinates and vectors and outputs new coordinates; pressing [ INV ] takes two coordinate pairs and outputs distance and bearing in one keystroke.

docs.title: Concept 3: Traverse Misclosure and the Shoelace Formula
docs.text:
When a survey crew walks around a parcel of land and returns to the starting benchmark, the sum of all North departures (\(\sum \Delta N\)) and East departures (\(\sum \Delta E\)) should theoretically equal zero. In practice, slight optical and taping tolerances leave a small gap: the linear error of closure (\(c\)):

\[c = \sqrt{\left(\sum \Delta E\right)^2 + \left(\sum \Delta N\right)^2}\]

If the crew walked \(2{,}500\text{ feet}\) in total perimeter, and the closure error is \(0.15\text{ feet}\), the precision ratio is:

\[\text{Precision} = \frac{2500}{0.15} \approx 16{,}667 \implies \mathbf{1:16{,}667}\]

This exceeds the standard \(1:10{,}000\) legal code requirement for suburban boundary surveys.

To find the enclosed acreage, the SC-35 applies Gauss's Shoelace Formula across the sequential coordinates as they are entered into the Σ+ register:

\[\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (E_i N_{i+1} - E_{i+1} N_i) + (E_n N_1 - E_1 N_n) \right|\]

Dividing square feet by \(43{,}560\) yields acres.

docs.title: Concept 4: The Wind Triangle and Ground Speed
docs.text:
When an airplane flies through the atmosphere, the air mass itself is moving over the ground. The aircraft's actual path across the countryside (Ground Track) is the vector sum of its True Airspeed Vector (\(\vec{V}_{\text{TAS}}\)) and the Wind Vector (\(\vec{V}_{\text{wind}}\)).

          True Airspeed (TAS) along Heading (TH)
        *----------------------------------------->
         \                                       /
   Wind   \                                     / 
   Vector  \                                   / Ground Track & Speed (GS)
            v                                 v

By applying the Law of Sines to the triangle: - Wind Correction Angle (WCA): The angle the nose of the plane must be turned into the wind so the airplane doesn't drift sideways off course. - Ground Speed (GS): The actual speed the plane covers ground over the trees and runways.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Field Walkthroughs
Field Case 1: Checking a Disputed Rural Boundary (r/Surveying)
docs.text: A land surveyor is verifying a boundary line between two iron boundary monuments. - Benchmark 1 is at coordinates: \(1000.00\text{ N}, 1000.00\text{ E}\). - Benchmark 2 is at coordinates: \(1385.20\text{ N}, 1412.60\text{ E}\). What is the exact boundary distance and quadrant bearing between the monuments?

docs.title: How to Solve It on the SC-35
docs.text:
1. Compute \(\Delta E = 1412.60 - 1000.00 = 412.60\text{ ft}\).
  2. Compute \(\Delta N = 1385.20 - 1000.00 = 385.20\text{ ft}\).
  3. Enter into the RPN stack:
  4. 412.60 [ENTER] 385.20
  5. Tap [g] [POL] (Rectangular to Polar / Inverse COGO):
  6. Register \(X\) displays: 564.4842 (Distance in feet).
  7. Register \(Y\) displays: 46.9745 (Azimuth in decimal degrees: \(46.97^\circ\)).
  8. Convert decimal degrees to sexagesimal:
  9. Tap [f] [→HR] \(\to\) Register \(Y\) shows 46.5828 (\(46^\circ 58' 28''\)).
  10. Press [BRG] then [g] [SHOW]:
  11. The LCD transiently displays: N 46° 58' 28" E (The exact quadrant bearing to write on the legal map).

docs.title: Field Case 2: Flying with a \(25\text{-Knot}\) Crosswind (r/flying)
docs.text: You are cruising in a light aircraft at a True Airspeed of \(120\text{ knots}\) heading on a True Course of \(070^\circ\). Flight Service reports winds aloft at \(120^\circ\) at \(25\text{ knots}\). What heading should you fly, and what is your actual ground speed?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Find the Wind Angle: \(120^\circ - 070^\circ = 50^\circ\) (wind is blowing from \(50^\circ\) to your right).
  2. Find the Crosswind Component:
  3. 25 [ENTER] 50 [SIN] [×] \(\to\) 19.15 knots.
  4. Find the Headwind Component:
  5. 25 [ENTER] 50 [COS] [×] \(\to\) 16.07 knots.
  6. Compute the Wind Correction Angle (WCA):
  7. \(\sin(WCA) = \frac{19.15}{120} = 0.1596\)
  8. 19.15 [ENTER] 120 [÷] [g] [ASIN] \(\to\) +9.18°.
  9. You must turn \(9.2^\circ\) right into the wind: Heading = \(079.2^\circ\).
  10. Compute Actual Ground Speed:
  11. \(GS = 120 \cdot \cos(9.18^\circ) - 16.07 = 118.46 - 16.07 = \mathbf{102.39\text{ knots}}\).

docs.title: 4. Try It Yourself: Practice Problems
Problem 1: Circular Highway Curve Tangent
docs.text: A civil engineering plan calls for a highway curve with an intersection deflection angle \(\Delta = 36^\circ 30' 00''\) (\(36.5^\circ\)) and a centerline radius \(R = 1{,}200.00\text{ ft}\). Calculate the tangent distance \(T = R \tan(\Delta / 2)\). (Solution: \(\Delta / 2 = 18.25^\circ\). \(1200 \times \tan(18.25^\circ) = \mathbf{395.73\text{ ft}}\).)

docs.title: Problem 2: Differential Leveling Loop
docs.text: At setup 1, your optical level sights a rod on Bench Mark 1 (Elevation \(= 842.15\text{ ft}\)) with a backsight (\(BS\)) of \(5.32\text{ ft}\). The foresight (\(FS\)) to Turning Point 1 is \(6.88\text{ ft}\). What is the height of instrument (\(HI\)) and the elevation of Turning Point 1? (Solution: \(HI = 842.15 + 5.32 = \mathbf{847.47\text{ ft}}\). Elevation = \(847.47 - 6.88 = \mathbf{840.59\text{ ft}}\).)

docs.title: Problem 3: Density Altitude Check
docs.text: An airport is at \(3{,}500\text{ ft}\) elevation. On a hot summer day, ambient temperature is \(35^\circ\text{C}\) (\(95^\circ\text{F}\)) with an altimeter setting of \(29.72\text{ inHg}\). Standard pressure altitude \(PA = 3500 + (29.92 - 29.72) \times 1000 = 3{,}700\text{ ft}\). Standard temperature at \(3{,}700\text{ ft}\) is \(15 - 2 \times 3.7 = 7.6^\circ\text{C}\). Calculate Density Altitude: \(DA = PA + 120 \times (T_{\text{actual}} - T_{\text{standard}})\). (Solution: \(DA = 3700 + 120 \times (35 - 7.6) = \mathbf{6{,}988\text{ ft}}\). The airplane will perform on takeoff as if it were nearly \(7{,}000\) feet up!)

docs.title: SC-14 Industrial Trades, Electrical & Mechanical Handbook
docs.text: Who this is for: Anyone who knows Ohm's Law (\(V = IR\)) and basic right-triangle trigonometry, but wants to understand the hidden physics behind electrical breaker panels, industrial motors, and bending steel pipes around structural obstacles.

docs.title: 1. When Ohm's Law Meets Heavy Copper
docs.text:
Have you ever noticed the lights in your home dim for a split second when the air conditioner compressor kicks on?

That momentary dip is Ohm's Law playing out along fifty feet of copper hidden behind your drywall. A copper wire is not an imaginary, zero-resistance superconductor; it is a very long, very thin resistor. When a heavy electric motor draws a sudden surge of current, that current passing through the wire's physical resistance drops voltage right in the line. The voltage at the appliance sags, and the missing energy turns directly into heat inside the wall.

In a home, an undersized wire might merely cause flickering lamps or a tripped breaker. But in a commercial hospital, a high-rise data center, or an industrial chemical plant, excessive electrical heat can melt insulation and cause electrical fires. To prevent this, the National Fire Protection Association publishes NFPA 70, known universally as the National Electrical Code (NEC).

The NEC is essentially applied physics and geometry codified into law. Electricians, pipefitters, and precision machinists work in an environment where math must be calculated quickly, accurately, and without paper: - Sizing a feeder cable so that a \(480\text{-volt}\) industrial pump doesn't suffer brownout over a \(300\text{-foot}\) run. - Calculating how much steel conduit shrinks when bending around an overhead structural I-beam. - Figuring out the exact spindle RPM for a carbide milling cutter so it cuts clean metal without overheating and dulling.

The StackCalc 14 (SC-14) puts these trade formulas, conductor tables, and mechanical calculations directly onto a rugged 4-level RPN stack.

docs.title: Why Not Just Use a Smartphone?
docs.text:
• The Scissor Lift Environment: Picture standing on a scissor lift platform thirty feet in the air, wearing leather work gloves coated in greasy wire-pulling lubricant. A glass smartphone requires bare hands, risks cracking if dropped onto concrete, and turns off its screen mid-calculation. The SC-14 is built for one-handed operation with tactile mechanical switches that click clearly even through thick gloves.
  • Scrap Conduit is Expensive: A single 10-foot stick of 3-inch or 4-inch rigid metal pipe costs over \(\$150\). If you miscalculate the offset travel or forget the shrinkage when bending around an obstacle, the pipe dog-legs, misses the junction box, and has to be thrown in the scrap bin.
  • Licensing Exams: Journeyman and Master Electrician licensing exams strictly ban smartphones and internet-connected devices. Candidates must be able to calculate conductor ampacity, conduit fill, and three-phase motor loads on an approved standalone instrument.

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts: How Electricians and Machinists Think
Concept 1: The Vanishing Volts & Circular Mils (\(CM\))
docs.text:
Why do electricians measure wire thickness in "Circular Mils" rather than square millimeters or inches?

A mil is one-thousandth of an inch (\(0.001\text{ in}\)). In standard geometry, the area of a circle is \(\frac{\pi}{4} d^2\). But when sizing thousands of cables, carrying \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) through every calculation is tedious.

Electrical pioneers invented a brilliant shortcut: A Circular Mil (\(CM\)) is simply the diameter in mils, squared:

\[CM = (d_{\text{mils}})^2 = (d_{\text{inches}} \times 1000)^2\]

A wire with a diameter of \(0.10\text{ inches}\) is \(100\text{ mils}\) thick, which means its area is simply \(100^2 = 10{,}000\text{ CM}\). The circle's \(\pi\) factor is baked directly into the material resistivity constant \(K\): - Copper (\(K_{\text{Cu}}\)): \(\approx 12.9\,\Omega\cdot\text{cmil/ft}\) at normal operating temperatures. - Aluminum (\(K_{\text{Al}}\)): \(\approx 21.2\,\Omega\cdot\text{cmil/ft}\).

docs.title: The Voltage Drop Formula
docs.text:
For a single-phase two-wire circuit carrying current \(I\) over a one-way distance \(L\) (total wire loop length is \(2L\)):

\[\text{Voltage Drop } (VD) = \frac{2 \cdot K \cdot I \cdot L}{CM}\]

The NEC recommends that voltage drop never exceed 3% on a branch circuit (e.g. no more than \(3.6\text{ V}\) drop on a \(120\text{ V}\) line). If the calculated drop is too high, you must step up to a thicker wire gauge with more circular mils.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Power of Three (\(\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\))
docs.text:
Why do commercial buildings and factories run on Three-Phase AC rather than the single-phase AC in our homes?

In single-phase power, voltage pulses like a heartbeat: it peaks, drops through zero, and reverses 60 times a second. A single-phase motor vibrates and needs auxiliary starting capacitors.

In three-phase power, three independent alternating voltage waves travel together, staggered evenly \(120^\circ\) apart. When one wave is passing through zero, the other two are delivering strong power. The total electrical power delivered is continuous and smooth, allowing motors to be smaller, lighter, and self-starting.

Because the three waves are separated by \(120^\circ\) on a circle, the line-to-line voltage is not simply double: it is multiplied by the geometric factor \(\mathbf{\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732}\):

\[V_{\text{line-to-line}} = \sqrt{3} \cdot V_{\text{phase-to-neutral}} \approx 1.732 \times 120\text{ V} \approx 208\text{ V}$$ $$1.732 \times 277\text{ V} \approx 480\text{ V}\]

docs.title: Sizing Three-Phase Motor Circuits
docs.text:
For a 3-phase motor delivering horsepower (\(1\text{ HP} = 746\text{ Watts}\)) at efficiency \(\eta\) and power factor \(PF\):

\[\text{Full Load Amps } (FLA) = \frac{\text{HP} \cdot 746}{\sqrt{3} \cdot V_{\text{line}} \cdot \eta \cdot PF}\]

Under NEC Article 430, because electric motors draw a heavy inductive inrush current when starting up, conductors must be sized to \(125\%\) of motor FLA. On the SC-14, pressing [f] [3PH÷] automatically incorporates \(\sqrt{3}\) in one keystroke.

docs.title: Concept 3: Bending Steel Pipe with Right Triangles
docs.text:
When routing conduit across a ceiling, electricians frequently hit obstacles: air ducts, fire sprinkler lines, or structural steel columns. To get around them, you bend the pipe out and back in an offset bend:

                       Offset Depth (D)
                      |---|
    ------------------\
                       \   Travel (Hypotenuse = D * csc θ)
                        \
                         \---------------------

An offset is simply two equal and opposite right triangles: - Travel Distance (Hypotenuse): \(\text{Travel} = \text{Depth} \cdot \csc\theta = \frac{\text{Depth}}{\sin\theta}\) - Conduit Shrinkage: Because the hypotenuse is longer than the straight horizontal path, bending an offset pulls the end of the pipe backward toward the bender. If you don't account for this "shrinkage," your pipe will end up too short to reach the next junction box!

\[\text{Shrinkage} = \text{Depth} \times \left(\frac{1}{\tan\theta} - \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)\]

docs.title: Bending Multipliers Quick Reference
docs.text:
• \(30^\circ\) Bend: Multiplier \(= 2.0\) (Travel is exactly twice the depth; shrinks \(1/4\text{ in}\) per inch of depth).
  • \(45^\circ\) Bend: Multiplier \(= 1.414\) (Travel is \(1.414 \times \text{Depth}\); shrinks \(3/8\text{ in}\) per inch of depth).

docs.title: Concept 4: Machining Feeds and Speeds
docs.text:
In a machine shop, cutting metal on a milling machine or lathe obeys a simple physical rule: the cutting tool must slide through the workpiece at a specific linear velocity called Surface Feet per Minute (\(SFM\)): - Mild steel cuts at roughly \(100\text{ SFM}\) with high-speed steel. - Aluminum can be machined at \(600\text{ SFM}\) or higher.

To turn linear surface feet into rotational spindle speed (\(RPM\)):

\[RPM = \frac{SFM \times 12}{\pi \cdot \text{Diameter}} \approx \frac{3.82 \cdot SFM}{\text{Diameter (inches)}}\]

A tiny \(1/8\text{-inch}\) drill bit must spin at high RPM to achieve the proper cutting speed, while a massive \(3\text{-inch}\) face mill must turn much slower to avoid overheating its carbide inserts.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Field Walkthroughs
Field Case 1: Sizing a 480V Sub-Panel Feeder (r/electricians)
docs.text: An electrician is running a continuous \(65\text{-amp}\) balanced 3-phase load from a main switchboard to a sub-panel located \(220\text{ feet}\) away. The supply voltage is \(480\text{ V}\) 3-phase copper. 1. What minimum ampacity wire is required under the NEC \(125\%\) continuous load rule? 2. If using #4 AWG copper wire (\(41{,}740\text{ CM}\)), what is the expected voltage drop and percentage drop?

docs.title: How to Solve It on the SC-14
docs.text:
1. Apply the 125% Continuous Rule (NEC 210.20):
  2. 65 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] \(\to\) 81.25 Amps.
  3. Looking at NEC Table 310.16 via [TBL]: #4 AWG copper (rated for \(85\text{ A}\) at \(75^\circ\text{C}\)) is required.
  4. Calculate 3-Phase Voltage Drop:
  5. Formula: \(VD = \frac{\sqrt{3} \cdot K \cdot I \cdot L}{CM}\) (\(K = 12.9\) for Cu, \(I = 65\text{ A}\), \(L = 220\text{ ft}\), \(CM = 41740\)).
  6. 1.732 [ENTER] 12.9 [×] 65 [×] 220 [×]
  7. Stack displays: 319485
  8. 41740 [÷] \(\to\) 7.65 Volts.
  9. Calculate Percentage Drop:
  10. 7.65 [ENTER] 480 [÷] 100 [×] \(\to\) 1.59%.
  11. Since \(1.59\% < 3.0\%\), the wire easily satisfies code requirements without excessive heat.

docs.title: Field Case 2: Bending a 4-Inch Offset Around an I-Beam (Practical Machinist)
docs.text: An electrician running \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT conduit must clear a steel ceiling beam that hangs \(4\text{ inches}\) lower than the roof deck. The electrician chooses a standard \(30^\circ\) offset. 1. How far apart should the two bend marks be made on the pipe (Travel)? 2. How much will the pipe shrink toward the bender?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Compute Travel Distance:
  2. Multiplier for \(30^\circ\) is \(\frac{1}{\sin(30^\circ)} = 2.0\).
  3. 4 [ENTER] 30 [SIN] [÷] \(\to\) 8.00 inches.
  4. The electrician places the two bend arrows exactly \(8\text{ inches}\) apart on the conduit.
  5. Compute Pipe Shrinkage:
  6. For \(30^\circ\), shrink is \(1/4\text{ inch}\) per inch of offset depth.
  7. 4 [ENTER] 0.25 [×] \(\to\) 1.00 inch.
  8. The electrician shifts the first bend mark forward by \(1\text{ inch}\) so the final end lands flush in the junction box.

docs.title: 4. Try It Yourself: Practice Problems
Problem 1: Motor Full Load Current
docs.text: A three-phase \(480\text{-volt}\) induction motor produces \(25\text{ HP}\) on a factory conveyor line. The motor nameplate lists an operating efficiency of \(88\%\) (\(\eta = 0.88\)) and a power factor of \(0.85\) (\(PF = 0.85\)). Calculate the motor Full Load Amps (\(FLA\)). (Solution: \(25 \times 746 = 18{,}650\text{ W}\). Denominator \(= 1.732 \times 480 \times 0.88 \times 0.85 = 622.3\). \(FLA = 18650 / 622.3 = \mathbf{29.97\text{ Amps}}\). Branch conductors must be sized to \(125\% \times 29.97 = \mathbf{37.5\text{ A}}\).)

docs.title: Problem 2: Conduit Raceway Fill
docs.text: Under NEC Chapter 9 Table 1, a conduit raceway with more than two conductors may be filled to a maximum of 40% of its cross-sectional area. A \(1\text{-inch}\) EMT conduit has an internal cross-sectional area of \(0.864\text{ sq in}\). If each #10 THHN conductor has a cross-sectional area of \(0.0211\text{ sq in}\), what is the maximum number of #10 wires allowed in this pipe? (Solution: Usable area \(= 0.864 \times 0.40 = 0.3456\text{ sq in}\). Max wires \(= 0.3456 / 0.0211 = 16.38 \implies \mathbf{16\text{ wires}}\).)

docs.title: Problem 3: CNC Spindle Speed
docs.text: A machinist is facing an aluminum block (\(SFM = 500\)) using a \(2.5\text{-inch}\) diameter carbide face mill. Calculate the proper spindle speed in \(RPM\). (Solution: \(RPM = 3.82 \times 500 / 2.5 = \mathbf{764\text{ RPM}}\).)

docs.title: SC-16 Systems Programming, Embedded & Cyber Operations
docs.text: Who this is for: Anyone who writes software in high-level languages like Python, C, Rust, or JavaScript, but wants to understand what actually happens when variables turn into electrical signals, registers, and memory addresses inside a CPU.

docs.title: 1. When Numbers Hit the Silicon Ceiling
docs.text:
In high school math, numbers are smooth and infinite. You can start at zero and count upward forever, or take any two numbers and divide them into smaller and smaller fractions.

In a computer chip, numbers are neither smooth nor infinite. They live in fixed-width boxes of silicon.

A physical register in a microprocessor is made of microscopic flip-flops—transistor circuits that can hold either high voltage (\(1\)) or low voltage (\(0\)). An 8-bit register has eight switches; a 32-bit register has thirty-two; a 64-bit register has sixty-four. Because there are only so many switches in the box, numbers in computing behave like an old mechanical car odometer.

If your car’s odometer has five digit wheels and you drive past \(99{,}999\text{ miles}\), the odometer doesn't expand to six digits; it clicks over to \(00{,}000\).

In 1996, the European Space Agency learned this lesson the hard way during the maiden launch of the Ariane 5 rocket. A routine software function tried to cram a 64-bit floating-point measurement of horizontal drift velocity into a 16-bit signed integer register. In pure math, the measured velocity of \(32{,}768\) was completely valid. But the maximum positive number that fits into a 16-bit signed integer is \(32{,}767\). The number overflowed, the CPU threw an unhandled hardware exception, the rocket's flight computers misread diagnostic dump data as an emergency command, and the rocket tore itself apart thirty-seven seconds into flight.

In the 1980s, Hewlett-Packard built the beloved HP-16C Computer Scientist to help programmers see and master these discrete boundaries. The StackCalc 16 (SC-16) modernizes that workflow: it lets you switch between Hex, Decimal, Octal, and Binary at a single touch, configure word sizes from 8 to 64 bits, mask bitfields, inspect compiler struct padding, and decode IEEE-754 floating-point bits directly on an RPN stack.

docs.title: Why Not Just Use Python or an On-Screen Calculator?
docs.text:
• The SCIF and Air-Gap Security Reality: In defense aerospace, cybersecurity red-teams, and secure government facilities (governed by DoD ICD 705 standards), smartphones, fitness trackers, and internet-connected devices are strictly prohibited and locked outside the vault door. Engineers debugging secure crypto chips or flight avionics work in clean rooms with zero web access. The SC-16 provides a compliant, non-communicating physical instrument permitted inside secure areas.
  • Bare-Metal Hardware Bring-Up: When a new prototype circuit board comes back from the factory, the microcontroller often crashes before the operating system or USB serial port even initializes. An engineer staring at raw hexadecimal addresses on a logic analyzer or JTAG debugger needs dedicated [A] through [F] keys to mask bits and calculate offsets without switching away from the oscilloscope.
  • Thinking in Hexadecimal: Generic calculators force you to convert hex addresses into decimal before doing math. On the SC-16, you add 0x1000 to 0x0F80 and bit-shift directly in native hexadecimal.

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts: How Systems and Cyber Engineers Think
Concept 1: The Odometer in Reverse (Two's Complement)
docs.text:
How does a computer represent negative numbers using only ones and zeros?

Early computer pioneers tried using the first bit as a simple plus/minus flag. But this created two separate zeros (\(+0\) and \(-0\)), requiring complicated arithmetic circuits.

The industry settled on a clever mechanical trick called Two's Complement. Think back to our five-digit car odometer: - If you start at \(00{,}000\) and drive forward 1 mile, the odometer reads \(00{,}001\). - What happens if you put the car in reverse and drive backward 1 mile? The wheels click backward from zero to \(99{,}999\)!

In a 16-bit binary register: - \(0\) is 0000 0000 0000 0000. - Rolling backward by 1 gives 1111 1111 1111 1111 (\(65{,}535\) if unsigned, or \(-1\) if signed!).

To negate any binary number in two's complement, you simply invert all the bits and add 1: $\(\text{Negate}(x) = (\sim x) + 1\)$

Because of this symmetry, a CPU does not need a separate subtraction circuit. To compute \(A - B\), the silicon simply computes \(A + ((\sim B) + 1)\) using standard addition gates.

docs.title: Word Sizes and the Sign Bit
docs.text:
The most significant (leftmost) bit acts as the sign flag: - 0 means positive. - 1 means negative.

Word Size Bit Width Unsigned Range Signed Two's Complement Range BYTE 8 bits \(0\) to \(255\) \(-128\) to \(+127\) WORD 16 bits \(0\) to \(65{,}535\) \(-32{,}768\) to \(+32{,}767\) DWORD 32 bits \(0\) to \(4{,}294{,}967{,}295\) \(-2{,}147{,}483{,}648\) to \(+2{,}147{,}483{,}647\) QWORD 64 bits \(0\) to \(\approx 1.84 \times 10^{19}\) \(\approx -9.22 \times 10^{18}\) to \(+9.22 \times 10^{18}\)

docs.title: Concept 2: Speaking in Hexadecimal (Base-16)
docs.text:
Humans have ten fingers, so we count in decimal (base-10). Computers have binary switches, so they count in binary (base-2).

Writing long binary strings like 1101111010101101 is dizzying and prone to transcription errors. Hexadecimal (base-16) solves this because \(16 = 2^4\). Every single hexadecimal digit represents exactly four binary bits (a "nibble"):

Hex Digit Binary Decimal Hex Digit Binary Decimal 0–9 0000–1001 \(0\)–\(9\) C 1100 \(12\) A 1010 \(10\) D 1101 \(13\) B 1011 \(11\) E / F 1110 / 1111 \(14\) / \(15\)

The 16-bit binary number 1101 1110 1010 1101 splits cleanly into four nibbles: DE AD \(\implies\) 0xDEAD.

docs.title: Concept 3: Bitwise Logic & Masking
docs.text:
In high-level programming, you write conditions like if (user.isActive). In firmware and network packet drivers, you interact directly with hardware registers where each individual bit controls a physical circuit (like turning on an LED, enabling an antenna, or resetting a timer).

We control individual bits using Boolean logic: - AND (&): Clears bits to zero. To check if bit 3 is set, you "mask" with 0000 1000. - OR (|): Sets bits to one without touching other bits. - XOR (^): Toggles bits, or checks if two values differ. - Bit Shifts (<<, >>): Multiplying or dividing by powers of 2. Shifting left by 1 multiplies by 2; shifting right by 1 divides by 2.

docs.title: Concept 4: Memory Alignment & Struct Padding
docs.text:
Modern 32-bit and 64-bit processors do not read memory one single byte at a time; they fetch 4-byte or 8-byte chunks across wide silicon buses.

If an 8-byte variable (like a 64-bit float) sits at an odd memory address (like 0x1001), the CPU has to make two separate memory accesses, stitch the halves together, and burn clock cycles. To prevent this, compilers insert invisible padding bytes between struct variables:

    struct SensorData {
        uint8_t  sensorId;   // 1 byte  at offset 0
        // [3 PADDING BYTES INSERTED BY COMPILER]
        uint32_t timestamp;  // 4 bytes at offset 4 (must align to multiple of 4!)
        uint16_t reading;    // 2 bytes at offset 8
        // [2 PADDING BYTES INSERTED AT END]
    }; // Total size = 12 bytes, NOT 7 bytes!

The SC-16's ALIGN softkeys calculate struct offsets and padding gaps automatically.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Field Walkthroughs
Field Case 1: Isolating a Hardware Status Bit (r/embedded)
docs.text: An engineer is reading an SPI status register from a radio transceiver. The hardware datasheet says: - Register address: 0x4001 - Bit 5 is the TX_READY flag (\(1 = \text{ready to transmit}\), \(0 = \text{busy}\)). - The microcontroller reads raw byte: 0x7A. Is the radio ready to transmit?

docs.title: How to Solve It on the SC-16
docs.text:
1. Put the SC-16 in HEX mode: softkey [ HEX ].
  2. Enter the raw byte: 7A [ENTER].
  3. Create a bitmask for bit 5 (\(2^5 = 32 = \text{0x20}\)):
  4. 20
  5. Execute bitwise AND:
  6. Tap [f] [AND].
  7. Register \(X\) displays: 0x20.
  8. Because the result is non-zero (0x20), bit 5 is high: The radio is ready to transmit!

docs.title: Field Case 2: Subnetting an IPv4 Network (Hacker News)
docs.text: A network architect is dividing a corporate network with IP block 192.168.10.0/26. 1. What is the subnet mask in dotted-decimal and hex? 2. How many total host IP addresses are available in each subnet?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Mechanics
docs.text:
1. A /26 prefix means the first 26 bits are 1s, and the remaining \(32 - 26 = 6\text{ bits}\) are 0s.
  2. In the 4th byte, there are two 1s followed by six 0s: 1100 0000 in binary.
  3. On the SC-16, type 11000000 in BIN mode \(\to\) switch to DEC: displays 192.
  4. Subnet mask is 255.255.255.192 (or 0xFFFFFFC0 in hex).
  5. Compute total host count from the 6 host bits:
  6. 2 [ENTER] 6 [yˣ] \(\to\) 64 total addresses.
  7. Subtract network ID (all 0s) and broadcast ID (all 1s): \(64 - 2 = \mathbf{62\text{ usable hosts}}\).

docs.title: 4. Try It Yourself: Practice Problems
Problem 1: Two's Complement Negative Conversion
docs.text: Using an 8-bit word size (BYTE mode on SC-16), enter decimal value \(+42\). Convert it to signed negative \(-42\) using two's complement. (Solution: \(+42 = \text{0x2A} = \text{0010 1010}_2\). Invert bits: \(\text{1101 0101}_2 = \text{0xD5}\). Add 1: \(\text{0xD5} + 1 = \mathbf{0xD6}\). In 8-bit signed decimal, \(\text{0xD6} = \mathbf{-42}\).)

docs.title: Problem 2: Circular Ring-Buffer Masking
docs.text: A high-speed UART driver allocates a ring buffer of size \(256\text{ bytes}\) (\(2^8\)). The head pointer is currently at index 310. Using bitwise AND masking instead of an expensive division/modulo operator (%), find the buffer index. (Solution: Mask with size minus one: \(256 - 1 = 255 = \text{0xFF}\). 310 & 0xFF \(\implies\) 310 [ENTER] 255 [AND] \(\to\) 54. Fast, single-cycle ring-buffer wrapping!)

docs.title: Problem 3: Decoding an IEEE-754 Single-Precision Float
docs.text: A binary packet dumps the 32-bit hex word 0x41440000. On the SC-16, enter 41440000 in HEX mode, then tap [FLT] followed by [g] [SHOW]. (Solution: Sign bit \(= 0\) (+). Exponent bits \(= 10000010_2 = 130\). Unbias: \(130 - 127 = 3\). Mantissa bits \(= 0.28125\). Value \(= +1.28125 \times 2^3 = \mathbf{12.25}\).)

docs.title: SC-24 Cinema Optics, Broadcast Timecode & Sound Handbook
docs.text: Who this is for: Anyone who loves photography, filmmaking, or audio production and wants to understand the exact mathematical physics connecting lenses, camera sensors, decibels, and broadcast video sync.

docs.title: 1. When Light and Sound Become Numbers
docs.text:
Every motion picture you have ever watched is an optical illusion. A projector or screen flashes twenty-four still photographs in front of your eyes every second. Because of the human brain's persistence of vision, our visual cortex fuses those discrete snapshots into the seamless illusion of continuous motion.

Our ears, by contrast, are far more sensitive to time. While our eyes are easily fooled by 24 frames a second, our hearing can detect an acoustic echo or phase delay of just a few milliseconds.

On a professional movie set or live broadcast production, these two worlds of physics—photons hitting camera sensors and sound waves striking microphones—must be synchronized down to the microsecond. A film crew operates under relentless pressure: - When the sun is setting during "magic hour," the light drops by an entire exposure stop every five minutes. - If a camera operator chooses the wrong f-stop, an actor leaning forward by two inches blurs completely out of focus. - If a live sports broadcast drifts by a few frames, audio loses lip-sync, and the transmission misses satellite commercial break windows.

The StackCalc 24 (SC-24) puts frame-accurate SMPTE timecode arithmetic, optical depth-of-field geometry, Exposure Value (\(EV\)) lighting photometrics, and acoustic decibel summing onto a fast, dedicated RPN stack.

docs.title: Why Not Just Use a Phone App?
docs.text:
• The Magic Hour Window: When racing against fading daylight on an exterior film set, every minute costs thousands of dollars in crew wages. Unlocking a phone, squinting against glare, and tapping through menus wastes precious light. The SC-24 lets a 1st AC (Focus Puller) or Director of Photography calculate hyperfocal distances and neutral density filter factors in two tactile clicks.
  • Set Discipline & Silence: Phone screens illuminate dark cinema sets and notifications distract actors during rehearsals. The SC-24 is a silent, non-radiating tool designed for professional working environments.
  • Frame-Accurate Arithmetic: Standard calculators work in base-10 decimals, but film and broadcast video operate in mixed radices: 24 frames per second for film, 25 fps for European TV, and \(29.97\text{ fps}\) for North American broadcast. Trying to add 01:14:22:18 to 00:45:10:12 on a decimal calculator requires endless manual conversions.

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts: How Cinematographers and Sound Engineers Think
Concept 1: The 0.1% Color Mystery (SMPTE Drop-Frame Timecode)
docs.text:
Timecode is the universal coordinate system of media:

\[\mathbf{HH:MM:SS:FF} \quad (\text{Hours : Minutes : Seconds : Frames})\]

Why does North American television run at the bizarre rate of \(29.97\text{ frames per second}\) instead of an even \(30.00\)?

In the 1940s, black-and-white television ran at exactly \(30\text{ fps}\). But in 1953, when color television was invented, engineers discovered that the new high-frequency color subcarrier (\(3.58\text{ MHz}\)) caused electrical interference with the audio carrier wave. To eliminate this interference, the broadcast industry decided to slow down the television frame rate by exactly \(0.1\%\):

\[\text{Color Framerate} = \frac{30}{1.001} \approx 29.97002997\text{ fps}\]

This tiny \(0.1\%\) difference creates a giant headache: - At \(30\text{ fps}\), 108,000 frames equal exactly 1 hour of wall-clock time. - At \(29.97\text{ fps}\), 108,000 frames take 1 hour, 3 seconds, and 18 frames!

Over an hour of broadcast, video drifts nearly \(3.6\text{ seconds}\) behind the wall clock. To fix this, the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) created Drop-Frame Timecode (DF): - Every minute, the timecode counter skips frame numbers 00 and 01. - Exception: To prevent over-correcting, it does not skip frames on minute numbers ending in zero (minutes 00, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50).

No actual video frames are deleted; only the numerical labels are dropped so the timecode display stays locked to real-world clocks. The SC-24 handles this drop-frame arithmetic automatically.

docs.title: Concept 2: The Slippery Edge of Focus (Depth of Field & Hyperfocal Distance)
docs.text:
A camera lens can only bring one exact distance into sharp mathematical focus. Points closer or farther away project onto the camera sensor as small, blurred discs of light called Circles of Confusion (\(CoC\)).

              Lens
             |      |
    ---------\      /------------------- Sensor Plane
              \    /
               \  /  Focal Point
                \/
                /\   Blur Circle (Circle of Confusion)
    -----------/  \---------------------

As long as the circle of confusion is smaller than the human eye can distinguish at a standard viewing distance (roughly \(0.03\text{ mm}\) on a Full Frame sensor, or \(0.02\text{ mm}\) on Super 35mm cinema), the image appears tack-sharp. The region where blur is imperceptible is the Depth of Field (DOF).

docs.title: Hyperfocal Distance (\(H\))
docs.text:
If you focus a lens on infinity, half the light is wasted on stars, and nearby foreground objects blur.

If you instead focus at the Hyperfocal Distance (\(H\)), everything from half that distance (\(H/2\)) all the way to infinity remains in sharp focus:

\[H \approx \frac{f^2}{N \cdot c}\]

where \(f\) is focal length (in mm), \(N\) is f-stop number, and \(c\) is circle of confusion (in mm).

docs.title: Concept 3: The Decibel Mystery & Acoustic Summation
docs.text:
Why is human hearing logarithmic rather than linear?

If you hear one person talking at a dinner table, and a second person speaks at the exact same volume, your ear does not perceive the room as twice as loud. To sound twice as loud to a human ear, sound energy must increase by roughly ten times!

Sound engineers measure acoustic pressure on a logarithmic decibel scale:

\[L_p = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) \quad [\text{dBSPL}]\]

where \(P_0 = 20\,\mu\text{Pa}\) is the quietest sound a human ear can detect.

docs.title: Adding Two Sound Sources (\(dB\oplus\))
docs.text:
If a guitar amplifier produces \(90\text{ dBSPL}\), and a second identical amplifier is turned on producing \(90\text{ dBSPL}\), what is the total volume?

You cannot add decibels directly (\(90 + 90 \ne 180\)). You must convert back to linear power, add the energies, and take the logarithm again:

\[L_{\Sigma} = 10 \log_{10}\left(10^{90/10} + 10^{90/10}\right) = 10 \log_{10}(2 \times 10^9) = 90 + 3.01 \approx \mathbf{93\text{ dBSPL}}\]

Two identical uncorrelated sound sources always add exactly \(+3\text{ dB}\). The SC-24 features a dedicated [dB⊕] key that sums sound levels in one step.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Field Walkthroughs
Field Case 1: Editing a 2-Hour Live Concert (Cinematography.com)
docs.text: A post-production editor is assembling two live camera reels recorded at \(29.97\text{ fps}\) Drop-Frame: - Reel 1 Duration: 01:14:28:12 - Reel 2 Duration: 00:52:45:20 What is the exact combined running time of the broadcast cut?

docs.title: How to Solve It on the SC-24
docs.text:
1. Set framerate to \(29.97\text{ DF}\) using softkey [ TC ].
  2. Enter Reel 1: 01142812 [ENTER].
  3. Enter Reel 2: 00524520 [+].
  4. Register \(X\) displays: 02:07:14:02 (2 hours, 7 minutes, 14 seconds, and 2 frames). The editor knows the exact master duration without manually tracking dropped frames.

docs.title: Field Case 2: Deep-Focus Landscape Cinematography (r/cinematography)
docs.text: A filmmaker is shooting an exterior scene with a \(35\text{mm}\) lens on a Full Frame cinema sensor (\(c = 0.030\text{ mm}\)) at \(f/8\). 1. What is the hyperfocal distance? 2. If the lens is focused at the hyperfocal distance, how close can an actor stand to the camera and still remain sharp?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Compute Hyperfocal Distance:
  2. Formula: \(H = \frac{f^2}{N \cdot c} = \frac{35^2}{8 \times 0.030} = \frac{1225}{0.24} = 5{,}104\text{ mm} \approx \mathbf{5.10\text{ meters}}\) (\(16.7\text{ feet}\)).
  3. On the SC-24: 35 [x²] 8 [÷] 0.03 [÷] \(\to\) 5104 mm.
  4. Compute Minimum Sharp Distance:
  5. Near limit \(= H / 2 = 5.10 / 2 = \mathbf{2.55\text{ meters}}\) (\(8.4\text{ feet}\)).
  6. Everything from \(8.4\text{ feet}\) out to the distant mountains on the horizon will be in focus.

docs.title: 4. Try It Yourself: Practice Problems
Problem 1: Acoustic Decibel Summing
docs.text: At a live concert, three uncorrelated noise sources are measured at the soundboard: - Main PA: \(96\text{ dBSPL}\) - Crowd cheering: \(92\text{ dBSPL}\) - Stage monitor bleed: \(88\text{ dBSPL}\) Calculate the total combined sound pressure level at the mixing console using [dB⊕]. (Solution: \(10^{9.6} + 10^{9.2} + 10^{8.8} = 3.981 \times 10^9 + 1.585 \times 10^9 + 0.631 \times 10^9 = 6.197 \times 10^9\). \(10 \log_{10}(6.197 \times 10^9) = \mathbf{97.92\text{ dBSPL}}\).)

docs.title: Problem 2: Neutral Density (ND) Filter Selection
docs.text: A cinematographer is filming outdoors at ISO 100 with a shutter speed of \(1/50\text{ second}\). A light meter reading indicates an Exposure Value of \(EV = 15\) (which requires \(f/16\) for proper exposure). However, the director wants a shallow depth of field at \(f/2.0\) (an increase of 6 full stops of light: \(f/16 \to 11 \to 8 \to 5.6 \to 4 \to 2.8 \to 2\)). What optical density (\(OD\)) neutral density filter is required to cut 6 stops of light? (Solution: Each stop is \(0.3\text{ OD}\). \(6\text{ stops} \times 0.3 = \mathbf{1.8\text{ ND}}\) (an ND64 filter, transmitting only \(1/64 = 1.56\%\) of light).)

docs.title: Problem 3: Sound Delay Tower Alignment
docs.text: At an outdoor music festival, a secondary speaker delay tower is positioned \(175\text{ feet}\) away from the main stage. The air temperature is \(20^\circ\text{C}\) (speed of sound \(c \approx 1{,}125\text{ ft/s}\)). Calculate the required delay in milliseconds to sync the speakers. (Solution: \(\text{Time} = \frac{175\text{ ft}}{1125\text{ ft/s}} = 0.1555\text{ seconds} = \mathbf{155.6\text{ milliseconds}}\).)

docs.title: SC-50 RF Spectrum, Transmission Lines & Microwave Handbook
docs.text: Who this is for: Anyone who understands complex numbers (\(a + jb\)) and alternating current, but wants to know why high-frequency radio waves behave like sound echoes bouncing off canyon walls, and how engineers tune antennas to prevent expensive amplifiers from melting.

docs.title: 1. When Wires Stop Acting Like Wires
docs.text:
If you shout into a wide canyon, your voice travels outward through the air until it hits the opposite cliff face. Because solid granite has a vastly different acoustic density than thin air, the rock cannot absorb the sudden wave of kinetic energy. The sound wave bounces straight back as an audible echo.

At normal household frequencies (\(60\text{ Hz}\) AC), electrical current travels along a copper wire smoothly and uniformly. The electromagnetic wavelength at \(60\text{ Hz}\) is over \(3{,}000\text{ miles}\) long—far larger than your house—so voltage is virtually identical everywhere along the cord.

Now crank the frequency up to \(1\text{ Gigahertz}\) (\(1{,}000{,}000{,}000\text{ cycles per second}\)), the realm of Wi-Fi, cellular 5G, and aircraft radar.

At \(1\text{ GHz}\), the wavelength shrinks to just 30 centimeters (about one foot). A coaxial cable running from a radio transmitter to an antenna on a tower is no longer a simple static connection: it is a distributed transmission line. The electrical signal travels along the wire as an electromagnetic wave.

When that forward-traveling wave hits the antenna terminals, one of two things happens: 1. If the antenna’s electrical impedance matches the cable, the wave steps cleanly into the air and radiates into space as radio waves. 2. If the impedance does not match, the antenna acts like the granite cliff in our canyon: it cannot absorb the energy, and a portion of the wave bounces backward down the cable toward the transmitter.

That reflected wave collides with the incoming wave, creating standing hot spots of voltage along the feedline. Worse, when that reflected power hits the delicate output transistors of the transmitter, it is dissipated as instant heat. In a \(100\text{-watt}\) or \(1{,}000\text{-watt}\) transmitter, a mismatched antenna can melt a \(\$500\) Gallium-Nitride (GaN) power transistor in milliseconds.

The StackCalc 50 (SC-50) is designed specifically to calculate these wave reflections. It pairs a native complex-number RPN stack with dedicated reflection engines, one-touch characteristic impedance toggles (\(50\,\Omega \leftrightarrow 75\,\Omega\)), Friis receiver noise figure accumulators, and transmission line matching tools.

docs.title: Why Not Just Use a Phone App?
docs.text:
• The Tower Climbing Reality: When a broadcast or cellular technician is climbing a 150-foot radio tower in gusty winds, tethered to a safety harness, a delicate touchscreen smartphone is an accident waiting to happen. The SC-50 features tactile keys that can be operated reliably with one hand while tethered to a climbing lanyard.
  • The \(50\,\Omega\) vs. \(75\,\Omega\) Compromise: Why is the entire RF world built on \(50\,\Omega\) and \(75\,\Omega\)? In the 1930s, electrical researchers discovered that for coaxial cables with air insulation, minimum signal loss (attenuation) occurs at \(77\,\Omega\), while maximum power-handling capability occurs at \(30\,\Omega\). Radio transmitters standardized on \(50\,\Omega\) as the sweet-spot compromise between power and loss. Cable television (CATV), which carries tiny microvolt signals over long neighborhood runs, standardized on \(75\,\Omega\) to minimize attenuation. The SC-50 lets you toggle between \(50\,\Omega\) and \(75\,\Omega\) reference systems with a single key.

docs.title: 2. Core Concepts: How RF and Microwave Engineers Think
Concept 1: The Bouncing Wave and Reflection Coefficient (\(\Gamma\))
docs.text:
When a transmission line with characteristic impedance \(Z_0\) (usually \(50\,\Omega\)) connects to an antenna with complex load impedance \(Z_L = R + jX\), the ratio of the reflected voltage wave to the forward voltage wave is the Voltage Reflection Coefficient (\(\Gamma\), Greek gamma):

\[\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0} = \rho \angle \theta\]

Because \(Z_L\) is a complex number, \(\Gamma\) is also a complex phasor with a magnitude (\(\rho = |\Gamma| \le 1.0\)) and a phase angle (\(\theta\)): - Perfect Match (\(Z_L = 50\,\Omega\)): \(\Gamma = \frac{50 - 50}{50 + 50} = \mathbf{0}\). Zero reflected wave; 100% of power radiates into the sky! - Open Circuit (\(Z_L = \infty\)): \(\Gamma = \mathbf{+1.0} \angle 0^\circ\). All voltage reflects back in-phase. - Short Circuit (\(Z_L = 0\)): \(\Gamma = \mathbf{-1.0} = 1.0 \angle 180^\circ\). All voltage reflects back inverted.

docs.title: Concept 2: Standing Waves (VSWR) & Return Loss
docs.text:
When forward and reflected waves pass through each other inside a cable, their peaks and troughs interfere constructively and destructively, creating a stationary wave pattern.

The ratio of the maximum voltage peak to the minimum voltage valley is the Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR):

\[VSWR = \frac{1 + |\Gamma|}{1 - |\Gamma|} = \frac{1 + \rho}{1 - \rho}\]
  • Ideal Match: \(VSWR = \mathbf{1.0 : 1}\) (smooth, uniform voltage along the cable).
  • Good Commercial Antenna: \(VSWR \le \mathbf{1.5 : 1}\) (\(4\%\) power reflected).
  • Dangerous Mismatch: \(VSWR \ge \mathbf{3.0 : 1}\) (\(25\%\) or more power reflected backward into the transmitter!).

docs.title: Return Loss (\(RL\))
docs.text:
Engineers often prefer to express reflection efficiency on a decibel scale called Return Loss:

\[RL = -20 \log_{10}|\Gamma| \quad [\text{dB}]\]

A high return loss means the reflected wave has been heavily attenuated: - \(RL = 20\text{ dB} \iff |\Gamma| = 0.10 \iff 99\%\) of power is absorbed by the antenna. - \(RL = 10\text{ dB} \iff |\Gamma| = 0.316 \iff 90\%\) of power is absorbed (\(10\%\) bounces back).

docs.title: Concept 3: Folding Infinity into a Circle (The Smith Chart)
docs.text:
In 1939, RCA engineer Phillip Smith grew tired of solving complex hyperbolic tangent equations to figure out how impedance changes as you travel along a transmission line.

He noticed something magical: if you map the infinite right half of the complex impedance plane (\(R \ge 0\)) onto the complex reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\), the entire infinite plane folds into a compact circular disk with a radius of 1.0:

                 Short Circuit 
                   (Γ = -1)
                      *
                     / \
                    /   \     Center = 50 Ω Perfect Match (Γ = 0)
                   |  +  |
                    \   /
                     \ /
                      *
                  Open Circuit
                   (Γ = +1)
  • The exact center of the circle is the \(50\,\Omega\) perfect match (\(\Gamma = 0\)).
  • The outer boundary rim is total reflection (\(|\Gamma| = 1.0\)).
  • Moving down a coaxial cable corresponds simply to rotating clockwise around the center of the chart!

On the SC-50, pressing [SMTH] lets you navigate impedance transformations and design matching networks without needing paper charts.

docs.title: Concept 4: Listening to the Stars (Friis Cascaded Noise)
docs.text:
When a satellite dish points at deep space, the signal arriving from a spacecraft millions of miles away is unimaginably faint: often less than a billionth of a microwatt (\(-120\text{ dBm}\)).

Every electronic component generates natural thermal noise (random motion of electrons). To amplify a faint signal without burying it in hiss, engineers use a chain of amplifiers.

Harald Friis at Bell Labs discovered that the total noise figure (\(F\)) of an entire multi-stage receiver is dominated by the very first stage:

\[F_{\text{total}} = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3 - 1}{G_1 G_2} + \dots\]

Notice the denominator: any noise added by stage 2 (\(F_2\)) is divided by the gain of stage 1 (\(G_1\))!

This explains why satellite dishes and cellular base stations always place a high-gain, Low Noise Amplifier (LNA) right at the antenna feedhorn on the mast, rather than down inside the warm building at the other end of a long, lossy cable.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Field Walkthroughs
Field Case 1: Checking an Amateur Radio Antenna Match (Microwaves101)
docs.text: An antenna analyzer measures the feedpoint impedance of a newly installed dipole antenna at \(14.2\text{ MHz}\): - Load impedance: \(Z_L = 35 - j25\,\Omega\) - Reference line: \(Z_0 = 50\,\Omega\) What is the reflection coefficient magnitude (\(|\Gamma|\)), the VSWR, and the Return Loss?

docs.title: How to Solve It on the SC-50
docs.text:
1. Enter \(Z_L\) on the complex stack:
  2. 35 [ENTER] 25 [+/-] (Stack holds \(35 - j25\)).
  3. Enter \(Z_0\):
  4. 50
  5. Tap [SWR]:
  6. Register \(X\) displays: 1.884 (VSWR = \(1.88 : 1\)).
  7. Register \(Y\) displays: 0.3065 (Reflection coefficient \(|\Gamma| = 0.307\)).
  8. Tap [f] [RL]:
  9. Register \(X\) displays: 10.27 dB (Return Loss).
  10. About \(90.6\%\) of the transmitter's power is radiating into the air, and \(9.4\%\) is reflected back. A simple L-matching network can tune this to \(1.0 : 1\).

docs.title: Field Case 2: Satellite Downlink Low-Noise Preamplifier (EEVblog)
docs.text: A satellite ground station receiver consists of: - Stage 1 (Masthead LNA): Noise Figure \(= 0.8\text{ dB}\) (\(F_1 = 1.202\)), Gain \(= 20\text{ dB}\) (\(G_1 = 100\)). - Stage 2 (Coax Cable Run): Loss \(= 3.0\text{ dB}\) (\(F_2 = 2.0\), \(G_2 = 0.50\)). - Stage 3 (Indoor Receiver): Noise Figure \(= 6.0\text{ dB}\) (\(F_3 = 3.98\)). What is the total cascaded noise figure of the receiving system?

docs.title: Step-by-Step Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Apply Friis Equation: $\(F_{\text{total}} = F_1 + \frac{F_2 - 1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3 - 1}{G_1 \cdot G_2}\)$ $\(F_{\text{total}} = 1.202 + \frac{2.0 - 1.0}{100} + \frac{3.98 - 1.0}{100 \times 0.50} = 1.202 + 0.010 + 0.0596 = \mathbf{1.2716}\)$
  2. Convert Back to Decibels: $\(NF_{\text{total}} = 10 \log_{10}(1.2716) = \mathbf{1.04\text{ dB}}\)$ Even though the indoor receiver has a noisy \(6\text{ dB}\) noise figure and the cable is lossy, the masthead LNA's \(20\text{ dB}\) gain keeps the total system noise figure down to an ultra-clean \(1.04\text{ dB}\)!

docs.title: 4. Try It Yourself: Practice Problems
Problem 1: Transmission Line Quarter-Wave Transformer
docs.text: A high-frequency load has a purely resistive impedance \(Z_L = 100\,\Omega\). You need to match it to a \(50\,\Omega\) coaxial generator using a quarter-wavelength (\(\lambda / 4\)) section of transmission line. Calculate the required characteristic impedance of the quarter-wave line: \(Z_{\text{match}} = \sqrt{Z_0 \cdot Z_L}\). (Solution: \(Z_{\text{match}} = \sqrt{50 \times 100} = \sqrt{5000} \approx \mathbf{70.71\,\Omega}\).)

docs.title: Problem 2: Return Loss from Power Measurements
docs.text: A forward-power directional coupler measures \(100\text{ Watts}\) forward power toward an antenna and \(4\text{ Watts}\) reflected power bouncing back. 1. What is the reflection coefficient magnitude \(\rho = \sqrt{P_{\text{ref}} / P_{\text{fwd}}}\)? 2. What is the Return Loss (\(RL = -20 \log_{10}\rho\))? 3. What is the VSWR? (Solution: \(\rho = \sqrt{4 / 100} = \mathbf{0.20}\). \(RL = -20 \log_{10}(0.20) = \mathbf{13.98\text{ dB}}\). \(VSWR = (1 + 0.20) / (1 - 0.20) = 1.20 / 0.80 = \mathbf{1.50 : 1}\).)

docs.title: Problem 3: Resonant LC Tank Frequency
docs.text: A resonant filter circuit consists of an inductor \(L = 47\text{ nH}\) (\(47 \times 10^{-9}\text{ H}\)) and a capacitor \(C = 10\text{ pF}\) (\(10 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}\)). Calculate the resonant frequency \(f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\) in Megahertz.
